name: UPSC Civil Services (IAS/IPS/IFS)
tagline: India's premier exam for the IAS, IPS, IFS and other Central Civil Services

overview.about: The Civil Services Examination is conducted every year by the Union Public Service Commission to recruit officers for the IAS, IPS, IFS and other Group A and Group B central services. It has three stages — Preliminary (objective, screening), Main (descriptive) and Personality Test (interview). The final merit list is based on 2025 marks: 1750 from Mains and 275 from the interview.
eligibility: Nationality: must be a citizen of India for IAS, IPS and IFS (other services allow certain specified categories — check the notification)
Education: a bachelor's degree from a recognised university; final-year students may appear in Prelims
Age: 21–32 years as on 1 August of the exam year for General/EWS
Age relaxation: OBC +3 years, SC/ST +5 years, PwBD up to +10 years, plus others as notified
Attempts: General/EWS 6, OBC 9, SC/ST unlimited (within age limit); PwBD (General/EWS/OBC) 9
Appearing in either Prelims paper counts as an attempt; always verify the latest UPSC notification

pattern.note: Objective; decides Prelims cut-off; 1/3 negative marking
Qualifying – 25%; language from the Eighth Schedule (exemptions as notified)

pattern.paper: Mains Papers II–V – General Studies I–IV
Mains Papers VI–VII – Optional Subject I & II

overview.frequency: Once a year — Prelims around May/June, Mains around August/September, interviews in the following months

cards.title: Three stages, one rank
cards.body: UPSC CSE is held once a year in three stages: **Prelims** (screening, objective), **Mains** (descriptive, 9 papers) and the **Personality Test** (interview). Prelims marks only decide who reaches Mains. Your final rank comes from Mains written marks plus the interview.
points: Prelims → Mains → Interview
Final merit = 1750 (Mains) + 275 (Interview) = 2025 marks

cards.title: Prelims at a glance
cards.body: Two objective papers on the same day, each 200 marks and 2 hours. **GS Paper I** has 100 questions and decides the cut-off. **Paper II (CSAT)** has 80 questions and is only qualifying, but you must score at least **33%** (66/200). Wrong answers cost one-third of the question's marks.

cards.title: Mains at a glance
cards.body: Nine descriptive papers of 3 hours each. Two are qualifying language papers — **Paper A** (an Eighth Schedule Indian language) and **Paper B** (English), 300 marks each, 25% needed. Seven papers count for merit: **Essay**, **GS I–IV** and **Optional I & II**, 250 marks each = 1750.
points: Essay 250
GS I: Heritage, History, Geography, Society
GS II: Polity, Governance, IR
GS III: Economy, Environment, S&T, Security
GS IV: Ethics
Optional I + II: 500

cards.title: Who can apply
cards.body: You need a bachelor's degree (final-year students may write Prelims). General/EWS candidates must be **21–32 years** on 1 August of the exam year, with **6 attempts**. Relaxations: OBC +3 years and 9 attempts; SC/ST +5 years and unlimited attempts; PwBD up to +10 years.
points: Appearing in even one Prelims paper counts as an attempt

cards.title: Golden rule
cards.body: Always read the latest UPSC notification (usually released in January/February). Rules on age, attempts, service allocation and documents can change, and the notification is the only binding source.

cards.q: What is the total marks on which the UPSC CSE final merit list is prepared?
cards.explain: Mains merit papers (Essay, GS I–IV, two Optionals) = 1750, plus Interview 275 = 2025. Language papers and CSAT are qualifying only.

cards.q: The minimum qualifying score in Prelims Paper II (CSAT) is:
cards.explain: CSAT is qualifying with a 33% minimum (66 out of 200). Only GS Paper I marks decide the Prelims cut-off.

cards.q: How many attempts does a General category candidate get?
cards.explain: General and EWS candidates get 6 attempts; OBC and General/EWS/OBC PwBD get 9; SC/ST are unlimited within the age limit.

notes.p:
The Civil Services Examination (CSE) is conducted by the **Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)**, a constitutional body set up under **Articles 315–323** of the Constitution. Through one common exam it selects officers for the **IAS, IPS, IFS** and many other Group A and Group B central services.

The exam is not a test of memory alone. It checks whether you can **understand issues, connect facts across subjects and express a balanced view** — the same skills an officer needs when handling a district, a ministry or a crisis. Keep this purpose in mind: every fact you read should help you explain *why* something matters for governance.
points: UPSC releases the notification and calendar every year — always read the latest official notification
Eligibility (age, attempts, education) has relaxations by category; check the notification instead of relying on coaching posters

notes.p:
CSE has three stages, and each one filters candidates for the next.

**Stage 1 – Preliminary exam (Prelims):** two objective papers. **GS Paper I** decides who clears the cut-off. **Paper II (CSAT)** is only qualifying, but you must score at least **33%** in it. Both papers have **negative marking of one-third** of the marks for a wrong answer. Prelims marks are **not** added to the final merit.

**Stage 2 – Main exam (Mains):** nine descriptive papers. Two are qualifying (an Indian language paper and English). Seven count for merit: Essay, GS I–IV and two papers of your Optional subject.

**Stage 3 – Personality Test (Interview):** a board judges your personality, balance, clarity and suitability for public service.
points: Final merit = Mains (1750) + Interview (275) = 2025 marks
Prelims is a screening test only — its marks vanish once you clear it
The language and English papers in Mains are qualifying; if you fail them, your other papers are not evaluated

notes.p: Knowing which topic goes to which paper helps you study once and use it many times.
points: **GS I:** Indian heritage and culture, modern Indian history, world history, society, geography of India and the world
**GS II:** Polity, Constitution, governance, social justice, international relations
**GS III:** Economy, agriculture, science and technology, environment, disaster management, internal security
**GS IV:** Ethics, integrity and aptitude, including case studies
**Essay:** two essays, usually one from each section of the paper, on philosophical or issue-based topics
**Prelims GS Paper I** draws from all of the above plus current events

notes.p:
Prelims rewards **breadth and accuracy**: you must eliminate wrong options quickly and avoid careless negative marks. Mains rewards **depth, structure and speed of writing**: around 20 questions in 3 hours per GS paper, with word limits.

The smart approach is **integrated preparation** — read a topic once with both lenses. Ask: *What facts could be asked as MCQs?* and *What analysis could be asked in 150–250 words?*
points: Prelims: facts, concepts, elimination, maps, current affairs
Mains: causes, impact, way forward, examples, data
Interview: your DAF (Detailed Application Form), opinions, current issues, calm attitude

notes.p: Questions about the exam itself do not appear, but understanding its pattern shapes your strategy. Recent trends show that Prelims questions often use **statement-based formats** ("Which of the statements given above is/are correct?") and **pair-matching** formats such as "How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?". Such formats reduce guessing, so conceptual clarity matters more than rote facts. Mains questions increasingly use directive words like *discuss, critically examine, analyse* and expect a balanced answer.
points: Read the official syllabus line by line and keep it printed near your desk
Solve previous years' questions (PYQs) early — they are the best guide to what matters

notes.p: Key points to remember before you start planning.
points: UPSC is a constitutional body (Articles 315–323)
Three stages: Prelims → Mains → Interview
Prelims GS I decides cut-off; CSAT is qualifying at 33%
Negative marking in Prelims: one-third of the question's marks
Merit list total: 2025 marks (1750 Mains + 275 Interview)
Mains has 9 papers: 2 qualifying + 7 counted
GS I culture/history/geography/society; GS II polity/IR; GS III economy/S&T/environment/security; GS IV ethics
Always confirm eligibility and dates in the latest notification

cards.title: Why NCERTs first
cards.body: NCERT textbooks (Classes 6–12) explain basics in simple language and are written by subject experts. Many Prelims questions test concepts these books cover. Finishing them first builds the vocabulary you need to understand advanced books and newspapers.
points: Free PDFs at ncert.nic.in/textbook.php

cards.title: Smart NCERT order
cards.body: Read subject by subject, not class by class across all subjects at once. For each subject go from Class 6 upwards so ideas build gradually. Give priority to History, Geography, Polity (Indian Constitution at Work), Economy and Class 11–12 Biology/Chemistry chapters on environment.

cards.title: Then one standard book per subject
cards.body: After NCERTs, pick **one** trusted book per subject and revise it many times instead of reading five. Popular choices among aspirants include Laxmikanth for Polity, Spectrum (Rajiv Ahir) for Modern History, G.C. Leong for Physical Geography and a standard Indian Economy text.
points: One book × many revisions > many books × one reading

cards.title: A 3-read method
cards.body: **Read 1:** understand, no notes. **Read 2:** underline and make short notes or mind-maps. **Read 3:** revise only notes and solve PYQs on that topic. Example: after finishing the Parliament chapter, attempt every Prelims PYQ on Parliament from the last ten years.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use the official UPSC syllabus as a checklist. Print it, keep it on your desk, and tick topics as you finish them. If a topic is not in the syllabus, do not go deep into it.

cards.q: Which approach is most recommended for static subjects?
options: Read one standard book and revise it several times
Skip NCERTs and start with coaching notes
cards.explain: Repeated revision of one reliable source builds recall far better than a single pass over many books.

cards.q: Where can you download NCERT textbooks free of cost?
cards.explain: NCERT hosts official free PDFs of its textbooks at ncert.nic.in/textbook.php.

notes.p:
**NCERT textbooks** (Classes 6–12) are written in simple language and explain basic concepts clearly. UPSC often frames questions on ideas that first appear in these books. If your base is weak, standard reference books will feel heavy and confusing.

Think of NCERTs as the **foundation** of a building and standard books as the **floors** above. Skipping the foundation makes later floors unstable.
points: Read for understanding first, not for notes
On the second reading, underline key terms and make short notes
Old and new NCERTs both have value; pick one set and finish it rather than collecting everything

notes.p: Go from easier to harder and from general to specific.
points: **History:** Class 6–8 social science for basics → Class 11–12 history books → a standard book on modern India

**Geography:** Class 6–10 for basics → Class 11 *Fundamentals of Physical Geography* and *India: Physical Environment* → Class 12 *Fundamentals of Human Geography* and *India: People and Economy* → an atlas daily
**Polity:** Class 9–11 political science (including *Indian Constitution at Work*) → a standard polity reference book → the bare text of important Articles
**Economy:** Class 9–12 economics → a standard Indian economy book → Economic Survey and Budget highlights
**Environment & Science:** Class 6–10 science and Class 12 biology ecology chapters → current affairs

notes.p:
After NCERTs, choose **one standard book per subject** and read it many times. Repeated revision of one good source beats a single reading of five books. Many toppers follow the rule **"limited sources, multiple revisions"**.

While reading a standard book, keep connecting it with the **syllabus** and **previous year questions**. If a chapter has never been asked and is not in the syllabus, read it lightly.
points: Mark PYQ-linked topics in the margin of your book
Add current affairs examples in the margins of the relevant chapter
Do not switch books mid-way because someone else is using a different one

notes.p: Notes should be **short, structured and revisable**. Long copied paragraphs are not notes. Use headings, bullets, flowcharts and small tables. Some aspirants prefer digital notes so they can add current affairs later; others prefer handwritten notes for memory. Either works if you **revise** them.
points: Write in your own words — it improves Mains writing
Keep one page per big topic for last-month revision
Combine static notes with current affairs under the same heading

notes.p: UPSC does not test which book you read, but many Prelims questions are built on **basic concepts** found in NCERTs — for example, how a type of rainfall forms, what a term in economics means, or the features of an art form. Mains questions also expect simple, clear explanations, which come from strong basics. When a question looks unfamiliar, a strong concept base helps you **eliminate options logically**.
Remember these rules of reading.
points: NCERTs first, standard books next, current affairs on top
Read once for understanding, then again for notes
One standard source per subject, revised many times
Use the syllabus and PYQs as filters
Keep notes short, in your own words, and easy to revise
Use an atlas regularly while reading geography and current affairs
Avoid collecting too many books — revision matters more

cards.title: What Mains tests
cards.body: Mains is not about knowing more facts — it is about presenting them clearly within time. In each GS paper you usually write 20 answers in 3 hours: 10-mark answers (~150 words) and 15-mark answers (~250 words). That is roughly 7–9 minutes per answer.

cards.title: Decode the directive word
cards.body: Every question has a command word. Answer what it asks.
points: **Discuss** – cover various aspects, both sides
**Critically examine** – analyse merits and limits, then judge
**Analyse** – break into parts, show causes and effects
**Comment** – give your opinion backed by evidence
**Elucidate** – explain clearly with examples

cards.title: Intro – Body – Conclusion
cards.body: **Intro (2–3 lines):** define the term, give context, a fact or a recent event. **Body:** sub-headings or points covering every part of the question. **Conclusion (2–3 lines):** balanced, forward-looking, ideally linking to a constitutional value, SDG or government scheme.

cards.title: Mini model
cards.body: Q: 'Discuss the significance of the 73rd Amendment.' Intro: it gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj in 1992. Body: three-tier structure, regular elections, one-third seats for women, finance commission; then challenges like funds, functions, functionaries. Conclusion: true devolution needs the '3Fs' to reach panchayats.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Add value with simple diagrams, flowcharts or a map of India sketch. Quote Articles, committee names, Supreme Court judgments and official data from the Economic Survey. Practise daily and get answers reviewed.

cards.q: For a 15-mark GS Mains answer, the usual word limit is about:
cards.explain: UPSC typically sets ~150 words for 10-mark and ~250 words for 15-mark questions.

cards.q: 'Critically examine' asks you to:
options: Weigh merits and limitations and reach a judgement
cards.explain: Critical examination means a balanced analysis of both sides ending with a reasoned verdict.

notes.p:
Mains is a **written exam**. Two aspirants with the same knowledge can score very differently based on how they write. In each GS paper you must answer about **20 questions in 3 hours**, so roughly 7–9 minutes per answer. That needs **practice**, not just reading.

Good answers are **relevant, structured, balanced and readable**. Examiners check many copies, so a clean layout with clear points helps them see your ideas quickly.
points: Typical limits: around 150 words for 10-mark and 250 words for 15-mark questions — follow what the paper states
Attempting all questions usually matters more than writing one perfect answer

notes.p: The directive word tells you **what kind of answer** is expected.
points: **Discuss:** explain different aspects, with pros and cons
**Critically examine / Critically analyse:** look at merits and limits, then give a reasoned judgement
**Examine:** go into the details and find the main facts and reasons
**Explain / Elucidate:** make it clear with reasons and examples
**Comment:** give your opinion, supported by facts
**Evaluate / Assess:** judge the value or impact, with evidence

notes.p:
Most answers fit into three parts.

**Introduction (2–3 lines):** define the term, give a fact, a recent example or the context. Do not repeat the question.

**Body (bulk of the answer):** use sub-headings or points. Cover multiple dimensions — social, economic, political, legal, environmental, ethical. Add **examples, Article numbers, committee names, data or judgments** where you are sure of them.

**Conclusion (2–3 lines):** give a balanced, forward-looking way out. Link to constitutional values, the Sustainable Development Goals or a relevant government vision.
points: Use simple diagrams, flowcharts or maps where they save words
Underline a few key words — not whole lines
Keep paragraphs short; use points for the body

notes.p: Content comes from your static reading plus current affairs. Make small **"value-addition" lists** for each topic: key reports, committees, Supreme Court cases, schemes and examples. For data, use official sources such as the Economic Survey, and if you are unsure of a number, write the trend ("has risen", "remains low") instead of inventing a figure.

Mains questions often have **two or more parts** joined by "and" — for example, asking for both challenges and solutions. Many marks are lost by answering only one part. Questions also mix current affairs with static concepts, so a question on a recent event may expect constitutional or historical background. Read each question twice and underline its demands before writing.
points: Break the question into its parts and answer each one
Map your answer to what is asked, not to everything you know

notes.p: A checklist for every answer.
points: Read the question twice and spot the directive word
Answer every part of the question
Intro – Body – Conclusion structure
Use headings, points and simple diagrams
Add examples, Articles, cases or reports only when sure
Keep within the word limit and time per question
End with a balanced, positive way forward
Practise daily and get answers reviewed

cards.title: Static + dynamic
cards.body: UPSC rarely asks pure news. It asks the concept behind the news. If a new tiger reserve is in the news, the question may test the Wildlife (Protection) Act or the Project Tiger history. Always link a news item back to your syllabus topic.

cards.title: Daily routine (60–90 min)
cards.body: Read one national newspaper such as The Hindu or The Indian Express, focusing on editorials, government policy, economy, environment, S&T and international relations. Skip politics gossip, crime and sports results unless they connect to the syllabus.
points: Check PIB for official scheme details
Use PRS for bills and Acts

cards.title: Make notes topic-wise
cards.body: Do not keep notes by date. File each news item under a syllabus heading — 'Polity: Election Commission', 'Economy: Inflation'. Keep short points: what happened, why it matters, related Article/Act, and one data point from an official source.

cards.title: Monthly cycle
cards.body: Week 1–4: daily paper + short notes. End of month: revise one monthly compilation and the Yojana issue. Every 3 months: revise all notes. Before Prelims: revise government schemes, reports and indices from the last 12–18 months.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Prefer official sources for facts — PIB, ministry websites, Economic Survey, Union Budget documents and RBI reports. Many coaching summaries contain errors; verify numbers before memorising them.

cards.q: The best way to organise current affairs notes is:
cards.explain: Topic-wise notes connect news to the syllabus and make revision faster.

cards.q: Which website gives official press releases of the Government of India?
cards.explain: The Press Information Bureau publishes official releases from all ministries.

notes.p:
UPSC does not test news for its own sake. It tests whether you can **link news to the syllabus**. A news report on a new species, a court judgment, an international summit or a government scheme becomes a question when it connects to a static topic like biodiversity, Fundamental Rights, international relations or economy.

So the goal is not to remember every headline but to ask: **Which syllabus topic does this belong to, and what is the background?**
Keep it light but regular.
points: Read **one** national newspaper daily (for example *The Hindu* or *The Indian Express*) for about 1–1.5 hours
Focus on editorials, national news, economy, environment, science and international pages
Skip political blame games, crime stories and celebrity news
Use **PIB (Press Information Bureau)** for official facts on schemes and government decisions
Make short notes under syllabus headings, not by date

notes.p: Daily reading is the base. Add a **monthly compilation** to fill gaps and revise. Once a year, read the **Economic Survey** (at least summaries and key chapters) and **Union Budget** highlights for the economy. Government reports and official websites help verify facts.
points: Use one monthly compilation, not many
Revise the compilation at least twice before Prelims
For changing numbers (rankings, GDP figures, rates), always check the latest official figures

notes.p: For each important issue, note the following:
points: **What happened** (1–2 lines)
**Background:** the static concept, Article, Act or institution involved
**Prelims angle:** places on the map, species, organisations, terms
**Mains angle:** significance, challenges, way forward
**Linkage:** GS paper and topic in the syllabus

notes.h: Linking news to the GS papers
notes.p:
A simple way to file every news item is to ask which GS paper it serves. Many issues fit more than one paper — note all of them, because UPSC often asks the same issue from different angles.

For example, a heatwave story can serve **GS I** (climate and geography), **GS II** (disaster governance and the role of local bodies) and **GS III** (impact on agriculture, labour and energy demand). A Supreme Court judgment on privacy links to **GS II** (Fundamental Rights) and **GS III** (data protection and technology).
points: **GS I:** heritage sites in news, natural phenomena, social issues like urbanisation and gender
**GS II:** bills and Acts, judgments, schemes for vulnerable sections, bilateral visits and summits
**GS III:** economic data releases, budget, agriculture, space missions, environment reports, internal security
**GS IV:** real incidents showing integrity, compassion or misuse of power — useful as examples
**Essay:** broad themes such as technology and society, or development and environment

notes.p: Prelims frequently picks **places in the news, species, international organisations, scientific terms and schemes**, often in pair-matching or statement formats. Mains questions take an ongoing issue and ask for analysis, often blending it with static background. Questions are usually based on issues of the past one to two years, not just the latest week.
Keep these habits.
points: Link every news item to a syllabus topic
One newspaper + PIB + one monthly compilation is enough
Make notes topic-wise, not date-wise
Note both Prelims facts and Mains analysis
Use an atlas for places in the news
Verify numbers with official sources; do not memorise unverified figures
Revise current affairs several times before the exam

chapters.title: Current Events for Prelims: What & How

cards.title: What the syllabus says
cards.body: GS Paper I begins with '**Current events of national and international importance**'. In practice, UPSC uses news as a **hook** and tests the static concept behind it — the convention behind a new Ramsar site, the physics behind a space mission, or the article behind a court judgment.

cards.title: Categories to track
points: Government schemes and missions — ministry, aim, beneficiaries
Reports and indices — publisher
Places in the news — map location
Species in the news — habitat, status
Science and space missions
International groupings and summits
Bills, Acts and Supreme Court judgments
Economic data — Budget, Economic Survey, RBI policy

cards.title: Sources
cards.body: Daily: one national newspaper and **PIB** releases. Monthly: a compilation. Yearly: **Economic Survey**, **Union Budget**, **India Year Book** (Publications Division) for schemes, and **Yojana/Kurukshetra** magazines. Cover roughly the **12–18 months** before the exam.

cards.title: From news to question
cards.body: News: India launches a solar mission. Static links: **Aditya-L1** (launched September 2023) studies the sun from the **Lagrange point L1**, about 1.5 million km from earth. A likely question tests what a Lagrange point is — not the launch time.

cards.title: Another example
cards.body: News: India's **Chandrayaan-3** lander touched down near the **lunar south pole** on **23 August 2023**; the date is now **National Space Day**. Static links: why the south pole matters (possible **water ice** in permanently shadowed craters).

cards.title: International example
cards.body: News: Under India's **G20 presidency (2023)**, the **African Union** became a permanent member of the G20 at the New Delhi summit. Static links: G20 origins (1999, after the Asian financial crisis), its members and its 'troika' system.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Never memorise news without its **static anchor**. For every item, ask: which Article, which convention, which scientific idea, which place on the map? That is what UPSC asks.

cards.q: Aditya-L1 observes the sun from:
cards.explain: It is placed in a halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L1 point.

cards.q: National Space Day in India marks the anniversary of:
cards.explain: Chandrayaan-3 landed on 23 August 2023.

cards.q: Which body became a permanent member of the G20 at the New Delhi summit (2023)?
cards.explain: The African Union joined as a permanent member in 2023; the EU was already a member.

notes.p: Recent Prelims papers contain many questions that are **triggered by news** but answered from **static knowledge**. Pure news questions (who won what award) are rare. Therefore, current-affairs study should be organised by GS subject — polity, economy, environment, science, international relations — and each news item should be linked to its static base. Earlier strategy chapters cover a daily method; this chapter focuses on what Prelims asks.

Ask four questions of any news item:
1. Is there a **constitutional, legal or institutional** angle?
2. Is there a **conceptual** angle (science, economy, environment)?
3. Is there a **map** angle?
4. Is it likely to matter a year later?

If none applies — for example, political statements, crime stories or celebrity news — skip it. This keeps notes short and useful.
Themes that recur in news-linked questions:
points: **Economy:** RBI policy tools, inflation measures, budget terms, new financial instruments, trade agreements
**Polity:** Supreme Court judgments, constitutional amendments, new Acts, statutory bodies
**Environment:** new protected areas or Ramsar sites, species status changes, climate conferences (COP), pollution rules
**Science:** ISRO and global space missions, vaccines and diseases, AI, quantum, semiconductors
**International:** groupings (G20, BRICS, SCO, Quad, IPEF), conflicts and the places involved
**Schemes:** new missions announced in the Budget

notes.p: Keep one page per subject, adding news under the relevant static heading. Record the **who, what and why** in one or two lines. Before the exam, revise these pages along with standard books. Use **elimination** in the exam: if a statement contains an extreme word ('only', 'all', 'never') about a fast-changing policy, it is often false. When facts change often — scheme amounts, rankings, membership of groupings such as **BRICS**, which expanded from 2024 — check the latest official source close to the exam.

Headline: 'A new wetland is designated a Ramsar site.'

Step 1 — Convention: Ramsar Convention, signed in **Ramsar, Iran (1971)**; India joined in 1982.
Step 2 — Concepts: the **Montreux Record** lists sites where ecological change has occurred or is threatened.
Step 3 — Map: locate the wetland and its state.
Step 4 — Related: India's wetland rules (2017) and the Amrit Dharohar initiative.
Now any question on this news can be answered, whatever angle UPSC chooses.

Expect two-to-four-statement questions that mix a news fact with static facts, and 'consider the following pairs' with places or species in the news. Precise wording matters, so read the question twice.
Recall.
points: News is the hook; static concept is the answer
Track schemes, reports, places, species, science, groupings, judgments
Cover 12–18 months before the exam
PIB, a national daily, Economic Survey, Budget, India Year Book
Aditya-L1 at L1; Chandrayaan-3 landed 23 Aug 2023
African Union joined G20 in 2023
Check fast-changing facts close to the exam

cards.title: The Constituent Assembly
cards.body: Formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), the Assembly first met on **9 December 1946**. Dr Rajendra Prasad was its President. On 13 December 1946 Nehru moved the **Objectives Resolution**, which later shaped the Preamble. The Drafting Committee, set up on 29 August 1947, was chaired by **Dr B.R. Ambedkar**.

cards.title: Key dates
points: Adopted: **26 November 1949** (Constitution Day)
Fully in force: **26 January 1950** (Republic Day)
Took about 2 years, 11 months, 18 days
Original: 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules

cards.title: Borrowed features
cards.body: The framers studied many constitutions.
points: UK: parliamentary system, rule of law, single citizenship
USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, impeachment of President
Ireland: Directive Principles
Canada: federation with strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre
Former USSR: Fundamental Duties
Government of India Act 1935: much of the administrative framework

cards.title: The Preamble
cards.body: It declares India a **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic** and promises Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity. The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** — the only amendment to the Preamble so far.

cards.title: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution?
cards.body: In **Berubari (1960)** the Supreme Court said no. In **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** it reversed this and held the Preamble **is** part of the Constitution and can be amended, but not in a way that destroys the basic structure. It is not enforceable in courts by itself.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Prelims loves the order of words: 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic' and 'Justice – Liberty – Equality – Fraternity'. Remember that 'Republic' means the head of state is elected, not hereditary.

cards.q: Which amendment added 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble?
cards.explain: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, added Socialist, Secular and Integrity.

cards.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble is part of the Constitution?
cards.explain: Kesavananda Bharati overruled the Berubari view and also gave the basic structure doctrine.

cards.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution?
cards.explain: Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee; Rajendra Prasad was President of the Constituent Assembly.

notes.h: How the Constituent Assembly was formed
notes.p:
The idea of a Constituent Assembly for India was put forward by **M.N. Roy** in 1934, and the Indian National Congress officially demanded it in 1935. The Assembly was finally formed under the **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)**. Its members were **indirectly elected** by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies, while princely states were to send nominated representatives.

The Assembly first met on **9 December 1946**, with **Dr Sachchidananda Sinha** as temporary President. **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946. After Partition, the Muslim League members from areas going to Pakistan left, and the Assembly also acted as the first **legislature (Dominion Parliament)** of free India.
points: Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru: 13 December 1946; adopted: 22 January 1947
Drafting Committee set up: 29 August 1947, chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar
Constitution adopted: 26 November 1949 (now celebrated as Constitution Day)
Came fully into force: 26 January 1950 (Republic Day) — chosen to honour the Purna Swaraj declaration of 1930
Some provisions (citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament) came into force on 26 November 1949 itself

notes.p: The framers borrowed ideas but adapted them to Indian conditions. The **Government of India Act, 1935** is the biggest single source — it gave the federal scheme, the office of Governor, the judiciary structure, public service commissions and emergency provisions.
points: **UK:** parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, Cabinet system, bicameralism
**USA:** Fundamental Rights, independence of judiciary, judicial review, impeachment of the President, Vice-President's office
**Ireland:** Directive Principles of State Policy, nomination to Rajya Sabha, method of electing the President
**Canada:** federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre
**Australia:** Concurrent List, joint sitting of Parliament, freedom of trade and commerce
**Former USSR:** Fundamental Duties, ideal of justice (social, economic, political) in the Preamble
**France:** ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity; republic
**Weimar Germany:** suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency
**South Africa:** procedure for amendment and election of Rajya Sabha members

notes.h: Reading the Preamble word by word
notes.p: The Preamble is the **introduction** to the Constitution and reflects its philosophy. It tells us the **source** of authority ("We, the people of India"), the **nature** of the Indian state, its **objectives**, and the **date of adoption** (26 November 1949).
points: **Sovereign:** India is free to decide its internal and external affairs
**Socialist:** democratic socialism — a mixed economy aiming to reduce inequality (added in 1976)
**Secular:** the State has no official religion and treats all religions equally (added in 1976)
**Democratic:** power comes from the people through elections
**Republic:** the head of state (President) is elected, not hereditary
**Justice:** social, economic and political
**Liberty:** of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
**Equality:** of status and opportunity
**Fraternity:** assuring dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation ('Integrity' added in 1976)

notes.p:
In the **Berubari Union case (1960)** the Supreme Court said the Preamble is **not** a part of the Constitution. In **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** the Court changed this view and held that it **is** a part of the Constitution. The Preamble was amended only once — by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, which added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'.

The Preamble is **not justiciable** — you cannot go to court to enforce it directly — but courts use it to interpret unclear provisions. Kesavananda Bharati also gave the **basic structure doctrine**: Parliament can amend the Constitution under **Article 368**, but it cannot destroy its basic structure.

Prelims often tests the **sources** of features, **dates** linked to the Constituent Assembly, the **keywords** of the Preamble and their meaning, and the **status of the Preamble** in court cases. Statement-based questions may mix correct and wrong claims, such as whether the Preamble is enforceable or how many times it has been amended. Mains (GS II) may ask about the **philosophy** of the Constitution, the meaning of secularism in India, or the significance of the basic structure doctrine.
Lock in these facts.
points: First meeting: 9 Dec 1946; adopted: 26 Nov 1949; in force: 26 Jan 1950
President: Dr Rajendra Prasad; Drafting Committee chair: Dr B.R. Ambedkar
Objectives Resolution: moved by Nehru, 13 Dec 1946
Largest source: Government of India Act, 1935
DPSP from Ireland; Fundamental Duties idea from USSR; Concurrent List from Australia
Preamble amended once: 42nd Amendment (1976) — Socialist, Secular, Integrity
Berubari (1960): not part; Kesavananda Bharati (1973): part of the Constitution
Preamble is non-justiciable but guides interpretation

cards.title: Fundamental Rights (Part III)
cards.body: Articles **12–35** guarantee six rights, enforceable in court.
points: Equality (14–18)
Freedom (19–22)
Against exploitation (23–24)
Freedom of religion (25–28)
Cultural & educational (29–30)
Constitutional remedies (32)

cards.title: Article 32 and writs
cards.body: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. The Supreme Court (Art 32) and High Courts (Art 226) can issue five writs.
points: Habeas corpus – produce the detained person
Mandamus – 'we command' a public duty
Prohibition – stop a lower court
Certiorari – quash a lower court's order
Quo warranto – 'by what authority' a public office is held

cards.title: Key changes
cards.body: The **44th Amendment (1978)** removed the Right to Property from Part III; it is now a legal right under **Article 300A**. It also ensured Articles **20 and 21** cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency. The **86th Amendment (2002)** added **Article 21A** — free and compulsory education for ages 6–14.

cards.title: Directive Principles (Part IV)
cards.body: Articles **36–51**, inspired by the Irish Constitution, guide the State towards a welfare state — equal pay, living wage, uniform civil code (Art 44), separation of judiciary (Art 50), village panchayats (Art 40). Under **Article 37** they are **not enforceable** in court but are 'fundamental in the governance of the country'.

cards.title: Fundamental Duties (Part IVA)
cards.body: Added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation, in **Article 51A**. Originally ten; the **86th Amendment (2002)** added the eleventh — parents/guardians must provide education opportunities to children aged 6–14. Duties are non-justiciable.

cards.title: Balance between Parts III and IV
cards.body: In **Minerva Mills (1980)** the Supreme Court held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure. Neither can be given absolute primacy over the other.

cards.q: Which writ is issued to examine the legality of a person's claim to a public office?
cards.explain: Quo warranto ('by what authority') questions the right of a person to hold a public office.

cards.q: Right to Property is now a:
cards.explain: The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted it from Part III and placed it in Article 300A.

cards.q: Fundamental Duties were added on the recommendation of:
cards.explain: The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) led to Part IVA via the 42nd Amendment.

notes.p:
**Part III (Articles 12–35)** contains the Fundamental Rights, often called the **Magna Carta** of India. They protect individuals against arbitrary action by the **State** (defined in Article 12). They are **justiciable** — a person can go to court if they are violated.

Originally there were seven rights. The **44th Amendment (1978)** removed the **Right to Property** from Part III and made it a legal right under **Article 300A**. Today there are six groups.
points: **Right to Equality:** Articles 14–18 (equality before law, no discrimination, equal opportunity in public jobs, abolition of untouchability, abolition of titles)

**Right to Freedom:** Articles 19–22 (six freedoms in Article 19, protection in respect of conviction, life and personal liberty in Article 21, education in Article 21A, protection against arbitrary arrest)
**Right against Exploitation:** Articles 23–24 (no forced labour or trafficking; no child labour in factories, mines or hazardous work below 14)
**Right to Freedom of Religion:** Articles 25–28
**Cultural and Educational Rights:** Articles 29–30 (protection of minorities)
**Right to Constitutional Remedies:** Article 32 — called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution by Dr Ambedkar

notes.p: Under **Article 32** the Supreme Court, and under **Article 226** the High Courts, can issue five writs. High Courts can use writs for legal rights too, so their writ power is wider.
points: **Habeas corpus:** produce a detained person before court
**Mandamus:** order a public official to do their duty
**Prohibition:** stop a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction
**Certiorari:** quash an order already passed by a lower court or tribunal
**Quo warranto:** ask by what authority a person holds a public office

notes.p:
Article 21 says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. In **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** the Supreme Court said this procedure must be **fair, just and reasonable**. Since then courts have read many rights into Article 21, such as the right to livelihood, clean environment, speedy trial, and the **right to privacy** (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017).

The **86th Amendment (2002)** added **Article 21A** (free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14), a new DPSP in Article 45 (early childhood care) and a new Fundamental Duty in Article 51A(k).

**Part IV (Articles 36–51)** contains DPSPs, borrowed from the Irish Constitution. They are guidelines for the State to build a welfare state. They are **non-justiciable** (Article 37) but 'fundamental in the governance of the country'.
points: **Socialist principles:** e.g. Article 39 (adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work), Article 41, Article 43
**Gandhian principles:** e.g. Article 40 (village panchayats), Article 43 (cottage industries), Article 47 (prohibition of intoxicating drinks), Article 48 (ban on cow slaughter)
**Liberal-intellectual principles:** e.g. Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code), Article 48A (environment), Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive), Article 51 (international peace)
Conflict with FRs: in **Minerva Mills (1980)** the Court held that a **balance** between FRs and DPSPs is part of the basic structure

notes.p: **Part IVA, Article 51A**, was added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**. It originally had **10 duties**; the 86th Amendment added the 11th (parents/guardians to provide education opportunities to children aged 6–14). Duties are **non-justiciable**, but courts may consider them when judging the reasonableness of a law. Unlike some FRs, duties apply only to **citizens**.

Prelims frequently asks which right falls under which Article, which writs apply to whom, which DPSPs are Gandhian, and which rights are available to foreigners as well (for example Articles 14, 20, 21). Questions on recent Supreme Court judgments linked to Article 21 are common. Mains GS II asks about the **relationship between FRs and DPSPs**, the expanding scope of Article 21, or the debate on the Uniform Civil Code.
Revise these anchors.
points: Part III = FRs (Art 12–35); Part IV = DPSP (Art 36–51); Part IVA = Duties (Art 51A)
Right to Property moved to Article 300A by 44th Amendment (1978)
Article 32 = 'heart and soul'; Article 226 gives HCs wider writ power
Maneka Gandhi (1978): procedure must be fair, just and reasonable
Puttaswamy (2017): privacy is a fundamental right
86th Amendment (2002): Article 21A, new Art 45, 11th duty
Duties added by 42nd Amendment on Swaran Singh Committee advice
Minerva Mills (1980): FR–DPSP balance is basic structure

cards.title: Structure
cards.body: Under **Article 79**, Parliament = the **President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha**. The President is part of Parliament though not a member of either House, because a bill becomes law only with the President's assent.

cards.title: The two Houses
points: **Lok Sabha:** directly elected, normal term 5 years, maximum strength 550 (after the 104th Amendment ended Anglo-Indian nomination)
**Rajya Sabha:** maximum 250 (238 elected by state/UT legislators + 12 nominated by the President)
Rajya Sabha is permanent — one-third members retire every second year
Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha

cards.title: Money Bill (Art 110)
cards.body: A Money Bill can be introduced only in Lok Sabha with the President's recommendation. The **Speaker** certifies whether a bill is a Money Bill. Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations and must return it within **14 days**; Lok Sabha may accept or reject them.

cards.title: Joint sitting (Art 108)
cards.body: If the two Houses disagree on an ordinary bill, the President can summon a joint sitting, presided over by the **Speaker**. There is **no joint sitting** for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills. Because Lok Sabha has more members, it usually prevails.

cards.title: Parliamentary tools
points: **Question Hour** – first hour of a sitting
**Zero Hour** – Indian innovation, not in the rules
**No-confidence motion** – only in Lok Sabha, needs 50 members' support to be admitted
**Quorum** – one-tenth of total members
Committees: Public Accounts Committee (chaired by an Opposition member by convention), Estimates, Public Undertakings

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Compare the Houses in a table: who can be dissolved, who passes Money Bills, who can create All-India Services (Rajya Sabha, Art 312), and who can authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject (Rajya Sabha, Art 249).

cards.q: Who decides whether a bill is a Money Bill?
cards.explain: Article 110(3): the Speaker's decision is final.

cards.q: A joint sitting of Parliament is NOT possible for:
options: Financial bills other than Money Bills
cards.explain: Article 368 requires each House to pass an amendment separately, so joint sittings are excluded. Money Bills are also excluded.

notes.p:
Under **Article 79**, Parliament consists of the **President, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People)**. The President is not a member of either House but is an integral part, because bills need the President's assent and the President summons and prorogues the Houses and can dissolve the Lok Sabha.

**Lok Sabha (Article 81):** members are directly elected. The term is **five years** unless dissolved earlier (Article 83). **Rajya Sabha (Article 80):** maximum strength 250, with **12 nominated** members having special knowledge in literature, science, art and social service. It is a **permanent body**; one-third of members retire every second year, and each member serves six years.
points: Rajya Sabha members from states are elected by elected MLAs using proportional representation by single transferable vote
Minimum age: 25 for Lok Sabha, 30 for Rajya Sabha
Presiding officers: Speaker (Lok Sabha); Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha

notes.p: Knowing bill types is essential for both Prelims and Mains.
points: **Ordinary bill:** can be introduced in either House; deadlock solved by a **joint sitting** (Article 108) presided over by the Speaker

**Money bill (Article 110):** only in Lok Sabha, with the President's recommendation; Speaker certifies it; Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes and must return it within **14 days**; no joint sitting
**Financial bills:** Article 117 — some features like money bills, but Rajya Sabha has fuller powers
**Constitutional Amendment bill (Article 368):** either House; special majority; no joint sitting; President must give assent (24th Amendment, 1971)

notes.p: These tools help Parliament hold the government accountable.
points: **Question Hour:** usually the first hour of a sitting; starred questions get oral answers with supplementaries, unstarred get written answers
**Zero Hour:** an Indian innovation, not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure; starts right after Question Hour
**Adjournment motion:** draws attention to an urgent matter of public importance; only in Lok Sabha
**No-confidence motion:** only in Lok Sabha; needs support of at least 50 members to be admitted; if passed, the Council of Ministers must resign (collective responsibility, Article 75(3))
**Cut motions:** used during the demands for grants in the Budget

notes.p: Much of Parliament's detailed work happens in **committees**. The **Public Accounts Committee (PAC)** examines the CAG's audit reports; its chairperson is by convention from the Opposition. The **Estimates Committee** has members from Lok Sabha only and suggests economies. **Departmentally Related Standing Committees** examine bills and budgets of ministries.
points: PAC: 22 members (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha)
Estimates Committee: 30 members, all from Lok Sabha
Committee on Public Undertakings: examines PSUs

notes.p: Parliament must meet so that the gap between two sessions is **not more than six months** (Article 85). Usually there are three sessions: Budget, Monsoon and Winter.
points: **Adjournment:** suspends a sitting for some time
**Prorogation:** ends a session (by the President)
**Dissolution:** ends the life of Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved
**Lapse of bills:** on dissolution, bills pending in Lok Sabha lapse; a bill pending in Rajya Sabha but not passed by Lok Sabha does not lapse

notes.p: Prelims often asks about **money bill vs ordinary bill**, joint sittings, the role of the Speaker, which motions apply only to Lok Sabha, and the composition of committees. Mains GS II asks about the **decline in parliamentary productivity**, the role of committees, anti-defection law (**Tenth Schedule**, added by the 52nd Amendment, 1985), or the use of money bills to bypass the Rajya Sabha.
Core facts.
points: Parliament = President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha (Article 79)
Rajya Sabha: max 250, 12 nominated, permanent house
Money bill: Article 110; only in Lok Sabha; Speaker certifies; 14 days for Rajya Sabha
Joint sitting: Article 108; not for money or amendment bills
Max gap between sessions: six months (Article 85)
PAC examines CAG reports; Opposition chairs it by convention
No-confidence and adjournment motions: only Lok Sabha
Anti-defection: Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985)

cards.title: The President
cards.body: Elected indirectly by an electoral college of **elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies** (including Delhi and Puducherry). Nominated members do not vote. Under **Article 74**, the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers; after the 44th Amendment the President may return advice once for reconsideration.

cards.title: Key presidential powers
points: Art 72 – pardon, reprieve, remission, commutation
Art 123 – ordinances when Parliament is not in session
Art 352 – National Emergency
Art 356 – President's Rule in a state
Art 360 – Financial Emergency (never imposed so far)

cards.title: PM and Council of Ministers
cards.body: The President appoints the Prime Minister (Art 75) and other ministers on the PM's advice. The Council is **collectively responsible to Lok Sabha**. The **91st Amendment (2003)** capped the total number of ministers at **15%** of Lok Sabha strength.

cards.title: Supreme Court
cards.body: Established under **Article 124**. Judges retire at **65** (High Court judges at 62). Key Articles:
points: Art 32 – writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights
Art 137 – review its own judgments
Art 141 – its law binds all courts
Art 142 – 'complete justice'
Art 143 – advisory opinion to President

cards.title: Appointment of judges
cards.body: Judges are appointed through the **collegium** system that evolved from the Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges cases. In **2015** the Supreme Court struck down the **National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC)** as violating judicial independence, a basic feature.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Remember: High Courts' writ power (Art 226) is wider than the Supreme Court's (Art 32) — HCs can issue writs for legal rights too, not only Fundamental Rights.

cards.q: The 91st Amendment limited the size of the Council of Ministers to:
cards.explain: Total ministers, including the PM, cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of Lok Sabha.

cards.q: Which Article lets the Supreme Court pass orders for 'complete justice'?
cards.explain: Article 142 empowers the SC to pass any decree or order necessary for complete justice.

cards.q: Who does NOT vote in the Presidential election?
cards.explain: Only elected members take part; nominated members of Parliament and of assemblies are excluded.

notes.p:
The **President** is the head of the State and the first citizen of India (Article 52). Executive power of the Union is vested in the President (Article 53), but it is exercised on the **aid and advice of the Council of Ministers** headed by the Prime Minister (Article 74). The 42nd Amendment made this advice binding, and the 44th Amendment allowed the President to send advice back **once** for reconsideration.

The President is elected **indirectly** by an **electoral college** of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of states and the Union Territories of Delhi and Puducherry (Article 54), using proportional representation by single transferable vote. Nominated members do not vote.
points: Term: five years (Article 56); removal by **impeachment** for 'violation of the Constitution' (Article 61)
Ordinance power: Article 123 (when Parliament is not in session)
Pardoning power: Article 72
Veto types: absolute, suspensive and pocket veto; a money bill cannot be returned for reconsideration, and the President must give assent to a Constitutional Amendment bill (24th Amendment, 1971)

notes.h: Vice-President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
notes.p:
The **Vice-President** (Article 63) is the ex-officio **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** and is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament (including nominated members).

The **Prime Minister** is appointed by the President (Article 75) and is the real head of the government. The Council of Ministers is **collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha** (Article 75(3)). The **91st Amendment (2003)** limited the size of the Council of Ministers to **15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha** (including the PM).

The Supreme Court is established under **Article 124**. Judges are appointed by the President, and in practice through the **collegium system**, which came from the 'Judges Cases' (1981, 1993, 1998). In 2015 the Supreme Court struck down the **National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC)** created by the 99th Amendment.
points: **Original jurisdiction (Article 131):** disputes between the Centre and states, or between states
**Writ jurisdiction (Article 32)**
**Appellate jurisdiction:** appeals in civil, criminal and constitutional matters
**Advisory jurisdiction (Article 143):** President may seek the Court's opinion; the opinion is not binding
**Court of record (Article 129):** can punish for contempt
**Article 142:** power to pass any order for 'complete justice'
Removal of judges: by an order of the President after an address by each House passed by a special majority, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Article 124(4))

notes.p:
High Courts are covered from **Article 214**. Article 226 gives them writ powers, and Article 227 gives supervision over subordinate courts. **Judicial review** — the power of courts to strike down laws or executive actions that violate the Constitution — is part of the basic structure.

**Public Interest Litigation (PIL)** grew in the late 1970s and 1980s, allowing any public-spirited person to approach courts for those who cannot. Supporters see it as a tool for justice; critics warn of **judicial overreach**.

Prelims asks about **who elects whom** (President vs Vice-President electoral colleges), ordinance and pardoning powers, jurisdictions of the Supreme Court, and comparisons such as Article 32 vs Article 226. Mains GS II asks about **judicial activism vs overreach**, collegium vs NJAC, pendency of cases, the role of the Governor or President in a hung assembly, and the discretionary powers of constitutional heads.
Revise these.
points: Article 74: aid and advice of Council of Ministers (binding since 42nd Amendment)
President elected by elected MPs + elected MLAs (incl. Delhi, Puducherry)
Article 123 ordinances; Article 72 pardons; Article 61 impeachment
91st Amendment: Council of Ministers capped at 15% of Lok Sabha
Supreme Court: Article 124; original (131), writ (32), advisory (143)
Article 142: complete justice; Article 129: court of record
NJAC struck down in 2015; collegium continues
High Courts: Article 226 writs, Article 227 superintendence

cards.title: A 'Union of States'
cards.body: **Article 1** calls India a 'Union of States', meaning states cannot secede. India is federal in structure with a strong Centre — scholars call it 'quasi-federal'. Features: division of powers, written constitution, independent judiciary; but also single citizenship, emergency powers and an appointed Governor.

cards.title: Seventh Schedule
cards.body: Legislative powers are split into three lists.
points: **Union List** – defence, foreign affairs, banking, railways
**State List** – police, public order, public health, agriculture
**Concurrent List** – education, forests, marriage, criminal law
**Residuary powers** rest with Parliament (Art 248)

cards.title: Cooperative federalism bodies
points: Inter-State Council – Article 263
GST Council – Article 279A (101st Amendment, 2016)
Finance Commission – Article 280
NITI Aayog (2015) – created by executive resolution, not constitutional

cards.title: 73rd Amendment – Panchayats
cards.body: Passed in 1992 (in force 1993), it added **Part IX** and the **Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects)**. Three tiers — village, intermediate, district (states under 20 lakh population may skip the middle tier). Five-year terms, **at least one-third seats for women**, SC/ST reservation, State Election Commission and State Finance Commission.

cards.title: 74th Amendment – Municipalities
cards.body: Also 1992, it added **Part IXA** and the **Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects)** for urban local bodies: Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban area) and Municipal Corporation (larger urban area). The idea of three-tier PRIs goes back to the **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957)**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Answer-writing hook: local bodies still lack the '3Fs' — Funds, Functions and Functionaries. Use this phrase in GS II answers on decentralisation.

cards.q: The Eleventh Schedule contains how many subjects for Panchayats?
cards.explain: The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects; the Twelfth Schedule (municipalities) lists 18.

cards.q: Residuary powers of legislation in India are with:
cards.explain: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List vest residuary powers in Parliament.

notes.p:
The Constitution does not use the word 'federation'. **Article 1** calls India a **'Union of States'**. Dr Ambedkar explained that the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among states and that states have **no right to secede**. Scholars like **K.C. Wheare** called India 'quasi-federal'.

India has federal features (two levels of government, written Constitution, division of powers, independent judiciary, bicameral Parliament) and **unitary features** (strong Centre, single Constitution, single citizenship, all-India services, emergency provisions, appointment of Governors by the Centre, Parliament's power to change state boundaries under Article 3).

notes.h: Division of powers: the Seventh Schedule
notes.p: **Article 246** and the **Seventh Schedule** divide subjects into three lists.
points: **Union List:** defence, foreign affairs, banking, currency, railways, etc.
**State List:** police, public order, public health, agriculture, land, etc.
**Concurrent List:** education, forests, criminal law, marriage, etc. — if there is conflict, Union law prevails (Article 254)
**Residuary powers:** with Parliament (Article 248), as in Canada
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** moved five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List, including education, forests and protection of wild animals and birds

notes.p:
Tension points include the **role of the Governor**, use of **Article 356** (President's Rule), financial dependence of states, and Centre's directions to states (Articles 256–257). In **S.R. Bommai (1994)** the Supreme Court said the floor of the House is the right place to test majority and that President's Rule is subject to judicial review.

Important commissions:
points: **Sarkaria Commission (1983):** Centre–state relations; Article 356 only as a last resort
**Punchhi Commission (2007):** further review of Centre–state relations
**Inter-State Council (Article 263):** set up in 1990 based on Sarkaria's advice
**Finance Commission (Article 280):** recommends sharing of central taxes with states
**GST Council (Article 279A):** a key example of cooperative federalism, added by the 101st Amendment (2016)

notes.p: The **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957)** recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj system; Rajasthan (Nagaur district) was the first to adopt it in 1959. Constitutional status came in **1992**.
points: **73rd Amendment (1992):** Part IX, Articles 243 to 243-O, **Eleventh Schedule** (29 subjects) — panchayats
**74th Amendment (1992):** Part IXA, Articles 243-P to 243-ZG, **Twelfth Schedule** (18 subjects) — municipalities
Three-tier system: village, intermediate (block) and district (intermediate tier optional for states with population under 20 lakh)
Five-year term; elections within six months if dissolved early
At least **one-third** seats reserved for women (several states have chosen 50%)
**State Election Commission** conducts local elections; **State Finance Commission** reviews finances every five years
**Gram Sabha:** all registered voters of a village
PESA Act, 1996 extends panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas with special powers for Gram Sabhas

notes.p: Prelims tests **which subject is in which list**, articles on local government, Schedules (Eleventh vs Twelfth), and committees like Balwant Rai Mehta and Ashok Mehta. Mains GS II asks about **cooperative and competitive federalism**, the role of the Governor, fiscal federalism, the misuse of Article 356, and why local bodies remain weak — the **'3Fs' problem: funds, functions and functionaries**.
Key anchors.
points: Article 1: India is a 'Union of States'
Seventh Schedule + Article 246: three lists; residuary power with Parliament (Article 248)
Article 254: Union law prevails in Concurrent List conflict
S.R. Bommai (1994): floor test; Article 356 is reviewable
Inter-State Council: Article 263; Finance Commission: Article 280; GST Council: Article 279A
73rd Amendment: panchayats, Part IX, Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects)
74th Amendment: municipalities, Part IXA, Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects)
At least one-third reservation for women in local bodies

cards.title: Constitutional bodies
cards.body: Created directly by the Constitution, so changing them needs a constitutional amendment.
points: Election Commission – Art 324
UPSC – Art 315
Finance Commission – Art 280
CAG – Art 148
Attorney General – Art 76
National Commission for SCs – Art 338; for STs – Art 338A; for Backward Classes – Art 338B

cards.title: Statutory and executive bodies
points: NHRC – Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
Central Vigilance Commission – statutory since CVC Act, 2003
Lokpal – Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013
National Green Tribunal – NGT Act, 2010
NITI Aayog – executive resolution, 2015

cards.title: CAG: guardian of the public purse
cards.body: The Comptroller and Auditor General audits accounts of the Union, states and bodies financed by them. Reports on Union accounts go to the President, who places them before Parliament, where the **Public Accounts Committee** examines them. The CAG holds office for 6 years or until age 65.

cards.title: Finance Commission
cards.body: Set up by the President every five years to recommend how central taxes are shared between the Centre and states (vertical devolution) and among states (horizontal devolution). The **16th Finance Commission**, chaired by **Arvind Panagariya**, covers the period 2026–31.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: A favourite Prelims trap: 'NITI Aayog is a constitutional body' — false. It replaced the Planning Commission through a Cabinet resolution in January 2015.

cards.q: Which of these is a constitutional body?
cards.explain: The Finance Commission is created under Article 280. The others are statutory or executive bodies.

cards.q: The National Commission for Backward Classes got constitutional status through:
cards.explain: The 102nd Amendment (2018) inserted Article 338B.

notes.h: Constitutional vs statutory vs executive bodies
notes.p: A **constitutional body** is created directly by the Constitution (for example the Election Commission). A **statutory body** is created by an Act of Parliament (for example the National Human Rights Commission). An **executive body** is created by a government resolution (for example NITI Aayog). This difference matters because constitutional bodies have stronger protection of independence, and changing them needs a constitutional amendment.
Remember the Article for each body.
points: **Election Commission of India — Article 324:** superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, state legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President
**UPSC — Articles 315–323;** State PSCs in the same Part (Part XIV)
**Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) — Articles 148–151:** audits accounts of the Union and states; reports go to the President/Governor and are discussed by the PAC
**Attorney General — Article 76:** highest law officer of the Union; can speak in Parliament but cannot vote
**Advocate General of a state — Article 165**
**Finance Commission — Article 280:** every five years, recommends tax devolution
**National Commission for Scheduled Castes — Article 338**; **National Commission for Scheduled Tribes — Article 338A** (separated by the 89th Amendment, 2003)
**National Commission for Backward Classes — Article 338B** (given constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment, 2018)
**GST Council — Article 279A**

notes.p: The Constitution protects these bodies so they can work without fear.
points: The **Chief Election Commissioner** can be removed only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge
The **CAG** can be removed like a Supreme Court judge; his/her salary and conditions cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment
Expenses of bodies like UPSC and CAG are **charged** on the Consolidated Fund of India (not voted)
UPSC members can be removed by the President only on specific grounds, and for misbehaviour only after an inquiry by the Supreme Court

notes.p: These often appear in news.
points: **National Human Rights Commission:** Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
**Central Vigilance Commission:** statutory status by the CVC Act, 2003 (first set up in 1964 on the Santhanam Committee's advice)
**Central Bureau of Investigation:** works under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 — not a statutory body in its own name
**Lokpal:** Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013
**NITI Aayog:** executive body formed in 2015, replacing the Planning Commission
**National Commission for Women:** National Commission for Women Act, 1990

notes.p: Prelims frequently asks **'Which of the following are constitutional bodies?'** — so separate constitutional, statutory and executive bodies clearly. Questions also test Articles, appointment and removal processes, and reporting lines (to whom does CAG submit reports?). Mains GS II asks about the **independence and effectiveness** of bodies like the Election Commission, CAG and Lokpal, and about reforms in their appointments.
Article memory list.
points: ECI: Article 324
UPSC/SPSC: Articles 315–323
CAG: Articles 148–151
Attorney General: Article 76; Advocate General: Article 165
Finance Commission: Article 280
NCSC 338, NCST 338A, NCBC 338B
NHRC, CVC, Lokpal, NCW = statutory; NITI Aayog = executive
CAG reports are examined by the Public Accounts Committee

cards.title: Article 368: three methods
points: **Simple majority** (outside Art. 368): new states, citizenship, quorum, Fifth/Sixth Schedule changes
**Special majority**: majority of total membership + two-thirds of those present and voting, in each House — most provisions including Fundamental Rights and DPSPs

**Special majority + ratification by half the states**: federal provisions — President's election, Supreme Court and High Courts, distribution of powers, GST Council, states' representation in Parliament, Art. 368 itself

cards.title: Procedure facts
cards.body: An amendment bill can be introduced in **either House**, by a minister or a private member, **without** the President's prior permission. There is **no joint sitting** for amendment bills. Since the **24th Amendment (1971)**, the President **must** give assent.

cards.title: Basic structure
cards.body: **Golaknath (1967)** held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** held Parliament can amend any part but **not the basic structure**. **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down clauses that made amendment power unlimited.

cards.title: Landmark amendments
points: 1st (1951): Ninth Schedule
42nd (1976): 'socialist', 'secular', 'integrity'; Fundamental Duties
44th (1978): property no longer a Fundamental Right; 'armed rebellion' replaces 'internal disturbance'
52nd (1985): anti-defection (Tenth Schedule)
61st (1989): voting age 21 → 18
73rd & 74th (1992): Panchayats & Municipalities
86th (2002): Art. 21A, right to education
106th (2023): one-third seats for women in Lok Sabha & state assemblies

cards.title: Three emergencies
cards.body: **National (Art. 352)** — war, external aggression or **armed rebellion**; proclaimed in 1962, 1971 and 1975. **President's Rule (Art. 356)** — failure of constitutional machinery in a state. **Financial (Art. 360)** — never proclaimed.

cards.title: Approval timelines
points: Art. 352: within 1 month, special majority; renew every 6 months
Art. 356: within 2 months, simple majority; max 3 years (beyond 1 year only with conditions)
Art. 360: within 2 months, simple majority; continues until revoked

cards.title: Twelve Schedules
points: 1 States & UTs; 2 Emoluments; 3 Oaths; 4 Rajya Sabha seats
5 Scheduled Areas; 6 Tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
7 Union, State, Concurrent Lists; 8 Languages; 9 Protected laws
10 Anti-defection; 11 Panchayats (29 subjects); 12 Municipalities (18 subjects)

cards.q: Which amendment made the President's assent to amendment bills obligatory?
cards.explain: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971.

cards.q: A proclamation of National Emergency must be approved by Parliament within:
cards.explain: Since the 44th Amendment, within one month by special majority.

cards.q: The basic structure doctrine was laid down in:
cards.explain: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973).

notes.p: The Constitution is described as **partly rigid and partly flexible**. Article 368 sets out the procedure, but some changes can be made by ordinary law outside it. Parliament's amending power is wide, but the **basic structure** doctrine sets limits. Elements held to be basic include supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, judicial review, federalism, secularism, separation of powers, free and fair elections and the parliamentary system — the list is not closed.

1. The bill is introduced in either House of Parliament (not in a state legislature).
2. Each House must pass it separately by the required majority — no joint sitting if they disagree.
3. If it affects federal provisions, at least **half the state legislatures** must ratify it by simple majority; there is no time limit for states.
4. It goes to the President, who must assent.

An amendment is valid only if it survives judicial review on the basic-structure test.

The **First Amendment (1951)** created the Ninth Schedule to protect land-reform laws from challenge on Fundamental Rights grounds. In **I.R. Coelho (2007)**, the Supreme Court held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after **24 April 1973** (the Kesavananda date) can be reviewed if they violate the basic structure.

During a **National Emergency**, the Centre can give directions to states, Parliament can legislate on State List subjects, and Lok Sabha's term can be extended one year at a time. **Article 358** suspends Article 19 automatically — but, after the 44th Amendment, only when the emergency is due to war or external aggression. **Article 359** lets the President suspend enforcement of other Fundamental Rights, **except Articles 20 and 21**.

**President's Rule** has been used many times. In **S.R. Bommai (1994)**, the Supreme Court held that it is subject to judicial review, that a majority must be tested on the **floor of the House**, and that secularism is part of the basic structure. A **Financial Emergency** would allow the Centre to direct states on finances and to reduce salaries, including those of judges.

The **105th Amendment (2021)** restored states' power to prepare their own lists of socially and educationally backward classes. The **106th Amendment (2023)** — the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam — reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha, state assemblies and the Delhi assembly, to take effect after **delimitation based on the first census after its commencement**, for 15 years initially. Proposals for **simultaneous elections** have been introduced as bills; check their latest status.

Typical questions: which provisions need state ratification, which emergency needs what majority, what each Schedule contains, and what an amendment did. Tip: when an option says 'the Rajya Sabha cannot amend' or 'joint sitting can resolve deadlock on an amendment bill', it is false.
Recall.
points: Art. 368; three methods
No joint sitting; President must assent (24th)
Kesavananda 1973 — basic structure
Emergency: 352 (1 month, special), 356 (2 months), 360 (never used)
Arts. 20 & 21 cannot be suspended
Twelve Schedules — 10th anti-defection, 11th/12th local bodies
106th Amendment: women's reservation after delimitation

cards.title: Election Commission of India
cards.body: Created under **Article 324**; supervises elections to Parliament, state legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President. It became **multi-member** (CEC + two ECs) in 1993 (briefly also in 1989). The CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge.

cards.title: Appointment law (2023)
cards.body: Under the **Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023**, a selection committee of the **Prime Minister**, the **Leader of Opposition** (or leader of the largest opposition party) in the Lok Sabha, and a **Union Cabinet Minister** nominated by the PM recommends names.

cards.title: Representation of the People Acts
cards.body: **RPA 1950** — allocation of seats, delimitation-related matters and **electoral rolls**. **RPA 1951** — conduct of elections, qualifications and **disqualifications**, corrupt practices and election disputes. Election petitions go to the **High Court**.

cards.title: Anti-defection law
cards.body: The **Tenth Schedule** (52nd Amendment, 1985) disqualifies members who voluntarily give up party membership or defy the whip. The **Speaker/Chairman** decides, subject to judicial review (**Kihoto Hollohan**, 1992). A **merger** supported by two-thirds of the legislature party is exempt; the 'split' exception was removed by the **91st Amendment (2003)**.

cards.title: Party recognition
cards.body: A party becomes a **national party** if it meets any one of: 6% votes in four or more states plus 4 Lok Sabha seats; or 2% of Lok Sabha seats from at least three states; or recognition as a state party in four states. Recognition is under the **Election Symbols Order, 1968**.

cards.title: Electoral reforms
cards.body: **EVMs** (first used in 1982 in Kerala); **VVPAT** slips; **NOTA** (2013, after the PUCL judgment); voter-ID linking efforts. In **February 2024** the Supreme Court struck down the **electoral bonds** scheme as unconstitutional.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: The **Model Code of Conduct** is not a statute — it is a consensus-based code enforced by the ECI from the announcement of elections. Delimitation of constituencies is done by a **Delimitation Commission** whose orders cannot be questioned in court.

cards.q: Which Act deals with disqualification of members and election disputes?
cards.explain: The RPA 1951 covers conduct of elections, disqualifications and disputes.

cards.q: Which exception to anti-defection was removed by the 91st Amendment?
cards.explain: The 'split' exception was deleted in 2003.

cards.q: NOTA was introduced following a Supreme Court judgment in:
cards.explain: PUCL v. Union of India (2013).

notes.p: India uses **first-past-the-post** for Lok Sabha and state assemblies. The President is elected by an **electoral college** of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and state (and Delhi and Puducherry) assemblies using **proportional representation by single transferable vote**; the Vice-President by members of both Houses of Parliament. **Rajya Sabha** members are elected by state assembly members using STV. The voting age was lowered from 21 to **18** by the **61st Amendment (1989)**.

Seat allocation and constituency boundaries are revised by a **Delimitation Commission**. The **84th Amendment (2001)** froze the number of Lok Sabha seats per state (based on the 1971 census) until the first census after **2026**, while allowing boundaries to be readjusted using the 2001 census. Seats are reserved for **SCs and STs** in proportion to population; the nomination of Anglo-Indians was discontinued by the **104th Amendment (2019)**. Women's reservation will follow the next delimitation.

notes.h: Powers and independence of the ECI
notes.p: The ECI prepares and revises **electoral rolls**, recognises parties and allots **symbols**, enforces the Model Code, and can **postpone or countermand** polls. Its independence is protected by security of tenure for the CEC and a bar on varying the CEC's service conditions to his disadvantage. Other ECs can be removed on the CEC's recommendation. Debates continue on whether the appointment process is sufficiently independent.

Parties are not mentioned in the original Constitution; they entered through the **Tenth Schedule**. Funding transparency remains a major issue: the **electoral bonds** scheme (2018) allowed anonymous donations through banks, but the Supreme Court in **Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2024)** held it violated voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a).
