Candidates must disclose criminal records, assets and education in affidavits, following Supreme Court directions.

A high-level committee chaired by former President **Ram Nath Kovind** recommended **simultaneous elections** to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies (report 2024), followed by local bodies. Constitution amendment bills for this were introduced in Parliament and referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee — check the latest status. Other long-standing reform ideas include state funding of elections, curbing criminalisation and strengthening the ECI's power over parties.

UPSC asks about who elects whom, ECI powers, anti-defection rules and RPA provisions. Worked check: 'A nominated member joining a party within six months of taking seat is disqualified' — **false**; a nominated member may join a party **within** six months without disqualification. Another: 'Election petitions are heard by the Supreme Court in the first instance' — **false** for Parliament and assembly elections (they go to the **High Court**); disputes over the election of the **President and Vice-President** go directly to the **Supreme Court**.
Recall.
points: Art. 324 — ECI; multi-member since 1993
2023 Act: PM, LoP, Cabinet Minister select ECs
RPA 1950 (rolls) vs RPA 1951 (conduct, disqualification)
Tenth Schedule — Speaker decides; merger exception
NOTA 2013; EVMs; VVPAT
Electoral bonds struck down 2024
Seats frozen till first census after 2026

cards.title: Committees before 1992
cards.body: **Balwant Rai Mehta (1957)** — three-tier 'democratic decentralisation'; first adopted at **Nagaur, Rajasthan (2 October 1959)**. **Ashok Mehta (1977)** — two-tier system. **G.V.K. Rao (1985)** and **L.M. Singhvi (1986)** — Singhvi recommended constitutional status.

cards.title: 73rd Amendment (1992)
cards.body: Added **Part IX** (Articles 243 to 243-O) and the **Eleventh Schedule** with **29 subjects**. In force from **24 April 1993** — celebrated as **National Panchayati Raj Day**. Created a uniform three-tier structure: village, intermediate (block) and district.

cards.title: Compulsory vs voluntary provisions
points: Compulsory: Gram Sabha; three tiers (intermediate tier optional for states under 20 lakh population); direct elections; SC/ST reservation; at least one-third seats for women; 5-year term; State Election Commission; State Finance Commission; minimum age 21
Voluntary: reservation for backward classes; devolution of powers and functions; financial powers; representation of MPs/MLAs

cards.title: PESA 1996
cards.body: The **Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act** extends Part IX to **Fifth Schedule** areas with modifications. It empowers the **Gram Sabha** over community resources, **minor forest produce**, **minor minerals**, prevention of land alienation, and consultation before land acquisition.

cards.title: 74th Amendment (1992)
cards.body: Added **Part IXA** (243P to 243ZG) and the **Twelfth Schedule** with **18 subjects**. Three types: **Nagar Panchayat** (transitional area), **Municipal Council** (smaller urban area), **Municipal Corporation** (larger urban area). Wards committees for municipalities with 3 lakh+ population.

cards.title: Planning bodies
cards.body: **District Planning Committee** (Art. 243ZD) consolidates panchayat and municipal plans. **Metropolitan Planning Committee** (Art. 243ZE) for metropolitan areas with population of **10 lakh or more**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Part IX does **not** automatically apply to Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, certain hill areas of Manipur and the Darjeeling hill areas, nor to Scheduled Areas (covered via PESA). Parliament can extend it by law.

cards.q: How many subjects are in the Eleventh Schedule?
cards.explain: The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects for Panchayats.

cards.q: Which body conducts elections to panchayats?
cards.explain: Article 243K vests it in the State Election Commission.

cards.q: PESA 1996 gives special powers to the Gram Sabha over:
cards.explain: Ownership of minor forest produce is among the Gram Sabha's powers under PESA.

notes.p: Article 40 (a Directive Principle) asks the state to organise village panchayats. Early Panchayati Raj institutions after 1959 declined because of irregular elections, lack of funds and domination by local elites. The **64th Amendment Bill (1989)** failed in the Rajya Sabha; the **73rd and 74th Amendments** (passed in 1992) finally gave constitutional status to rural and urban local governments.

1. **Gram Sabha**: all registered voters of a village; powers set by state law.
2. **Three tiers**, with members of all tiers **directly elected**; chairpersons of the intermediate and district tiers elected indirectly.
3. **Reservation** for SCs and STs in proportion to population; **not less than one-third** for women (including among SC/ST seats) — many states now reserve **50%**; offices of chairpersons also reserved.
4. **Term**: five years; fresh elections before expiry or within **six months** of dissolution.
5. **State Election Commissioner**: appointed by the Governor; removable only like a High Court judge.
6. **State Finance Commission**: every five years, reviews panchayat finances (Art. 243-I).
7. The Union Finance Commission recommends measures to augment state funds for local bodies (Art. 280(3)(bb)).

The 74th Amendment mirrors Part IX for towns. The Governor specifies whether an area is a Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council or Corporation based on population, density, revenue and employment. Other urban bodies such as **cantonment boards**, **townships**, **port trusts** and **special purpose agencies** exist outside the elected municipal system. Mayors are elected directly in some states and indirectly in others.

Local bodies often lack **funds** (weak own-revenue such as property tax), **functions** (states have not fully devolved the listed subjects) and **functionaries** (staff remain under state departments). Other issues: proxy representation of women by male relatives ('sarpanch-pati'), elite capture, and delays in elections. In 2021 the Supreme Court required a **'triple test'** (dedicated commission, ward-wise data, 50% ceiling) for OBC reservation in local bodies. Initiatives such as **e-Gram Swaraj**, the **SVAMITVA** property-card scheme using drones, and **Gram Panchayat Development Plans** aim to strengthen local governance.

Statement check: 'A person aged 21 is eligible to contest panchayat elections; disputes about panchayat elections can be taken to any court.'

Part 1: The minimum age is **21** — correct.
Part 2: Article 243-O bars courts from interfering in electoral matters, and election disputes go only through an **election petition** as provided by state law — so 'any court' is wrong.
Answer: only the first part is correct.
Expect statement questions on compulsory vs voluntary provisions, Schedules, PESA, and planning committees. UPSC also links local governance to schemes and Finance Commission grants.
Recall.
points: Balwant Rai Mehta 1957; Nagaur 1959
73rd: Part IX, 11th Schedule, 29 subjects
74th: Part IXA, 12th Schedule, 18 subjects
Women ≥ one-third seats
SEC and SFC every five years
PESA 1996 for Fifth Schedule areas
DPC 243ZD; MPC 243ZE

chapters.title: Rights Issues, Rights Bodies & Public Policy

cards.title: Human rights bodies
cards.body: The **National Human Rights Commission** (NHRC) was set up under the **Protection of Human Rights Act 1993**. Its chairperson is a former Chief Justice of India or former Supreme Court judge. It recommends; it cannot punish. States have **SHRCs**.

cards.title: Constitutional vs statutory commissions
points: Constitutional: NCSC (Art. 338), NCST (Art. 338A, 89th Amendment), NCBC (Art. 338B, 102nd Amendment, 2018)
Statutory: NHRC (1993), National Commission for Women (1990 Act), National Commission for Minorities (1992 Act), NCPCR (2005 Act)

cards.title: Key rights laws
cards.body: **Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955**; **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989**; **RTI Act 2005**; **RTE Act 2009**; **POCSO 2012**; **Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016** (21 disabilities); **Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019**; **Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023**.

cards.title: Landmark judgments
cards.body: **Vishaka (1997)** — workplace sexual harassment guidelines (later the 2013 POSH Act). **NALSA (2014)** — transgender persons as 'third gender'. **Puttaswamy (2017)** — privacy is a Fundamental Right. **Navtej Johar (2018)** — decriminalised consensual same-sex relations.

cards.title: RTI basics
cards.body: Any citizen can seek information from a **public authority**; reply normally within **30 days** (48 hours if life or liberty is involved). Appeals go to the **Central/State Information Commissions**. Section 8 lists exemptions. A 2019 amendment let the Centre set the tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners.

cards.title: Public policy cycle
cards.body: **Agenda setting → formulation → adoption → implementation → evaluation**. Inputs come from Parliament, ministries, **NITI Aayog** (since 2015, replacing the Planning Commission), courts, civil society and pressure groups. Tools: **social audit**, citizen charters, RTI and outcome budgets.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Know which bodies are **constitutional** vs **statutory**: NCW, NHRC, NCM and NCPCR are statutory; NCSC, NCST and NCBC are constitutional. This is a recurring trap.

cards.q: Which commission got constitutional status through the 102nd Amendment?
cards.explain: The 102nd Amendment (2018) inserted Article 338B.

cards.q: Under the RTI Act, information concerning life or liberty must be supplied within:
cards.explain: Section 7(1) prescribes 48 hours for such information.

cards.q: Privacy was declared a Fundamental Right in:
cards.explain: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).

notes.p: The syllabus phrase 'Rights Issues' covers the rights of citizens and vulnerable groups — **women, children, SCs and STs, minorities, persons with disabilities, transgender persons, elderly persons** — and the institutions and laws that protect them. Questions mix constitutional provisions (Articles 14–32, DPSPs), statutes, and bodies.
Major safeguards:
points: **SCs/STs:** Art. 17 (untouchability abolished), Art. 46, reservations (Arts. 15(4), 16(4), 330, 332), Atrocities Act
**Women:** Art. 15(3), 39(d) equal pay, 42 maternity relief; Domestic Violence Act 2005; POSH Act 2013; Maternity Benefit (Amendment) 2017 — 26 weeks
**Children:** Art. 21A, 24, 39(f), 45; RTE, POCSO, Juvenile Justice Act 2015; Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act
**Minorities:** Arts. 29–30 — culture and educational institutions
**Disability:** RPwD Act 2016 — 4% reservation in government jobs, 5% in higher education
**Elderly:** Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007

notes.p: The NHRC can inquire **suo motu** or on petition, visit jails, review laws and promote human rights literacy. It cannot inquire into matters more than **one year** old. For the armed forces it can only seek a report from the Centre. Members are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the **Prime Minister**. Critics call it a 'toothless tiger' because its recommendations are not binding, but its reports influence policy.

The **RTI Act 2005** made information a right flowing from Article 19(1)(a). The **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013** created an anti-corruption ombudsman; the first Lokpal was appointed in **2019**. **Social audits** — first mandated under **MGNREGA** — let communities verify spending. The **Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014** and citizen charters complete the toolkit, though implementation varies.

Take the policy problem 'low school learning outcomes':
1. **Agenda**: survey data (e.g., ASER, NAS) put it in the news.
2. **Formulation**: options such as teacher training, foundational literacy missions, remedial classes.
3. **Adoption**: a national programme (e.g., **NIPUN Bharat**, 2021) under the **National Education Policy 2020**.
4. **Implementation**: states, schools, funding through Samagra Shiksha.
5. **Evaluation**: learning surveys and feedback lead to revisions.
This cycle explains how most schemes evolve.

Questions test the status of bodies, provisions of key laws, landmark judgments and RTI details. Statements often hinge on one word — 'binding', 'constitutional', 'suo motu'. Read slowly.

Also connect rights to the courts: **Public Interest Litigation**, developed in the late 1970s and 1980s (e.g., *Hussainara Khatoon*, *S.P. Gupta*), relaxed the rule of locus standi so that anyone acting in good faith could approach the courts for people unable to do so. Many rights now taken for granted — speedy trial, legal aid, clean environment, livelihood — were read into **Article 21** this way.
Recall.
points: NHRC 1993 — recommendatory; PM-led selection
NCSC 338, NCST 338A, NCBC 338B — constitutional
NCW, NCM, NCPCR — statutory
RTI: 30 days; 48 hours for life/liberty
Vishaka 1997; NALSA 2014; Puttaswamy 2017
RPwD 2016 — 21 disabilities, 4% job quota
Lokpal Act 2013; first Lokpal 2019

cards.title: Sources of the Constitution
points: **UK**: parliamentary system, rule of law, single citizenship, cabinet, writs
**USA**: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independent judiciary, impeachment of President
**Ireland**: DPSP, nomination to Rajya Sabha
**Canada**: federation with strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre
**Australia**: Concurrent List, joint sitting
**Weimar Germany**: suspension of FRs during emergency
**USSR**: Fundamental Duties

cards.title: Basic structure doctrine
cards.body: In **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** a 13-judge bench held (7:6) that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution under Article 368 but **cannot destroy its basic structure**.

cards.title: Elements recognised by courts
points: Supremacy of the Constitution
Republican, democratic form; free and fair elections
Secularism and federalism
Separation of powers
Judicial review and independence of judiciary
Rule of law; balance between FRs and DPSPs

cards.title: Key cases
points: **Golaknath (1967)**: Parliament cannot amend FRs (later overruled)
**Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975)**: free and fair elections basic
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: limited amending power and FR–DPSP balance
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: secularism, federalism
**NJAC case (2015)**: judicial independence

cards.title: India vs USA
points: Parliamentary vs presidential executive
Single vs dual citizenship
Integrated vs dual judiciary
"Indestructible union of destructible states" vs indestructible states
Flexible-rigid amendment vs very rigid

cards.title: India vs UK
points: Written vs largely unwritten constitution
Constitutional supremacy with judicial review vs parliamentary sovereignty
Elected President vs hereditary monarch
Federal structure vs unitary state

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In comparison questions, always end with **why India chose differently** — its diversity, colonial experience and goals of social revolution.

cards.q: The basic structure doctrine was laid down in:
cards.explain: Kesavananda Bharati established that the basic structure cannot be amended away.

cards.q: Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from the constitution of:
cards.explain: DPSPs were inspired by the Irish Constitution.

notes.p:
The Constitution is the **lengthiest written constitution**, drawing from many sources yet adapted to Indian needs. Key features: a blend of **rigidity and flexibility**, **federal system with unitary bias**, **parliamentary government**, synthesis of **parliamentary sovereignty and judicial supremacy**, integrated and independent judiciary, Fundamental Rights, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties, a **secular state**, universal adult franchise, single citizenship, emergency provisions, and independent bodies like the Election Commission and CAG.

Ambedkar defended borrowing: the fundamentals of a constitution are known to the world; what matters is adapting them to the country's conditions.

Article 368 provides three ways to amend: simple majority (for provisions outside Article 368 itself, like creating new states), **special majority** of each House, and special majority plus **ratification by half the states** for federal provisions.

The tussle over Parliament's amending power ran from **Shankari Prasad (1951)** and **Golaknath (1967)** to **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, which created the **basic structure doctrine**. The **42nd Amendment (1976)** tried to bar judicial review of amendments; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down those clauses, holding that limited amending power is itself basic. **Waman Rao (1981)** applied the doctrine to Ninth Schedule laws inserted after 24 April 1973, and **I.R. Coelho (2007)** confirmed such laws are open to review.

The Court has never given a closed list. Elements recognised across cases include: supremacy of the Constitution; sovereign, democratic, republican nature; **secularism**; **federalism**; separation of powers; **judicial review**; independence of the judiciary; rule of law; free and fair elections; parliamentary system; harmony between FRs and DPSPs; the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21; welfare state; and limited amending power.

**USA:** presidential system with fixed terms and strict separation of powers; India's executive is responsible to the legislature. The US has dual citizenship and dual courts; India has single citizenship and an **integrated judiciary**. The US Supreme Court relies on "due process of law"; India adopted "procedure established by law" (from Japan) but after **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** reads in fairness and reasonableness.

**UK:** largely unwritten constitution and **parliamentary sovereignty**; India has a written constitution and judicial review. India borrowed the Westminster model but with an elected head of state.

**Canada and Australia:** India's federation resembles Canada's strong-centre model and borrowed the Concurrent List from Australia. Unlike the USA, Indian states did not come together by agreement and have no right to secede; Parliament can alter state boundaries (Article 3).

Question type: "Compare the Indian and US models of federalism."
**Intro:** both are federations with written constitutions and independent judiciaries.
**Differences:** origin (holding-together vs coming-together), single vs dual citizenship and constitution, residuary powers (Centre vs states), Article 3 power, governor appointed by Centre, emergency provisions, all-India services.
**Assessment:** India's design reflects concerns for unity after Partition; cooperative federalism and the GST Council show evolution.
**Conclusion:** a "federation with a centralising tendency" (K.C. Wheare called it "quasi-federal").
Key points.
points: Borrowings: UK, USA, Ireland, Canada, Australia, Weimar, USSR, Japan
Article 368: three methods of amendment
Kesavananda 1973 (7:6): basic structure
Minerva Mills 1980: limited amending power; FR–DPSP balance
I.R. Coelho 2007: Ninth Schedule laws reviewable
India vs USA: parliamentary, single citizenship, integrated judiciary
India vs UK: written, judicial review, elected head

cards.title: Areas of friction
points: Role of **Governors**: assent to bills, government formation
Misuse of **Article 356** (President's Rule)
Fiscal imbalance: Centre raises more, states spend more
**Cesses and surcharges** outside the divisible pool
Central agencies and law & order
Inter-state water and boundary disputes

cards.title: Fiscal federalism
points: **Finance Commission** (Art 280): shares central taxes vertically and horizontally
**GST Council** (Art 279A, 101st Amendment 2016)
Grants-in-aid (Art 275, 282)
16th Finance Commission covers 2026–31: check its accepted recommendations

cards.title: Reform commissions
points: **Rajamannar Committee** (Tamil Nadu, 1969)
**Sarkaria Commission** (1983–88)
**Punchhi Commission** (2007–10)
Second ARC reports

cards.title: Bodies for coordination
points: **Inter-State Council** (Art 263)
**Zonal Councils** (States Reorganisation Act, 1956)
NITI Aayog Governing Council
GST Council

cards.title: Devolution to local bodies
cards.body: The 73rd and 74th Amendments require devolution of **funds, functions and functionaries (3Fs)**. **State Finance Commissions** (Art 243I, 243Y) recommend sharing of state resources; **District Planning Committees** (Art 243ZD) consolidate plans. Many states lag in real devolution.

cards.title: S.R. Bommai safeguards
cards.body: The Supreme Court (1994) held that a government's majority must be tested on the **floor of the House**, Article 356 proclamations are subject to judicial review, and secularism is part of the basic structure — curbing arbitrary dismissal of state governments.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Present federal issues as "cooperative and competitive federalism under strain", then give specific reforms: Sarkaria/Punchhi on governors, reducing cesses, empowering the Inter-State Council, timely SFC devolution.

cards.q: Which Article provides for the Inter-State Council?
cards.explain: Article 263 allows the President to establish an Inter-State Council.

cards.q: The GST Council was created under:
cards.explain: Article 279A, inserted by the 101st Amendment, provides for the GST Council.

notes.p:
India is described as a **"Union of States"** (Article 1) with a strong Centre — a "holding-together" federation. Federal features include a written constitution, division of powers (Seventh Schedule), an independent judiciary and bicameralism. Unitary features include a strong Centre, single citizenship, emergency provisions, governors appointed by the Centre, all-India services and Parliament's power to alter state boundaries.

The Supreme Court has held **federalism to be a basic feature** (S.R. Bommai). In practice, India oscillates between **cooperative federalism** (GST Council, NITI Aayog) and **competitive federalism** (states competing for investment), with periods of **confrontational** relations.
Key areas of tension:
points: **Governor's office:** delays in assent to bills, role in government formation, use of discretion; the Supreme Court has examined timelines for assent (Tamil Nadu Governor case, 2025, and a subsequent Presidential Reference) — check the latest position
**Article 356:** frequent use before 1994; Bommai made it judicially reviewable
**Fiscal:** vertical imbalance; rising share of **cesses and surcharges** not shared with states; GST compensation ended in 2022; borrowing limits
**Agencies:** use of central investigative agencies and the need for state consent
**Legislative:** central laws on Concurrent List subjects affecting state priorities
**Inter-state:** river-water disputes (Article 262; tribunals under the 1956 Act) and boundary disputes

notes.p:
The **Finance Commission** recommends the share of states in the divisible pool of central taxes (vertical devolution) and its distribution among states (horizontal devolution) using criteria such as population, area, income distance, forest cover and demographic performance. The 15th Finance Commission recommended 41% for states for 2021–26; for 2026–31, refer to the **16th Finance Commission** report and the government's action-taken report.

The **GST Council**, chaired by the Union Finance Minister with state finance ministers, is a model of pooled sovereignty: the Centre has one-third of the vote weight and states two-thirds, with decisions needing a three-fourths majority. The Supreme Court (Mohit Minerals, 2022) held its recommendations are persuasive, not binding.

The **Sarkaria Commission** recommended consulting the Chief Minister on governors' appointment, sparing use of Article 356 and a permanent Inter-State Council (which was set up in 1990). The **Punchhi Commission** suggested fixed tenure for governors and localised emergency provisions. Coordination bodies include the **Inter-State Council**, **Zonal Councils**, NITI Aayog's Governing Council and the GST Council. Critics note the Inter-State Council meets rarely.

Federalism does not end at states. The **73rd and 74th Amendments (1992)** created a third tier but left devolution of the 29 (Eleventh Schedule) and 18 (Twelfth Schedule) functions to state laws. Problems: limited own revenue, dependence on grants, parallel bodies, delayed State Finance Commissions and weak staff. Reforms: activity mapping, untied funds, property tax reform, capacity building, and holding local elections on time.

Question type: "Cooperative federalism in India is under stress. Examine."
**Intro:** constitutional design and cooperative ideal.
**Stress points:** governors, cesses, GST disputes, agencies, Article 356 history.
**Counter-points:** GST Council functioning by consensus, joint responses in COVID-19, Aspirational Districts.
**Way forward:** Sarkaria and Punchhi reforms, regular Inter-State Council meetings, reduced cesses, empowered local bodies.
**Conclusion:** "Team India" requires trust and institutions.
Key points.
points: India: "Union of States", holding-together federation
Issues: governors, Art 356, cesses, agencies, water disputes
Finance Commission (Art 280); GST Council (Art 279A)
Sarkaria 1983–88; Punchhi 2007–10; Rajamannar 1969
Inter-State Council (Art 263); Zonal Councils (1956 Act)
Local devolution: 3Fs, SFCs (243I/243Y), DPCs (243ZD)

chapters.title: Separation of Powers & Dispute Redressal Mechanisms

cards.title: Separation of powers in India
cards.body: India follows **separation of functions with checks and balances**, not rigid separation. The executive is drawn from the legislature; the judiciary reviews both. **Article 50** directs separating the judiciary from the executive.

cards.title: Checks and balances
points: Judiciary: **judicial review** (Art 13, 32, 226)
Legislature: no-confidence motion, questions, impeachment of President and removal of judges
Executive: appoints judges (with collegium), issues **ordinances** (Art 123, 213)
Art 121/211: legislatures cannot discuss judges' conduct; Art 122/212: courts cannot question House proceedings

cards.title: Judicial activism vs overreach
cards.body: **Activism**: PILs expanding rights — clean air, prisoners' rights, environment. **Overreach**: courts stepping into policy or administration (e.g. framing detailed guidelines, managing bodies). The line is debated; restraint and institutional respect are key.

cards.title: Dispute redressal mechanisms
points: Courts (Supreme Court, High Courts, subordinate courts)
**Tribunals** (Art 323A, 323B; added by 42nd Amendment)
**Lok Adalats** (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987)
**Gram Nyayalayas** (2008)
Arbitration (1996 Act), **Mediation Act, 2023**
Consumer Commissions (Consumer Protection Act, 2019)

cards.title: Pendency remedies
points: Fill judicial vacancies; more judges per population
Case management, e-Courts, virtual hearings
Promote ADR and pre-litigation mediation
Reduce government litigation
Strengthen subordinate judiciary infrastructure

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Cite Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) for "no rigid separation" and Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975) for separation of powers as part of the basic structure.

cards.q: Tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B were added by the:
cards.explain: The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Part XIV-A on tribunals.

cards.q: Lok Adalats get statutory status under the:
cards.explain: The 1987 Act gives Lok Adalat awards the status of a civil court decree.

notes.p:
**Montesquieu** argued that liberty requires separating legislative, executive and judicial power. The US follows a stricter version; India, with a parliamentary system, has a **fusion of legislature and executive** and an independent judiciary that checks both.

In **Ram Jawaya Kapur v State of Punjab (1955)** the Supreme Court said the Constitution does not recognise absolute separation but differentiates functions. In **Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975)** and later cases, separation of powers was treated as part of the **basic structure**.

The **legislature** controls the executive through questions, debates, motions, committees and the budget, and can remove judges by a special process. The **executive** can issue ordinances when Parliament is not in session, frames delegated legislation and plays a role in judicial appointments. The **judiciary** can strike down unconstitutional laws and executive actions. Mutual restraints include Articles 121 and 211 (no discussion of a judge's conduct except in removal proceedings) and Articles 122 and 212 (courts cannot question legislative procedure). **Article 361** gives the President and Governors personal immunity.
Areas of debate:
points: **Judicial appointments:** the collegium system versus the NJAC, struck down in 2015 as violating judicial independence
**Judicial activism vs overreach:** PIL successes vs policy-making by courts
**Ordinances:** re-promulgation criticised in **Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)** as a fraud on the Constitution
**Money bill route** to bypass the Rajya Sabha
**Legislative privileges** versus judicial review
**Tribunalisation:** executive control over appointments to tribunals (Madras Bar Association cases; Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021)

notes.p: Beyond regular courts, India has built several mechanisms:
points: **Tribunals** for service, tax, company, environment and other matters (CAT, ITAT, NCLT, NGT)
**Lok Adalats** for compromise settlement; awards are final and non-appealable
**Legal services authorities** (NALSA, state and district) for free legal aid (Article 39A)
**Gram Nyayalayas** for accessible rural justice
**Arbitration and conciliation**; institutional arbitration being promoted
**Mediation Act, 2023** encouraging pre-litigation mediation
**Consumer commissions** at district, state and national levels
**Ombudsman schemes** in banking and insurance; Lokpal and Lokayuktas for corruption

notes.p: Millions of cases are pending across courts (see the National Judicial Data Grid for current figures). Causes include vacancies, low judge-population ratio, frequent adjournments, government as the largest litigant, and procedural complexity. Reforms: timely appointments, **All India Judicial Service** proposals, e-Courts and virtual hearings, case management, specialised commercial courts, plea bargaining, and wider use of ADR.

Question type: "Is judicial activism a threat to separation of powers?"
**Define** activism and separation.
**Positive role:** filling governance gaps (Vishaka guidelines, environment cases, prisoners' rights).
**Concerns:** overreach into policy, lack of expertise and accountability, implementation issues.
**Balance:** courts as sentinels when institutions fail; restraint in policy domains.
**Conclusion:** mutual respect among organs is the essence of constitutionalism.
Key points.
points: Separation of functions + checks and balances, not rigid separation
Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955); Raj Narain (1975)
NJAC struck down (2015); Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) on ordinances
Tribunals: Art 323A/323B (42nd Amendment)
Lok Adalats (1987 Act); Mediation Act 2023; Gram Nyayalayas 2008

chapters.title: Parliament & State Legislatures: Functioning, Business & Privileges

cards.title: Syllabus focus
cards.body: "Parliament and State legislatures — structure, functioning, conduct of business, powers and privileges and issues arising out of these." Prelims basics are in the Parliament chapter; this chapter covers **Mains issues**.

cards.title: Parliamentary privileges
points: **Art 105** (Parliament), **Art 194** (state legislatures)
Freedom of speech in the House
Immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given
Power to punish for **contempt**
Not codified — debate on codification

cards.title: Sita Soren (2024)
cards.body: A seven-judge bench held that legislators who take **bribes** to vote or speak are **not protected** by privilege, overruling P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).

cards.title: Issues in functioning
points: Fewer sitting days and frequent **disruptions**
Bills passed with little debate or committee scrutiny
Use of **money bill** route and ordinances
Anti-defection law and Speaker's role
Long vacancy in Deputy Speaker's post
Weak private members' business

cards.title: Committees: Parliament's workshops
points: Financial: Public Accounts, Estimates, Public Undertakings
**Department-related Standing Committees** (since 1993)
Joint and Select Committees for specific bills
Committees allow detailed, less partisan scrutiny

cards.title: Legislative Councils
cards.body: A state may create or abolish a Council under **Article 169**: the Assembly passes a resolution by special majority and Parliament legislates. Six states currently have councils: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For "parliamentary effectiveness" questions, give data-free but concrete reforms: minimum sitting days, mandatory committee scrutiny of bills, a parliamentary budget office, a code of conduct, and an independent Speaker.

cards.q: Parliamentary privileges for state legislatures are provided under:
cards.explain: Article 194 deals with privileges of state legislatures.

cards.q: In Sita Soren v Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court held that:
options: MPs have absolute immunity for bribes
Bribery by legislators is not protected by parliamentary privilege
cards.explain: The Court overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998) on this point.

cards.q: Which Article governs creation or abolition of Legislative Councils?
cards.explain: Article 169 lets Parliament create or abolish a council on the Assembly's resolution.

notes.p: Parliament consists of the President, Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha; state legislatures consist of the Governor and one or two Houses. Legislatures **make laws**, **control the executive**, **approve finance**, **represent** the people and **deliberate** national issues. They also have constituent (amendment), electoral (President, Vice-President) and judicial (impeachment, removal) roles.

Business follows the **Rules of Procedure** of each House: Question Hour and Zero Hour, calling attention notices, adjournment motions, short-duration discussions, legislation, financial business (budget, demands for grants, appropriation and finance bills) and motions such as no-confidence. The **Speaker/Chairman** regulates proceedings, certifies money bills (Article 110) and decides disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.

The **anti-defection law** (Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment in 1985 and tightened by the 91st Amendment in 2003) disqualifies members who voluntarily give up party membership or defy the whip; the merger exception requires two-thirds of the legislature party. **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** upheld the law and made the Speaker's decision subject to judicial review.

Privileges ensure that legislators can work without fear. Under Articles 105 and 194: freedom of speech in the House (subject to rules), immunity from court proceedings for speeches and votes, and publication of proceedings. Collective privileges include the power to regulate internal affairs, exclude strangers and punish for **breach of privilege or contempt**.

Privileges are **not codified**, so their scope is uncertain; critics argue codification would protect free speech of citizens and media. In **Sita Soren (2024)**, the Supreme Court held bribery is not protected by privilege because it is not essential to legislative functioning.
Concerns raised by analysts and committees:
points: Declining sitting days and productivity loss due to disruptions
Bills referred to committees less often; short debates
Money bill certification controversies (Aadhaar Act case, 2018; the issue was later referred to a larger bench — check the latest position)
Ordinance use and re-promulgation
Speakers delaying disqualification petitions — Supreme Court has asked for decisions within a reasonable time (Keisham Meghachandra Singh, 2020)
Criminalisation and declining quality of debate
State legislatures meet for very few days in many states

notes.p: Fixed minimum sittings; mandatory committee referral for major bills; strengthening **Department-related Standing Committees**; research support through a **Parliamentary Budget Office**; a code of conduct and ethics committees with teeth; independent Speakers (some suggest Speakers resign from party, as in the UK); timely disqualification decisions; live data on legislative performance; and pre-legislative consultation.

Question type: "Discuss the need for codifying parliamentary privileges."
**Intro:** Articles 105/194 and uncodified status.
**For codification:** clarity, protection of citizens' and media freedoms, consistency with FRs, judicial review.
**Against:** loss of flexibility, courts may encroach on legislative domain.
**Middle path:** codify core privileges, keep procedure flexible.
**Conclusion:** privileges exist to serve the people, not to shield members.
Key points.
points: Privileges: Art 105 (Parliament), Art 194 (states)
Sita Soren 2024: bribery not protected
Tenth Schedule: 52nd (1985), 91st (2003); Kihoto Hollohan 1992
Money bill: Art 110, Speaker certifies
Councils: Art 169; six states have them
DRSCs since 1993; PAC, Estimates, COPU
Reforms: sittings, committee scrutiny, PBO, impartial Speaker

chapters.title: Representation of the People Acts & Pressure Groups

cards.title: RPA 1950 vs RPA 1951
points: **RPA 1950**: allocation of seats, delimitation-related matters, qualification of voters, **electoral rolls**
**RPA 1951**: **conduct of elections**, qualifications and disqualifications of members, corrupt practices, election disputes, registration of parties

cards.title: Key sections of RPA 1951
points: **Sec 8**: disqualification on conviction (sentence of 2+ years for many offences)
**Sec 29A**: registration of political parties
**Sec 33(7)**: contest from at most two constituencies
**Sec 77**: account of election expenses
**Sec 123**: corrupt practices (bribery, undue influence, appeals on religion/caste)
**Sec 126**: campaign silence before poll

cards.title: Judicial milestones
points: **Lily Thomas (2013)**: Sec 8(4) protection for sitting members struck down
**PUCL (2013)**: NOTA introduced
**ADR (2002)/PUCL (2003)**: candidates disclose criminal, assets, education details
**ADR v Union of India (2024)**: electoral bonds scheme struck down

cards.title: Pressure groups
cards.body: Organised groups that try to **influence public policy without seeking to form government**. Examples: business associations (FICCI, CII), trade unions (INTUC, BMS, CITU), farmers' bodies, professional bodies (IMA, Bar Council), student unions, environmental and caste/community associations.

cards.title: Pressure groups vs political parties
points: Parties contest elections; pressure groups do not
Parties have broad programmes; groups focus on specific interests
Groups use lobbying, petitions, protests, litigation, media
Some groups are affiliated with parties (e.g. trade union wings)

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Present pressure groups as a feature of a healthy democracy (voice, information, accountability) with risks (capture by powerful lobbies, violent agitation, narrow interests). Suggest transparency in lobbying and dialogue platforms.

cards.q: Which Act deals with the preparation of electoral rolls?
cards.explain: Electoral rolls and voter qualification come under RPA 1950.

cards.q: Under RPA 1951, a candidate can contest a general election from at most:
cards.explain: Section 33(7) limits it to two constituencies.

cards.q: Which is a key difference between pressure groups and political parties?
options: Pressure groups seek to influence policy without forming government
cards.explain: Pressure groups influence policy from outside government.

notes.p: Article 324 vests superintendence of elections in the **Election Commission**, and Article 327 lets Parliament make laws on elections. Parliament enacted two key laws: the **Representation of the People Act, 1950** and the **Representation of the People Act, 1951**. Together with the Conduct of Election Rules (1961), the Registration of Electors Rules (1960) and the Delimitation Acts, they form India's electoral framework.

**RPA 1950:** allocation of seats in Parliament and state legislatures, delimitation-related provisions, qualifications of voters, preparation and revision of **electoral rolls**, and filling of Rajya Sabha seats from Union Territories.

**RPA 1951:** administrative machinery (returning officers), **qualifications and disqualifications** for membership (Sections 8–11), notification and conduct of elections, nomination and scrutiny, registration of parties (**Section 29A**), contributions to parties (Section 29B, 29C reporting), election expenses (Section 77), **corrupt practices** (Section 123) and electoral offences, and **election disputes** — election petitions are tried by the **High Court**, with appeal to the Supreme Court.
Key points for answers:
points: **Section 8** disqualifies those convicted of specified offences; **Lily Thomas (2013)** removed the three-month protection for sitting legislators
**Section 62(5)** bars persons in prison from voting
**Section 123(3)** makes appeals on grounds of religion, race, caste, community or language corrupt practices; **Abhiram Singh (2017)** read it broadly
**Section 125A** penalises false affidavits
Disclosure of criminal antecedents, assets and education following the ADR and PUCL judgments
**NOTA** option (PUCL, 2013)
**Electoral bonds** scheme struck down in ADR v Union of India (2024)

notes.p: Issues include criminalisation of politics, money power, the limit of two constituencies, simultaneous elections, remote voting for migrants, de-registration of inactive parties (the ECI lacks explicit power to de-register under the Act), and transparency of party funding. Committees such as the **Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990)**, **Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998)** on state funding, and the **Law Commission** have proposed reforms.

Pressure groups are **interest or promotional groups** that seek to influence policy. Gabriel Almond classified them as **institutional** (within institutions, e.g. civil service associations), **associational** (formal interest groups like FICCI or trade unions), **non-associational** (kinship, caste or religious groups) and **anomic** (spontaneous protests).

Methods: lobbying ministers and MPs, submitting memoranda, public campaigns, strikes and protests, litigation including PILs, and media advocacy. Contributions: representing interests between elections, providing expertise, and holding government accountable. Concerns: unequal access (powerful corporate lobbies), opaque lobbying, violent agitations, and capture of parties by narrow interests. Formal and informal **associations** — NGOs, RWAs, cooperatives, SHGs — form the wider civil society.
Key points.
points: RPA 1950: seats, voters, electoral rolls
RPA 1951: conduct, disqualification, parties, corrupt practices, disputes
Lily Thomas 2013; PUCL NOTA 2013; electoral bonds struck down 2024
Election petitions: High Court
Pressure groups influence policy, do not seek power
Almond: institutional, associational, non-associational, anomic

cards.title: Three categories
points: **Statutory bodies**: created by an Act of Parliament (NHRC, NCW, CVC, Lokpal)
**Regulatory bodies**: oversee a sector to protect competition and consumers (SEBI, TRAI, IRDAI, CCI)
**Quasi-judicial bodies**: decide disputes with court-like powers (NGT, CAT, NCLT, consumer commissions, Information Commissions)

cards.title: Major regulators
points: **SEBI**: securities markets (statutory 1992)
**IRDAI**: insurance (1999 Act)
**TRAI**: telecom (1997)
**CCI**: competition (Competition Act, 2002)
**PFRDA**: pensions; **FSSAI**: food safety (2006 Act)
**CERC**: electricity (Electricity Act, 2003)

cards.title: Quasi-judicial bodies
points: **NGT** (2010): environmental cases
**CAT** (1985): service matters of central employees
**NCLT/NCLAT**: company law and insolvency
**Consumer Commissions** (2019 Act)
**Central/State Information Commissions** (RTI Act, 2005)

cards.title: Why regulators?
cards.body: Independent regulators bring **expertise, stability and insulation from day-to-day politics**, handling sectors opened up after liberalisation where government is also a player.

cards.title: Common issues
points: Independence: appointments, tenure, government control
**Regulatory capture** by industry
Overlapping jurisdictions
Vacancies and delays
Accountability to Parliament
Tribunals overloaded; appeals clog Supreme Court

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use the "independence–accountability balance": regulators must be insulated from political pressure yet answerable to Parliament and the public through reports, audits and reasoned orders.

cards.q: Which body was set up under the Competition Act, 2002?
cards.explain: The Competition Commission of India enforces the Competition Act.

cards.q: The National Green Tribunal was established in:
cards.explain: The NGT Act was passed in 2010.

notes.p:
**Constitutional bodies** (Election Commission, UPSC, CAG, Finance Commission) are covered in the Constitutional Bodies chapter. This chapter covers bodies created by **statute** or **executive resolution** that regulate sectors or decide disputes.

A **quasi-judicial** body has powers resembling a court — it hears parties, takes evidence and gives binding decisions — but is not part of the regular judiciary. **Regulatory** bodies frame rules, license participants, monitor compliance and penalise violations in a sector.

notes.h: Statutory bodies for rights and integrity
notes.p: Important statutory bodies include the **National Human Rights Commission** (Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993), **National Commission for Women** (1990 Act), **National Commission for Protection of Child Rights** (2005 Act), **Central Vigilance Commission** (statutory under the CVC Act, 2003), **Lokpal** (Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013), **Central Bureau of Investigation** (functions under the DSPE Act, 1946) and **National Investigation Agency** (2008 Act). Many have only **recommendatory** powers, a common criticism.
After the 1991 reforms, independent regulators were created for opened-up sectors:
points: **SEBI** — investor protection and market regulation
**IRDAI** — insurance
**TRAI** — telecom tariffs and quality; disputes go to TDSAT
**CCI** — anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominance, mergers
**CERC/SERCs** — electricity tariffs
**PNGRB** — downstream petroleum and gas
**AERA** — airport tariffs
**FSSAI** — food standards
**RBI** remains the banking and payments regulator

notes.p:
**Tribunals** like the **Central Administrative Tribunal** (Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985), **NGT** (2010), **NCLT/NCLAT** (company law and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code), **Income Tax Appellate Tribunal**, **Securities Appellate Tribunal** and **Armed Forces Tribunal** reduce the burden on courts and bring specialisation. **Consumer commissions** and **Information Commissions** also act quasi-judicially.

The Supreme Court in **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** held that tribunal decisions are subject to High Court review. The **Madras Bar Association** cases have repeatedly insisted on judicial dominance in tribunal selection and adequate tenure; the **Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021** abolished several appellate tribunals.

Common problems: **independence** compromised by executive control over appointments and service conditions; **post-retirement** appointments of judges and officials; **vacancies**; overlapping mandates (e.g. between sector regulators and CCI); limited **parliamentary oversight**; and risk of **regulatory capture**.

Reforms suggested by the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission and others: a common framework law for regulators, transparent selection, fixed tenure, regulatory impact assessment, reasoned public orders, parliamentary committee review of annual reports, and a **National Tribunals Commission** for uniform administration of tribunals.

Question type: "Regulatory bodies in India lack real independence. Critically examine."
**Intro:** why independent regulators emerged after 1991.
**Arguments for the statement:** government controls appointments and removals; budgets depend on ministries; officials move to regulated firms or post-retirement posts; vacancies leave bodies weak.
**Counter-arguments:** SEBI and CCI have imposed significant penalties; statutes give fixed tenure; orders are appealable and reasoned.
**Way forward:** a common regulatory framework law, transparent selection committees, cooling-off periods, parliamentary review.
**Conclusion:** credibility of regulators is central to investor and citizen trust.
Key points.
points: Statutory: NHRC 1993, NCW 1990 Act, NCPCR 2005, CVC 2003, Lokpal 2013
Regulators: SEBI, IRDAI, TRAI, CCI, CERC, PNGRB, FSSAI, PFRDA
Quasi-judicial: CAT 1985, NGT 2010, NCLT, consumer and information commissions
L. Chandra Kumar 1997: tribunals under HC review
Tribunals Reforms Act 2021
Balance independence with accountability

cards.title: From traders to rulers
cards.body: The English East India Company came as traders in 1600. Two battles made it a political power in Bengal.
points: **Plassey (1757):** Robert Clive defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, helped by Mir Jafar's betrayal
**Buxar (1764):** the Company defeated Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II
**Treaty of Allahabad (1765):** the Company got the Diwani (revenue rights) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa

cards.title: Tools of expansion
points: **Subsidiary Alliance** – Lord Wellesley (from 1798): Indian rulers kept British troops at their own cost; Hyderabad was among the first to accept
**Doctrine of Lapse** – Lord Dalhousie: a state without a natural heir was annexed; Satara (1848) was the first, Jhansi and Nagpur followed
Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of 'misgovernance'

cards.title: Land revenue systems
points: **Permanent Settlement (1793)** – Cornwallis; Bengal, Bihar, Orissa; zamindars fixed revenue permanently
**Ryotwari** – Thomas Munro and Alexander Read; Madras and Bombay; direct settlement with peasants
**Mahalwari** – village (mahal) as unit; North-West Provinces, Punjab, parts of central India

cards.title: Economic drain
cards.body: **Dadabhai Naoroji** explained in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' that India's wealth was being drained to Britain through salaries, pensions, home charges and profits without equal return. This 'Drain Theory' became the core economic critique of colonial rule.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Make a timeline of Governors-General with one signature policy each — Cornwallis (Permanent Settlement), Wellesley (Subsidiary Alliance), Bentinck (abolition of Sati, 1829), Dalhousie (Doctrine of Lapse, railways, telegraph).

cards.q: The Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa was granted to the Company by:
cards.explain: After Buxar, Shah Alam II granted the Diwani through the Treaty of Allahabad in 1765.

cards.q: Which was the first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse?
cards.explain: Satara was annexed in 1848. Awadh was annexed in 1856 for alleged misgovernance, not lapse.

notes.p:
The **English East India Company** received its charter from Queen Elizabeth I in **1600**. It first came to trade in spices, textiles and indigo, competing with the Portuguese, Dutch and French. After the death of Aurangzeb in **1707**, the Mughal Empire weakened and regional powers such as Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad, the Marathas and Mysore rose. This political vacuum allowed the Company to turn trade into territorial power.

The misuse of trade privileges (dastaks) and the fortification of Calcutta led to conflict with **Siraj-ud-Daulah**, the Nawab of Bengal.

notes.h: Key battles and treaties — a timeline
notes.p: These are the turning points of British expansion.
points: **1757 – Battle of Plassey:** Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, helped by Mir Jafar's betrayal
**1764 – Battle of Buxar:** the Company defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II — a more decisive military victory than Plassey
**1765 – Treaty of Allahabad:** the Company got the **Diwani** (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
**1767–1799 – Anglo-Mysore Wars:** four wars against Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan; Tipu died at Srirangapatnam in 1799
**1775–1818 – Anglo-Maratha Wars:** three wars ending Maratha power
**1845–1849 – Anglo-Sikh Wars:** Punjab annexed in 1849

notes.p: The British did not rely only on war. They used clever political tools.
points: **Dual government in Bengal (1765–1772):** the Company held revenue rights while the Nawab carried administrative responsibility — power without responsibility
**Subsidiary Alliance (Lord Wellesley, 1798):** Indian rulers kept British troops at their own cost and accepted a British Resident; Hyderabad was the first to accept it
**Doctrine of Lapse (Lord Dalhousie):** a state whose ruler died without a natural heir was annexed — Satara (1848), Jhansi and Nagpur (1854) among others
Awadh was annexed in **1856** on the ground of 'misgovernance', not under the Doctrine of Lapse

notes.p: Parliament in Britain slowly increased its control over the Company.
points: **Regulating Act, 1773:** Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings first); Supreme Court at Calcutta set up (1774)
**Pitt's India Act, 1784:** Board of Control created — dual system of control
**Charter Act, 1813:** ended the Company's trade monopoly in India except tea and trade with China; ₹1 lakh a year set aside for education
**Charter Act, 1833:** Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck first); Company's commercial activities ended
**Charter Act, 1853:** open competition introduced for civil services

notes.p: British rule led to the **drain of wealth** (explained by Dadabhai Naoroji), **de-industrialisation** of handicrafts, and new land revenue systems.
points: **Permanent Settlement (1793, Lord Cornwallis):** Bengal, Bihar, Orissa — zamindars as owners with fixed revenue
**Ryotwari:** Madras and Bombay regions — revenue directly from cultivators (associated with Thomas Munro)
**Mahalwari:** north-western provinces and Punjab — revenue settled with the village community (mahal)

notes.p: Prelims often tests the **chronology** of battles, governors-general and their policies, and features of revenue systems. Pair-matching of 'Act – provision' is common. Mains GS I asks about the **economic impact** of colonial rule, why Indian powers failed against the British, and the nature of early colonial administration.
Fix the timeline.
points: 1600: Company charter; 1707: Aurangzeb's death
1757 Plassey; 1764 Buxar; 1765 Diwani via Treaty of Allahabad
Subsidiary Alliance: Wellesley (1798); Hyderabad first
Doctrine of Lapse: Dalhousie; Awadh annexed in 1856 for misgovernance
Regulating Act 1773; Pitt's India Act 1784
Charter Acts: 1813 (monopoly ends), 1833 (GG of India), 1853 (open competition)
Permanent Settlement 1793 (Cornwallis); Ryotwari; Mahalwari
Drain theory: Dadabhai Naoroji

cards.title: The Revolt of 1857
cards.body: It began at **Meerut on 10 May 1857**; sepoys marched to Delhi and proclaimed **Bahadur Shah Zafar** emperor. Causes included annexations, heavy revenue demands, social interference and the greased cartridge issue of the Enfield rifle.
points: Delhi – Bahadur Shah Zafar (with General Bakht Khan)
Kanpur – Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope
Lucknow – Begum Hazrat Mahal
Jhansi – Rani Lakshmibai
Bihar (Jagdishpur) – Kunwar Singh

cards.title: Aftermath
cards.body: The **Government of India Act 1858** ended Company rule; power passed to the British Crown. A Secretary of State for India was created, and the Governor-General became the **Viceroy**. Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) promised to respect Indian princes and religions.

cards.title: Reformers you must know
points: Raja Ram Mohan Roy – Brahmo Sabha (1828); campaign led to abolition of Sati (1829)
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar – Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856)
Jyotiba Phule – Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)
Swami Dayanand Saraswati – Arya Samaj (1875)
Swami Vivekananda – Ramakrishna Mission (1897)
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan – Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, Aligarh (1875)

cards.title: Linking to Mains
cards.body: GS I asks about social reform's role in nationalism. Example line: 'Reform movements spread rational thought, women's education and pride in Indian heritage, preparing the middle class that later led the national movement.' Then give two reformers as evidence.

cards.q: The Revolt of 1857 began at:
cards.explain: The organised outbreak began at Meerut on 10 May 1857 (Mangal Pandey's earlier incident at Barrackpore was in March 1857).

cards.q: Who founded the Satyashodhak Samaj?
cards.explain: Jyotiba Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873 to fight caste discrimination.

notes.p: The revolt began at **Meerut on 10 May 1857**, when sepoys rose up and marched to Delhi, proclaiming **Bahadur Shah Zafar** as emperor. Its causes had built up over a century.
points: **Political:** annexations under the Doctrine of Lapse and the annexation of Awadh (1856)
**Economic:** heavy land revenue, ruin of artisans, loss of jobs for those dependent on Indian courts
**Socio-religious:** fear of forced conversion and interference in customs
**Military:** poor pay and promotion for Indian sepoys; General Service Enlistment Act (1856)
**Immediate cause:** the new **Enfield rifle** cartridges, rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat

notes.p: The revolt spread mainly across north and central India.
points: **Delhi:** Bahadur Shah Zafar (symbolic), Bakht Khan (real military leadership)
**Kanpur:** Nana Saheb, with Tantia Tope
**Lucknow:** Begum Hazrat Mahal
**Jhansi:** Rani Lakshmibai
**Bihar (Arrah/Jagdishpur):** Kunwar Singh
**Faizabad:** Maulvi Ahmadullah
Mangal Pandey's act of rebellion at Barrackpore took place in March 1857, before Meerut

notes.h: Why it failed and what changed
notes.p:
The revolt failed because of **limited geographic spread**, lack of a common plan and modern weapons, and the support many rulers and sections gave to the British. Yet it changed India's governance.

The **Government of India Act, 1858** ended Company rule and transferred power to the **British Crown**. The Governor-General was now also called **Viceroy** (Lord Canning first). A **Secretary of State for India** was created. **Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858)** promised no further annexations and respect for Indian customs. The army was reorganised to increase the ratio of European soldiers and to follow 'divide and rule'.
points: Historians debate its nature: 'sepoy mutiny', 'first war of independence' (V.D. Savarkar's term) or a popular revolt — Mains may ask you to discuss this

notes.p: In the 19th century, educated Indians began questioning social evils such as sati, child marriage, caste discrimination and the ban on widow remarriage.
points: **Raja Ram Mohan Roy:** Brahmo Sabha (1828), later Brahmo Samaj; campaigned against sati — banned by Regulation XVII of **1829** under Lord William Bentinck
**Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar:** led the campaign for the **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856**
**Swami Dayananda Saraswati:** Arya Samaj (1875); 'Go back to the Vedas'
**Swami Vivekananda:** Ramakrishna Mission (1897)
**Jyotiba Phule:** Satyashodhak Samaj (1873); worked for lower castes and girls' education with Savitribai Phule
**Sir Syed Ahmad Khan:** Aligarh Movement; Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (1875)
**Narayana Guru:** Kerala; 'one caste, one religion, one God for man'

notes.p: Prelims tests **leader–centre** pairs, reformers and their organisations, and the provisions of the 1858 Act. Mains GS I may ask about the **nature and consequences** of the 1857 revolt or the **contribution of reform movements** to modern India and women's emancipation.
Key points.
points: Revolt began at Meerut, 10 May 1857; immediate cause: greased cartridges
Leaders: Nana Saheb (Kanpur), Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Kunwar Singh (Bihar)
GoI Act 1858: Crown rule, Viceroy, Secretary of State
Sati banned 1829 (Bentinck) with Ram Mohan Roy's efforts
Widow Remarriage Act 1856: Vidyasagar
Arya Samaj 1875; Satyashodhak Samaj 1873; Ramakrishna Mission 1897
Aligarh Movement: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan

cards.title: Birth of the Congress
cards.body: The **Indian National Congress** was founded in **1885** with help from retired civil servant A.O. Hume. Its first session at **Bombay** was presided over by **W.C. Bonnerjee**. The early **Moderates** (Naoroji, Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta) used petitions, prayers and protests within constitutional limits.

cards.title: Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi
cards.body: Lord **Curzon** partitioned Bengal in **1905**, officially for administration but in effect to divide Bengali nationalists along religious lines. The response was the **Swadeshi and Boycott movement**. The partition was annulled in **1911**, and the capital shifted from Calcutta to Delhi.

cards.title: Key milestones
points: 1906 – All-India Muslim League founded at Dacca
1907 – Surat Split: Moderates vs Extremists (Lal-Bal-Pal)
1909 – Morley-Minto Reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims
1916 – Lucknow Pact between Congress and Muslim League; Moderates and Extremists reunited
1916 – Home Rule Leagues of Tilak and Annie Besant

cards.title: Moderates vs Extremists
cards.body: Moderates believed British rule could be reformed and relied on the educated elite. Extremists like Tilak ('Swaraj is my birthright') demanded self-rule and used mass mobilisation, festivals and boycott. Both contributed: Moderates built economic critique; Extremists widened the movement's base.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Prelims frequently asks chronology. Write 1885 → 1905 → 1906 → 1907 → 1909 → 1911 → 1916 on one card and revise it weekly.

cards.q: Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced by:
cards.explain: The Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced separate electorates.

cards.q: Who presided over the first session of the INC?
cards.explain: W.C. Bonnerjee presided over the 1885 Bombay session.

notes.p:
The **Indian National Congress (INC)** was founded in **December 1885** at Bombay with the help of **A.O. Hume**, a retired British civil servant. Its first session was presided over by **W.C. Bonnerjee** and had 72 delegates. Earlier bodies like the **Indian Association (1876)** of Surendranath Banerjea had prepared the ground.

The period **1885–1905** is called the **Moderate phase**. Leaders included Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Surendranath Banerjea.
points: Moderate methods: petitions, prayers, protests through constitutional means — sometimes called '3P'
Demands: more Indians in councils and services, reduction in military expenditure, economic critique of British rule
Biggest contribution: the **economic critique** of colonialism and the drain theory

notes.p:
**Lord Curzon** announced the **Partition of Bengal** in 1905; it took effect on **16 October 1905**. The official reason was administrative convenience, but the real aim was to divide Bengali Hindus and Muslims and weaken nationalism.

The response was the **Swadeshi and Boycott Movement**: boycott of foreign goods, use of Indian goods, national education, and mass participation. Rabindranath Tagore wrote 'Amar Sonar Bangla' during this time. The partition was **annulled in 1911**, and the capital moved from Calcutta to **Delhi** (announced in 1911).
Differences between the two groups grew, leading to the **Surat Split (1907)**.
points: **Extremist leaders:** Lal-Bal-Pal (Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal) and Aurobindo Ghosh
Tilak's slogan: 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'
Extremists relied on mass action, self-reliance and boycott; Moderates on gradual constitutional reform
**Muslim League** founded in **1906** at Dacca
**Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act, 1909):** introduced **separate electorates** for Muslims

notes.p:
Alongside mainstream politics, revolutionary groups arose: **Anushilan Samiti** and **Jugantar** in Bengal, **Abhinav Bharat** in Maharashtra, and the **Ghadar Party (1913)** in the USA led by Lala Har Dayal.

During World War I, the **Home Rule Leagues** were started in **1916** by **Tilak** (April, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Central Provinces, Berar) and **Annie Besant** (September, rest of India). The **Lucknow Pact (1916)** brought Congress and the Muslim League together, and Moderates and Extremists reunited in the Congress in the same year.

The **Montagu Declaration (August 1917)** promised gradual development of self-governing institutions, leading to the **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919)**, which introduced **dyarchy** in provinces.

Critics say the Moderates were too dependent on British goodwill and failed to involve the masses. Yet they built the **first all-India political platform**, trained Indians in public debate and exposed the economic exploitation of India through writings such as Naoroji's *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India*. The Extremists widened the movement and gave it self-confidence. A balanced Mains answer shows how both phases **prepared the ground** for the mass movements under Gandhi.

Prelims asks about **sessions and presidents**, founders of organisations, the Morley-Minto and Montagu-Chelmsford reforms, and revolutionary groups. Mains GS I may ask you to evaluate the **contribution of Moderates**, the significance of the Swadeshi movement, or the role of revolutionaries in the freedom struggle.
Timeline.
points: 1885: INC founded; first president W.C. Bonnerjee
1905: Partition of Bengal (Curzon) → Swadeshi Movement
1906: Muslim League at Dacca
1907: Surat Split
1909: Morley-Minto Reforms, separate electorates
1911: Partition annulled; capital shift to Delhi announced
1913: Ghadar Party; 1916: Home Rule Leagues and Lucknow Pact
1919: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms — dyarchy in provinces

cards.title: Early experiments
points: **Champaran (1917)** – indigo farmers in Bihar; first civil disobedience in India
**Ahmedabad (1918)** – mill workers' strike; Gandhi's hunger strike
**Kheda (1918)** – peasants seeking revenue remission, with Sardar Patel

cards.title: 1919–1922: mass politics
cards.body: The **Rowlatt Act (1919)** allowed detention without trial. On **13 April 1919** General Dyer's troops fired on a peaceful crowd at **Jallianwala Bagh**, Amritsar. The **Non-Cooperation Movement** (1920–22), merged with the Khilafat cause, was withdrawn after violence at **Chauri Chaura** (February 1922).

cards.title: Towards Purna Swaraj
points: 1927 – Simon Commission appointed (no Indian member); 'Simon Go Back'
Dec 1929 – Lahore Session under Nehru demands **Purna Swaraj**
26 Jan 1930 – first 'Independence Day' celebrated
12 Mar–6 Apr 1930 – **Dandi March** starts Civil Disobedience
1931 – Gandhi-Irwin Pact; Gandhi attends Second Round Table Conference
1932 – Poona Pact (Gandhi–Ambedkar) on depressed classes' representation

cards.title: Final phase
points: 1935 – Government of India Act: provincial autonomy
1942 – Cripps Mission fails; **Quit India** resolution on **8 August 1942** in Bombay; 'Do or Die'
1946 – Cabinet Mission; Constituent Assembly elected
3 June 1947 – Mountbatten Plan for partition
15 August 1947 – Independence under the Indian Independence Act 1947

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Link Gandhi's methods to ethics papers too — satyagraha, non-violence and means-ends purity are frequently quoted in GS IV answers.

cards.q: The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn after:
cards.explain: Violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922, where policemen were killed, led Gandhi to call off the movement.

cards.q: The Purna Swaraj resolution was passed at the Congress session of:
cards.explain: The Lahore Session (December 1929), presided by Jawaharlal Nehru, adopted Purna Swaraj.

cards.q: The Poona Pact (1932) was signed between:
cards.explain: It replaced separate electorates for depressed classes with reserved seats in joint electorates.

notes.p: **Mahatma Gandhi** returned from South Africa in **January 1915**, where he had developed **satyagraha** (truth-force, non-violent resistance). His first experiments in India were local struggles:
points: **Champaran (1917):** indigo farmers in Bihar against the tinkathia system
**Ahmedabad mill strike (1918):** Gandhi used a hunger strike for workers
**Kheda (1918):** peasants in Gujarat seeking revenue remission after crop failure; Sardar Patel joined
**Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919):** against the Rowlatt Act, which allowed detention without trial
**Jallianwala Bagh massacre:** 13 April 1919 at Amritsar, ordered by General Dyer

notes.p: Gandhi turned the national movement into a mass movement.
points: **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22):** linked with the Khilafat issue; boycott of schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth; withdrawn after the **Chauri Chaura** incident (February 1922)
**Swaraj Party (1923):** C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru, to enter councils
**Simon Commission (1927, arrived 1928):** boycotted because it had no Indian member
**Lahore Session (December 1929):** under Jawaharlal Nehru, adopted **Purna Swaraj** as the goal; 26 January 1930 celebrated as Independence Day
**Civil Disobedience Movement (1930):** began with the **Dandi March** (12 March – 6 April 1930)
**Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)** and the **Second Round Table Conference** (Gandhi attended)
**Poona Pact (1932):** Gandhi and Ambedkar; reserved seats for depressed classes within joint electorates instead of separate electorates
**Quit India Movement (August 1942):** 'Do or Die'; launched at Bombay

notes.p: Alongside mass movements, the British introduced reforms.
points: **Government of India Act, 1935:** provincial autonomy, proposed All-India Federation (never formed), federal court, dyarchy at the Centre (not implemented)
**1937 elections:** Congress formed ministries in most provinces; resigned in 1939 over India being dragged into World War II
**August Offer (1940)**, **Cripps Mission (1942)** — Gandhi reportedly called Cripps' offer a 'post-dated cheque'
**INA:** Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army; INA trials (1945) at the Red Fort sparked national sympathy
**Royal Indian Navy mutiny (1946)**
**Cabinet Mission (1946):** proposed a Constituent Assembly and a loose federation
**Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947)** → **Indian Independence Act, 1947** → independence on **15 August 1947**

notes.p: Gandhi's methods brought **peasants, women, workers and students** into politics on a large scale. Non-violence gave the movement moral strength and wide appeal. Critics point to the sudden withdrawal of Non-Cooperation, differences with revolutionaries, and the failure to prevent Partition. A balanced Mains answer should present both sides.

**Satyagraha** means holding firmly to truth. A satyagrahi resists injustice through **non-violence, self-suffering and moral persuasion**, aiming to change the opponent's heart rather than defeat them. Gandhi combined mass struggle (Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience) with constructive work: **khadi, removal of untouchability, Hindu–Muslim unity, village industries and basic education (Nai Talim)**. This mix of struggle and constructive phases is sometimes described by historians as a **'struggle–truce–struggle'** strategy.

Prelims tests **chronology** (which came first), features of the 1935 Act, sessions of Congress, and pacts. Mains GS I asks about the role of **women, peasants or tribals** in the movement, the **evolution of Gandhian strategy**, or the significance of the Quit India Movement.
Timeline to memorise.
points: 1915 return; 1917 Champaran; 1918 Kheda and Ahmedabad
1919 Rowlatt Act; Jallianwala Bagh (13 April)
1920–22 Non-Cooperation; ended after Chauri Chaura
1929 Lahore Session: Purna Swaraj
1930 Dandi March; 1931 Gandhi-Irwin Pact; 1932 Poona Pact
1935 GoI Act: provincial autonomy
1942 Cripps Mission and Quit India
1946 Cabinet Mission; 1947 Mountbatten Plan and Independence

cards.title: The Portuguese
cards.body: **Vasco da Gama** reached **Calicut** in **1498** and was received by the Zamorin. **Francisco de Almeida**, the first viceroy, followed a 'blue water' naval policy. **Afonso de Albuquerque** captured **Goa** from Bijapur in **1510**. The Portuguese controlled sea trade with the **cartaz** (pass) system.

cards.title: The Dutch
cards.body: The Dutch **VOC** (1602) set up a factory at **Masulipatnam** (1605) and focused on spices from Indonesia. They lost to Travancore's **Marthanda Varma** at **Colachel (1741)** and to the English at **Bedara (1759)**.

cards.title: The English
cards.body: The **East India Company** got its charter from Queen Elizabeth I on **31 December 1600**. After **Hawkins** (1608) and **Sir Thomas Roe** (1615) at Jahangir's court, it set up a factory at **Surat** (1613). Key bases: **Madras** (Fort St George, 1639–40), **Bombay** (dowry, 1661), **Calcutta** (1690s).

cards.title: The French
cards.body: The French **Compagnie des Indes Orientales** (1664) founded factories at Surat (1668) and **Pondicherry** (1674). Governor **Dupleix** tried to build influence by backing claimants to thrones in the Carnatic and Hyderabad.

cards.title: Carnatic wars
points: First (1746–48): French victory at Adyar / St Thome; ended by Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle
Second (1749–54): Clive's defence of Arcot (1751); Treaty of Pondicherry
Third (1758–63): Battle of Wandiwash (1760) — Eyre Coote defeated Lally; French power ended

cards.title: Farrukhsiyar's farman
cards.body: In **1717** the Mughal emperor **Farrukhsiyar** granted the English duty-free trade in Bengal for a fixed annual payment, plus rights in Hyderabad and Surat. Historian Orme called it the Company's '**Magna Carta**'; misuse of its **dastaks** angered Bengal's nawabs.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Remember the sequence of arrival: **Portuguese → Dutch → English → Danes → French**. The Danes had bases at **Tranquebar** (Tamil Nadu) and **Serampore** (Bengal), later sold to the English.

cards.q: Goa was captured by the Portuguese in 1510 under:
cards.explain: Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur sultanate.

cards.q: The Battle of Wandiwash (1760) was fought between:
cards.explain: The English under Eyre Coote defeated the French under Lally.

cards.q: The Dutch were defeated at Colachel in 1741 by:
cards.explain: Marthanda Varma of Travancore defeated the Dutch at Colachel.

notes.p: The fall of **Constantinople** to the Ottomans (1453) and Venetian–Arab control of the spice trade encouraged Europeans to seek a **direct sea route** to India. Advances in navigation, shipbuilding and state-backed trading companies made long voyages possible. Pepper, cloves, cinnamon, cotton textiles, indigo and saltpetre were prized commodities.
The Portuguese built a maritime empire rather than a land empire.
points: **1498:** Vasco da Gama at Calicut
**Almeida (1505–09):** fortresses and naval supremacy; defeated a combined fleet at Diu (1509)
**Albuquerque (1509–15):** Goa (1510), Malacca, Hormuz; encouraged Portuguese marriages with local women
Bases: **Goa, Daman, Diu**, Salsette, Bassein, Hooghly, Cochin
Cartaz: licence for Asian ships; ships without it could be seized
Introduced **printing press** at Goa (1556) and crops like tobacco, potato and chillies

notes.p: The **Dutch** built factories at Masulipatnam, Pulicat, Surat, Chinsura, Cochin and Nagapatnam, but preferred the Indonesian spice islands. The **Danes** were minor players. The **English** company gradually outgrew rivals. A grant from a local nayaka under the Vijayanagara (Chandragiri) ruler gave them land for **Madras (1639)**. Charles II received **Bombay** from Portugal as dowry (1661) and leased it to the Company (1668). **Job Charnock**'s settlement and the purchase of three villages (**Sutanuti, Gobindapur, Kalikata**) in 1698 created Calcutta, protected by **Fort William**.

In the 1740s, European wars spilled into India. **Dupleix** showed that small, disciplined European-trained armies could defeat large Indian armies — a lesson the British learnt. In the First Carnatic War the French under Paradis defeated the Nawab of Arcot's army at **Adyar (St Thome)**. In the Second, **Robert Clive**'s defence of **Arcot** (1751) restored English prestige, and Dupleix was recalled (1754). The Third ended with **Wandiwash (1760)** and the fall of Pondicherry (1761). France kept Pondicherry and a few enclaves only as trading posts.

The English company enjoyed advantages: a **powerful navy**, a stable home government, support of the Crown and merchants, and a strong financial base — especially after the **Battle of Plassey (1757)** gave them Bengal's revenues. The French company depended heavily on its state and its directors were less committed to India. Rivalries among Indian rulers allowed Europeans to play one against another.

Questions test chronological order, bases of each power, the cartaz system, and wars or treaties that ended rivalry. A favourite type is 'Consider the following pairs: settlement — European power' (e.g., Tranquebar — Danes; Chinsura — Dutch; Chandernagore — French).

Link this chapter to the next stage: the English used their Bengal base, the 1717 farman and the weakness of the post-Aurangzeb Mughal state to move from trade to territory — **Plassey (1757)** and **Buxar (1764)**, followed by the **Diwani** of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha (1765). Those events are covered in the chapter on the rise of British power. Also note that Portuguese **Goa** was liberated only in **1961**, and French Pondicherry was transferred de facto in **1954**, showing how long European enclaves survived.
Recall.
points: Vasco da Gama 1498, Calicut
Albuquerque took Goa 1510
VOC 1602; Colachel 1741; Bedara 1759
EIC charter 1600; Surat 1613; Madras 1639
French: Pondicherry 1674; Dupleix
Wandiwash 1760 ended French ambitions
Farrukhsiyar's farman 1717

cards.title: Bengal to India
cards.body: Under the **Regulating Act 1773**, **Warren Hastings** became the first **Governor-General of Bengal**. The **Charter Act 1833** made **William Bentinck** the first **Governor-General of India**. After **1858**, the GG was also **Viceroy**; **Canning** was the first.

cards.title: Cornwallis and Wellesley
cards.body: **Cornwallis** (1786–93): **Permanent Settlement** of Bengal (1793), the Cornwallis Code, and organised civil services. **Wellesley** (1798–1805): **Subsidiary Alliance** (Hyderabad first, 1798), defeated **Tipu** in 1799, set up Fort William College (1800).

cards.title: Bentinck's reforms
cards.body: **Abolition of sati** (Regulation XVII, **1829**) with support from Raja Rammohan Roy; suppression of **thuggee**; **English Education Act 1835** following Macaulay's Minute; checks on female infanticide.

cards.title: Dalhousie (1848–56)
cards.body: **Doctrine of Lapse** (Satara 1848, Jhansi 1853, Nagpur 1854, and others); annexed **Punjab** (1849) and **Awadh** (1856, on grounds of misgovernance). First railway **Bombay–Thane (1853)**, telegraph, Post Office Act 1854, Public Works Department, and **Wood's Despatch** (1854).

cards.title: Lytton and Ripon
cards.body: **Lytton**: Delhi Durbar 1877, **Vernacular Press Act 1878**, Arms Act 1878. **Ripon**: repealed the VPA (1882), **resolution on local self-government (1882)**, Hunter Education Commission, first Factory Act (1881), Ilbert Bill controversy (1883).

cards.title: Curzon (1899–1905)
