cards.body: **Partition of Bengal (1905)**, **Indian Universities Act 1904**, **Ancient Monuments Preservation Act 1904**, police and universities commissions, and agricultural research at **Pusa**.

cards.title: Twentieth-century viceroys
points: Minto II — Morley–Minto Reforms 1909
Hardinge II — Delhi Durbar 1911; partition annulled; capital to Delhi
Chelmsford — Montford Reforms 1919, Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala
Irwin — Simon Commission, Gandhi–Irwin Pact 1931
Willingdon — Communal Award, Poona Pact 1932, GoI Act 1935
Linlithgow — August Offer, Cripps Mission, Quit India
Wavell — Shimla Conference 1945; Mountbatten — 3 June Plan 1947

cards.q: The first Governor-General of India was:
cards.explain: The Charter Act of 1833 designated Bentinck as Governor-General of India.

cards.q: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was repealed by:
cards.explain: Ripon repealed it in 1882.

cards.q: Which Governor-General introduced the Subsidiary Alliance?
cards.explain: Lord Wellesley introduced it; Hyderabad was the first to accept (1798).

notes.p: UPSC often frames modern history around **who did what when**. Learning administrators in sequence gives a skeleton on which wars, reforms and movements hang. Focus on the major figures rather than every holder of the office.
Key Governors-General and their landmarks:
points: **Warren Hastings (1773–85):** dual government ended (1772); Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774); Asiatic Society founded by **William Jones** (1784) with his support; First Anglo-Maratha War (Treaty of Salbai 1782); later impeached in Britain, but acquitted
**Cornwallis (1786–93):** Permanent Settlement; separation of revenue and judicial work; Third Anglo-Mysore War (Treaty of Seringapatam 1792)
**Wellesley (1798–1805):** Subsidiary Alliance; Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799); Second Anglo-Maratha War
**Lord Hastings (1813–23):** Third Anglo-Maratha War; Peshwaship abolished (1818); Pindaris suppressed
**Bentinck (1828–35):** sati, thuggee, English education
**Dalhousie (1848–56):** lapse, railways, telegraph, Punjab and Awadh annexed

notes.p:
**Canning** (1856–62) handled the Revolt of 1857, saw the **universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** founded (1857), the **Indian Penal Code** (1860) and the **Indian Councils Act 1861**. **Mayo** (1869–72) began financial decentralisation (1870) and a census attempt (1872); he was assassinated in the Andamans. **Ripon** (1880–84) is called the 'father of local self-government'; the first **synchronous census** took place in 1881. The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 during **Dufferin**'s tenure. **Lansdowne** saw the Indian Councils Act 1892 and the **Durand Line** (1893).

**Curzon**'s partition of Bengal triggered the Swadeshi movement. Later viceroys presided over the constitutional reforms and national movement phases covered in other chapters. **Mountbatten** was the last Viceroy and first Governor-General of independent India; **C. Rajagopalachari** was the only Indian Governor-General.

Group by theme instead of memorising a list:
- **Press**: Metcalfe freed the press (1835) → Lytton gagged it (1878) → Ripon freed it (1882).
- **Education**: Bentinck (1835 Act) → Dalhousie (Wood's Despatch 1854) → Canning (universities 1857) → Ripon (Hunter Commission) → Curzon (Universities Act 1904).
- **Annexation**: Wellesley (alliances) → Hastings (Maratha territories) → Dalhousie (lapse and misgovernance).

Typical questions: 'With reference to the period of X, consider the following statements', or chronological ordering of Acts. Be careful with close calls — e.g., the **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act** was enacted in July **1856**, in **Canning**'s early tenure, though often linked with Dalhousie's era.
Recall.
points: Warren Hastings — first GG of Bengal (1773)
Bentinck — first GG of India (1833); sati abolished 1829
Canning — first Viceroy (1858)
Cornwallis — Permanent Settlement 1793
Wellesley — Subsidiary Alliance
Dalhousie — Doctrine of Lapse, railways 1853
Ripon — local self-government 1882; Curzon — Bengal partition 1905

cards.title: Why reform began
cards.body: Western education, the printing press, Christian missionary critiques and a new **rational, humanist** outlook led Indian thinkers to re-examine customs such as **sati, child marriage, caste rigidity, purdah** and the ban on widow remarriage. Most reformers argued from both reason and ancient scripture.

cards.title: Raja Rammohan Roy
cards.body: Called the 'father of the Indian Renaissance'. Founded the **Atmiya Sabha (1815)** and the **Brahmo Sabha (1828)**, later the **Brahmo Samaj**. Campaigned against **sati**, supporting its abolition (1829), and backed modern education and press freedom.

cards.title: Bengal after Rammohan
cards.body: **Debendranath Tagore** — Tattvabodhini Sabha (1839). **Keshab Chandra Sen** — Brahmo Samaj of India (1866), Native Marriage Act 1872. **Henry Derozio** — Young Bengal. **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** — **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856**, girls' education.

cards.title: Western India
cards.body: **Prarthana Samaj** (1867, Bombay; Atmaram Pandurang, M.G. Ranade). **Jyotiba Phule** — **Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)**, book **Gulamgiri**, girls' school in Pune with **Savitribai Phule** (1848). **Gopal Hari Deshmukh 'Lokhitwadi'** wrote on social reform.

cards.title: Revivalist-reform movements
cards.body: **Arya Samaj** (1875, Bombay) by **Dayanand Saraswati** — 'Back to the Vedas', **Satyarth Prakash**, shuddhi, DAV schools. **Ramakrishna Mission** (1897) by **Swami Vivekananda** — social service. **Theosophical Society** (1875, New York; HQ at Adyar) — Annie Besant.

cards.title: Muslim, Sikh and Parsi reform
cards.body: **Aligarh movement** — Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, **MAO College 1875** (Aligarh Muslim University from 1920). **Deoband** (1866) — orthodox seminary. **Singh Sabha** (1873) and **Akali movement** for Sikhs. **Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha** (1851) for Parsis.

cards.title: Anti-caste movements in the south
cards.body: **Sree Narayana Guru** — SNDP Yogam (1903), 'one caste, one religion, one God for man'. **E.V. Ramasamy 'Periyar'** — Self-Respect Movement (1925). **Vaikom Satyagraha** (1924–25) for access to temple roads. **Ayyankali** fought for Dalit rights in Travancore.

cards.q: The Satyashodhak Samaj was founded by:
cards.explain: Jyotiba Phule founded it in 1873.

cards.q: Satyarth Prakash was written by:
cards.explain: Dayanand Saraswati, founder of the Arya Samaj.

cards.q: The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856) is most associated with the efforts of:
cards.explain: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar campaigned for it.

notes.p: The 19th century saw a cultural awakening often called the **Indian Renaissance**. It had two broad strands:
points: **Reformist**: used reason and humanism to change society (Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj, Aligarh movement)
**Revivalist**: sought to restore what was seen as a purer ancient tradition (Arya Samaj, Deoband)
Both strands challenged ritualism, superstition and priestly dominance to varying degrees
Their impact was mostly among the **urban educated classes** at first

notes.p:
**Rammohan Roy** (1772–1833) believed in monotheism and opposed idol worship. He wrote **Precepts of Jesus**, ran the Persian newspaper **Mirat-ul-Akhbar** and the Bengali **Sambad Kaumudi**, and founded **Vedanta College** (1825). The Brahmo movement later split: Keshab Chandra Sen's group pushed radical reforms; when Keshab married his minor daughter in 1878, dissenters formed the **Sadharan Brahmo Samaj**.

**Young Bengal**, inspired by Derozio at Hindu College, attacked orthodoxy with radical ideas. **Vidyasagar** used scriptural arguments for widow remarriage and simplified Bengali education with Barna Parichay.

In Maharashtra the **Paramahansa Mandali** (1849) and **Prarthana Samaj** (1867) promoted inter-dining, widow remarriage and women's education. **Jyotiba Phule** offered the most radical critique of caste and brahmanical dominance. **Pandita Ramabai** worked for widows (Sharada Sadan). The **Arya Samaj** became strong in Punjab and western UP, combining Vedic revival with campaigns against idolatry, untouchability and child marriage.

Reform campaigns produced legislation:
1. Abolition of **sati** — Bengal Regulation XVII, **1829** (Bentinck).
2. **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856**.
3. **Native Marriage Act, 1872** — civil marriage for Brahmos; set minimum ages.
4. **Age of Consent Act, 1891** — campaign by **B.M. Malabari**; opposed by Tilak as interference.
5. **Child Marriage Restraint (Sarda) Act, 1929** — minimum age 14 for girls and 18 for boys.

Laws were often weakly enforced, showing the limits of legal reform without social change.

**Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** urged Muslims to embrace modern scientific education and loyalty to the British; his journal was **Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq**. **Deoband** (founded by Muhammad Qasim Nanotvi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi) stressed religious learning and opposed British rule. The **Ahmadiyya** movement (1889) was founded by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad. Among Sikhs, the Akali movement led to the **Sikh Gurdwaras Act 1925**, placing gurdwaras under the SGPC.

Expect questions on founders, years, books and journals, and ideas (for example, 'which organisation opposed idol worship'). Cross-link with the national movement: reformers built confidence and a public sphere that nationalism later used. Treat statements such as 'all reform movements were anti-British' with caution — many were not political at all.

Women reformers deserve separate attention: **Savitribai Phule** (often called India's first woman teacher of the modern era), **Pandita Ramabai**, **Tarabai Shinde** (Stri Purush Tulana, 1882) and **Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain** (Sultana's Dream) questioned patriarchy directly.
Recall.
points: Atmiya Sabha 1815; Brahmo Sabha 1828
Sati abolished 1829; widow remarriage 1856
Prarthana Samaj 1867; Satyashodhak 1873
Arya Samaj 1875; Ramakrishna Mission 1897
Theosophical Society 1875; Adyar
MAO College 1875; Deoband 1866
SNDP 1903; Self-Respect 1925; Vaikom 1924–25

cards.title: Early civil and tribal uprisings
cards.body: **Sanyasi–Fakir** revolt (late 18th century, Bengal); **Paika rebellion** (1817, Odisha, Bakshi Jagabandhu); **Kol** rising (1831–32); **Santhal Hul** (1855–56, Sidhu and Kanhu); **Munda Ulgulan** (1899–1900, Birsa Munda); **Rampa** rebellion (1922–24, Alluri Sitarama Raju).

cards.title: Peasant movements before Gandhi
cards.body: **Indigo revolt** (1859–60, Bengal; play **Nil Darpan** by Dinabandhu Mitra). **Pabna** agrarian league (1873–76) against zamindars. **Deccan riots** (1875) against moneylenders, leading to the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879).

cards.title: Gandhian-era peasant struggles
cards.body: **Champaran** (1917, indigo/tinkathia system), **Kheda** (1918, revenue remission), **Bardoli** (1928, Vallabhbhai Patel earned the title 'Sardar'). **Awadh Kisan Sabha** (1920) and the **Eka** movement. **Mappila** uprising (1921, Malabar).

cards.title: Organised kisan politics
cards.body: The **All India Kisan Sabha** was formed at **Lucknow in 1936** with **Swami Sahajanand Saraswati** as president. Late struggles: **Tebhaga** (1946, Bengal — sharecroppers demanded two-thirds of the crop) and **Telangana** (1946–51, against Nizam's feudal order).

cards.title: First phase of revolutionaries
cards.body: **Chapekar brothers** (1897, Poona); **Anushilan Samiti** and **Jugantar** (Bengal); **Abhinav Bharat** (V.D. Savarkar). **Khudiram Bose** and **Prafulla Chaki** (1908, Muzaffarpur). Abroad: **India House** (London), the **Ghadar Party** (1913, San Francisco; Lala Hardayal).

cards.title: Second phase
cards.body: **Hindustan Republican Association** (1924) → **Kakori** train action (1925). Reorganised as **HSRA** (1928) under **Chandrashekhar Azad** and **Bhagat Singh**. Assembly bomb (1929) by Bhagat Singh and **B.K. Dutt**; hanged on 23 March 1931 with Rajguru and Sukhdev. **Chittagong armoury raid** (1930) led by **Surya Sen**.

cards.title: INA and 1946
cards.body: The **Indian National Army**, first raised under **Mohan Singh**, was led by **Subhas Chandra Bose** from 1943; he proclaimed the **Provisional Government of Free India** in Singapore (October 1943). The **INA trials** at the Red Fort (1945) and the **Royal Indian Navy mutiny** (Bombay, February 1946) stirred the country.

cards.q: Birsa Munda's movement is known as:
cards.explain: The Munda 'Ulgulan' (great tumult) of 1899–1900.

cards.q: The All India Kisan Sabha was founded in 1936 at:
cards.explain: It was formed at Lucknow with Swami Sahajanand Saraswati as president.

cards.q: The Chittagong armoury raid (1930) was led by:
cards.explain: Surya Sen ('Masterda') led the raid.

notes.h: Why rural and tribal India rose
notes.p: Colonial rule disrupted agrarian and forest life. High **land revenue**, new **landlords and moneylenders**, **commercial crops** under coercion (indigo), loss of **forest rights** under forest laws, and outsiders (dikus) entering tribal areas created anger. Movements were often local and short-lived but showed deep resistance; many later merged into the national movement.
Tribal resistance was rooted in land and forest rights:
points: **Santhal Hul (1855–56):** against zamindars, moneylenders and police in the Rajmahal hills; led to creation of the Santhal Parganas
**Munda Ulgulan:** Birsa Munda attacked the breakdown of the **khuntkatti** (communal land) system; the **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908** followed
**Rampa rebellion:** Alluri Sitarama Raju in the Godavari agency against forest restrictions
**Tana Bhagat** (Oraon, from 1914): later linked with Gandhian ideas
**Rani Gaidinliu** (Naga): resisted British rule in the 1930s; Nehru called her 'Rani'

notes.p: The **Indigo revolt** saw peasants refuse to grow indigo under unfair contracts; the Indigo Commission (1860) followed. The **Pabna** movement was largely legal and non-violent, and contributed to the **Bengal Tenancy Act 1885**. Under Gandhi's leadership, local satyagrahas in **Champaran, Kheda** and **Bardoli** won concessions and mobilised peasants for the Congress. From the 1930s, socialists and communists organised kisan sabhas; the Kisan Manifesto demanded the abolition of zamindari.

Disillusionment with moderate politics, the **partition of Bengal**, and repression led some youth to armed action. Early groups relied on individual action and secret societies. The **Alipore bomb case** (1908) put **Aurobindo Ghose** on trial; he was acquitted. The **Ghadar** movement planned an uprising in 1915 that failed; the **Komagata Maru** incident (1914) radicalised Punjabi migrants.

After the **Non-Cooperation Movement** was withdrawn (1922), revolutionaries regrouped. HSRA, under Bhagat Singh's influence, adopted **socialism** as a goal. Bhagat Singh's trial statements and the slogan 'Inquilab Zindabad' made him a national hero. Women such as **Pritilata Waddedar** and **Kalpana Dutt** took part in Bengal.

Revolutionaries did not overthrow British rule, but they **inspired** many, kept anti-colonial spirit alive, and showed courage that the public admired. Peasant and tribal movements broadened nationalism's social base and pushed issues like **land reform** onto the agenda of independent India. The INA and naval mutiny of 1945–46 showed the British that the loyalty of Indian armed forces could no longer be assumed.

Questions usually pair a movement with its leader, region or demand, or ask which statements about an organisation are correct. Watch for close distractors: **Hul** (Santhal) vs **Ulgulan** (Munda); **HRA** (1924) vs **HSRA** (1928); **Tebhaga** (Bengal) vs **Telangana** (Hyderabad).

Also keep apart the religious-tinged movements: the **Wahabi** movement of Syed Ahmad of Rae Bareli, the **Faraizi** movement of Haji Shariatullah in Bengal, and the **Kuka (Namdhari)** movement of Ram Singh in Punjab.
Recall.
points: Santhal Hul 1855–56; Munda Ulgulan 1899–1900
Indigo revolt 1859–60; Pabna 1873–76; Deccan riots 1875
Champaran 1917, Kheda 1918, Bardoli 1928
AIKS 1936, Lucknow
Ghadar 1913; Kakori 1925; HSRA 1928

cards.title: Government of India Act 1858
cards.body: Ended Company rule; power passed to the **Crown**. Created the **Secretary of State for India** with a 15-member **Council of India**. The Governor-General became the **Viceroy**. Abolished the Board of Control and Court of Directors (ending **double government**).

cards.title: Councils Acts 1861 and 1892
cards.body: **1861**: Indians nominated as non-official members of the legislative council; **portfolio system** legalised; legislative powers restored to Bombay and Madras; Viceroy could issue **ordinances**. **1892**: members could discuss the budget and ask questions; an **indirect** (nomination on recommendation) method introduced.

cards.title: Morley–Minto Reforms 1909
cards.body: Enlarged legislative councils; members could ask **supplementary questions** and move resolutions on the budget. Introduced **separate electorates for Muslims** — Minto is called the 'father of communal electorate'. **S.P. Sinha** became the first Indian on the Viceroy's Executive Council.

cards.title: Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms 1919
cards.body: **Dyarchy** in provinces: 'transferred' subjects under Indian ministers; 'reserved' subjects under the Governor. **Bicameral** central legislature with **direct elections** on a limited franchise. Separate electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans. Provided for a **Public Service Commission** (set up 1926).

cards.title: Government of India Act 1935
cards.body: Proposed an **All-India Federation** (never formed). **Provincial autonomy** replaced provincial dyarchy; **dyarchy at the centre** (not implemented). **Three lists** — Federal, Provincial, Concurrent; residuary powers with the Viceroy. **Federal Court** (1937). Council of India abolished. Burma separated.

cards.title: Road to 1947
points: August Offer 1940 (Linlithgow)
Cripps Mission 1942 — dominion status after the war
Wavell Plan / Shimla Conference 1945
Cabinet Mission 1946 — Constituent Assembly, three groups of provinces
Attlee's statement, 20 February 1947
Mountbatten (3 June) Plan 1947 → Indian Independence Act 1947

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: The Constitution of India borrowed heavily from the **1935 Act**: federal scheme, office of Governor, emergency provisions, public service commissions and the judiciary's structure. Expect cross-linking questions with Polity.

cards.q: Dyarchy at the provincial level was introduced by the:
cards.explain: The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in provinces; the 1935 Act replaced it with provincial autonomy.

cards.q: Separate electorates for Muslims were first introduced in:
cards.explain: The Morley–Minto Reforms of 1909.

cards.q: Which body did the Government of India Act 1935 establish in 1937?
cards.explain: The Federal Court was set up in 1937 under the 1935 Act.

notes.p: After the Revolt of 1857, Queen Victoria's **Proclamation (1 November 1858)**, read at Allahabad by Canning, promised religious tolerance, respect for treaties with princes, and equal access to public office. The **Government of India Act 1858** centralised control in London through the Secretary of State. The **Indian Civil Services Act 1861** and the **Indian Councils Act 1861** started the gradual and limited association of Indians with law-making.

Each Act added a little more representation while keeping real power with the British.

1. **1861** — Indians nominated (e.g., Raja of Benares, Maharaja of Patiala, Sir Dinkar Rao).
2. **1892** — budget discussion and questions; members nominated on the recommendation of bodies such as universities and municipalities.
3. **1909** — elections (indirect), separate Muslim electorates, supplementary questions.
4. **1919** — direct elections, dyarchy, bicameral centre, separate budgets for centre and provinces (from 1921).
5. **1935** — provincial autonomy, wider franchise (about a tenth of the population), federal structure on paper.

**Montagu's August Declaration (1917)** promised 'progressive realisation of responsible government'. The 1919 Act disappointed nationalists. The all-white **Simon Commission** (1927) was boycotted ('Simon go back'); Indians replied with the **Nehru Report (1928)**, which asked for dominion status and a list of fundamental rights. Three **Round Table Conferences** (1930–32) followed; Gandhi attended only the second (1931) after the **Gandhi–Irwin Pact**. The **Communal Award (1932)** of Ramsay MacDonald gave separate electorates to depressed classes; Gandhi's fast led to the **Poona Pact** (September 1932), which instead reserved seats for them within joint electorates.

Elections under the Act were held in **1937**; Congress formed ministries in most provinces and resigned in **1939** when Britain declared India a party to the Second World War without consulting Indians. The federation never materialised because princely states did not join. Yet the Act became a **blueprint** for the Constitution — its schedules, lists and emergency provisions appear in modified form today.

The **Cripps Mission (1942)** offered dominion status after the war and the right of provinces to stay out — rejected by the Congress. The **Cabinet Mission (1946)** proposed a united India with a weak centre, provincial groupings and a **Constituent Assembly** elected indirectly by provincial assemblies. An **Interim Government** under Nehru was formed in **September 1946**. Communal violence and political deadlock led to **Attlee's announcement** that Britain would leave by June 1948, and Mountbatten's **3 June Plan** for partition. The **Indian Independence Act 1947** created two dominions — India and Pakistan — from **15 August 1947**, and made the Constituent Assemblies sovereign.

Questions focus on 'which Act introduced X' (portfolio system, dyarchy, separate electorates, Federal Court, bicameralism, PSC). A worked example: 'The Act that first provided for a Public Service Commission in India' — the **1919 Act** (the Commission came up in 1926 on the Lee Commission's recommendation). Another: 'Provincial autonomy' — **1935**, not 1919.
Recall.
points: 1858: Crown rule, Secretary of State, Viceroy
1861: portfolio system; Indians nominated; ordinances
1892: budget discussion
1909: separate electorates; S.P. Sinha
1919: dyarchy in provinces; bicameral centre
1935: provincial autonomy; three lists; Federal Court
1946: Cabinet Mission; 1947: Independence Act

cards.title: Challenges in 1947
points: Partition violence and refugee rehabilitation
Integrating hundreds of **princely states**
Framing the Constitution and holding elections
Economic backwardness, food scarcity
Linguistic and regional demands

cards.title: Integration of princely states
cards.body: **Sardar Patel** and **V.P. Menon** persuaded most rulers to sign the **Instrument of Accession** before 15 August 1947. Exceptions: **Junagadh** (plebiscite, 1948), **Hyderabad** (police action, "Operation Polo", September 1948) and **Jammu & Kashmir** (accession in October 1947 amid tribal invasion).

cards.title: Linguistic reorganisation
points: Dhar Commission and JVP Committee (1948) cautious
Potti Sriramulu's death after fast → **Andhra State (1953)**
**States Reorganisation Commission** (Fazl Ali, Kunzru, Panikkar)
**States Reorganisation Act, 1956**
Bombay split into Maharashtra and Gujarat (1960); Punjab–Haryana (1966)

cards.title: Later reorganisation
points: Nagaland (1963)
North-East reorganisation (1971–72)
Sikkim joins (1975)
Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand (2000)
Telangana (2014)
J&K reorganised into two UTs (2019)

cards.title: French and Portuguese enclaves
cards.body: Pondicherry and other French possessions came to India by agreement (de facto 1954, formally 1962). **Goa, Daman and Diu** were liberated by military action in **1961**; Dadra and Nagar Haveli had been freed earlier by local action.

cards.title: Nation-building pillars
points: First general elections (1951–52)
Planning Commission (1950) and Five-Year Plans
Land reforms, community development
Non-alignment in foreign policy
Tribal policy based on Nehru's Panchsheel and Verrier Elwin's ideas

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Mains questions on this period test evaluation: "Was linguistic reorganisation a threat or a strength for national unity?" Argue that accommodating identity strengthened unity.

cards.q: "Operation Polo" (1948) refers to the integration of:
cards.explain: The police action brought Hyderabad into the Indian Union.

cards.q: Which state was the first to be formed on a linguistic basis (1953)?
cards.explain: Andhra State was formed in 1953 after Potti Sriramulu's fast unto death.

notes.p: At independence India faced Partition's violence and the arrival of millions of refugees, the integration of princely states covering a large part of the territory, the need for a Constitution and democratic institutions, and deep poverty. Historians like **Bipan Chandra** describe the first two decades as a period of **nation-building**: territorial integration, political institutionalisation and planned development.

When British paramountcy lapsed, princely states could in theory join India, Pakistan or remain independent. The States Department under **Sardar Patel**, with **V.P. Menon** as secretary, used persuasion, the appeal of patriotism and the prospect of privy purses to secure accession on defence, external affairs and communications through the **Instrument of Accession**, followed by merger agreements.

Hard cases: **Junagadh** (ruler acceded to Pakistan; a plebiscite in 1948 confirmed joining India), **Hyderabad** (Nizam sought independence; integrated after police action in September 1948) and **Kashmir** (Maharaja acceded in October 1947 after a tribal invasion backed by Pakistan; the issue went to the UN). The **privy purses** were later abolished by the **26th Amendment (1971)**.

The Congress had accepted linguistic provinces in principle since 1920, but after Partition leaders feared further division. The **Dhar Commission** and the **JVP Committee** (Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya) in 1948 advised caution. The death of **Potti Sriramulu** after a fast in 1952 forced the creation of **Andhra State (1953)**.

The **States Reorganisation Commission** (Fazl Ali, H.N. Kunzru, K.M. Panikkar) reported in 1955, leading to the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956**, which reorganised states largely on linguistic lines and abolished the old Part A/B/C classification. Further changes followed: Maharashtra and Gujarat (1960), Nagaland (1963), Punjab and Haryana (1966), the North-East reorganisation (1971–72), Sikkim (1975), three new states in 2000, Telangana (2014) and the reorganisation of J&K into two Union Territories (2019).

Fears that linguistic states would lead to disintegration proved largely unfounded. Language-based states brought administration closer to people, strengthened regional cultures and **deepened democracy**. However, issues remain: inter-state border disputes (e.g. Belagavi), river-water disputes, and the position of linguistic minorities within states. Later states were created on grounds of **development and administrative convenience** (Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Telangana), not only language.

**Democracy:** the first general elections (1951–52) under universal adult franchise succeeded despite low literacy. **Economy:** the Planning Commission (1950), Five-Year Plans emphasising heavy industry (Mahalanobis model), land reforms and community development. **Society:** Hindu Code Bills reforming personal law, abolition of untouchability, reservation. **Foreign policy:** non-alignment, Panchsheel with China (1954). **Challenges:** the 1962 war with China, wars with Pakistan (1965, 1971), food crises leading to the **Green Revolution**, and the **Emergency (1975–77)**, which tested and ultimately reaffirmed democratic institutions.
Key points.
points: Patel and V.P. Menon: Instrument of Accession
Junagadh plebiscite, Hyderabad (Operation Polo, 1948), Kashmir (Oct 1947)
Privy purses abolished by 26th Amendment (1971)
Andhra State 1953; SRC (Fazl Ali); SR Act 1956
Goa liberated 1961; Pondicherry formally 1962; Sikkim 1975
New states 2000 and Telangana 2014; J&K UTs 2019
Linguistic states strengthened, not weakened, unity

cards.title: Harappan Civilisation
cards.body: A Bronze Age urban culture (mature phase roughly 2600–1900 BCE) known for planned cities, grid streets, covered drains and standard weights. Its script is still undeciphered.
points: Harappa (Ravi) – excavated by Daya Ram Sahni, 1921
Mohenjo-daro (Indus) – R.D. Banerji, 1922; Great Bath
Lothal (Gujarat) – dockyard
Dholavira (Gujarat) – water management; UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021)

cards.title: Vedic Age
cards.body: The **Rigveda** is the oldest Veda. The Early Vedic people were mainly pastoral, with assemblies called **sabha** and **samiti**. In the Later Vedic period, agriculture expanded, the varna system became more rigid and kingdoms grew larger.

cards.title: Buddhism and Jainism
points: Gautama Buddha – enlightenment at Bodh Gaya; first sermon at **Sarnath** (Dharmachakra Pravartana); died at Kushinagar
Mahavira – the **24th Tirthankara** of Jainism
Both rejected Vedic ritualism and spoke in people's languages (Pali, Prakrit)

cards.title: Mauryas and Guptas
cards.body: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan empire; Kautilya's **Arthashastra** discusses statecraft. **Ashoka** turned to Dhamma after the Kalinga war; his edicts are mostly in Prakrit, in **Brahmi** script (Kharosthi in the north-west). The **Gupta age** saw Aryabhata in astronomy and Kalidasa in literature.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Ancient history in Prelims is now mostly culture-linked: Buddhist sites, terms (Tirthankara, Bodhisattva), inscriptions and scripts. Focus on these rather than dynasty lists.

cards.q: Which Harappan site has a dockyard?
cards.explain: Lothal in Gujarat has a structure widely identified as a dockyard.

cards.q: Buddha delivered his first sermon at:
cards.explain: The first sermon was at Sarnath near Varanasi; enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, birth at Lumbini, death at Kushinagar.

notes.p: The **Indus Valley (Harappan) civilisation** flourished roughly in **2600–1900 BCE** (mature phase). It was a **Bronze Age** urban culture known for planned towns, grid streets, covered drains, baked bricks and standard weights.
points: **Harappa** (Punjab, Pakistan) — first site excavated (1921, Daya Ram Sahni)
**Mohenjo-daro** (Sindh) — Great Bath; bronze 'Dancing Girl'
**Lothal** (Gujarat) — dockyard
**Kalibangan** (Rajasthan) — ploughed field, fire altars
**Dholavira** (Gujarat) — water management; a UNESCO World Heritage Site
**Rakhigarhi** (Haryana) — one of the largest sites
The Harappan script has **not been deciphered**

notes.p: The **Early Vedic (Rig Vedic)** period (around 1500–1000 BCE) was centred in the Sapta Sindhu region; society was pastoral, and cattle were wealth. The **Later Vedic** period (around 1000–600 BCE) saw agriculture, iron use, bigger kingdoms and a rigid varna system.
points: Four Vedas: Rig, Sama, Yajur, Atharva
Assemblies: **sabha** and **samiti**
'Satyameva Jayate' comes from the **Mundaka Upanishad**
The Gayatri Mantra appears in the Rig Veda

notes.p:
By the 6th century BCE, there were **16 Mahajanapadas**; **Magadha** became the strongest under the Haryanka, Shishunaga and Nanda dynasties.

**Gautama Buddha** (born at Lumbini) taught the **Four Noble Truths** and the **Eightfold Path**, gave his first sermon at **Sarnath** and attained parinirvana at **Kushinagar**. **Vardhamana Mahavira**, the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism, taught **ahimsa** and the five vows; the **triratna** of Jainism are right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.
points: Buddhist councils: Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra (under Ashoka), Kashmir (under Kanishka)
Buddhist texts were written in **Pali**; Jain texts in **Prakrit**

notes.p:
The **Mauryan Empire** was founded by **Chandragupta Maurya** (around 321 BCE) with the help of **Kautilya** (author of the *Arthashastra*). **Ashoka** adopted Buddhism after the **Kalinga War** (around 261 BCE) and spread his policy of **Dhamma** through rock and pillar edicts, mostly in **Brahmi** script. Megasthenes wrote *Indica*.

The **Gupta age** (from about 320 CE) is often called a classical age: **Aryabhata** in mathematics and astronomy, **Kalidasa** in literature, and temple architecture's beginnings. In the south, the **Sangam age** saw the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas.
points: Sarnath Lion Capital (Ashokan) is India's national emblem
Fa-Hien, a Chinese pilgrim, visited during Chandragupta II's reign

notes.p: Historians use two kinds of sources to rebuild the past.
points: **Literary sources:** Vedas, Upanishads, epics, Puranas, Buddhist Jatakas, Jain texts, Sangam literature, Kautilya's *Arthashastra*
**Foreign accounts:** Megasthenes (*Indica*), Fa-Hien, Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang, during Harshavardhana's time)
**Archaeological sources:** inscriptions (Ashoka's edicts were deciphered by **James Prinsep** in 1837), coins, monuments, pottery
Inscriptions on stone or copper plates are among the most reliable dated sources

notes.p: Prelims asks about **Harappan sites and features**, Buddhist and Jain concepts, Ashokan edicts, and terms from ancient texts. Questions often use pair-matching of 'site – feature' or 'term – meaning'. Mains GS I asks about the **salient features** of art, architecture and literature from ancient times.
Points to remember.
points: Harappan mature phase ~2600–1900 BCE; script undeciphered
Lothal dockyard; Dholavira water system; Kalibangan ploughed field
Satyameva Jayate: Mundaka Upanishad
Buddha: Lumbini (birth), Bodh Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon), Kushinagar (death)
Mahavira: 24th Tirthankara
Chandragupta Maurya + Kautilya; Ashoka's Dhamma after Kalinga
Gupta age: Aryabhata, Kalidasa

cards.title: Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)
cards.body: Began with **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** and ended when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi. Five dynasties ruled: Mamluk (Slave), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi. **Alauddin Khalji** is known for market price control; **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** for token currency and shifting the capital to Daulatabad.

cards.title: The Mughals
points: Babur won the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)**
**Akbar** – mansabdari system, policy of Sulh-i-kul, Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri
Shah Jahan – Taj Mahal, Red Fort
Aurangzeb – largest territorial extent; reimposed jizya

cards.title: Vijayanagara Empire
cards.body: Founded in **1336** by **Harihara and Bukka**. Under **Krishnadevaraya** it reached its peak; he wrote the Telugu work Amuktamalyada. Its capital Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The empire declined after the **Battle of Talikota (1565)**.

cards.title: Bhakti and Sufi movements
cards.body: Both stressed personal devotion over ritual and caste.
points: Bhakti: Kabir, Guru Nanak, Mirabai, Tulsidas, Chaitanya; earlier the Alvars and Nayanars in Tamil Nadu
Sufi: Chishti order – Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi)

cards.q: The First Battle of Panipat (1526) was fought between:
cards.explain: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, ending the Delhi Sultanate and founding Mughal rule.

cards.q: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded by:
cards.explain: Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty founded it in 1336.

notes.p: Five dynasties ruled from Delhi: **Slave (Mamluk), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi**.
points: **Qutb-ud-din Aibak:** founder; began the Qutub Minar
**Iltutmish:** completed Qutub Minar; introduced the silver **tanka** and copper **jital**; organised the **iqta** system
**Razia Sultan:** first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate
**Alauddin Khalji:** market control reforms; resisted Mongol invasions
**Muhammad bin Tughlaq:** shifted the capital to Daulatabad; token currency experiment
**Firoz Shah Tughlaq:** canals and public works
**Ibrahim Lodi:** defeated by Babur at the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)**

notes.p:
In the south, the **Vijayanagara Empire** was founded in **1336** by **Harihara and Bukka**. Its greatest ruler, **Krishnadevaraya** (Tuluva dynasty), wrote the Telugu work *Amuktamalyada*. The capital **Hampi** is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The empire was weakened after the **Battle of Talikota (1565)** against the Deccan Sultanates.

The **Bahmani kingdom** was founded in 1347; **Mahmud Gawan** was its noted minister.
Major rulers and their contributions.
points: **Babur:** founder after Panipat (1526)
**Humayun:** lost to **Sher Shah Suri**, who introduced the silver **rupiya** and improved roads (e.g. Grand Trunk Road)
**Akbar:** **Mansabdari** system, **Sulh-i-kul** (peace with all), **Din-i-Ilahi**, land revenue system (Zabt/Dahsala) with Raja Todar Mal; built Fatehpur Sikri
**Jahangir:** Mughal painting flourished
**Shah Jahan:** Taj Mahal, Red Fort in Delhi, Peacock Throne
**Aurangzeb:** largest territorial extent; reimposed jizya; died in 1707

notes.p: Medieval India saw devotional movements that crossed caste and religious lines.
points: **Bhakti in the south:** Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva)
**Ramanuja** (Vishishtadvaita), **Kabir**, **Ravidas**, **Mirabai**, **Tulsidas**, **Chaitanya**
**Guru Nanak:** founder of Sikhism
**Sufi silsilas:** Chishti (Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi), Suhrawardi
Both movements used **local languages** and stressed love, devotion and equality

notes.p: Medieval rulers developed systems of revenue and military organisation that shaped later Indian administration.
points: **Iqta:** land revenue assignments given to officers in return for military and administrative service (Delhi Sultanate)
**Mansabdari:** under Akbar, every officer held a **mansab** (rank) with two parts — **zat** (personal rank) and **sawar** (number of cavalry to maintain)
**Jagir:** revenue assignment given in place of salary; frequent transfers prevented local power bases
**Zabt / Dahsala system:** revenue fixed on the average produce and prices of the past ten years, developed with **Raja Todar Mal**
**Amara-nayaka system:** in Vijayanagara, military commanders (nayakas) were given territories to govern
Persian was the court language; regional languages and Urdu developed in this period
Towns, crafts and trade grew; Indian textiles were in demand across Asia and Europe

notes.p: Prelims often asks about **administrative terms** (iqta, mansab, jagir), Bhakti and Sufi saints and their teachings, and architectural features. Mains GS I may ask about the **cultural synthesis** of the medieval period, or the role of Bhakti and Sufi movements in society.
Key anchors.
points: Delhi Sultanate: Slave → Khalji → Tughlaq → Sayyid → Lodi
Iltutmish: tanka and jital; iqta system
Vijayanagara founded 1336; Krishnadevaraya; Talikota 1565
Panipat I (1526): Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi
Sher Shah: rupiya; Akbar: mansabdari, Sulh-i-kul
Shah Jahan: Taj Mahal; Aurangzeb died 1707
Chishti silsila: Ajmer; Guru Nanak: Sikhism

cards.title: Temple architecture styles
points: **Nagara** – North India; curvilinear shikhara (e.g. Khajuraho, Konark)
**Dravida** – South India; pyramidal vimana and large gopurams (e.g. Brihadeeswara, Thanjavur)
**Vesara** – mix of both; Chalukya and Hoysala temples in the Deccan

cards.title: Classical dances
cards.body: The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises eight classical dance forms.
points: Bharatanatyam – Tamil Nadu
Kathak – North India
Kathakali – Kerala
Mohiniyattam – Kerala
Kuchipudi – Andhra Pradesh
Odissi – Odisha
Manipuri – Manipur
Sattriya – Assam

cards.title: Caves and monuments
points: **Ajanta** – Buddhist caves famous for murals
**Ellora** – Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves; Kailasa temple carved from a single rock under the Rashtrakutas
**Konark Sun Temple** – Odisha, built by Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, shaped like a chariot

cards.title: UNESCO Intangible Heritage
cards.body: India has several elements on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list, including **Kumbh Mela** (2017), **Durga Puja in Kolkata** (2021) and **Garba of Gujarat** (2023). Tangible sites like Dholavira and Ramappa Temple were inscribed as World Heritage in 2021.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Make a state-wise table: dance, folk art, painting style, major temple. One page per region helps answer both Prelims factual questions and GS I culture questions.

cards.q: Sattriya is a classical dance form of:
cards.explain: Sattriya originated in the Vaishnava monasteries (sattras) of Assam.

cards.q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was built under which dynasty?
cards.explain: It is attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (8th century).

notes.p: Art and culture is part of **GS Paper I** ('salient aspects of art forms, literature and architecture from ancient to modern times') and appears regularly in Prelims. It covers architecture, sculpture, painting, music, dance, theatre, festivals, languages and heritage. Because the area is vast, focus on **features, regions and examples** and revise with pictures.
Indian temples are mainly classified into three styles.
points: **Nagara (north):** curvilinear **shikhara**; no elaborate boundary walls; e.g. Khajuraho (Chandelas), Sun Temple at Konark (Odisha style)
**Dravida (south):** pyramidal tower called **vimana**; large gateway **gopuram**; enclosed courtyard; e.g. Brihadeeswara Temple at Thanjavur (Rajaraja Chola I)
**Vesara:** mix of Nagara and Dravida; associated with the later Chalukyas and Hoysalas
**Pallavas:** rock-cut **rathas** and Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram
Rock-cut caves: **Ajanta** (Buddhist paintings), **Ellora** (Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves; Kailasa temple)

notes.p: The **Sangeet Natak Akademi** recognises eight classical dances (the Ministry of Culture also includes Chhau in some lists — check the current official position).
points: **Bharatanatyam** – Tamil Nadu
**Kathak** – North India
**Kathakali** – Kerala
**Mohiniyattam** – Kerala
**Kuchipudi** – Andhra Pradesh
**Odissi** – Odisha
**Manipuri** – Manipur
**Sattriya** – Assam (introduced by Srimanta Sankaradeva)

notes.p:
Indian classical music has two traditions: **Hindustani** (north) and **Carnatic** (south). Hindustani forms include dhrupad, khayal and thumri. Carnatic music was systematised by figures such as **Purandara Dasa**, and the 'trinity' — Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri.

Painting traditions include **Ajanta murals**, **Mughal miniatures**, **Rajput** and **Pahari** schools, and folk forms such as **Madhubani (Bihar)**, **Warli (Maharashtra)**, **Pattachitra (Odisha)**, **Gond (Madhya Pradesh)** and **Kalamkari (Andhra Pradesh)**.

Indian puppetry (for example **Kathputli** of Rajasthan) and folk theatre forms such as **Yakshagana** (Karnataka), **Jatra** (Bengal), **Nautanki** (north India) and **Tamasha** (Maharashtra) are also frequently asked. Remember region–form pairs and one distinctive feature of each.

India has many **UNESCO World Heritage Sites** and elements on UNESCO's list of **Intangible Cultural Heritage** — for example Kumbh Mela, Yoga, Durga Puja in Kolkata, and Vedic chanting. Lists grow every year, so **check the latest count** before the exam. **Geographical Indication (GI)** tags for crafts and products are also frequently in the news.

Institutions to know include the **Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)**, set up in **1861** with Alexander Cunningham as its first Director-General, the **Sangeet Natak Akademi**, the **Lalit Kala Akademi** and the **Sahitya Akademi**.

Prelims asks about **features of a temple style**, dance–state pairs, folk painting–region pairs, and items in news (new UNESCO sites, GI tags). Questions often use the 'how many pairs are correctly matched' format. Mains GS I may ask about the **evolution of temple architecture**, the role of Buddhist art, or how heritage can be preserved and promoted.
Key pairs.
points: Nagara: shikhara; Dravida: vimana + gopuram; Vesara: mixed
Brihadeeswara: Thanjavur, Rajaraja Chola I
Mahabalipuram: Pallava rathas and Shore Temple
Ellora: Buddhist, Hindu, Jain caves; Kailasa temple
Sattriya: Assam; Kuchipudi: Andhra Pradesh
Madhubani: Bihar; Warli: Maharashtra; Pattachitra: Odisha
Check the latest UNESCO and GI lists

cards.title: A Bronze Age urban culture
cards.body: The **Harappan civilisation** flourished in the north-west of the subcontinent; its mature phase is usually dated to about **2600–1900 BCE**. It was first identified at **Harappa** (excavated by Daya Ram Sahni, 1921) and **Mohenjo-daro** (R.D. Banerji, 1922) under John Marshall's leadership of the ASI.

cards.title: Town planning
cards.body: Cities had a **grid pattern**, baked-brick houses, covered **drains**, and often a raised **citadel** with a lower town. Mohenjo-daro's **Great Bath** and Harappa's granaries are famous structures. Bricks followed a standard ratio of about 1:2:4.

cards.title: Site–feature pairs
cards.body: Remember the signature finds of each site.
points: Lothal (Gujarat): dockyard, bead-making
Kalibangan (Rajasthan): ploughed field, fire altars
Dholavira (Gujarat): water reservoirs, signboard; World Heritage Site (2021)
Rakhigarhi (Haryana): among the largest sites
Chanhudaro: bead-making, no citadel
Banawali (Haryana): toy plough

cards.title: Economy and trade
cards.body: Farmers grew wheat, barley, peas, sesame and cotton (Harappans were among the earliest cotton growers). Trade reached **Mesopotamia**, whose texts refer to **Meluhha**, generally identified with the Indus region. Standardised **weights** in binary multiples and steatite **seals** point to organised commerce.

cards.title: Religion and script
cards.body: Terracotta female figurines suggest a mother-goddess cult; the 'Proto-Shiva' (Pashupati) seal shows a seated figure with animals. **Fire altars** appear at Kalibangan and Lothal. The **script remains undeciphered**; it was mostly written right to left.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: UPSC likes matching sites with features and rivers, and asking what was **absent** — no iron, no evidence of the horse in a clear mature-phase context, no large temples or palaces. Learn negatives as carefully as positives.

cards.title: Elimination practice
cards.body: Statement: 'Harappans used iron tools.' Iron in India is associated with a much later period (the Painted Grey Ware / later Vedic phase). Harappans used **copper and bronze**. So the statement is wrong — eliminate options containing it.

cards.q: Which Harappan site is best known for a dockyard?
cards.explain: Lothal in Gujarat has a structure widely interpreted as a dockyard.

cards.q: Evidence of a ploughed field has been found at:
cards.explain: Kalibangan in Rajasthan shows furrows of a ploughed field.

cards.q: Which metal was NOT known to the mature Harappans?
cards.explain: Harappans used copper, bronze, gold and silver but not iron.

notes.p:
The civilisation is named after **Harappa** on the Ravi, the first site excavated (1921). Its sites spread across present-day Pakistan, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat and western Uttar Pradesh, with outposts such as **Shortughai** in Afghanistan. It is also called the **Sindhu–Sarasvati** civilisation by some scholars because many sites lie along the Ghaggar–Hakra channel.

Archaeologists divide it into **Early, Mature and Late** phases. The mature urban phase is generally placed around **2600–1900 BCE**.
points: Northernmost: Manda (J&K)
Southernmost: Daimabad (Maharashtra)
Westernmost: Sutkagen Dor (Balochistan)
Easternmost: Alamgirpur (Uttar Pradesh)

notes.p:
Harappan cities are celebrated for **planning**. Streets crossed at right angles, dividing towns into blocks. Houses of **standard burnt bricks** opened onto side lanes and had wells and bathrooms. A covered **drainage system** ran along streets.

Many towns had a **citadel** on a raised platform (public buildings) and a **lower town** (residential). Dholavira was divided into three parts and had elaborate **water-harvesting reservoirs**.
Agriculture was based on wheat and barley, with cotton, peas, sesame and mustard; rice evidence is limited (e.g., Lothal, Rangpur). Animals such as cattle, sheep and goats were domesticated.
points: **Crafts:** bead-making (Chanhudaro, Lothal), pottery, metallurgy in copper and bronze, the bronze 'Dancing Girl' from Mohenjo-daro
**Seals:** mostly steatite, often with a unicorn-like animal and script
**Weights:** cubical, in binary multiples (1, 2, 4, 8 … )
**Trade:** with Mesopotamia ('Meluhha' in Mesopotamian texts), Oman and Bahrain region

notes.p:
There is no clear evidence of a single ruler or large palaces, so scholars debate how authority worked. Religion is inferred from objects: **terracotta figurines** (fertility cult), the **Pashupati seal**, worship of trees such as the peepal, animals, and **fire altars** at Kalibangan and Lothal. The dead were mostly buried.

The **script**, with around 400 signs, is pictographic and still **undeciphered**, so our knowledge comes entirely from archaeology.

No single cause explains the decline after about 1900 BCE. Proposed causes include **climate change and declining rainfall**, **shifts in river courses** (drying of the Ghaggar–Hakra), floods, decline of trade with Mesopotamia and ecological strain. The old 'Aryan invasion' theory of sudden destruction is **not supported** by evidence. Late Harappan cultures continued in a de-urbanised, regional form.

Questions usually test **site–feature matching**, what Harappans did or did not know (iron, horse), crafts, and trade links. Recent attention to **Dholavira** (UNESCO World Heritage, 2021) and **Rakhigarhi** (DNA studies) makes them worth knowing.

A useful habit: make a two-column table of **site → state/river → signature find** and revise it before the exam. Also remember that much of what we 'know' about Harappan religion and polity is **interpretation** of objects, so options that use absolute words such as 'proved' or 'certainly' are usually unsafe. Note too that sites like **Mehrgarh** (Balochistan) belong to an earlier Neolithic phase and show the roots of farming in the region.
Lock these in.
points: Mature phase ~2600–1900 BCE; Bronze Age
Harappa 1921 (Sahni), Mohenjo-daro 1922 (Banerji)
Great Bath — Mohenjo-daro; dockyard — Lothal; ploughed field — Kalibangan
Dholavira — reservoirs, UNESCO site 2021
No iron; script undeciphered
Meluhha = Indus region in Mesopotamian texts
Decline: climate and river shifts, not a single invasion

cards.title: Two phases
cards.body: The **Early (Rig) Vedic** period (about 1500–1000 BCE) was centred on the **Sapta Sindhu** region (Punjab). The **Later Vedic** period (about 1000–600 BCE) saw expansion into the Ganga–Yamuna doab and is linked with **Painted Grey Ware** and the use of iron.

cards.title: The Vedic texts
cards.body: Four **Vedas**: Rig (hymns), Sama (melodies), Yajur (sacrificial formulae), Atharva (spells, charms, popular beliefs). Each has **Brahmanas** (ritual), **Aranyakas** (forest texts) and **Upanishads** (philosophy). Vedic literature is **shruti** (revealed).

cards.title: Rig Vedic society
cards.body: Society was **tribal and pastoral**; cattle (go) was wealth — a war was 'gavishthi', search for cows. The **sabha** and **samiti** were assemblies; women such as Apala and Ghosha composed hymns. Varna divisions were still fluid.

cards.title: Later Vedic changes
cards.body: Agriculture became central with iron tools. The **varna system** hardened; kings grew stronger through rituals like **Rajasuya**, **Ashvamedha** and **Vajapeya**. Women's status declined, and assemblies lost importance.

cards.title: Gods across phases
cards.body: Rig Vedic: **Indra** (most hymns), **Agni**, **Varuna** (cosmic order, *rita*), **Soma**. Later Vedic: **Prajapati** (creator), **Vishnu** and **Rudra** gain importance; ritual becomes complex.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Many UPSC questions are 'which is correctly matched' on texts and ideas — e.g., the **Purusha Sukta** (10th mandala of the Rig Veda) first mentions four varnas; the **Gayatri Mantra** is in the Rig Veda; **'Satyameva Jayate'** comes from the **Mundaka Upanishad**.

cards.q: India's national motto 'Satyameva Jayate' is taken from the:
cards.explain: It comes from the Mundaka Upanishad.

cards.q: Which Veda is mainly a collection of spells and charms?
cards.explain: The Atharva Veda deals with spells, charms and popular practices.

cards.q: The four-fold varna division is first mentioned in the:
options: Purusha Sukta of the Rig Veda
cards.explain: The Purusha Sukta in the tenth mandala of the Rig Veda is the earliest reference.

notes.p:
The Vedic period is known mainly from **texts**, unlike the Harappan period which is known from archaeology. It is divided into the **Early Vedic** (c. 1500–1000 BCE) and **Later Vedic** (c. 1000–600 BCE) phases. Dates are approximate and debated, so UPSC usually asks about features rather than exact years.

The Rig Vedic people lived in the **Sapta Sindhu** (land of seven rivers). Rivers named in the Rig Veda include the Sindhu, Sarasvati and Parushni (Ravi), along whose banks the **Battle of Ten Kings** (Dasarajna) was fought, won by **Sudas** of the Bharata tribe.
Vedic literature is grouped as **shruti** (heard/revealed).
points: **Rig Veda:** 10 mandalas, 1,028 hymns; oldest text
**Sama Veda:** hymns set to melody; roots of Indian music
**Yajur Veda:** sacrificial formulae; Shukla and Krishna branches
**Atharva Veda:** charms, spells, medicine and popular belief
**Brahmanas:** explain rituals (e.g., Shatapatha Brahmana)
**Aranyakas:** 'forest texts', bridge between ritual and philosophy
**Upanishads:** philosophy of **atman** and **brahman**; also called **Vedanta**

notes.p:
In the Early Vedic phase the **rajan** was a tribal chief, guided by assemblies — **sabha** (council of elders), **samiti** (folk assembly), **vidatha** and **gana**. There was no regular tax; **bali** was a voluntary offering.

In the Later Vedic phase territorial kingdoms (**janapadas**) emerged. Kings performed costly sacrifices to claim legitimacy. Bali became more regular, officials (ratnins) appear, and the assemblies declined. The **four varnas** hardened and the **ashrama** system (brahmacharya, grihastha, vanaprastha, sannyasa) took shape.

Early Vedic economy was largely **pastoral**; wealth was counted in **cattle**. Barley (**yava**) was grown. Later Vedic people used **iron** (krishna ayas / shyama ayas) to clear forests in the Gangetic plain, grew rice (vrihi), and practised crafts. Pottery: **Painted Grey Ware** is associated with Later Vedic settlements.

Rig Vedic religion was nature-based, centred on **Indra**, **Agni**, **Varuna** and **Soma**, with prayers for cattle, progeny and victory. Later, rituals became elaborate and priests powerful. The **Upanishads** reacted against ritualism and emphasised knowledge, the unity of **atman and brahman**, and ideas of **karma** and **rebirth** that later influenced Buddhism and Jainism.

Expect statement-based questions on assemblies, texts, gods and changes between the two phases. The six schools of philosophy (Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Sankhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta) and their founders are also asked.

Some terms worth knowing: **gotra** (lineage, literally 'cow-pen'), **rita** (cosmic order guarded by Varuna), **purohita** (priest), **senani** (army chief), **gramani** (village head) and **nishka** (a gold ornament used in exchange). The **Vedangas** — shiksha (phonetics), kalpa (ritual), vyakarana (grammar), nirukta (etymology), chhanda (metre) and jyotisha (astronomy) — are **smriti** texts that helped preserve the Vedas. Watch for statements that mix up the Early and Later Vedic phases; that is the most common trap.
Key facts.
points: Early Vedic: pastoral, Sapta Sindhu; Later Vedic: agrarian, Ganga plain, iron
Four Vedas; Upanishads = Vedanta
Purusha Sukta — first mention of four varnas
Indra most invoked Rig Vedic god
Sabha and samiti — tribal assemblies
Satyameva Jayate — Mundaka Upanishad
Battle of Ten Kings on the Parushni (Ravi)

cards.title: Sixteen Mahajanapadas
cards.body: Buddhist (Anguttara Nikaya) and Jain texts list **16 Mahajanapadas** in the 6th century BCE, such as Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, Avanti, Kashi, Anga, Vajji and Gandhara. **Vajji** and **Malla** were **ganasanghas** (republics); most others were monarchies.

cards.title: Rise of Magadha
cards.body: Magadha became dominant under the **Haryanka** (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru), **Shishunaga** and **Nanda** dynasties. Reasons: fertile Ganga plains, **iron ore** nearby, river transport, elephants for the army, and strong rulers. Capitals moved from **Rajagriha** to **Pataliputra**.

cards.title: Gautama Buddha
cards.body: Born at **Lumbini** (in present-day Nepal) in the Shakya clan; enlightenment at **Bodh Gaya**; first sermon at **Sarnath** (Dharmachakra-pravartana); death (mahaparinirvana) at **Kushinagar**. Taught the **Four Noble Truths** and the **Eightfold Path** — a Middle Way.

cards.title: Mahavira and Jainism
cards.body: **Vardhamana Mahavira** was the **24th tirthankara**; Rishabhanatha was the first and Parshvanatha the 23rd. Jainism's **five vows**: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, and brahmacharya (added by Mahavira). It stresses strict non-violence and the triratna.

cards.title: Buddhist councils
points: 1st — Rajagriha, under Ajatashatru (presided by Mahakassapa)
2nd — Vaishali, under Kalashoka
3rd — Pataliputra, under Ashoka (Moggaliputta Tissa)
4th — Kashmir (Kundalvana), under Kanishka; split into Hinayana and Mahayana

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Keep Buddhism and Jainism's **triratna** apart: Buddhism — Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha; Jainism — right faith, right knowledge, right conduct. Jain sects: **Shvetambara** (white-clad) and **Digambara** (sky-clad).

cards.q: The third Buddhist council was held at:
cards.explain: Under Ashoka, at Pataliputra, presided by Moggaliputta Tissa.

cards.q: Which Mahajanapada was a republic (ganasangha)?
cards.explain: The Vajji confederacy, with Vaishali as a centre, was a republic.

cards.q: Mahavira added which vow to the four of Parshvanatha?
cards.explain: Mahavira added brahmacharya (celibacy) as the fifth vow.

notes.p: By the 6th century BCE, iron tools, surplus agriculture and trade produced towns and states in the Ganga valley — the **second urbanisation**. **Punch-marked coins**, mostly silver, appear. Texts list **sixteen Mahajanapadas** stretching from Gandhara in the north-west to Assaka on the Godavari.
points: Monarchies: Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, Avanti
Republics (ganasanghas): Vajji, Malla — power with a council of clan heads
Assaka was the only Mahajanapada south of the Vindhyas

notes.p: Magadha's rise rested on geography and leadership. The **Ganga, Son and Gandak** gave fertile land and transport; **iron ore** deposits of the region supplied weapons; forests gave **elephants**. Bimbisara used marriage alliances and conquest of Anga; Ajatashatru defeated Vajji; the Nandas built a large army and treasury. Alexander's invasion (326 BCE) reached the Beas but did not touch Magadha.
Buddhism rejected ritual sacrifice and the authority of the Vedas, and emphasised ethical living.
points: **Four Noble Truths:** life involves suffering (dukkha); suffering has a cause (desire); it can end (nirvana); the path to end it is the **Eightfold Path**
**Eightfold Path:** right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration
**Tripitaka:** Vinaya (rules for monks), Sutta (discourses), Abhidhamma (philosophy) — in Pali
Mahayana worships Buddha images and bodhisattvas; Hinayana/Theravada holds to the original path; Vajrayana developed later

notes.p: Jainism holds that everything — even plants and stones — has a soul (**jiva**), hence extreme **ahimsa**. Liberation (kaivalya/moksha) comes through the **triratna** and severe austerity. Jain texts (Agamas) were compiled at the council of **Vallabhi** in the 5th–6th century CE. The split into **Shvetambara** and **Digambara** is linked by tradition with the migration under Bhadrabahu during a famine in the Mauryan period. Jain doctrines include **anekantavada** (many-sidedness) and **syadvada**.

Both appealed to **traders and urban groups** and to those excluded by costly rituals. They used **Prakrit and Pali**, the people's languages, and organised monastic orders. Royal patrons — Bimbisara, Ashoka, Kanishka for Buddhism; Chandragupta Maurya and later Kharavela of Kalinga for Jainism — helped. Other heterodox sects included the **Ajivikas** (Makkhali Gosala), associated with determinism.

Questions test places linked with the Buddha's life, councils, sects, schools and key terms such as **bodhisattva**, **tirthankara**, **anekantavada** and the triratna. Matching Mahajanapadas with capitals (e.g., Avanti–Ujjain, Kosala–Shravasti, Vatsa–Kaushambi) is also common.

Also revise Buddhist art terms that link this chapter to Art & Culture: a **stupa** holds relics, a **chaitya** is a prayer hall, and a **vihara** is a monastery. Key Mahayana philosophers include **Nagarjuna** (Madhyamika school). In Jainism, **sallekhana** is the vow of fasting unto death, and the 1st-century BCE Hathigumpha inscription of **Kharavela** of Kalinga shows royal Jain patronage. Statements that call either faith 'atheistic in every respect' or 'Vedic' should make you pause and check.
Recall list.
points: 16 Mahajanapadas; Vajji and Malla were republics
Magadha: Haryanka → Shishunaga → Nanda
Buddha: Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar
Four councils: Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra, Kashmir
Mahavira — 24th tirthankara; added brahmacharya
Buddhist texts in Pali; Tripitaka
Jain sects: Shvetambara, Digambara

cards.title: Foundation
cards.body: **Chandragupta Maurya** overthrew the Nandas around 321 BCE with the help of **Kautilya (Chanakya)**. He defeated **Seleucus Nikator**, who sent **Megasthenes** as envoy to his court at **Pataliputra**. Megasthenes' account is called **Indica** (surviving only in quotations).

cards.title: Ashoka and Kalinga
cards.body: **Ashoka** (c. 268–232 BCE) conquered **Kalinga** around 261 BCE. The bloodshed, described in **Major Rock Edict XIII**, led him to renounce war by conquest and promote **dhamma** — an ethical code of tolerance, respect for elders, and kindness to animals and slaves.

cards.title: Ashokan inscriptions
cards.body: Written mostly in **Prakrit** using **Brahmi**, with **Kharosthi** in the north-west and **Greek and Aramaic** in Afghanistan. **James Prinsep** deciphered Brahmi in 1837. The **Maski** and **Gujarra** edicts name him 'Ashoka'; elsewhere he is 'Devanampiya Piyadasi'.

cards.title: Administration
cards.body: A centralised state with a council of ministers (mantriparishad), a strong army, spies, and officials such as the **samaharta** (revenue collector) and **sannidhata** (treasurer). Provinces were ruled by princes (kumaras). Pataliputra was run by committees, according to Megasthenes.

cards.title: Mauryan art
cards.body: **Pillars** of polished sandstone with animal capitals — the **Sarnath lion capital** is India's national emblem. Other works: **Barabar caves** (for Ajivikas), stupas such as the early Sanchi stupa, and the **Didarganj Yakshi** (often dated to the Mauryan period).

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: 'Arthashastra' is a treatise on statecraft attributed to Kautilya; its date is debated. Phrase answers safely: it **describes** an ideal administration and need not prove actual Mauryan practice.

cards.q: Who deciphered the Brahmi script of Ashokan edicts?
cards.explain: James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837.

cards.q: The Kalinga war is described in Ashoka's:
cards.explain: Major Rock Edict XIII records the Kalinga war and Ashoka's remorse.

cards.q: Megasthenes came to India as ambassador of:
cards.explain: Seleucus Nikator sent Megasthenes to Chandragupta's court.

notes.p:
**Chandragupta Maurya** founded the first large empire of the subcontinent, from the north-west to Bengal and much of central India. After the war with **Seleucus**, he gained territories in the north-west (Arachosia, Gedrosia etc.), and a marriage alliance followed. Jain tradition holds that he abdicated and died at **Shravanabelagola** (Karnataka) as a Jain ascetic.

**Bindusara**, his son, extended control into the Deccan; Greek writers call him **Amitrochates**. He had links with the **Ajivikas**.

Ashoka's **dhamma** was not a narrow sectarian faith but a moral code. It stressed **tolerance of all sects**, respect to parents and teachers, generosity to brahmanas and shramanas, humane treatment of slaves, and non-killing of animals. He appointed **dhamma-mahamattas** to spread it, undertook dhamma tours (dhamma-yatras), and sent missions abroad — tradition credits his son **Mahendra** and daughter **Sanghamitra** with taking Buddhism to **Sri Lanka**.
Ashoka's inscriptions are the first deciphered written records of Indian history.
points: **Major Rock Edicts** (14): e.g., Girnar, Kalsi, Dhauli, Jaugada, Shahbazgarhi
**Minor Rock Edicts:** e.g., Maski, Brahmagiri; Maski first gave the name 'Ashoka'
**Pillar Edicts:** e.g., Delhi-Topra, Lauriya-Nandangarh
**Rummindei pillar:** marks Lumbini; mentions tax reduction
Scripts: Brahmi, Kharosthi, Greek, Aramaic

notes.p:
The Mauryas ran a large bureaucracy. The **Arthashastra** lists superintendents (adhyakshas) for trade, mines, agriculture and more. Revenue came mainly from land (often described as one-fourth to one-sixth of produce), and the state controlled mining and some trade. Punch-marked silver coins circulated. A royal road connected Pataliputra with the north-west.

Megasthenes described **seven classes** of society and a city administration of **six committees** of five members each — but he was an outsider, so his account is used with caution.

Mauryan art includes polished **monolithic pillars** (Sarnath, Rampurva bull, Lauriya-Nandangarh lion), the **Barabar and Nagarjuni caves** gifted to the Ajivikas, and stupas. After Ashoka the empire weakened: weak successors, financial strain, provincial revolts and pressure in the north-west. The last ruler, **Brihadratha**, was killed by his general **Pushyamitra Shunga** around 185 BCE.

UPSC has repeatedly asked about edict content, scripts, Ashokan sites, Arthashastra terms and Mauryan art. Learn which edict says what and which sites are pillars versus rocks.

A frequent trap is treating Megasthenes, the Arthashastra and the edicts as equally reliable. The **edicts** are contemporary first-hand records in Ashoka's own voice; the **Indica** survives only in later Greek and Roman quotations; the **Arthashastra** is normative and possibly compiled over centuries. Also remember that the **Junagadh (Girnar) inscription** of the Shaka ruler Rudradaman later mentions the **Sudarshana lake**, built under Chandragupta's governor and repaired in Ashoka's time — a classic link question.
Recall.
points: Chandragupta + Kautilya overthrew Nandas c. 321 BCE
Megasthenes — Indica; envoy of Seleucus
Kalinga war — Major Rock Edict XIII
Dhamma = ethical code, not a sect
Brahmi deciphered by Prinsep (1837)
Sarnath lion capital = national emblem
End: Pushyamitra Shunga killed Brihadratha c. 185 BCE

cards.title: After the Mauryas
cards.body: The **Shungas** (Pushyamitra) and **Kanvas** ruled Magadha. In the Deccan the **Satavahanas** rose; in the north-west came **Indo-Greeks**, **Shakas** and **Kushanas**. This was an age of trade with Rome, new art schools and the growth of Mahayana Buddhism.

cards.title: Foreign rulers to remember
points: Indo-Greek **Menander** (Milinda) — dialogue with monk Nagasena in the Milindapanho
Shaka **Rudradaman I** — Junagadh inscription (c. 150 CE), an early long inscription in chaste Sanskrit
Kushana **Kanishka** — Shaka era (78 CE) is usually linked to him; patron of the 4th Buddhist council

cards.title: Art schools
cards.body: **Gandhara** art (north-west) mixed Greco-Roman style with Buddhist themes, often in grey schist. **Mathura** art used spotted red sandstone and showed indigenous features. **Amaravati** (Andhra) used white marble-like limestone and narrative panels.

cards.title: The Guptas
cards.body: **Chandragupta I** (Gupta era from 319–20 CE) married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi. **Samudragupta**'s conquests are listed in the **Allahabad (Prayag) pillar** prashasti by **Harisena**. **Chandragupta II** defeated the western Shakas; **Fa-hien** (Faxian) visited in his reign.

cards.title: Science and literature
cards.body: **Aryabhata** (Aryabhatiya, 499 CE) explained that the earth rotates on its axis and gave a value of π; **Varahamihira** wrote the Brihat Samhita. **Kalidasa** wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam and Meghaduta. The **Mehrauli iron pillar** shows advanced, rust-resistant metallurgy.

cards.title: Harsha and the Chalukyas
cards.body: **Harshavardhana** (606–647 CE) ruled from Kannauj; **Banabhatta** wrote the Harshacharita and **Hiuen Tsang** (Xuanzang) studied at Nalanda. Harsha was checked on the Narmada by **Pulakeshin II** of the Badami Chalukyas, as recorded in the **Aihole inscription** by Ravikirti.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: The Gupta period is often called a 'classical age', but avoid absolute claims. Feudal tendencies grew through **land grants** (agrahara) to brahmanas and temples, and the position of women and lower varnas worsened in some respects.

cards.q: The Allahabad pillar inscription of Samudragupta was composed by:
cards.explain: Harisena, Samudragupta's court poet, composed the prashasti.

cards.q: Which art school typically used spotted red sandstone?
cards.explain: The Mathura school used locally available spotted red sandstone.

cards.q: The Chinese pilgrim who visited during Chandragupta II's reign was:
cards.explain: Fa-hien (Faxian) travelled in India in the early 5th century CE.

notes.p: After about 185 BCE, **Pushyamitra Shunga** ruled Magadha and revived Vedic sacrifices; the Bharhut stupa railings were built in this broad period. The **Kanvas** followed. In the Deccan, the **Satavahanas** (also called Andhras in the Puranas) ruled from Pratishthana (Paithan). **Gautamiputra Satakarni** is praised in the **Nasik inscription** of his mother Gautami Balashri for defeating the Shakas. The Satavahanas issued lead and potin coins and are known for land grants to Buddhist monks — among the earliest such grants.

The **Indo-Greeks** issued the first gold coins in India with clear portraits and legends. The **Shakas** ruled western India as **Kshatrapas**; Rudradaman's **Junagadh inscription** records the repair of the Sudarshana lake. The **Kushanas** built an empire from Central Asia to the Ganga plain. **Kanishka** patronised Buddhism (the fourth council in Kashmir), scholars such as **Ashvaghosha** (Buddhacharita), Vasumitra and the physician **Charaka**. Kushanas issued many gold coins.

Trade with the **Roman empire** flourished; Roman coins are found in south India and sites like **Arikamedu** (near Puducherry) show Roman contact.
The Guptas built a large empire from the early 4th century CE.
points: **Chandragupta I:** founded the Gupta era (319–20 CE)
**Samudragupta:** conquests in Aryavarta and the south (dakshinapatha) listed by Harisena; V.A. Smith called him the 'Napoleon of India'; coins show him playing the veena
**Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya):** ended Shaka rule in western India; Ujjain as a second centre; Fa-hien visited
**Kumaragupta I:** Nalanda's foundation is generally credited to his time
**Skandagupta:** repulsed the **Hunas**; their later invasions weakened the empire

notes.p:
Sanskrit literature flourished: **Kalidasa** (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha), **Shudraka** (Mrichchhakatika), and **Vishakhadatta** (Mudrarakshasa). The Puranas were given their present form. In science, **Aryabhata** worked on the place-value system, π and eclipses; Varahamihira wrote on astronomy and astrology.

Structural Hindu **temples** began: the **Dashavatara temple at Deogarh** and the brick temple at **Bhitargaon**. Ajanta's later caves were made under the **Vakatakas**, Gupta contemporaries. Gold coins (**dinara**) were plentiful, though their purity declined later.

Regional powers rose: the Maitrakas of Valabhi, Maukharis, and the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar. **Harsha** moved his capital to **Kannauj**, held assemblies at Kannauj and Prayag, and wrote plays such as **Nagananda**, **Ratnavali** and **Priyadarshika**. Hiuen Tsang's account describes Nalanda as a great centre of learning. After Harsha, Kannauj became the prize in the **tripartite struggle** among the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas.

Expect matching of inscriptions to rulers (Nasik — Gautamiputra Satakarni; Junagadh — Rudradaman; Allahabad — Samudragupta; Aihole — Pulakeshin II; Mehrauli — 'Chandra'), art schools to materials, and authors to works. The Mehrauli inscription refers to a king called 'Chandra', generally identified with Chandragupta II — phrase it that way if asked.
Recall.
points: Shungas → Kanvas; Satavahanas in Deccan
Menander–Nagasena; Rudradaman–Junagadh; Kanishka–4th council
Gandhara (schist, Greek style) vs Mathura (red sandstone)
Gupta era 319–20 CE; Samudragupta–Harisena
Fa-hien under Chandragupta II; Hiuen Tsang under Harsha
Aryabhata 499 CE; Kalidasa
Harsha checked by Pulakeshin II (Aihole)

cards.title: The Sangam age
cards.body: Early Tamil poems, compiled in **Sangam** literature, describe the land of the **Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas**. Tradition speaks of three Sangams (assemblies of poets) under Pandya patronage at **Madurai**. The age is broadly placed in the early centuries BCE–CE; exact dates are debated.

cards.title: Sangam texts
cards.body: **Tolkappiyam** — Tamil grammar; **Ettuthogai** (eight anthologies) and **Pattuppattu** (ten idylls); **Tirukkural** by Tiruvalluvar — ethics. Epics: **Silappadikaram** (Ilango Adigal) and **Manimekalai** (Sittalai Sattanar).

cards.title: Three crowned kings
points: Cheras — Kerala coast; port Muziris; emblem bow
Cholas — Kaveri delta; port Puhar (Kaveripattinam); Karikala; emblem tiger
Pandyas — Madurai; port Korkai; famed for pearls; emblem fish

cards.title: Pallavas and Chalukyas
cards.body: **Pallavas** of Kanchi: Mahendravarman I (rock-cut temples), Narasimhavarman I **Mamalla** (Mamallapuram rathas), Rajasimha (**Shore Temple**, **Kailasanatha** at Kanchi). **Chalukyas** of Badami: Pulakeshin II; temples at **Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal**.

cards.title: Rashtrakutas and Cholas
cards.body: **Rashtrakuta** Krishna I built the **Kailasa temple at Ellora**; Amoghavarsha wrote **Kavirajamarga** (Kannada). The **imperial Cholas** — **Rajaraja I** built the **Brihadeeswara temple** at Thanjavur; **Rajendra I** led a naval expedition to **Srivijaya** and founded Gangaikondacholapuram.

cards.title: Chola village assemblies
cards.body: The **Uttaramerur inscriptions** of Parantaka I describe election to village committees by lot (**kudavolai**). Assemblies: **ur** (general village), **sabha** (brahmadeya villages) and **nagaram** (merchants).

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Know the Dravida temple features — **vimana** (tower over sanctum), **gopuram** (gateway tower, larger in later periods) — and the dynasty linked to each landmark temple.

cards.q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was built under the:
cards.explain: Rashtrakuta king Krishna I is credited with it.

cards.q: The Uttaramerur inscriptions are a source for:
cards.explain: They describe the functioning and election of Chola village assemblies.

cards.q: Silappadikaram was written by:
cards.explain: Ilango Adigal wrote Silappadikaram, the story of Kannagi and Kovalan.

notes.p:
Sangam poems divide the land into five **tinais** (landscapes) — kurinji (hills), mullai (forests), marutam (farmland), neytal (coast) and palai (dry land) — each linked to occupations and moods. Poems are classed as **akam** (inner, love) and **puram** (outer, war and ethics).

The economy combined agriculture, crafts and flourishing **Indo-Roman trade** through ports such as **Muziris**, **Puhar** and **Korkai**. Pepper, pearls, ivory and textiles went west; Roman gold coins came in. **Karikala Chola** is traditionally credited with the **Kallanai** (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri.

With their capital at **Kanchipuram**, the Pallavas pioneered south Indian temple architecture in stages: **rock-cut** cave temples under **Mahendravarman I**; **monolithic rathas** at Mamallapuram under **Narasimhavarman I**, who also captured Badami from the Chalukyas; and **structural** temples such as the **Shore Temple** and **Kailasanatha temple** under **Rajasimha (Narasimhavarman II)**. The Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Pallava period also saw the Tamil devotional poets — **Nayanars** (Shaiva) and **Alvars** (Vaishnava).

The **Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi)** experimented with both northern (nagara) and southern (dravida) temple styles at **Aihole**, **Badami** and **Pattadakal** (a World Heritage Site). Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha, but lost to the Pallavas.

The **Rashtrakutas** (from Dantidurga, 8th century) ruled from Manyakheta and joined the **tripartite struggle** for Kannauj. Krishna I's **Kailasa temple** at Ellora was carved top-down from a single rock. Amoghavarsha patronised Jain scholars and Kannada literature.
Founded by **Vijayalaya** in the 9th century at Thanjavur, the Chola empire peaked under:
points: **Rajaraja I:** conquests in Sri Lanka and the Maldives; Brihadeeswara (Rajarajeshwaram) temple, c. 1010
**Rajendra I:** expedition to the Ganga; title Gangaikonda; naval raid on **Srivijaya** (Southeast Asia)
Administration: mandalam → valanadu → nadu → village; strong local self-government
Art: famous **bronze sculptures** such as **Nataraja**, made by the lost-wax method
Three 'Great Living Chola Temples' (Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram, Darasuram) are a UNESCO site

notes.h: The Palas and Pratiharas in brief
notes.p: For completeness: in the east, the **Palas** of Bengal (founded by Gopala, reportedly elected by chiefs) patronised Buddhism; **Dharmapala** founded **Vikramashila** university. In the west, the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** resisted Arab advances from Sindh. Their three-way rivalry with the Rashtrakutas for **Kannauj** lasted for much of the 8th–10th centuries.

Expect questions on Sangam terms, ports, Chola local government, temple-dynasty matching and devotional poets. UPSC also likes 'which of these is a UNESCO World Heritage Site' type questions for Pattadakal, Mahabalipuram and the Chola temples.

Watch the term **brahmadeya** (tax-free land granted to brahmanas, whose villages had a **sabha**) and **devadana** (land granted to temples). Remember that the Nayanars' hymns were compiled as the **Tirumurai** and the Alvars' as the **Nalayira Divya Prabandham**. Finally, avoid dating traps: the Sangam age predates the Pallavas, and the imperial Cholas (from the 9th century) are different from the early Sangam Cholas such as Karikala.
Recall.
points: Sangam: Cheras, Cholas, Pandyas; Madurai assemblies
Tolkappiyam grammar; Tirukkural ethics; two epics
Pallavas: Kanchi, Mamallapuram rathas, Shore Temple
Chalukyas: Aihole, Badami, Pattadakal
Rashtrakutas: Kailasa temple, Ellora
Cholas: Brihadeeswara; Srivijaya expedition; Uttaramerur
Ur, sabha, nagaram — village assemblies

cards.title: Five dynasties
points: Mamluk / Slave (1206–1290): Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia, Balban
Khalji (1290–1320): Jalaluddin, Alauddin
Tughlaq (1320–1414): Ghiyasuddin, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firoz Shah
Lodi (1451–1526): Bahlul, Sikandar, Ibrahim

cards.title: Iltutmish and Balban
