cards.body: **Iltutmish** consolidated the Sultanate, organised the **iqta** system, issued the silver **tanka** and copper **jital**, and formed the 'Forty' (**Chahalgani**) nobles. **Balban** crushed the Forty, raised royal prestige with **sijda** and **paibos**, and saw kingship as divine.

cards.title: Alauddin Khalji
cards.body: Fixed prices through **market reforms** with officers (shahna-i-mandi), introduced **dagh** (branding horses) and **huliya** (descriptive roll of soldiers), measured land for revenue, and resisted Mongol raids. His general **Malik Kafur** raided the Deccan and south.

cards.title: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
cards.body: Known for bold but failed experiments: shifting the capital to **Daulatabad**, **token currency** in copper/brass, raised taxes in the **Doab**, and a planned Khurasan expedition. Moroccan traveller **Ibn Battuta** served at his court.

cards.title: Firoz Shah Tughlaq
cards.body: Built **canals**, towns (Hisar, Firozabad), and departments for charity (**Diwan-i-Khairat**) and employment. He made the **iqtas hereditary**, which weakened central control, and had two Ashokan pillars moved to Delhi.

cards.title: Architecture
cards.body: The **Qutub Minar** was begun by Aibak and completed by Iltutmish; **Alai Darwaza** (Alauddin) shows true arch and dome. The **Quwwat-ul-Islam** mosque is in the Qutub complex. Lodi tombs introduced double domes.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Pair rulers with their 'one big idea': Iltutmish — iqta and coins; Balban — theory of kingship; Alauddin — markets; MBT — experiments; Firoz — welfare and canals; Sikandar Lodi — founded Agra (1504).

cards.q: The 'Chahalgani' was a group of nobles organised by:
cards.explain: Iltutmish organised the Forty; Balban later broke their power.

cards.q: Token currency was introduced by:
cards.explain: Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued bronze/copper token coins.

cards.q: Who introduced dagh and huliya?
cards.explain: Alauddin Khalji introduced branding of horses and descriptive rolls of soldiers.

notes.p: After **Muhammad Ghori** defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in the **Second Battle of Tarain (1192)** — having lost the first in 1191 — his slave-general **Qutbuddin Aibak** became the first Sultan of Delhi in 1206. Aibak was known as **Lakh Bakhsh** for his generosity and died after a fall during chaugan (polo). **Iltutmish** received investiture from the **Abbasid Caliph** (1229), giving legal standing to the Sultanate. His daughter **Razia** (1236–40) was the first and only woman ruler of the Sultanate.
The Sultanate's state structure set patterns used later.
points: **Iqta:** land revenue assignment to officers (iqtadars/muqtis) in return for military and administrative service
**Diwan-i-Wizarat:** finance; **Diwan-i-Arz:** military (established by Balban); **Diwan-i-Insha:** correspondence; **Diwan-i-Risalat:** religious matters
**Kharaj:** land tax; **jaziya:** tax on non-Muslims; **zakat:** on Muslims
Coins: silver **tanka**, copper **jital**

notes.p:
**Alauddin Khalji** (1296–1316) built a large standing army paid in cash. To make that affordable he controlled prices of grain, cloth and horses, and collected land revenue at up to half of produce based on **measurement**. He defeated repeated **Mongol** invasions and raided Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai through Malik Kafur.

**Muhammad bin Tughlaq** (1325–51) was learned but impatient. His capital shift (1327) caused hardship; token coins were easily forged; Doab tax increase coincided with famine. He created a department of agriculture (**Diwan-i-Kohi**). **Firoz Shah** focused on welfare, canals and orthodox policies, including levying jaziya on brahmanas, and translated Sanskrit works into Persian.

Hereditary iqtas, weak successors, provincial revolts (Bengal, Bahmani, Vijayanagara) and **Timur's invasion of Delhi (1398)** fractured the Sultanate. The Sayyids ruled a small territory. The Lodis, Afghan in origin, revived it briefly; **Sikandar Lodi** founded **Agra** and introduced the **gaz-i-Sikandari** for land measurement. **Ibrahim Lodi** lost to **Babur** at the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)**.

**Amir Khusrau** (a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya) wrote in Persian and Hindavi, and is credited by tradition with musical innovations. Indo-Islamic architecture introduced the **true arch**, **dome**, minarets and calligraphy. Persian became the court language, and Urdu began to develop through interaction of Persian and local dialects.

UPSC asks statement-based questions on administrative terms (iqta, kharaj), rulers' reforms, travellers (Ibn Battuta's **Rihla**) and monuments. Learn the exact distinctions between rulers, since options often swap names.

Also note the Sufi and Bhakti currents of this era (covered in a separate chapter), and the **Chishti** saint **Nizamuddin Auliya**, contemporary of several sultans. Historians such as **Ziauddin Barani** (Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi) and **Minhaj-us-Siraj** (Tabaqat-i-Nasiri) are the main sources; Barani's views were coloured by his own preferences, so statements quoting him should be read as his opinion. Sultanate rule also saw growth of towns, the **Persian wheel** for irrigation, and spread of paper.
Recall.
points: Tarain 1191 & 1192; Sultanate from 1206
Iltutmish: iqta, tanka & jital, Chahalgani
Balban: sijda, paibos, Diwan-i-Arz
Alauddin: market control, dagh, huliya
MBT: Daulatabad, token currency, Ibn Battuta
Firoz: canals, hereditary iqtas
Timur 1398; Panipat 1526 ends Sultanate

cards.title: Vijayanagara founded
cards.body: **Harihara and Bukka** of the **Sangama** dynasty founded Vijayanagara in **1336**, with the capital at **Hampi** on the Tungabhadra. Four dynasties ruled: **Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu**.

cards.title: Krishnadevaraya
cards.body: The greatest ruler, **Krishnadevaraya** (Tuluva, 1509–1529), won wars against the Deccan sultans and Gajapatis of Odisha. He wrote **Amuktamalyada** in Telugu and patronised the **Ashtadiggajas** (eight poets), including Allasani Peddana.

cards.title: Administration
cards.body: The **nayankara** system gave military chiefs (**nayakas / amara-nayakas**) territories in return for troops and tribute. Village-level **ayagar** officials served for land grants. Temples were key economic institutions.

cards.title: The Bahmani kingdom
cards.body: Founded in **1347** by **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah** (Hasan Gangu), capital first at **Gulbarga**, later **Bidar**. Minister **Mahmud Gawan** reformed administration and built a madrasa at Bidar. The kingdom split into five sultanates.

cards.title: Five Deccan sultanates
points: Bijapur — Adil Shahi (Gol Gumbaz)
Golconda — Qutb Shahi (Charminar)
Ahmadnagar — Nizam Shahi
Berar — Imad Shahi
Bidar — Barid Shahi

cards.title: Talikota, 1565
cards.body: An alliance of Deccan sultanates crushed Vijayanagara at the **Battle of Talikota** (Rakshasi-Tangadi) in **1565**, and Hampi was sacked. The Aravidu dynasty continued from Penukonda and Chandragiri.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Foreign visitors to Vijayanagara: **Niccolò de' Conti** (Italian), **Abdur Razzaq** (Persian, envoy of Shah Rukh), **Domingo Paes** and **Fernão Nuniz** (Portuguese). Afanasy Nikitin (Russian) visited the Bahmani kingdom.

cards.q: Amuktamalyada was written by:
cards.explain: Krishnadevaraya wrote it in Telugu.

cards.q: The Battle of Talikota was fought in:
cards.explain: In 1565 the Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara.

cards.q: Gol Gumbaz is located in:
cards.explain: Gol Gumbaz, the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah, is at Bijapur.

notes.p:
Vijayanagara emerged in the 14th century as Delhi's control over the south collapsed after Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Tradition links the founders, **Harihara and Bukka**, with the sage **Vidyaranya**. The kingdom fought for control of the fertile **Raichur doab** (between the Krishna and Tungabhadra) with the Bahmanis for nearly two centuries.

**Deva Raya II** (Sangama) recruited Muslim cavalry and archers to strengthen the army; Abdur Razzaq visited in his reign.

Vijayanagara was a rich trading state. It imported **horses** from Arabia and Central Asia (first through Arab traders, later the Portuguese) and exported spices, textiles and precious stones. The capital had large **water works**, bazaars and temple complexes.
points: **Vitthala temple** with musical pillars and the stone chariot
**Virupaksha temple** with tall **raya gopurams**
**Mahanavami dibba** — platform for festivals
Literature in Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit
Group of Monuments at **Hampi** — UNESCO World Heritage Site

notes.p: The king was supreme, assisted by ministers. Provinces (**rajyas/mandalams**) were governed by princes or nobles. The **amara-nayaka** system was the backbone of the military: nayakas held territory (amaram) and maintained troops. After 1565 many nayakas — of **Madurai, Thanjavur** and **Ikkeri** — became independent rulers. Women held some prominent roles as poets, wrestlers and palace guards, as foreign travellers noted.

notes.h: The Bahmani kingdom and its successors
notes.p: The Bahmani sultanate grew in the northern Deccan. Its nobility was divided between **Deccanis** (old settlers) and **Afaqis/pardesis** (newcomers), a rivalry that weakened it. **Mahmud Gawan**, an Afaqi, was executed in 1481 on false charges; soon after, the kingdom fragmented into five sultanates. These sultanates allied briefly to defeat Vijayanagara in 1565, then fought each other and were absorbed by the Mughals in the 17th century (Ahmadnagar 1600/1633, Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687).

Before Vijayanagara, the south was ruled by the **Yadavas** of Devagiri, the **Kakatiyas** of Warangal (Rudramadevi, a woman ruler admired by Marco Polo), the **Hoysalas** of Dwarasamudra (star-shaped temples at **Belur and Halebidu**), and the **Pandyas** of Madurai. In the east, the **Gajapatis** of Odisha and, in the north, the sultanates of **Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa** and **Jaunpur**, and the **Rajput** states such as **Mewar** were important.

Questions focus on travellers, temples, the nayaka system, and pairs like dynasty–monument. The Hoysala temples of Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura were inscribed together as a UNESCO site in 2023 — the kind of current-linked fact UPSC enjoys.

Other frequently tested points: the Raichur doab as the core of the Vijayanagara–Bahmani conflict; the use of **firearms and cavalry** on both sides; the Portuguese role in the horse trade after they took **Goa** from Bijapur in 1510; and the Qutb Shahi patronage of **Telugu** and Deccani Urdu at Golconda, which was also famous for **diamonds** such as those from the Kollur mines. When a statement says Vijayanagara 'ended' in 1565, be careful — the empire survived in reduced form under the Aravidus until the 17th century.
Recall.
points: Vijayanagara 1336, Hampi; four dynasties
Krishnadevaraya — Amuktamalyada, Ashtadiggajas
Amara-nayaka system
Bahmani 1347; Gulbarga → Bidar; Mahmud Gawan
Five Deccan sultanates
Talikota 1565
Paes, Nuniz, Abdur Razzaq, Nicolo de Conti

chapters.title: The Mughals, the Surs & the Marathas

cards.title: Babur's battles
points: First Panipat 1526 — defeated Ibrahim Lodi; field artillery and tulughma tactics
Khanwa 1527 — defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar
Chanderi 1528 — Medini Rai
Ghaghra 1529 — Afghans of Bihar and Bengal

cards.title: Sher Shah Sur
cards.body: Defeated Humayun at **Chausa (1539)** and **Kannauj (1540)**. Introduced the silver **rupiya**, measured land for revenue, built sarais and revived the road from Sonargaon to the north-west (today's Grand Trunk Road). His tomb is at **Sasaram**.

cards.title: Akbar's institutions
cards.body: **Mansabdari** — ranks (zat and sawar) for nobles and officers. **Zabt / dahsala** revenue system developed by **Raja Todar Mal** (from 1580), based on average produce and prices over ten years. Abolished pilgrim tax (1563) and **jaziya (1564)**.

cards.title: Akbar's religious policy
cards.body: Built the **Ibadat Khana** at Fatehpur Sikri (1575) for debates, proclaimed **sulh-i-kul** (peace with all), and started **Tauhid-i-Ilahi / Din-i-Ilahi** (1582), a discipleship with very few followers. Abul Fazl wrote the **Akbarnama** and **Ain-i-Akbari**.

cards.title: Jahangir to Aurangzeb
cards.body: **Jahangir** — 'chain of justice', English envoys Hawkins and **Sir Thomas Roe**. **Shah Jahan** — Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Shahjahanabad, Peacock Throne. **Aurangzeb** — reimposed jaziya (1679), long Deccan wars, annexed Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687); died 1707.

cards.title: The Marathas
cards.body: **Shivaji** crowned at **Raigad (1674)**; council of eight ministers (**Ashtapradhan**); levies **chauth** (one-fourth) and **sardeshmukhi** (one-tenth). After him the **Peshwas** — Balaji Vishwanath, **Baji Rao I** — expanded Maratha power until the **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)** against Ahmad Shah Abdali.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Don't confuse the three Panipats: **1526** Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi; **1556** Akbar (Bairam Khan) vs **Hemu**; **1761** Marathas vs Ahmad Shah Abdali.

cards.q: The dahsala revenue system is associated with:
cards.explain: Todar Mal developed Akbar's zabt/dahsala system.

cards.q: Chauth was a levy of:
cards.explain: Chauth = one-fourth; sardeshmukhi = an additional one-tenth.

cards.q: Who defeated Humayun at Chausa in 1539?
cards.explain: Sher Khan (later Sher Shah) defeated Humayun at Chausa and Kannauj.

notes.p: **Babur**, a Timurid from Ferghana, used **field artillery** and the Central Asian **tulughma** flanking tactic to win at Panipat (1526). He wrote his memoirs, the **Baburnama**, in Turki. **Humayun** lost his kingdom to the Afghan **Sher Shah Sur** and spent about fifteen years in exile, partly in Persia, returning in 1555 with Safavid help. He died in 1556 after a fall from his library stairs. His tomb in Delhi, built by his widow, is an early **charbagh garden tomb** and a UNESCO site.

Under regent **Bairam Khan**, Akbar defeated **Hemu** at the Second Battle of Panipat (1556). He expanded the empire through conquest and **Rajput alliances** (marriage with Amber's ruling family), though Mewar under **Maharana Pratap** resisted — Battle of **Haldighati (1576)**.
points: **Mansabdari:** every officer held a rank; **jagirs** (revenue assignments) paid many mansabdars
**Zabt:** cash revenue based on measured land and average yields
**Provinces (subas):** each with a subedar, diwan, bakhshi
**Sulh-i-kul:** policy of tolerance; translation bureau (Mahabharata as **Razmnama**)
**Navratnas** of tradition include Birbal, Tansen, Abul Fazl, Faizi, Todar Mal

notes.p:
**Jahangir** (1605–27) was a patron of painting; **Mansur** painted birds and animals. Empress **Nur Jahan** was influential. He ordered the execution of **Guru Arjan Dev** (1606). **Shah Jahan** (1628–58) was the great builder — Taj Mahal (Agra), Red Fort and Jama Masjid (Delhi). The war of succession (1657–58) brought **Aurangzeb** to power after he defeated Dara Shikoh.

**Aurangzeb** (1658–1707) expanded the empire to its largest extent but faced revolts by Jats, Satnamis, Sikhs (he executed **Guru Tegh Bahadur**, 1675), Rajputs and the Marathas. The long Deccan wars drained resources and strained the **jagirdari** system.

After 1707 weak successors, factional nobles (Turani, Irani, Hindustani), the **jagirdari crisis**, regional assertion (Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh), Maratha expansion and foreign invasions weakened the empire. **Nadir Shah** sacked Delhi in **1739** after the Battle of Karnal, taking the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-noor. **Ahmad Shah Abdali** invaded repeatedly. Farrukhsiyar's 1717 farman gave the English duty-free trade in Bengal, an early sign of shifting power.

**Shivaji** (d. 1680) built a state in the western Deccan through hill forts and guerrilla warfare. He signed the **Treaty of Purandar (1665)** with Raja Jai Singh, escaped from Agra (1666) and was crowned in 1674. His **Ashtapradhan** included the Peshwa (prime minister), Amatya (finance) and Senapati.

Under the **Peshwas**, the Marathas spread across India; Baji Rao I raided as far as Delhi (1737). The defeat at **Panipat (1761)** under **Sadashivrao Bhau** checked them, but Mahadji Scindia later revived Maratha power in the north. The confederacy (Peshwa, Scindia, Holkar, Gaekwad, Bhonsle) fell to the British in three Anglo-Maratha wars, ending in 1818.

Questions target administrative terms (mansab, jagir, zabt, chauth), cultural works (Ain-i-Akbari, Razmnama, Baburnama), and sequence of events. Expect statement pairs such as 'Akbar abolished jaziya' (true) vs 'Aurangzeb abolished jaziya' (false — he reimposed it). Also remember that **Dara Shikoh** translated the Upanishads into Persian as **Sirr-i-Akbar**.
Recall.
points: Sher Shah: rupiya, roads, Sasaram tomb
Akbar: mansabdari, zabt, sulh-i-kul, Ibadat Khana
Jahangir: Roe; Shah Jahan: Taj; Aurangzeb: jaziya 1679
Nadir Shah 1739
Shivaji: Ashtapradhan, chauth & sardeshmukhi
Peshwas led Maratha expansion

cards.title: Roots in the south
cards.body: Bhakti began with the Tamil **Alvars** (12 Vaishnava saints) and **Nayanars** (63 Shaiva saints) between roughly the 6th and 9th centuries. They sang in Tamil, rejected caste rigidity in devotion, and included women saints like **Andal** and **Karaikkal Ammaiyar**.

cards.title: Acharyas and philosophies
points: Shankaracharya — Advaita (non-dualism)
Ramanuja — Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism)
Madhva — Dvaita (dualism)
Nimbarka — Dvaitadvaita
Vallabhacharya — Shuddhadvaita; Pushti Marg

cards.title: Nirguna and saguna
cards.body: **Nirguna** saints worshipped a formless God — **Kabir**, **Guru Nanak**, **Ravidas**. **Saguna** saints worshipped God with form — **Tulsidas** (Rama; Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi), **Surdas** (Krishna; Sursagar), **Mirabai** (Krishna).

cards.title: Regional movements
cards.body: Maharashtra — **Varkari** saints of **Vithoba (Pandharpur)**: Jnaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram. Bengal — **Chaitanya** (kirtan). Assam — **Shankaradeva** (Ekasarana dharma, namghars, sattras). Karnataka — **Basavanna** (Virashaiva/Lingayat, vachanas).

cards.title: Sufi orders (silsilas)
cards.body: **Chishti** — Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi), Salim Chishti (Fatehpur Sikri). **Suhrawardi** — Bahauddin Zakariya (Multan). **Naqshbandi** — Ahmad Sirhindi (orthodox). **Qadiri** — Mian Mir; Dara Shikoh was associated with it.

cards.title: Sufi terms
cards.body: **Khanqah** — hospice; **pir/shaikh** — master; **murid** — disciple; **sama** — devotional music; **dargah** — shrine; **urs** — death anniversary of a saint; **wahdat-ul-wujud** — unity of being.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Many questions are pairs: saint–region–language–deity. Build a single table and you can answer most of them. Note that Chishtis kept distance from the state; Suhrawardis accepted royal patronage.

cards.q: Ekasarana dharma and namghars are associated with:
cards.explain: Shankaradeva founded the Ekasarana dharma in Assam.

cards.q: Vishishtadvaita was propounded by:
cards.explain: Ramanuja taught qualified non-dualism.

cards.q: The Sufi saint whose dargah is at Ajmer is:
cards.explain: Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti's dargah is at Ajmer.

notes.p: **Bhakti** is personal, loving devotion to God. The medieval movement stressed that devotion — not ritual, priestly mediation or birth — leads to salvation. Saints composed in **regional languages**, helping literatures in Tamil, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Assamese and Punjabi to flourish. Many came from artisan and lower-caste groups: Kabir was a weaver, Ravidas a leather worker, Namdev a tailor.

The Alvars' hymns are compiled in the **Nalayira Divya Prabandham**; the Nayanars' in the **Tirumurai**. Philosophers then gave bhakti intellectual foundations. **Shankaracharya** (8th century) taught Advaita and established mathas. **Ramanuja** (11th–12th century) gave a theistic interpretation that accommodated devotion. **Basavanna** (12th century), a minister in the Kalachuri court, founded the **Virashaiva** tradition, opposed caste and ritual, and built the **Anubhava Mantapa**, a hall for spiritual discussion.
**Ramananda** is traditionally seen as a bridge who took Ramanuja's ideas north and accepted disciples from all castes.
points: **Kabir** (15th century): dohas; rejected idol worship and ritual of both Hindus and Muslims; verses in the Bijak and the Guru Granth Sahib
**Guru Nanak** (1469–1539): founder of Sikhism; nam japna, kirat karni, vand chakna; langar
**Mirabai**: Rajput princess devoted to Krishna
**Surdas**: Sursagar in Braj
**Tulsidas**: Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi
**Chaitanya**: Gaudiya Vaishnavism; sankirtan in Bengal and Odisha

notes.p:
Sufism is the mystical tradition in Islam. Sufi orders came to India from the 12th century. The **Chishti** order became the most popular; its saints shunned state service, used music (**sama**), and adapted local customs. **Nizamuddin Auliya** of Delhi had famous disciples including **Amir Khusrau**. **Baba Farid**'s verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.

Sufis were classified as **ba-shara** (following sharia) and **be-shara** (free of it). The Naqshbandi **Ahmad Sirhindi** opposed Akbar's liberal ideas and stressed orthodoxy (**wahdat-ul-shuhud**).

Bhakti and Sufi movements created a shared devotional culture: common shrines, music (qawwali, kirtan), and **syncretic** ideas. They challenged caste hierarchy in religious practice — though they did not end the caste system — and improved the status of vernacular languages. Sikhism grew into a distinct faith under the ten Gurus, with the **Adi Granth** compiled by **Guru Arjan Dev** (1604).

UPSC asks direct matching (saint–sect–region), questions on philosophical schools, and Sufi vocabulary. It also tests nuanced statements such as whether a saint opposed idol worship or wrote in a particular language. Read options carefully: Mirabai and Surdas are saguna, Kabir is nirguna.

Other names worth a line each: **Dadu Dayal** (Rajasthan, nirguna; followers called Dadupanthis), **Purandara Dasa** (Karnataka, regarded as the father of Carnatic music), **Lal Ded** (Lalleshwari, a Kashmiri Shaiva mystic poet), **Narsinh Mehta** (Gujarat, author of 'Vaishnava Jana To', Gandhi's favourite hymn) and **Shankaradeva**'s disciple **Madhavadeva**. Knowing one identifying fact for each is usually enough to eliminate wrong options.
Recall.
points: Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva) — Tamil
Shankara Advaita; Ramanuja Vishishtadvaita; Madhva Dvaita
Kabir, Nanak — nirguna; Tulsidas, Surdas, Mira — saguna
Varkaris — Vithoba, Pandharpur
Shankaradeva — Assam; Basavanna — Lingayats
Chishti: Ajmer, Delhi, Fatehpur Sikri
Khanqah, sama, urs, dargah

chapters.title: Indian Heritage for Mains: Sculpture, Indo-Islamic Architecture, Literature & Philosophy

cards.title: Mains scope
cards.body: GS I asks for "salient aspects of **art forms, literature and architecture** from ancient to modern times". Mains questions want **features, evolution and significance**, not just names. Revise temple styles and dances from the Art & Culture chapter alongside this.

cards.title: Schools of sculpture
points: **Gandhara**: Greco-Roman influence, grey schist, wavy hair, drapery
**Mathura**: indigenous, red sandstone, fleshy figures; Buddhist, Jain and Hindu images
**Amaravati**: white marble, narrative panels, dynamic figures

cards.title: Rock-cut heritage
points: **Ajanta**: Buddhist caves with celebrated murals
**Ellora**: Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves; **Kailasa temple** carved from a single rock under the Rashtrakutas
**Elephanta**: Shaiva sculpture, the Trimurti/Maheshmurti

cards.title: Indo-Islamic features
points: True **arch** and **dome**
Minarets, calligraphy, geometric and arabesque designs
**Pietra dura** inlay (Taj Mahal)
**Charbagh** gardens
Examples: Qutub Minar, Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, Taj Mahal, Gol Gumbaz

cards.title: Colonial architecture
points: **Indo-Saracenic**: Indian and Islamic motifs with Western techniques
**Victorian Gothic**: Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus (Mumbai)
New Delhi by Lutyens and Baker

cards.title: Schools of Indian philosophy
points: **Astika** (accept Vedas): Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta
**Nastika**: Buddhism, Jainism, Charvaka (materialist), Ajivika
Vedanta sub-schools: Advaita (Shankara), Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja), Dvaita (Madhva)

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In 150-word culture answers, use the formula: definition → 3–4 distinguishing features → one or two examples → significance (synthesis, continuity, soft power).

cards.q: Grey schist stone and Greco-Roman influence are features of which school of sculpture?
cards.explain: Gandhara art blended Hellenistic styles with Buddhist themes.

cards.q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was carved under the:
cards.explain: It is attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (8th century).

cards.q: Which is NOT one of the six orthodox (astika) schools?
cards.explain: Charvaka is a materialist heterodox (nastika) school.

notes.p: Prelims rewards recall of names; Mains rewards understanding of **evolution, features and significance**. Typical questions: compare schools of art, trace the evolution of temple or Indo-Islamic architecture, explain the contribution of a dynasty to culture, or discuss how culture reflects social change. Always show **synthesis** — India's culture grew by absorbing and adapting influences.
The Mauryan period gave **polished pillars** with animal capitals (Sarnath lion capital, India's national emblem). In the early centuries CE, three schools flourished:
points: **Gandhara** (north-west): Hellenistic realism, Buddha with wavy hair and heavy drapery, grey schist and stucco; patronised under the Kushanas
**Mathura**: indigenous style in spotted red sandstone, fleshy and energetic figures; produced Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical images
**Amaravati** (Andhra): white marble, lively narrative panels from the Buddha's life, patronised by Satavahanas and successors

notes.p: Cave architecture evolved from simple Mauryan **Barabar caves** to elaborate Buddhist **chaityas** (prayer halls) and **viharas** (monasteries) at Karle, Bhaja and Ajanta. **Ajanta** is famous for murals depicting Jataka tales. **Ellora** shows the coexistence of Buddhist, Hindu and Jain traditions, with the monolithic **Kailasa temple**. **Elephanta** has the great Shaiva sculpture of the three-faced Mahesha. The Pallava **rathas** at Mahabalipuram show the transition from rock-cut to structural temples.

From the Delhi Sultanate onwards, the **true arch and dome**, lime mortar, minarets, calligraphy and geometric ornament entered India and blended with Indian craftsmanship (lotus motifs, brackets, chhatris). Phases: Sultanate (Qutub Minar, Alai Darwaza), provincial styles (Gol Gumbaz of Bijapur, Jaunpur and Bengal mosques), and the **Mughal** synthesis — Humayun's Tomb with charbagh, Fatehpur Sikri, and the Taj Mahal with **pietra dura** and perfect symmetry.

Colonial India saw **Indo-Saracenic** buildings mixing Indian, Islamic and European elements, **Victorian Gothic** buildings in Mumbai, and the planned imperial capital of **New Delhi**.

Literature: Vedic texts and Upanishads; epics; **Sangam** poetry in Tamil; classical Sanskrit (Kalidasa's *Abhijnanashakuntalam*, *Meghaduta*); Bhakti poetry in regional languages (Kabir, Tulsidas, Mirabai, Alvars and Nayanars); Persian and Urdu literature (Amir Khusrau, Ghalib); and modern literature from Tagore onwards.

Philosophy: six **astika** schools — **Nyaya** (logic), **Vaisheshika** (atomism), **Samkhya** (dualism of purusha and prakriti), **Yoga** (Patanjali), **Mimamsa** (ritual) and **Vedanta** (Upanishadic metaphysics) — and **nastika** schools: Buddhism, Jainism, Charvaka (materialism) and Ajivika. Vedanta's major sub-schools are Shankara's Advaita, Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita and Madhva's Dvaita.

Question type: "Indo-Islamic architecture was a synthesis. Discuss."
**Intro:** arrival of the arch and dome with the Sultanate.
**Islamic elements:** arch, dome, minaret, calligraphy, geometric design.
**Indian elements:** lotus and bell motifs, brackets, chhatris, jaali work, local craftsmen and stone.
**Examples:** Qutub complex, Gol Gumbaz, Fatehpur Sikri, Taj Mahal.
**Conclusion:** a shared heritage reflecting cultural dialogue.
Key points.
points: Gandhara (schist, Hellenistic), Mathura (red sandstone), Amaravati (white marble)
Ajanta murals; Ellora Kailasa (Rashtrakuta); Elephanta Shaiva
Indo-Islamic: arch, dome, minaret, calligraphy, pietra dura, charbagh
Colonial: Indo-Saracenic, Victorian Gothic, Lutyens' Delhi
Six astika schools; nastika: Buddhism, Jainism, Charvaka, Ajivika
Answer with features, examples and significance

cards.title: Earth's interior
cards.body: The Earth has three main layers: **crust** (thin, rocky), **mantle** (the upper part includes the partly molten asthenosphere) and **core** (iron-nickel; outer core liquid, inner core solid). Much of our knowledge comes from studying earthquake (seismic) waves — S-waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core.

cards.title: Plate tectonics
cards.body: The lithosphere is broken into plates that move over the asthenosphere.
points: Convergent – plates collide; fold mountains like the Himalayas
Divergent – plates separate; mid-ocean ridges
Transform – plates slide past; earthquakes (e.g. San Andreas Fault)

cards.title: Rocks
points: **Igneous** – from cooled magma (granite, basalt)
**Sedimentary** – layered deposits; may contain fossils (sandstone, limestone)
**Metamorphic** – changed by heat/pressure (limestone → marble, shale → slate)

cards.title: Atmosphere layers
points: **Troposphere** – all weather; about 8 km at poles, 18 km at equator
**Stratosphere** – ozone layer; ideal for jet planes
**Mesosphere** – meteors burn up
**Thermosphere** – contains the ionosphere, reflects radio waves
**Exosphere** – outermost

cards.title: Coriolis force
cards.body: Due to Earth's rotation, moving air and water are deflected to the **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and to the **left in the Southern**. The force is **zero at the equator** and maximum at the poles — which is why cyclones do not form right at the equator.

cards.q: The ozone layer is mainly found in the:
cards.explain: Most atmospheric ozone lies in the stratosphere, where it absorbs harmful UV radiation.

cards.q: Marble is a metamorphic form of:
cards.explain: Heat and pressure change limestone into marble.

notes.p: Scientists study the interior mainly through **seismic waves**. The Earth has three main layers: **crust**, **mantle** and **core**.
points: **Crust:** thinnest layer; continental crust is thicker than oceanic crust
**Mantle:** upper part includes the **asthenosphere**, a weak, partly molten zone that is a source of magma
**Core:** outer core is liquid, inner core is solid; made mostly of nickel and iron
**P-waves** travel through solids, liquids and gases; **S-waves** travel only through solids — the S-wave shadow zone shows the outer core is liquid
Lithosphere = crust + uppermost solid mantle

notes.p: Alfred Wegener proposed **continental drift** (1912), suggesting a supercontinent **Pangaea** surrounded by the ocean **Panthalassa**. Later, **sea-floor spreading** and **plate tectonics** (1960s) explained how plates move.
points: **Divergent boundaries:** plates move apart — e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge
**Convergent boundaries:** plates collide — fold mountains (Himalayas: Indian and Eurasian plates), ocean trenches and volcanic arcs
**Transform boundaries:** plates slide past each other — e.g. San Andreas Fault
The **Pacific 'Ring of Fire'** has most of the world's active volcanoes and earthquakes

notes.p: Landforms are shaped by **endogenic** forces (from within: folding, faulting, volcanism) and **exogenic** forces (on the surface: weathering, erosion by rivers, wind, glaciers, waves).
points: **Igneous rocks:** formed from cooled magma — granite (intrusive), basalt (extrusive)
**Sedimentary rocks:** layers of deposits — sandstone, limestone; may contain fossils
**Metamorphic rocks:** changed by heat and pressure — limestone → marble, shale → slate
River landforms: V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, meanders, ox-bow lakes, deltas
Glacial landforms: U-shaped valleys, cirques, moraines; Wind (aeolian) landforms: barchans, mushroom rocks

notes.p: The atmosphere is made mainly of **nitrogen (about 78%)** and **oxygen (about 21%)**. Layers from the surface: **troposphere** (weather happens here), **stratosphere** (has the **ozone layer**), mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.
points: Pressure belts and planetary winds: trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies
**Coriolis force** deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere; it is zero at the equator
Tropical cyclones form over warm oceans (generally above about 26–27°C) and do not usually form right at the equator because the Coriolis force is too weak
Jet streams: fast winds high in the troposphere

notes.p: Ocean currents are moved by winds, temperature and salinity differences, and the Coriolis force. **Warm currents** (e.g. Gulf Stream, Kuroshio) raise coastal temperatures; **cold currents** (e.g. Labrador, Humboldt/Peru, Benguela) are linked to coastal deserts and rich fishing grounds where cold and warm currents meet. **El Niño** and **La Niña** are changes in the tropical Pacific that affect global weather, including India's monsoon.

Prelims asks **concept-based** questions: why a phenomenon happens, which current is warm or cold, which rock type is which, how seismic waves behave. Map-based questions on places, straits and volcanoes are common. Mains GS I asks about the **mechanism** of phenomena (cyclones, earthquakes, ocean currents) and their effects — diagrams help a lot.
Key concepts.
points: Crust → mantle → core; outer core liquid
S-waves don't pass through liquids
Himalayas: convergence of Indian and Eurasian plates
Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic rocks
Ozone layer in the stratosphere; weather in troposphere
Coriolis: right in NH, left in SH, zero at equator
Cold currents → coastal deserts; El Niño affects the Indian monsoon

cards.title: Location
cards.body: India lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere. The **Tropic of Cancer** passes through eight states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. The **Standard Meridian (82°30′E)** passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.

cards.title: Six physiographic divisions
points: The Himalayas (young fold mountains)
The Northern Plains (alluvial, made by Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra)
The Peninsular Plateau (oldest landmass, part of Gondwana)
The Indian Desert (Thar)
The Coastal Plains (Western and Eastern)
The Islands (Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep)

cards.title: Himalayan vs Peninsular rivers
points: Himalayan rivers are **perennial** (glaciers + rain), form meanders and large deltas
Peninsular rivers are mostly **seasonal** (rain-fed), with shorter, fixed courses
**Godavari** is the largest peninsular river, called 'Dakshin Ganga'
**Narmada** and **Tapi** flow west through rift valleys and form estuaries, not deltas

cards.title: Map practice
cards.body: Take a blank map and mark from north to south: Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra; then Narmada and Tapi (west-flowing) and Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri (east-flowing into the Bay of Bengal). Add one major dam on each. Five minutes daily for a month fixes the map in memory.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: UPSC often asks 'which river is a tributary of which' and 'arrange from north to south'. Learn rivers with their states and tributaries, not in isolation.

cards.q: Which river flows west through a rift valley?
cards.explain: The Narmada (and Tapi) flow west through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea.

cards.q: The Tropic of Cancer does NOT pass through:
cards.explain: It passes through 8 states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram — not Odisha.

notes.p: India lies entirely in the **Northern Hemisphere**. The **Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N)** passes through eight states: **Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram**. The **Standard Meridian** is **82.5°E**, passing near Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh). India is the seventh-largest country by area.
points: Southernmost point of India: Indira Point (Great Nicobar)
Southernmost point of the mainland: Kanyakumari
Palk Strait separates India and Sri Lanka

notes.p: India is divided into six major physiographic units.
points: **Northern mountains:** Himalayas — Himadri (Greater), Himachal (Lesser) and Shiwaliks (Outer); plus Trans-Himalaya and Purvachal hills
**Northern Plains:** formed by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; zones include bhabar, terai, bhangar (old alluvium) and khadar (new alluvium)
**Peninsular Plateau:** oldest landmass, part of Gondwana; includes the Deccan Plateau, Central Highlands, Western and Eastern Ghats
**Indian Desert:** Thar, west of the Aravallis
**Coastal Plains:** western (narrow) and eastern (broader, with deltas)
**Islands:** Andaman & Nicobar (Bay of Bengal), Lakshadweep (Arabian Sea, coral origin)

notes.p: Himalayan rivers are **perennial** (fed by rain and snowmelt) and form large plains and deltas.
points: **Indus:** rises near Mansarovar in Tibet; tributaries Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej; shared under the **Indus Waters Treaty (1960)**
**Ganga:** formed at **Devprayag** by the **Bhagirathi** and **Alaknanda**; Yamuna joins at Prayagraj
Ganga's tributaries: Yamuna, Son (right bank); Ramganga, Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi (left bank)
**Brahmaputra:** called Tsangpo in Tibet, Siang/Dihang in Arunachal Pradesh; with the Ganga forms the **Sundarbans delta**
Kosi is called the 'Sorrow of Bihar' due to floods

notes.p: Peninsular rivers are mostly **seasonal (rain-fed)** and flow in older, graded valleys.
points: **East-flowing (form deltas):** Mahanadi, Godavari (largest peninsular river, 'Dakshin Ganga'), Krishna, Kaveri
**West-flowing (form estuaries):** **Narmada** and **Tapi** flow through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea
Narmada rises at **Amarkantak** (Madhya Pradesh)
Kaveri is shared by Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry — subject of a long-running water dispute
**Mahanadi:** rises in Chhattisgarh; **Hirakud Dam** in Odisha
**Krishna:** rises near Mahabaleshwar; tributaries include Tungabhadra and Bhima
**Mahi** and **Sabarmati** also flow west into the Gulf of Khambhat

notes.p:
This comparison is a favourite for both stages.

Because Himalayan rivers carry heavy silt and are perennial, they support dense population and intensive farming in the plains, but also cause floods and course changes.
points: Origin: Himalayan glaciers vs Peninsular plateau/Western Ghats
Flow: perennial vs mostly seasonal
Valley: young, deep V-shaped gorges vs old, wide, shallow valleys
Course: meandering and shifting vs more fixed courses
Mouth: big deltas vs deltas (east-flowing) or estuaries (west-flowing)

notes.p: Prelims asks about **rivers and their tributaries in order**, states through which a line or river passes, mountain passes, national parks along rivers and places in the news on the map. Mains GS I asks about physiographic features, the **interlinking of rivers** debate, or how drainage patterns affect settlement and agriculture.
Key anchors.
points: Tropic of Cancer: 8 states (Gujarat to Mizoram)
Standard Meridian: 82.5°E
Himalayas: Himadri, Himachal, Shiwalik
Ganga forms at Devprayag (Bhagirathi + Alaknanda)
Indus Waters Treaty: 1960
Narmada and Tapi: west-flowing, rift valleys, estuaries
Godavari: largest peninsular river
Lakshadweep: coral islands

cards.title: What drives the monsoon
cards.body: The south-west monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds. Key drivers:
points: Differential heating of land and sea in summer
Northward shift of the **ITCZ** over the Gangetic plain
Heating of the **Tibetan Plateau** and the tropical easterly jet
High pressure east of Madagascar pushing winds towards India

cards.title: Onset and retreat
cards.body: The monsoon normally reaches **Kerala around 1 June** and covers the whole country by early-to-mid July. It withdraws from the north-west from September. During October–December, the **north-east monsoon** brings much of Tamil Nadu's annual rainfall.

cards.title: El Niño, La Niña and IOD
points: **El Niño** – warming of the central/eastern Pacific; often weakens the Indian monsoon
**La Niña** – cooler Pacific; usually supports good monsoon
**Positive Indian Ocean Dipole** – warmer western Indian Ocean; can offset El Niño's effect

cards.title: Local weather terms
points: **Western disturbances** – winter rain in north-west India, good for rabi wheat
**Mango showers** – pre-monsoon rain in Kerala and Karnataka
**Kal Baisakhi** – violent evening thunderstorms in West Bengal
**Loo** – hot, dry summer winds of the northern plains

cards.q: Winter rainfall in Punjab and Haryana is mainly due to:
cards.explain: Western disturbances originate over the Mediterranean region and bring winter rain to north-west India.

cards.q: Tamil Nadu receives a large share of its rainfall during:
cards.explain: The north-east (retreating) monsoon in Oct–Dec gives Tamil Nadu much of its rain.

notes.p:
India has a **tropical monsoon** type of climate. The word 'monsoon' comes from the Arabic word **'mausim'**, meaning season. The key feature is the **seasonal reversal of winds**: south-west winds in summer and north-east winds in winter.

The Himalayas act as a barrier that blocks cold Central Asian winds and traps monsoon winds, causing rain over north India.
There is no single theory, but several factors together explain the monsoon.
points: **Differential heating:** in summer, the land heats faster than the sea, creating low pressure over north-west India
**Shift of the ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone)** northward over the Gangetic plain in summer
**Tibetan Plateau heating** and the **Tropical Easterly Jet**
**Subtropical westerly jet** shifting north of the Himalayas allows the monsoon to set in
**El Niño** (warming of the central and eastern Pacific) is often linked to weaker Indian monsoons; **La Niña** often to stronger ones
**Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD):** a positive IOD generally supports the Indian monsoon

notes.p: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) recognises four seasons.
points: **Cold weather season (winter):** December–February; **western disturbances** bring rain to north-west India, useful for rabi crops

**Hot weather season (summer):** March–May; local storms like **'loo'** (hot winds in north India), **'mango showers'** (Kerala, Karnataka), **'Kal Baisakhi'** (Bengal) and **'Bardoli Chheerha'** (Assam)
**South-west monsoon season:** June–September; arrives at Kerala around **1 June** (normal date)
**Retreating monsoon / post-monsoon:** October–November; Tamil Nadu coast gets much of its rain from the **north-east monsoon** in this period

notes.p: The monsoon splits into two branches near the southern tip of India.
points: **Arabian Sea branch:** strikes the Western Ghats, causing heavy rain on the windward side; the leeward side (e.g. parts of the Deccan) is a **rain-shadow area**
**Bay of Bengal branch:** moves north-east, gets deflected by the Himalayas and moves west along the Gangetic plain
**Mawsynram** and **Cherrapunji** (Meghalaya) receive very high rainfall due to the funnel-shaped Khasi Hills
Western Rajasthan receives little rain because the Aravallis lie parallel to the Arabian Sea branch
**Break in monsoon:** dry spells during the rainy season

notes.p: A large share of Indian farmland is **rain-fed**, so the monsoon affects **food production, rural incomes, inflation, reservoir levels and power generation**. A delayed or weak monsoon can push up food prices. Climate change is making rainfall more **erratic**, with more extreme rain events and longer dry spells.

Prelims asks about **factors** affecting the monsoon (El Niño, IOD, jet streams), local winds, and why certain regions get more or less rain. Mains GS I asks about the **mechanism** of the monsoon and its variability, and GS III may link it to agriculture and food security.
Lock these in.
points: Monsoon = seasonal reversal of winds; from Arabic 'mausim'
ITCZ shifts north in summer
El Niño often weakens the Indian monsoon; positive IOD supports it
Normal onset at Kerala: around 1 June
Western disturbances: winter rain in north-west India
Tamil Nadu: rain from the north-east monsoon (Oct–Dec)
Mango showers: Kerala/Karnataka; Kal Baisakhi: Bengal; Loo: north India
Rain-shadow: leeward side of the Western Ghats

cards.title: Major soils
points: **Alluvial** – most widespread; Northern Plains; fertile
**Black (regur)** – Deccan basalt; holds moisture; ideal for cotton
**Red and yellow** – iron oxide gives colour; Peninsula
**Laterite** – formed by intense leaching in hot, wet areas; good for cashew, tea, coffee with manure
**Arid** – Rajasthan; sandy, saline

cards.title: Cropping seasons
points: **Kharif** (sown with monsoon, June–July): rice, maize, cotton, soybean, groundnut
**Rabi** (sown Oct–Nov, harvested spring): wheat, mustard, gram, barley
**Zaid** (short summer season): watermelon, cucumber, fodder

cards.title: Minerals and energy
cards.body: Most of India's coal comes from Gondwana coalfields in the **Damodar valley (Jharkhand, West Bengal), Odisha and Chhattisgarh**. Odisha is the leading iron ore producer. Diversifying into solar and wind energy is central to India's climate targets.

cards.title: Green Revolution
cards.body: From the mid-1960s, high-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and assured prices raised wheat output sharply, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western UP. It made India food-secure but also caused groundwater depletion, soil degradation and regional inequality — a common Mains theme.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Minimum Support Prices are announced by the government on the recommendation of the **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)**. Link MSP, procurement and the Public Distribution System when writing on food security.

cards.q: Black soil is best suited for:
cards.explain: Black (regur) soil retains moisture and suits cotton, hence called 'black cotton soil'.

cards.q: Which is a Rabi crop?
cards.explain: Mustard is sown in winter and harvested in spring — a Rabi crop.

notes.p: The **Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR)** classification is widely used. The main soil types are:
points: **Alluvial soil:** most widespread; northern plains and river deltas; rich in potash, poor in phosphorus and nitrogen
**Black soil (regur):** Deccan lava plateau; retains moisture; ideal for **cotton**; rich in iron, lime, magnesium
**Red and yellow soil:** red due to iron oxide; yellow when hydrated; eastern and southern parts of the plateau
**Laterite soil:** formed by intense leaching in high rainfall and high temperature; good for cashew, tea, coffee with fertilisers
**Arid soil:** Rajasthan; sandy, saline; low organic matter
**Saline and alkaline soils:** poor drainage; also called reh, kallar or usar
**Peaty soils:** high organic matter; humid areas such as parts of Kerala and Sundarbans
**Forest/mountain soils:** in the Himalayan and forest regions

notes.p: India has three main cropping seasons.
points: **Kharif:** sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon (June–July), harvested in September–October — rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra, groundnut, soybean
**Rabi:** sown in October–December, harvested in March–April — wheat, barley, gram, mustard
**Zaid:** short summer season between rabi and kharif — watermelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder

notes.p: Minerals are concentrated mainly in the **Peninsular Plateau** (especially the Chota Nagpur region).
points: **Iron ore:** Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa
**Coal:** mostly **Gondwana coal** in the Damodar, Mahanadi, Godavari and Son valleys; Jharia (Jharkhand) is a major field
**Bauxite:** Odisha is a leading producer
**Mica:** Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan
**Petroleum:** Mumbai High, Assam (Digboi, among India's oldest refineries), Gujarat
State rankings change — check the latest Ministry of Mines data before quoting

notes.p: Indian agriculture faces **small and fragmented landholdings**, dependence on monsoon, low productivity, soil degradation, groundwater depletion and price volatility. The **Green Revolution** (from the mid-1960s) used **high-yielding varieties (HYV)**, irrigation and fertilisers to raise wheat and rice output, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, but also caused problems such as falling water tables and soil health decline.
points: **Minimum Support Price (MSP):** announced by the government on the advice of the **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)**
Schemes such as soil health cards, crop insurance and micro-irrigation exist — check the latest scheme details and figures
Diversification into horticulture, dairy, fisheries and allied activities raises income

notes.p:
Water is the key input for Indian farming. Major irrigation sources are **wells and tube wells**, **canals** and **tanks**. Tube-well irrigation expanded rapidly with the Green Revolution, causing **groundwater depletion** in states such as Punjab and Haryana. Tank irrigation is common in peninsular India, where hard rocks limit groundwater.

Solutions include **micro-irrigation** (drip and sprinkler), crop diversification away from water-intensive crops in water-scarce areas, watershed management and rainwater harvesting.

Prelims asks about **soil characteristics**, crop–season and crop–climate requirements, and mineral–state pairs. Mains GS I covers distribution of resources; GS III covers **agricultural issues**: MSP, irrigation, cropping patterns, food security, and technology in farming.
Key points.
points: Alluvial: most widespread; Black soil: cotton; Laterite: leaching
Kharif: rice, cotton; Rabi: wheat, mustard; Zaid: summer crops
Gondwana coal: Damodar valley; Jharia field
Digboi: Assam oil; Mumbai High: offshore oil
MSP recommended by CACP
Green Revolution: HYV seeds, irrigation, fertilisers; side effects on soil and water
Always check latest production rankings

cards.title: Layers and discontinuities
cards.body: Earth has a **crust**, **mantle** and **core**. Boundaries: **Conrad** (within the crust), **Mohorovičić / Moho** (crust–mantle), **Repetti** (upper–lower mantle), **Gutenberg** (mantle–core) and **Lehmann** (outer–inner core). The outer core is liquid; the inner core is solid.

cards.title: Seismic waves
cards.body: **P-waves** (primary) are fastest and travel through solids, liquids and gases. **S-waves** (secondary) pass only through **solids**, so they do not cross the liquid outer core — creating an S-wave **shadow zone**. Surface waves cause most damage.

cards.title: Drift to plate tectonics
cards.body: **Wegener** proposed **continental drift** (Pangaea surrounded by Panthalassa). **Harry Hess**'s **sea-floor spreading** (1960s) showed new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges. **Plate tectonics** unites these: rigid lithospheric plates move over the asthenosphere.

cards.title: Plate boundaries
points: Divergent: plates move apart — Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift
Convergent: ocean–continent (Andes), ocean–ocean (Japan, Mariana Trench), continent–continent (Himalaya)
Transform: plates slide past — San Andreas Fault

cards.title: Volcanoes
cards.body: **Shield** volcanoes (gentle, basaltic — Hawaii); **composite/strato** (explosive, layered — Fuji, Vesuvius); **calderas** (collapsed craters); **flood basalts** (Deccan Traps). About three-fourths of active volcanoes lie on the Pacific **Ring of Fire**.

cards.title: Landforms by agent
points: Rivers: V-shaped valley, gorge, waterfall, meander, ox-bow lake, delta
Glaciers: U-shaped valley, cirque, arête, horn, moraine, esker, drumlin
Wind: barchan, seif, mushroom rock, loess
Groundwater (karst): sinkhole, stalactite (hangs), stalagmite (rises)
Sea: cliff, arch, stack, spit, lagoon

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Remember stalac**t**ite hangs from the **t**op (ceiling); stalag**m**ite rises from the ground. Earthquake **magnitude** (energy, Richter/moment magnitude) differs from **intensity** (observed damage, Mercalli scale).

cards.q: Which discontinuity separates the crust from the mantle?
cards.explain: The Moho separates crust and mantle.

cards.q: The Himalayas formed mainly through:
cards.explain: Collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates.

cards.q: Which seismic waves cannot travel through liquids?
cards.explain: S-waves need a rigid medium.

notes.p:
Direct observation of the interior is impossible, so knowledge comes mostly from **seismic waves**, meteorites, gravity and magnetic data. The **crust** is thin — thicker under continents (made largely of silica and aluminium, older 'SIAL') than under oceans ('SIMA', silica and magnesium). The **lithosphere** (crust plus upper mantle) is rigid; beneath it the **asthenosphere** is partly molten and plastic, the main source of magma. The **core** is mainly nickel and iron ('NIFE').

The P-wave shadow zone is roughly between **103° and 142°** from the epicentre, while S-waves are not recorded beyond about 103° — evidence of the liquid outer core.

notes.h: From continental drift to plate tectonics
notes.p:
**Alfred Wegener** argued (1912) that continents were once joined in **Pangaea**. Evidence: the jigsaw fit of South America and Africa, matching rocks and fossils (e.g., **Glossopteris**, Mesosaurus), and tillite deposits. He could not explain the force; later work on **convection currents** (Arthur Holmes), **palaeomagnetism** and **sea-floor spreading** supplied it.

Plate tectonics recognises about seven major plates (Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic) and many minor ones. The Indian plate moved north after breaking from Gondwana and collided with Eurasia, raising the Himalayas — which are still rising.

Most earthquakes and volcanoes cluster at plate boundaries. The point inside the earth where an earthquake begins is the **focus (hypocentre)**; the point on the surface above it is the **epicentre**. **Tsunamis** are generated by undersea earthquakes that displace water vertically.

Volcano types depend on magma: low-silica basaltic lava is runny and builds shields; high-silica lava is sticky and explosive. Intrusive igneous features include **batholiths, laccoliths, sills and dykes**.

Rocks are **igneous** (from magma — granite, basalt), **sedimentary** (layers, often with fossils — sandstone, limestone, shale) and **metamorphic** (changed by heat/pressure — limestone → **marble**, shale → **slate**, granite → **gneiss**, sandstone → **quartzite**). The **rock cycle** links them. **Weathering** can be physical (frost wedging, exfoliation), chemical (solution, oxidation, carbonation) or biological.

Mountains are classed as **fold** (Himalaya, Alps, Andes, Rockies), **block** (Vosges, Black Forest — formed by faulting; rift valleys are the sunken blocks), **volcanic** (Kilimanjaro, Fuji) and **residual** (Aravallis, worn-down old ranges). A river's course changes from youth (steep, V-valley, waterfalls) to maturity (meanders) to old age (flood plains, ox-bows, deltas). Delta shapes vary — arcuate (Nile), bird's-foot (Mississippi), and estuaries form where tides and currents remove sediment (Narmada, Tapi).

UPSC asks concept-based statements (e.g., why S-waves vanish), landform identification, and links to current events like earthquakes or volcanic eruptions. Practise explaining a feature in one line — that is the level of precision needed.
Recall.
points: Moho: crust–mantle; Gutenberg: mantle–core
S-waves only through solids; liquid outer core
Wegener → Hess → plate tectonics
Divergent, convergent, transform boundaries
Ring of Fire ~ most active volcanoes
Limestone → marble; shale → slate
Stalactite hangs; stalagmite rises

cards.title: Layers of the atmosphere
cards.body: **Troposphere** — weather happens here; about 8 km thick at the poles and about 18 km at the equator. **Stratosphere** — ozone layer; temperature rises with height. **Mesosphere** — coldest layer; meteors burn. **Thermosphere** (with the **ionosphere**) — reflects radio waves. **Exosphere** — outermost.

cards.title: Pressure belts
cards.body: Equatorial **low** (doldrums) → **subtropical highs** near 30° (horse latitudes) → **subpolar lows** near 60° → **polar highs**. Belts shift north and south with the apparent movement of the sun.

cards.title: Planetary winds
cards.body: **Trade winds** blow from subtropical highs towards the equator; **westerlies** from subtropical highs towards subpolar lows (the 'Roaring Forties' in the southern hemisphere); **polar easterlies** from the poles. The **Coriolis force** deflects winds right in the northern hemisphere and left in the southern; it is zero at the equator.

cards.title: Local winds
points: Loo — hot, dry, north India summer
Chinook — warm, dry, east of the Rockies ('snow eater')
Foehn — warm, dry, Alps
Sirocco — hot, Sahara to southern Europe
Harmattan — dry, West Africa ('the doctor')
Mistral — cold, Rhône valley, France
Bora — cold, Adriatic coast

cards.title: Tropical cyclones
cards.body: Form over warm seas (surface temperature above about **26–27°C**), need **Coriolis force** (so not at the equator), moist air and low vertical wind shear. Called **hurricanes** (Atlantic, E. Pacific), **typhoons** (W. Pacific), **cyclones** (Indian Ocean). They weaken over land.

cards.title: ENSO and IOD
cards.body: **El Niño** — unusual warming of the central/eastern equatorial Pacific; often linked with weaker Indian monsoons. **La Niña** — cooling phase. The **Indian Ocean Dipole** (positive phase: western Indian Ocean warmer) can support the Indian monsoon.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Lapse rate: temperature falls on average about **6.5°C per km** in the troposphere. A **temperature inversion** (warmer air above cold air) traps pollutants — a cause of winter smog in north India.

cards.q: In which layer of the atmosphere does the ozone layer mainly lie?
cards.explain: Most ozone is in the stratosphere.

cards.q: Tropical cyclones do not form at the equator mainly because:
cards.explain: Coriolis force is near zero at the equator, so rotation cannot develop.

cards.q: The 'Chinook' is a local wind of:
cards.explain: It blows down the eastern slopes of the Rockies.

notes.p: The earth receives solar energy as **insolation** and loses heat as long-wave **terrestrial radiation**. The fraction reflected is the **albedo** (high for snow and clouds, low for forests and oceans). The atmosphere is heated mainly from **below** by the earth's surface, through conduction, convection and radiation — which is why temperature normally falls with height in the troposphere. Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing long-wave radiation and keep the planet warm.

Unequal heating creates a **three-cell circulation** in each hemisphere: the **Hadley cell** (equator to about 30°), **Ferrel cell** (30–60°) and **Polar cell**. **Jet streams** are narrow, fast westerly winds near the tropopause; the **subtropical westerly jet** and the **tropical easterly jet** both influence the Indian monsoon.

The **ITCZ** (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone), where trade winds meet, shifts north in the northern summer, pulling the monsoon trough over the Ganga plain.

**Relative humidity** is the moisture present compared with what the air could hold at that temperature; air is saturated at the **dew point**. Clouds: **cirrus** (high, feathery), **cumulus** (heaped, fair weather), **stratus** (layered), **nimbus** (rain-bearing; cumulonimbus brings thunderstorms).
points: **Convectional rain:** heated air rises — equatorial afternoon showers
**Orographic rain:** moist wind rises over mountains; the leeward side is a **rain-shadow** (e.g., east of the Western Ghats)
**Cyclonic/frontal rain:** air masses meet along fronts — temperate regions

notes.p: **Tropical cyclones** have a calm **eye** with the strongest winds in the **eye wall**. They draw energy from latent heat of condensation. **Temperate (extra-tropical) cyclones** form along **fronts** where warm and cold air masses meet; they cover larger areas and can form over land. **Anticyclones** are high-pressure systems with clear, calm weather. In the northern hemisphere, winds circulate **anticlockwise** around a cyclone and **clockwise** around an anticyclone (reverse in the south).

**Köppen** classified climates by temperature and rainfall into groups A (tropical humid), B (dry), C (warm temperate), D (cold, snow-forest) and E (polar), with H for highlands. Examples: equatorial rainforest (Af), monsoon (Am), savanna (Aw), hot desert (BWh), Mediterranean (Cs — winter rain, dry summers), tundra (ET). Mediterranean climates grow citrus fruits and grapes; west-coast deserts often lie next to **cold currents**.

Questions test causes (why the troposphere is thicker at the equator — strong convection), definitions (albedo, inversion, jet stream), local winds, and current climate events such as El Niño years. Worked reasoning: 'Why do temperate cyclones bring rain for several days?' — fronts move slowly and lift large air masses gradually. Another: 'Why are deserts on western margins of continents?' — subtropical high pressure brings sinking dry air, and cold offshore currents cool the air so it cannot rise and rain.
Recall.
points: Troposphere ~8 km poles, ~18 km equator
Ozone in stratosphere; mesosphere coldest
Pressure belts: 0°, 30°, 60°, 90°
Coriolis: right in NH, left in SH, zero at equator
Cyclones need warm sea >26–27°C
El Niño often weakens the Indian monsoon
Lapse rate ~6.5°C/km; inversion traps smog

cards.title: Ocean floor relief
cards.body: From the coast: **continental shelf** (shallow, rich fishing and oil) → **continental slope** → **continental rise** → **abyssal plain**. Other features: **mid-ocean ridges**, **trenches** (Mariana Trench has the deepest point, Challenger Deep, about 11 km), **seamounts** and flat-topped **guyots**.

cards.title: Temperature and salinity
cards.body: Surface temperature falls from equator to poles. The **thermocline** is a layer where temperature drops sharply with depth. Average ocean salinity is about **35 parts per thousand**. Salinity is higher in subtropics (high evaporation) than at the equator (heavy rain) and low where rivers enter (Baltic Sea).

cards.title: Major currents
points: Warm: Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Kuroshio, Brazil, Agulhas, East Australian
Cold: Labrador, Canary, Benguela, Humboldt (Peru), California, Oyashio, Falkland, West Australian

cards.title: Currents and climate
cards.body: Cold currents along tropical **west coasts** help create deserts — **Atacama** (Humboldt), **Namib** (Benguela). The **North Atlantic Drift** keeps north-west Europe's ports ice-free. Where warm and cold currents meet, plankton thrive — **Grand Banks** off Newfoundland, waters off Japan.

cards.title: Tides
cards.body: Tides are caused mainly by the **moon's gravity**, aided by the sun. **Spring tides** (highest range) occur at new and full moon, when sun, moon and earth are aligned. **Neap tides** (lowest range) occur at the quarter phases. The **Bay of Fundy** (Canada) has among the world's highest tidal ranges.

cards.title: Coral reefs
cards.body: Corals are animals (polyps) living in symbiosis with **zooxanthellae** algae. They need warm (above about 20°C), clear, shallow, saline water. Types: **fringing**, **barrier** (Great Barrier Reef) and **atolls** (Lakshadweep). Heat stress causes **bleaching**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: UNCLOS zones from the baseline: **territorial sea 12 nautical miles**, **contiguous zone 24 nm**, **EEZ 200 nm**. The EEZ gives rights over resources but not full sovereignty.

cards.q: Which is a cold ocean current?
cards.explain: The Benguela is a cold current off south-west Africa.

cards.q: Spring tides occur when:
options: Sun, moon and earth are aligned
Moon is farthest from earth only
Sun and moon are at right angles
cards.explain: Alignment at new and full moon gives spring tides.

cards.q: The Exclusive Economic Zone extends up to:
cards.explain: EEZ extends up to 200 nm from the baseline.

notes.p: About **71%** of the earth's surface is covered by water, nearly all of it in the oceans. The **Pacific** is the largest and deepest ocean, followed by the Atlantic and Indian. The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country. Ocean basins are young compared with continents because oceanic crust is continuously created at ridges and destroyed at trenches.

The **continental shelf** is the submerged edge of a continent, usually less than 200 m deep. It is economically the most important zone — fisheries, petroleum (e.g., **Mumbai High**) and placer minerals. **Mid-ocean ridges** form the longest mountain system on earth; Iceland is part of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge above sea level. **Trenches** are found mostly in the Pacific at subduction zones. **Guyots** are seamounts whose tops were flattened by erosion and then submerged.

Factors affecting salinity: evaporation (raises), precipitation and river inflow (lower), freezing of sea ice (raises nearby water's salinity), and mixing by currents. Inland seas with high evaporation such as the **Red Sea** are very saline; some lakes such as the **Dead Sea** and **Lake Van** are far saltier than the ocean. Cold, saline water is dense and sinks, driving the global **thermohaline circulation** (the 'ocean conveyor belt').

Ocean currents are driven by **planetary winds**, differences in temperature and salinity (density), the **Coriolis force** and the shape of coastlines. Large circular systems called **gyres** move clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anticlockwise in the southern. Generally, warm currents flow along the **east coasts** of continents in low and middle latitudes, and cold currents along the **west coasts**.

In the north Indian Ocean, currents **reverse with the monsoon** — clockwise in summer and anticlockwise in winter — a unique feature.

Waves are mainly wind-generated energy moving through water; the water itself moves in circles. Tides have a period of about **12 hours 25 minutes** between highs because the moon rises about 50 minutes later each day. Tidal energy potential in India is often cited for the **Gulf of Khambhat**, **Gulf of Kutch** and the **Sundarbans**. **Tsunamis** have very long wavelengths and travel fast in deep water, growing in height near coasts — as in the **2004 Indian Ocean tsunami**.

Expect questions on currents and their effect on climate and fishing, salinity factors, coral conditions and bleaching, and maritime zones. Map-based thinking helps: picture which side of a continent a current flows along. Also link oceans with current affairs: marine heatwaves and coral bleaching events, deep-sea mining and India's **Deep Ocean Mission**, and disputes over EEZs in the South China Sea are common hooks for questions.
Recall.

cards.title: Mountain records
cards.body: **Himalaya** — highest range (Everest). **Andes** — longest continental range. **Urals** — traditional Europe–Asia divide. **Atlas** (north-west Africa), **Alps**, **Rockies**, **Great Dividing Range** (Australia), **Drakensberg** (South Africa).

cards.title: River facts
cards.body: The **Nile** is traditionally listed as the longest river (some studies argue for the Amazon). The **Amazon** carries the largest volume of water. The **Congo** crosses the equator twice. The **Mississippi–Missouri** is North America's main system; the **Danube** flows through more countries than any other river.

cards.title: Key straits
points: Malacca — Malay Peninsula & Sumatra
Hormuz — Persian Gulf & Gulf of Oman
Bab-el-Mandeb — Red Sea & Gulf of Aden
Gibraltar — Mediterranean & Atlantic
Bosporus — Black Sea & Sea of Marmara
Palk — India & Sri Lanka
Bering — Asia & North America

cards.title: Lakes and canals
cards.body: **Caspian Sea** — largest lake by area (bordered by Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, Azerbaijan). **Baikal** — deepest. **Superior** — largest freshwater lake by area. **Suez Canal** (1869) links Mediterranean and Red Sea; **Panama Canal** (1914) links Atlantic and Pacific.

cards.title: Grasslands of the world
points: Prairies — North America
Pampas — Argentina
Steppes — Eurasia
Veld — South Africa
Downs — Australia
Llanos — Venezuela/Colombia; Campos — Brazil (savanna types)

cards.title: Lines on the map
cards.body: The **Tropic of Cancer** passes through eight Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. The **International Date Line** roughly follows 180° longitude. India's standard meridian is **82°30′ E**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: UPSC often uses places in the news — conflict zones, straits, volcanoes, islands. Whenever a place appears in the news, locate it on a map and note its neighbours, water bodies and why it matters.

cards.q: Which strait connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden?
cards.explain: Bab-el-Mandeb lies between Yemen and Djibouti/Eritrea.

cards.q: 'Veld' grasslands are found in:
cards.explain: The veld is in southern Africa.

cards.q: Which of these does NOT border the Caspian Sea?
cards.explain: Uzbekistan is landlocked away from the Caspian; the five littoral states are Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan.

notes.p: Prelims routinely include **location-based** questions: which countries border a sea, which river flows through which countries, or which places lie on a given line. These are easy marks if you study with an **atlas** open. A good method is to trace one region at a time and attach facts to the map rather than to lists.
Quick anchors for each continent:
points: **Asia:** largest continent; Himalaya, Tibetan plateau, Gobi; rivers Yangtze, Mekong, Ob, Indus, Ganga
**Africa:** Sahara (largest hot desert), Great Rift Valley, Lake Victoria; equator and both tropics pass through it
**North America:** Rockies, Appalachians, Great Lakes, Mississippi
**South America:** Andes, Amazon, Atacama (among the driest places), Pampas
**Europe:** Alps, Rhine, Danube, North European Plain
**Australia:** Great Dividing Range, Murray–Darling, Great Barrier Reef, Great Artesian Basin
**Antarctica:** largest cold desert; ice sheet holds most of the world's fresh water

notes.p: Global trade depends on a few **chokepoints**. The **Strait of Malacca** links the Indian Ocean with the South China Sea; **Hormuz** carries a large share of seaborne oil; **Bab-el-Mandeb** and the **Suez Canal** connect Asia and Europe. Disruptions in these areas raise freight and oil costs for India. Learn which countries border the **Red Sea** (Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti on the African side; Saudi Arabia and Yemen on the Asian side), the **Black Sea** (Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine, Russia, Georgia) and the **South China Sea** (China, Vietnam, Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei, Indonesia's Natuna area and Taiwan nearby).

notes.h: Worked example: elimination with a map
notes.p:
Question type: 'Which of the following countries does the Equator pass through? Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Indonesia.'

Step 1: Recall that the equator crosses Africa through Gabon, Congo, DR Congo, **Uganda**, **Kenya** and Somalia (with São Tomé's islands nearby).
Step 2: **Tanzania** lies just south of the equator — it borders Lake Victoria, which the equator crosses, but the line does not pass through Tanzania's land.
Step 3: In Asia it passes through **Indonesia** (Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi).
Answer: Kenya, Uganda and Indonesia.

Climate shapes vegetation and economy. **Equatorial** regions (Amazon, Congo, Indonesia) have dense forests and plantation crops. **Savannas** support herding and wildlife. **Mediterranean** lands grow citrus, olives and grapes. **Temperate grasslands** are the world's 'granaries' for wheat. **Taiga** forests supply softwood timber. **Tundra** has mosses and lichens and is affected by thawing **permafrost**.

Expect 'consider the following pairs' with places and countries, rivers and seas, or questions sparked by current events (conflicts, disasters, new canals or corridors such as the **INSTC** or **IMEC**). Always check on a map before trusting memory. Keep a running list of 'places in the news' during the year, and for each one note the country, nearest water body and the reason it was in the news.
Recall.
