cards.title: Where minerals are
cards.body: Most metallic minerals lie in the old **Peninsular plateau**, especially the **Chota Nagpur** region (Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh). Petroleum and natural gas occur in **sedimentary basins** — Assam, Gujarat (Cambay), Mumbai High offshore, Krishna–Godavari basin and Barmer (Rajasthan).

cards.title: Mineral–place pairs
points: Iron ore — Bailadila (Chhattisgarh), Kudremukh (Karnataka), Keonjhar (Odisha)
Coal (Gondwana) — Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro, Talcher, Singareni
Bauxite — Panchpatmali/Koraput (Odisha)
Copper — Khetri (Rajasthan), Malanjkhand (MP)
Mica — Koderma (Jharkhand), Nellore (AP)
Uranium — Jaduguda (Jharkhand), Tummalapalle (AP)

cards.title: Coal types
cards.body: About 98% of India's coal is **Gondwana** coal (about 250 million years old), found in river valleys like the Damodar, Son, Mahanadi and Godavari. **Tertiary** coal (younger, lower quality, high sulphur) occurs in the north-east. India's coal is mostly bituminous with high ash content.

cards.title: Energy mix
cards.body: Thermal (coal) power is the largest source of electricity; **renewables** — solar and wind — are growing fastest. Nuclear plants include **Tarapur** (first, 1969), Rawatbhata, Kalpakkam, Narora, Kakrapar, Kaiga and Kudankulam. Thorium-rich **monazite** sands occur on the Kerala and Odisha coasts.

cards.title: Industrial location
cards.body: **Iron and steel** plants sit near coal and iron ore: **TISCO, Jamshedpur (1907)**; public-sector plants at **Bhilai** and **Bokaro** (Soviet help), **Rourkela** (German) and **Durgapur** (British). **Jute** mills cluster in the **Hooghly** belt; cotton textiles grew around Mumbai and Ahmedabad.

cards.title: Ports
cards.body: **Mumbai** — natural harbour; **JNPT** — largest container port; **Deendayal (Kandla)** — tidal port; **Kolkata/Haldia** — riverine; **Visakhapatnam** — deep, protected harbour; **Chennai** — artificial harbour; **Mormugao** — iron-ore exports; **Kamarajar (Ennore)** — corporate port.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: National Waterways: **NW-1** Ganga–Bhagirathi–Hooghly (Haldia–Prayagraj), **NW-2** Brahmaputra (Dhubri–Sadiya), **NW-3** West Coast Canal (Kerala). The National Waterways Act 2016 declared 111 waterways in total.

cards.q: Bailadila is famous for:
cards.explain: Bailadila in Chhattisgarh has high-grade hematite iron ore.

cards.q: Most of India's coal reserves are of:
cards.explain: Gondwana coal forms the bulk of reserves.

cards.q: Which steel plant was set up with German collaboration?
cards.explain: Rourkela was built with West German help.

notes.p: India's minerals are concentrated in a few belts:
points: **North-eastern plateau belt** (Chota Nagpur, Odisha plateau, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh): iron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite, mica — the richest belt
**South-western plateau belt** (Karnataka, Goa, Tamil Nadu uplands, Kerala): iron ore, manganese, limestone, monazite on beaches
**North-western belt** (Aravallis of Rajasthan, Gujarat): copper, zinc and lead (Zawar), building stones, petroleum in Gujarat and Barmer
The Himalayan belt and Indo-Gangetic plain are relatively poor in metallic minerals

notes.p:
**Coal** remains the backbone of power generation, but its high ash content and emissions are concerns. **Petroleum**: the first oil was struck at **Digboi** (Assam) in the late 19th century; today offshore Mumbai High and the KG basin are important. India imports most of its crude oil, which links energy to the external sector.

**Renewables**: Rajasthan and Gujarat lead in solar; large parks include **Bhadla** (Rajasthan) and **Pavagada** (Karnataka). Wind power is concentrated in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Karnataka and Maharashtra. India's three-stage nuclear programme, envisaged by **Homi Bhabha**, aims to use its large **thorium** reserves eventually. Hydropower projects include **Bhakra Nangal** (Sutlej), **Hirakud** (Mahanadi), **Tehri** (Bhagirathi), **Sardar Sarovar** (Narmada) and **Nagarjuna Sagar** (Krishna).

Industry locates where the sum of costs is lowest. Factors include **raw materials** (weight-losing raw materials such as sugarcane or iron ore pull industry close by), **power**, **labour**, **markets**, **transport**, **capital** and **government policy**. The first modern cotton mill was set up in **Mumbai (1854)**, and the first jute mill near Kolkata (Rishra, 1855). Sugar mills are found near cane fields in UP and Maharashtra because cane loses sucrose quickly after harvest. **Information technology** clusters (Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune) depend on skilled labour rather than raw materials.

India has one of the world's largest road and rail networks. Roads: National Highways, the **Golden Quadrilateral** connecting Delhi–Mumbai–Chennai–Kolkata, and expressways under newer programmes. Railways: the **Dedicated Freight Corridors** (Eastern and Western) separate freight from passenger traffic. Pipelines move crude and gas (e.g., the **HBJ** gas pipeline). Coastal shipping and inland waterways are cheaper and greener but underused. The **Sagarmala** programme focuses on port-led development.

Question: Match the following correctly — (1) Khetri: copper; (2) Koderma: mica; (3) Jaduguda: bauxite.

Step 1: Khetri (Rajasthan) — copper ✔.
Step 2: Koderma (Jharkhand) — 'mica capital' ✔.
Step 3: Jaduguda (Jharkhand) — **uranium**, not bauxite ✘.
So only pairs 1 and 2 are correct.
Questions are mostly pairs (mineral–place, port–feature, project–river) and concept questions on industrial location or energy security. Keep a map of mines, dams and ports; it saves time.
Recall.
points: Chota Nagpur = mineral heartland
Gondwana coal ~98%; tertiary coal in NE
Bauxite — Odisha; copper — Khetri; mica — Koderma
Uranium — Jaduguda; thorium — monazite sands
TISCO 1907; Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro
Kandla tidal; Chennai artificial; JNPT containers
NW-1 Ganga, NW-2 Brahmaputra, NW-3 Kerala

cards.title: Census basics
cards.body: The census is a **Union subject** (Seventh Schedule) conducted under the **Census Act 1948** by the **Registrar General and Census Commissioner**. The first synchronous census was in **1881**. The 2021 census was postponed; the next census was notified with reference date **1 March 2027** and is to include caste enumeration — check the latest updates.

cards.title: Census 2011 headline figures
points: Population ≈ 121 crore (1.21 billion)
Sex ratio 943 females per 1,000 males; child sex ratio 919
Literacy 74.04% (male ≈ 82%, female ≈ 65%)
Density 382 persons per sq km
Urban share ≈ 31%

cards.title: State extremes (2011)
cards.body: Most populous: **Uttar Pradesh**; least: **Sikkim**. Highest density: **Bihar**. Highest sex ratio: **Kerala**; lowest among states: **Haryana**. Highest literacy: **Kerala**; lowest: **Bihar**.

cards.title: Census town vs statutory town
cards.body: A **statutory town** has a municipality, corporation or cantonment. A **census town** has population ≥ **5,000**, density ≥ **400 per sq km**, and at least **75% of male main workers** in non-agricultural work. An **urban agglomeration** is a continuous urban spread around a core town.

cards.title: Scheduled Tribes
cards.body: STs were about **8.6%** of the population in 2011. The **Bhil** and **Gond** are among the largest tribes. There are **75 Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs)**. The **Fifth Schedule** governs Scheduled Areas; the **Sixth Schedule** covers tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

cards.title: Languages
cards.body: The **Eighth Schedule** lists **22 languages**. India has recognised **11 classical languages**: Tamil, Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, and (from 2024) Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Migration: in Census data the largest stream is **rural-to-rural**, and the main reason for female migration is **marriage**, while for men it is **work/employment**. UPSC likes such counter-intuitive facts.

cards.q: Which criterion is NOT part of the definition of a census town?
options: Density of at least 400 per sq km
75% of male main workers in non-farm work
cards.explain: A municipal body makes it a statutory town; census towns lack one.

cards.q: The Sixth Schedule does NOT apply to tribal areas of:
cards.explain: It covers Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

cards.q: According to Census 2011, which state had the highest population density?
cards.explain: Bihar had the highest density, about 1,106 per sq km.

notes.p: India has about **2.4% of world land area** but around **18%** of world population. Population is dense on the **Ganga plains**, coastal deltas and parts of Kerala, and sparse in deserts, high mountains and dense forests. Growth phases are often described as: **stagnant** (1901–21), **steady** (1921–51), **rapid/'population explosion'** (1951–81), and **high but slowing** (since 1981). **1921** is called the 'year of the great divide' because population fell only in the preceding decade (1911–21) owing to epidemics.

Key indicators: **sex ratio**, **age structure**, **literacy**, **rural–urban** split, and **occupational structure** (main workers, marginal workers, non-workers). A declining **child sex ratio** points to son preference and sex-selective practices, which led to laws such as the **PCPNDT Act** and the **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao** campaign. Work participation of women remains comparatively low, though recent labour surveys suggest it has risen.

**Rural settlements** may be **clustered** (plains), **semi-clustered**, **hamleted** (Himalayan valleys, parts of the Ganga plain) or **dispersed** (hills, forests). **Urban** places are classified by size: cities with one lakh or more; **million-plus** cities; and **megacities**. Problems of rapid urbanisation include **slums**, traffic, waste, water scarcity and heat islands. Programmes include **AMRUT**, the **Smart Cities Mission** and **PMAY-Urban**.

Migration is recorded by **place of birth** and **place of last residence**. Push factors: poverty, low wages, disasters; pull factors: jobs, education, amenities. Inter-state migrants commonly move from **UP and Bihar** to **Maharashtra, Delhi, Gujarat** and **Punjab**. Remittances support source households, while destination cities face pressure on housing and services. The COVID-19 lockdown in 2020 showed the vulnerability of migrant workers and led to the **One Nation One Ration Card** portability scheme.

Tribal communities are concentrated in central India (MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha) and the north-east; in some north-eastern states (Mizoram, Nagaland, Meghalaya) they form the large majority. In 2011, Hindus formed about 79.8% of the population and Muslims about 14.2%. Hindi is the most widely spoken language; India has hundreds of mother tongues grouped into four major families — **Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austro-Asiatic** and **Tibeto-Burman**.

Expect conceptual questions (census town definition, migration patterns, sex ratio vs child sex ratio), and constitutional links (Schedules, languages). Be careful with figures: quote Census **2011** numbers only and say so; newer survey numbers (NFHS, PLFS) differ.

The **demographic transition** model links all this: high birth and death rates → falling death rates (rapid growth) → falling birth rates → low birth and death rates. India is in the later stages; NFHS-5 (2019–21) reported a national **total fertility rate of about 2.0**, just below replacement level, with large differences between states.
Recall.
points: Census: Union List; Census Act 1948; first synchronous 1881
2011: 121 crore; sex ratio 943; literacy 74%
UP most populous; Bihar densest; Kerala top sex ratio & literacy
Census town: 5,000 / 400 per sq km / 75% non-farm
STs 8.6%; 75 PVTGs
22 scheduled languages; 11 classical languages
Female migration mainly due to marriage

cards.title: What the syllabus asks
cards.body: "Distribution of key natural resources across the world (including South Asia and the Indian sub-continent); factors responsible for the location of primary, secondary and tertiary sector industries in various parts of the world (including India)."

cards.title: Global resource map
points: Oil: Persian Gulf, Venezuela, Russia, USA, Canada
Iron ore: Australia, Brazil
Coal: China, India, USA, Russia, Australia
Lithium: Chile–Argentina–Bolivia "triangle", Australia
Rare earths: China dominant in processing

cards.title: South Asia's resources
points: India: coal and iron in **Chota Nagpur** and Odisha–Chhattisgarh; bauxite in Odisha
Bangladesh: natural gas
Nepal and Bhutan: **hydropower** potential
Himalayan and Indo-Gangetic water resources
Sri Lanka: graphite; Pakistan: Thar coal

cards.title: Weber's least-cost theory
cards.body: Industries locate where **transport plus labour costs** are lowest. **Weight-losing** raw materials (iron ore, sugarcane, limestone) pull industry to the source; **weight-gaining** or perishable products locate near markets.

cards.title: Factors by sector
points: **Primary**: where the resource is — mines, fisheries, fertile land
**Secondary**: raw material, power, labour, market, transport, capital, government policy
**Tertiary**: skilled labour, connectivity, markets, institutions (e.g. IT clusters)
**Footloose** industries: few location constraints

cards.title: Why sugar mills moved south
cards.body: Peninsular India offers higher sucrose content, a longer crushing season and cooperative organisation (Maharashtra). Sugarcane loses weight and sucrose after cutting, so mills must stay close to the fields — a classic raw-material orientation.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use one world example and one Indian example for each factor: e.g. iron & steel — Ruhr (Germany) and Jamshedpur; IT — Silicon Valley and Bengaluru.

cards.q: Under Weber's theory, an industry using a weight-losing raw material tends to locate:
cards.explain: Locating near the source reduces transport of waste weight.

cards.q: The "lithium triangle" includes:
cards.explain: Large lithium brine deposits lie in Chile, Argentina and Bolivia.

notes.p: Natural resources may be **renewable** (water, forests, solar, wind) or **non-renewable** (fossil fuels, minerals); **biotic** or **abiotic**; and **ubiquitous** or **localised**. Their uneven distribution explains trade, geopolitics and industrial location. Today's strategic focus is on **critical minerals** (lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earths, graphite) needed for batteries and electronics.
A broad picture (check latest data for rankings):
points: **Petroleum and natural gas:** sedimentary basins — Persian Gulf, Russia, USA, Venezuela, Canada (oil sands), Qatar and Iran for gas
**Coal:** China, India, USA, Russia, Australia, Indonesia
**Iron ore:** Australia (Pilbara), Brazil (Carajás), China, India
**Copper:** Chile, Peru; **cobalt:** Democratic Republic of Congo
**Bauxite:** Australia, Guinea, India
**Lithium:** Australia (hard rock), South America's lithium triangle (brines)
**Rare earths:** China dominates mining and especially processing

notes.p:
India's **Gondwana** coalfields lie along the Damodar, Mahanadi, Godavari and Son valleys; tertiary coal occurs in the North-East. Iron ore belts are in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Goa. **Bauxite** is concentrated in the Eastern Ghats of Odisha. Petroleum comes from Mumbai High, Assam and Gujarat, and the Krishna–Godavari basin has gas.

In the neighbourhood, **Nepal and Bhutan** hold large hydropower potential (Bhutan exports electricity to India), **Bangladesh** has natural gas, and the Himalayan rivers are a shared resource governed by treaties such as the Indus Waters Treaty and the Ganga Water Treaty.

**Alfred Weber's least-cost theory** argues that industries choose locations that minimise transport and labour costs, with agglomeration benefits. His **material index** (weight of localised raw materials ÷ weight of product) helps predict location: an index above 1 favours the raw-material site, below 1 favours the market.

Other factors: power (aluminium near cheap electricity), water, labour (skilled or cheap), markets, transport nodes and ports, capital, government incentives (SEZs, PLI schemes), and **agglomeration economies** where clusters share suppliers and talent.

**Primary:** mining towns like Jharia; fishing near continental shelves such as the Grand Banks.
**Secondary:** iron and steel in the Chota Nagpur plateau (coal, iron ore, limestone nearby) and Germany's Ruhr (coal, Rhine transport); cotton textiles in Mumbai and Ahmedabad (raw cotton, humid climate historically, port, market); jute along the Hooghly (raw jute, water, Kolkata port); automobiles in clusters around Chennai, Pune and the NCR.
**Tertiary:** IT services in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune (skilled graduates, institutions, connectivity, policy); finance in Mumbai, London and New York.

Industry is shifting towards **coasts and ports** for export, towards states with better infrastructure and policy, and globally towards diversified supply chains ("China plus one"). **Footloose** knowledge industries locate where talent prefers to live. Answers should mention how policy (PLI schemes, industrial corridors) now competes with classical factors.
Key points.
points: Critical minerals: lithium, cobalt, rare earths, graphite
India: Gondwana coal; Odisha–Jharkhand iron; Odisha bauxite
Neighbourhood: Bhutan/Nepal hydro, Bangladesh gas
Weber: least cost; material index > 1 → raw-material site
Factors: raw material, power, labour, market, transport, policy, agglomeration
Sugar shifted south: sucrose and crushing season
IT and finance: talent and connectivity driven

cards.title: Earthquakes
points: Sudden release of energy along faults
**Focus/hypocentre** below; **epicentre** on surface above
Waves: **P** (primary, fastest, through solids and liquids), **S** (secondary, solids only), surface waves (most damage)
Measured by magnitude (moment magnitude) and intensity scales

cards.title: India's seismic zones
cards.body: The Bureau of Indian Standards seismic map divides India into zones **II to V**; Zone V is the most severe — including the North-East, parts of the Himalaya, Rann of Kutch and Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Check the latest BIS code for revisions.

cards.title: Tsunami
cards.body: A series of long waves caused mainly by **undersea earthquakes** (also landslides or volcanic eruptions). The **26 December 2004** Indian Ocean tsunami followed a great earthquake off Sumatra and devastated coasts including Tamil Nadu and the Andamans. INCOIS now runs the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre.

cards.title: Volcanoes
points: Most lie on plate boundaries — the Pacific **Ring of Fire**
Hotspot volcanoes: Hawaii
**Barren Island** (Andaman Sea): India's only active volcano
Effects: lava, ash, gases; eruptions can cool global climate briefly

cards.title: Tropical cyclones
points: Form over warm seas (around 26–27°C or more)
Need Coriolis force — so not right at the equator
Low wind shear and pre-existing disturbance help
Bay of Bengal sees more cyclones than the Arabian Sea
Names from a regional WMO/ESCAP list

cards.title: Changing critical features
points: Retreat of Himalayan **glaciers**; glacial lake outburst floods
Shrinking **Arctic sea ice**, ice-sheet melt, sea-level rise
Shrinking lakes (e.g. Aral Sea)
Coral **bleaching**
Species shifting upslope and poleward

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For "effects" questions, link physical change to people: glacier melt → water security and GLOFs; sea-level rise → coastal displacement; coral loss → fisheries and tourism.

cards.q: Which seismic wave cannot pass through liquids?
cards.explain: S waves are shear waves and do not travel through liquids — evidence for a liquid outer core.

cards.q: India's only active volcano is located at:
cards.explain: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is active; Narcondam is considered dormant.

cards.q: Tropical cyclones do not form very close to the equator mainly because:
cards.explain: Coriolis force, needed for rotation, is near zero at the equator.

notes.p: The syllabus asks for "important geophysical phenomena such as earthquakes, tsunami, volcanic activity, cyclone etc., geographical features and their location — changes in critical geographical features (including water bodies and ice-caps) and in flora and fauna and the effects of such changes". Mains questions combine **process** (how it happens), **distribution** (where), and **impact and management** (so what). Revise plate tectonics from the geomorphology chapter alongside this one.

Earthquakes occur when stress on faults is suddenly released, mostly at **plate boundaries**. The point of origin is the **focus**; the point above it on the surface is the **epicentre**. **P waves** are compressional and fastest; **S waves** are shear waves and cannot pass through liquids; **surface waves** cause most destruction.

India's high seismicity comes from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates. The Himalaya, North-East and Andaman arc are highly active; the peninsula is not immune (Latur 1993, Bhuj 2001). Mitigation: enforcing **building codes**, retrofitting, seismic microzonation, early-warning research and community drills.

**Tsunamis** are generated mostly when undersea earthquakes vertically displace the sea floor. In deep water they travel very fast with low height; near the shore they slow and rise. After the **2004 Indian Ocean tsunami**, India set up a tsunami early warning centre at **INCOIS, Hyderabad**. Mangroves and coastal vegetation reduce damage.

**Volcanoes** occur at subduction zones (Ring of Fire), divergent boundaries (Iceland) and hotspots (Hawaii). Types range from shield volcanoes with gentle lava flows to explosive stratovolcanoes. Large eruptions inject sulphur aerosols that can temporarily cool the climate. **Barren Island** is India's only active volcano.

Cyclones form over warm oceans with sea surface temperatures around 26–27°C or higher, sufficient **Coriolis force** (generally beyond about 5° from the equator), low vertical wind shear and a pre-existing low-pressure disturbance. Latent heat from condensation fuels them; they weaken over land or cold water.

India's east coast is more cyclone-prone than the west. Damage comes from wind, **storm surge** and rain-driven floods. Improved IMD forecasts and evacuation — notably in Odisha after the 1999 super cyclone — have sharply reduced deaths, a good example of disaster-risk reduction.

Climate change and human activity are altering key features. Many **Himalayan glaciers are retreating**, forming glacial lakes that can burst (**GLOFs**). **Arctic sea ice** is shrinking and ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica are losing mass, adding to sea-level rise. Lakes such as the **Aral Sea** shrank due to irrigation diversion; Lake Chad has also shrunk greatly. Deltas sink due to reduced sediment and groundwater extraction.

Flora and fauna respond: **coral bleaching** with marine heatwaves, treelines and species moving upslope, changes in flowering and migration timing, and invasive species spreading. Effects on humans include water insecurity, coastal flooding, fisheries decline and new disease patterns.

Question type: "Why is the Bay of Bengal more cyclone-prone than the Arabian Sea?"
**Points:** warmer sea surface; lower salinity and stratified upper ocean from river inflow keep the surface warm; remnant low-pressure systems from the Pacific moving west; funnel-shaped coastline and shallow shelf amplify storm surge.
**Add:** recent studies suggest the Arabian Sea is seeing more intense cyclones as it warms.
**Conclude** with preparedness lessons.
Key points.
points: Focus vs epicentre; P, S and surface waves
India seismic zones II–V (BIS); Zone V most severe
2004 tsunami; INCOIS early warning
Ring of Fire; Barren Island active
Cyclone needs: warm sea, Coriolis, low shear, disturbance
Glacier retreat, GLOFs, sea-ice loss, Aral Sea shrinkage
Link changes to water, coasts, livelihoods

cards.title: Measuring output
cards.body: **GDP** is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year. **GNP** = GDP + net factor income from abroad. **Real GDP** removes the effect of price changes; **nominal GDP** uses current prices.
points: GDP (expenditure) = C + I + G + (X − M)

cards.title: Key identities
points: GVA at basic prices + product taxes − product subsidies = GDP
NDP = GDP − depreciation
GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100
Per capita income = National income ÷ population

cards.title: Inflation basics
points: **Demand-pull** – too much money chasing too few goods
**Cost-push** – rising input costs (fuel, wages)
**Stagflation** – high inflation + low growth + unemployment
**Deflation** – sustained fall in general prices
**Disinflation** – inflation still positive but slowing

cards.title: Price indices in India
cards.body: **CPI** (Consumer Price Index), compiled by the National Statistics Office, measures retail prices and is used by RBI for its inflation target. **WPI** (Wholesale Price Index) is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, and does not cover services.

cards.title: Inflation targeting
cards.body: Under the amended RBI Act, India follows **flexible inflation targeting** (adopted 2016). The CPI inflation target is **4%** with a tolerance band of **2% to 6%**. If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, RBI must explain the reasons to the government.

cards.q: Which index does RBI use for its inflation target?
cards.explain: The target is set in terms of headline CPI (Combined) inflation.

cards.q: GNP is equal to:
options: GDP + net factor income from abroad
cards.explain: GNP adds income earned by residents abroad minus income earned by foreigners in India.

notes.h: Measuring the economy: GDP and its cousins
notes.p:
**Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** is the market value of all **final** goods and services produced **within a country's borders** in a given period. Intermediate goods are not counted separately to avoid double counting.

**Gross National Product (GNP)** = GDP + **net factor income from abroad** (income earned by residents abroad minus income earned by foreigners in India). Subtracting **depreciation** gives the 'net' measures.
points: **GDP:** production inside the country
**GNP:** GDP + net factor income from abroad
**NDP:** GDP − depreciation
**NNP at factor cost** is traditionally called **National Income**
**GVA (Gross Value Added):** output minus intermediate consumption; GDP = GVA + product taxes − product subsidies
**Nominal GDP** uses current prices; **real GDP** uses constant prices of a base year, removing inflation
**GDP deflator** = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100

notes.p:
In India, the **National Statistical Office (NSO)** under the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)** releases GDP estimates. The base year for national accounts is revised from time to time to reflect changes in the economy — check the current base year and the latest growth figures in official releases.

GDP can be calculated using three methods: **production (value added)**, **income** and **expenditure** (C + I + G + (X − M)).
**Inflation** is a sustained rise in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money.
points: **Demand-pull inflation:** too much demand chasing too few goods
**Cost-push inflation:** rise in input costs like fuel or wages
**Consumer Price Index (CPI):** measures retail prices paid by consumers; released by NSO
**Wholesale Price Index (WPI):** measures wholesale prices; released by the Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry; does not cover services
The RBI uses **CPI (combined)** headline inflation for its inflation target
**Deflation:** fall in the general price level; **disinflation:** fall in the rate of inflation
**Stagflation:** high inflation with low growth and high unemployment
**Core inflation:** excludes volatile items such as food and fuel

notes.p:
**Economic growth** is an increase in output (GDP). **Economic development** is broader — it includes health, education, equality and quality of life. The **Human Development Index (HDI)**, published by the **UNDP**, combines life expectancy, education and per capita income (GNI). Rankings change every year, so check the latest report.

Other concepts: **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)** compares incomes after adjusting for price differences between countries; **per capita income** divides national income by population.
Unemployment questions are common in both stages.
points: **Disguised unemployment:** more people working than needed (common in agriculture) — their marginal productivity is near zero
**Seasonal unemployment:** work available only in certain seasons
**Structural unemployment:** mismatch between skills and jobs
**Frictional unemployment:** short-term, while changing jobs
**Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS):** NSO's main source of employment data

notes.p: Prelims asks **conceptual** questions: what is included in GDP, the difference between CPI and WPI, which agency publishes what, and effects of inflation on different groups. Statement-based questions on the GDP deflator or base year are common. Mains GS III asks about **inclusive growth**, jobless growth, measuring growth accurately, and inflation management.
Key definitions.
points: GDP = final goods and services within borders
GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad
National Income = NNP at factor cost
GDP = GVA + product taxes − product subsidies
CPI by NSO; WPI by Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT, Commerce Ministry)
RBI targets CPI inflation
Disinflation ≠ deflation
HDI by UNDP; check latest ranks and growth numbers

cards.title: Reserve Bank of India
cards.body: Established on **1 April 1935** under the RBI Act 1934 and nationalised in **1949**. It issues currency (except one-rupee notes and coins, issued by the Government), regulates banks, manages foreign exchange and acts as banker to the government.

cards.title: Monetary Policy Committee
cards.body: The **MPC** has **six members** — three from RBI (including the Governor, who has a casting vote) and three appointed by the Central Government. It decides the **policy repo rate** to meet the inflation target while keeping growth in mind.

cards.title: Policy tools
points: **Repo rate** – rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities
**Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** – floor of the corridor; banks park funds without collateral
**MSF** – emergency borrowing for banks, above repo
**CRR** – share of deposits kept with RBI; earns no interest
**SLR** – share of deposits held in liquid assets like government securities
**Open Market Operations** – buying/selling government securities

cards.title: How a rate cut works
cards.body: RBI cuts repo → banks borrow cheaper → loan rates fall → more spending and investment → growth rises (but inflation may also rise). To fight inflation, RBI does the opposite: raises repo, tightens liquidity.

cards.title: Money supply measures
points: **M0** – reserve money
**M1** – currency with public + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI (narrow money)
**M3** – M1 + time deposits with banks (broad money)

cards.q: Which instrument requires banks to keep cash with RBI without earning interest?
cards.explain: Cash Reserve Ratio balances are held with RBI and earn no interest.

cards.q: How many members does the Monetary Policy Committee have?
cards.explain: Six: three from RBI and three external members appointed by the government.

notes.p: Money serves as a **medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value** and standard of deferred payment. The RBI measures money supply through monetary aggregates.
points: **M0 (Reserve Money / High-powered money):** currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI
**M1 (Narrow money):** currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBI
**M3 (Broad money):** M1 + time deposits with banks — the most commonly used broad measure
**Money multiplier** = M3 ÷ M0; a higher reserve requirement reduces it

notes.p: The **RBI** was set up on **1 April 1935** under the **RBI Act, 1934**, and was **nationalised in 1949**. Its functions include:
points: Issuing currency (except ₹1 notes and coins, which are issued by the Government of India)
Banker to the government and banker's bank
Regulator and supervisor of banks and the financial system
Manager of foreign exchange under **FEMA, 1999**
Conducting **monetary policy** for price stability while keeping growth in mind
Lender of last resort

notes.p:
Under the amended RBI Act (2016), India adopted **flexible inflation targeting**. The target is **4% CPI inflation with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%**, set by the government in consultation with the RBI for five-year periods (check the current notification). A six-member **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** — three from the RBI (including the Governor, who has a casting vote) and three external members appointed by the government — decides the **policy repo rate**.

Current rates change frequently — always **check the latest RBI policy statement** for the repo rate and other figures.
Quantitative tools control the overall quantity of money; qualitative tools guide credit to particular sectors.
points: **Repo rate:** rate at which RBI lends to banks against government securities
**Reverse repo rate / Standing Deposit Facility (SDF):** tools to absorb liquidity from banks
**Marginal Standing Facility (MSF):** emergency overnight borrowing for banks at a higher rate
**Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR):** share of deposits banks must keep with RBI as cash; earns no interest
**Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR):** share of deposits banks must keep in liquid assets like government securities
**Open Market Operations (OMO):** buying/selling government securities to inject or absorb liquidity
**Qualitative tools:** margin requirements, moral suasion, credit rationing
To fight inflation the RBI generally **raises** rates (tightening); to support growth it **cuts** rates (easing)

notes.p: India's banking system includes **scheduled commercial banks** (public, private, foreign, regional rural banks, small finance banks), **payments banks**, **cooperative banks** and **NBFCs**. Bank nationalisation took place in **1969** (14 banks) and **1980** (6 banks).
points: **Non-Performing Asset (NPA):** a loan where interest or principal is overdue for more than 90 days
**Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016:** time-bound resolution of stressed assets
**Basel norms:** international standards on bank capital
**Financial inclusion:** Jan Dhan accounts, UPI and digital payments — check latest data

notes.p: Prelims tests **tools of monetary policy and their effects**, components of money supply, and functions of the RBI, often through statement questions such as 'If the RBI raises CRR, what happens?'. Mains GS III asks about the **NPA problem**, banking reforms, financial inclusion, and the effectiveness of inflation targeting.
Core facts.
points: RBI set up 1 April 1935; nationalised 1949
Inflation target: 4% CPI, band 2–6%
MPC: 6 members; Governor has casting vote
M3 = broad money; M0 = reserve money
Rate hike / CRR hike → less liquidity, lower inflation pressure
NPA: overdue more than 90 days
Bank nationalisation: 1969 (14), 1980 (6)
Check latest repo rate in the RBI's policy statement

cards.title: Constitutional basis
points: Art 112 – **Annual Financial Statement** (the 'Budget')
Art 265 – no tax without authority of law
Art 266 – Consolidated Fund and Public Account
Art 267 – Contingency Fund
Art 114 – Appropriation Bill
Art 110 – Money Bill

cards.title: Budget structure
cards.body: The budget has a **revenue account** (taxes, interest, subsidies, salaries — no asset created) and a **capital account** (borrowings, loan recoveries, disinvestment; spending that creates assets or reduces liabilities). Capital expenditure is seen as more growth-friendly.

cards.title: Deficits
points: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts
Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − (Revenue receipts + Non-debt capital receipts)
Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments
Fiscal deficit ≈ the government's total borrowing requirement

cards.title: FRBM and GST
cards.body: The **FRBM Act, 2003** sets fiscal discipline goals for the Centre. **GST** was launched on **1 July 2017** after the 101st Amendment, with the GST Council (Art 279A) recommending rates. In September 2025 GST was simplified mainly into two slabs — **5% and 18%** — with a special 40% rate for select luxury and sin goods.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In Mains, use the Economic Survey and Budget documents on indiabudget.gov.in for official numbers. Quote the source, e.g. 'as per the Economic Survey', instead of approximate figures from memory.

cards.q: Primary deficit is:
cards.explain: Primary deficit removes interest payments, showing borrowing needed for current policies alone.

cards.q: The 'Annual Financial Statement' is mentioned in Article:
cards.explain: Article 112 requires the President to lay the Annual Financial Statement before Parliament.

notes.p:
**Fiscal policy** is the government's use of **taxation, expenditure and borrowing** to influence the economy. It aims at growth, employment, price stability and fair distribution of income. While monetary policy is run by the RBI, fiscal policy is run by the **government** through the Ministry of Finance.

**Expansionary fiscal policy** (more spending or lower taxes) is used in a slowdown; **contractionary fiscal policy** (less spending or higher taxes) is used to cool an overheated economy.
The word 'Budget' is not used in the Constitution. It is called the **Annual Financial Statement** under **Article 112**. Key provisions:
points: **Article 112:** Annual Financial Statement laid before Parliament
**Article 113:** demands for grants (Lok Sabha votes on them)
**Article 114:** Appropriation Bill — no money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund without it
**Article 110:** Money Bills; the **Finance Bill** contains tax proposals
**Article 116:** vote on account (allows spending until the budget is passed)
**Article 266:** Consolidated Fund and Public Account of India; **Article 267:** Contingency Fund
Since 2017, the Budget is presented on **1 February**, and the **Railway Budget was merged** into the Union Budget

notes.p: Budget receipts and spending are split into **revenue** and **capital** accounts.
points: **Revenue receipts:** tax revenue (income tax, corporate tax, GST, customs) + non-tax revenue (dividends, fees, interest)
**Capital receipts:** borrowings, recovery of loans, disinvestment proceeds
**Revenue expenditure:** does not create assets — salaries, interest, subsidies
**Capital expenditure:** creates assets or reduces liabilities — roads, railways, loans given
**Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts
**Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts); shows total borrowing need
**Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit − interest payments
**Effective revenue deficit** = revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets

notes.p:
**Direct taxes** (income tax, corporate tax) are paid by the person on whom they are levied and are usually **progressive**. **Indirect taxes** (GST, customs) are passed on to consumers and can be **regressive**.

The **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** came into force on **1 July 2017** through the **101st Constitutional Amendment (2016)**. It replaced many central and state indirect taxes. The **GST Council (Article 279A)** is chaired by the Union Finance Minister.

The **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003** set rules to control deficits; the **N.K. Singh Committee** (2017) later reviewed it and suggested debt as a key anchor. The government's current deficit targets change each year — **check the latest Budget** for figures.

The **Finance Commission (Article 280)** recommends how central tax revenue is shared between the Centre and states (**vertical devolution**) and among states (**horizontal devolution**, based on criteria like population, area, income distance and forest cover). Check the current Finance Commission's share and award period.

Prelims frequently asks about **types of deficits**, what counts as capital vs revenue, constitutional articles on the budget, and features of GST. Mains GS III asks about **fiscal consolidation**, quality of public spending, GST's impact on federalism, and subsidies' rationalisation.
Key terms.
points: Budget = Annual Financial Statement (Article 112)
Appropriation Bill: Article 114; vote on account: Article 116
Fiscal deficit = total borrowing need
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments
Disinvestment = non-debt capital receipt
GST: 101st Amendment, in force 1 July 2017; GST Council Article 279A
FRBM Act 2003; N.K. Singh Committee review
Check the latest Budget for deficit targets

cards.title: Balance of Payments
cards.body: The BoP records all transactions with the rest of the world.
points: **Current account** – trade in goods, services, remittances, investment income
**Capital account** – FDI, portfolio investment, external loans, NRI deposits
A **current account deficit** must be financed by capital inflows or by drawing down reserves

cards.title: Strengths and weaknesses
cards.body: India usually runs a **merchandise trade deficit** (large imports of crude oil, electronics and gold) but a big **services surplus** (IT and business services). India has been the world's largest recipient of remittances according to World Bank data, which also cushions the current account.

cards.title: Exchange rate and convertibility
cards.body: India follows a **managed float** — market forces set the rupee's value, but RBI intervenes to smooth excess volatility. The rupee has been fully convertible on the **current account since 1994**, but capital account convertibility is only partial.

cards.title: Forex reserves and institutions
points: Reserves include foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and reserve tranche position in the IMF
**FEMA 1999** replaced the stricter FERA 1973
**WTO** (1995) replaced GATT; India is a founding member
IMF and World Bank were born at Bretton Woods (1944)

cards.title: Depreciation in practice
cards.body: If the rupee moves from ₹80 to ₹85 per dollar, it has depreciated. Exporters earn more rupees per dollar (good for exports), but oil and electronics imports become costlier, which can raise inflation.

cards.q: Which item is part of the capital account of BoP?
cards.explain: FDI is a capital account flow; the others are current account items.

cards.q: FEMA 1999 replaced:
cards.explain: The Foreign Exchange Management Act replaced the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, shifting from control to management.

notes.p: The **Balance of Payments** records all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world in a period. It has two main accounts.
points: **Current account:** trade in goods (merchandise), services (software, tourism), primary income (interest, dividends) and secondary income/transfers (remittances)
**Capital account / financial account:** FDI, FPI, external loans, banking capital
**Trade deficit:** imports of goods exceed exports
**Current Account Deficit (CAD):** total outflows on current account exceed inflows; India usually has a trade deficit in goods but a surplus in services and large remittance inflows
Changes in **foreign exchange reserves** balance the BoP

notes.p: An **exchange rate** is the price of one currency in terms of another. India follows a **managed float** — the rupee's value is mostly set by the market, but the **RBI intervenes** to reduce excess volatility.
points: **Depreciation:** fall in the rupee's value under a floating system (more rupees per dollar)
**Devaluation:** deliberate reduction by the government/central bank under a fixed system (India devalued in 1966 and 1991)
Depreciation makes **exports cheaper** and **imports costlier**
**REER (Real Effective Exchange Rate):** trade-weighted, inflation-adjusted measure of a currency's value

notes.p: Foreign capital enters as **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** or **Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI)**.
points: **FDI:** long-term, involves control or lasting interest; considered more stable
**FPI:** investment in shares and bonds without control; can be 'hot money' that leaves quickly
Routes for FDI: **automatic route** (no prior approval) and **government route**
Sector caps and rules change — check the latest FDI policy
**Convertibility:** the rupee is fully convertible on the current account and partially on the capital account

notes.p: In **1991** India faced a severe BoP crisis: foreign exchange reserves had fallen to cover only a few weeks of imports. The government pledged gold and took IMF support. This triggered the **LPG reforms — Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation** — under PM P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Dr Manmohan Singh: industrial delicensing, lower tariffs, opening to FDI and a market-based exchange rate.

India's trade policy uses tools like tariffs, export promotion schemes and **Free Trade Agreements (FTAs)**. India is a founding member of the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**, established on **1 January 1995**. India **did not join RCEP** in 2019. Trade figures, top partners and reserve levels change — **check the latest figures** from the Commerce Ministry and RBI.
points: IMF: deals with BoP support and global monetary stability
World Bank: long-term development lending
Special Drawing Rights (SDR): IMF's reserve asset based on a basket of currencies

notes.p: Prelims asks about **components of the BoP**, which items fall in the current vs capital account, effects of rupee depreciation, and FDI vs FPI. Mains GS III asks about managing the **current account deficit**, export competitiveness, the impact of global events on the rupee, and India's FTA strategy.
Key points.
points: BoP = current account + capital/financial account
Remittances are in the current account; FDI in the capital account
India: deficit in goods trade, surplus in services
Managed float; RBI intervenes to curb volatility
Depreciation → exports cheaper, imports costlier
Rupee: fully convertible on current account, partially on capital account
1991 BoP crisis → LPG reforms
WTO: 1 January 1995; India stayed out of RCEP

cards.title: Definition
cards.body: The **Brundtland Report** ('Our Common Future', 1987) defined sustainable development as development that **meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs**. It balances **economic, social and environmental** goals.

cards.title: Milestones
points: 1972 — Stockholm Conference; UNEP set up
1987 — Brundtland Report
1992 — Rio Earth Summit: Agenda 21; UNFCCC & CBD opened for signature
2000 — Millennium Development Goals (8 goals, to 2015)
2012 — Rio+20: 'The Future We Want'
2015 — 2030 Agenda: 17 SDGs, 169 targets

cards.title: The 17 SDGs (sample)
cards.body: Goal 1 No Poverty; 2 Zero Hunger; 3 Good Health; 4 Quality Education; 5 Gender Equality; 6 Clean Water; 7 Clean Energy; 8 Decent Work; 13 Climate Action; 14 Life Below Water; 15 Life on Land; 16 Peace and Justice; **17 Partnerships** for the Goals.

cards.title: India's SDG tracking
cards.body: **NITI Aayog** coordinates SDGs and publishes the **SDG India Index** (since 2018), ranking states and UTs. The **MoSPI** maintains the National Indicator Framework. Kerala has frequently ranked at or near the top — check the latest edition.

cards.title: Human Development Index
cards.body: Published by **UNDP** in the Human Development Report since **1990** (Mahbub ul Haq, with Amartya Sen's capability ideas). Dimensions: **long and healthy life** (life expectancy), **knowledge** (mean and expected years of schooling), **standard of living** (GNI per capita, PPP).

cards.title: Who publishes which index
points: Human Development Report, Global MPI — UNDP (MPI with OPHI)
Global Gender Gap Report — World Economic Forum
Global Hunger Index — Concern Worldwide & Welthungerhilfe
World Happiness Report — UN SDSN with partners
SDG India Index — NITI Aayog

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: UPSC often asks which organisation publishes a report — it is a cheap mark if you keep a one-page table and update it from the news during the year.

cards.q: The definition of sustainable development is most associated with:
cards.explain: The 1987 Brundtland Report gave the classic definition.

cards.q: How many Sustainable Development Goals are there?
cards.explain: 17 goals with 169 targets.

cards.q: The Global Gender Gap Report is published by:
cards.explain: The World Economic Forum publishes it.

notes.p: Sustainable development rejects the idea that growth and environment are always in conflict. It emphasises **inter-generational equity** (fairness to future generations), **intra-generational equity** (fairness within the present), the **precautionary principle**, and the **polluter pays principle** — the last two have been recognised by the Supreme Court as part of Indian environmental law (e.g., **Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum, 1996**).

The **MDGs** (2000–2015) focused mainly on developing countries and on social goals such as poverty, primary education and child mortality. The **SDGs** (2016–2030) are **universal** — they apply to all countries — and integrated, covering inequality, cities, consumption, climate, oceans, land and institutions. They were adopted by the UN General Assembly in **September 2015** as 'Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda'. The principle '**leave no one behind**' is central.
Beyond GDP, several measures track well-being and sustainability:
points: **HDI** — health, education and income
**Inequality-adjusted HDI** and **Gender Development Index** — from UNDP
**Multidimensional Poverty Index** — deprivations in health, education, living standards
**Green GDP** — adjusts output for resource depletion and environmental damage
**Ecological footprint** — demand on nature compared with biocapacity
**SDG India Index** — composite score from 0 to 100 for each state

notes.p: India has linked SDGs to its schemes — for example, **Swachh Bharat** (Goal 6), **Ujjwala** (Goal 7), **Jal Jeevan Mission** (Goal 6), **Ayushman Bharat** (Goal 3) and **Poshan Abhiyaan** (Goal 2). States prepare SDG vision documents and district indicator frameworks. India promoted **Mission LiFE** (Lifestyle for Environment, launched 2022), which emphasises mindful consumption by individuals, and the **circular economy** — reduce, reuse, recycle — through rules on plastics, e-waste and batteries.

Suppose two countries have the same per-capita income. Country A has higher life expectancy and schooling. Which has the higher HDI?

Step 1: HDI is a **geometric mean** of three dimension indices.
Step 2: Income is equal, so the difference comes from health and education indices.
Step 3: A scores higher on both.
Answer: **Country A**. This shows why HDI rankings can differ sharply from GDP rankings.

Expect questions on milestones, index publishers, HDI components and principles such as polluter pays. Link with environment and climate chapters, since UPSC often blends them.

Remember the difference between **weak sustainability** (natural capital can be replaced by man-made capital, as long as total capital does not fall) and **strong sustainability** (critical natural capital — such as the ozone layer or biodiversity — cannot be substituted). Also note the idea of **common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR)**, born at Rio 1992, which India uses in climate negotiations to stress that developed countries bear greater historical responsibility.
Recall.
points: Brundtland 1987 — classic definition
Rio 1992 — Agenda 21; UNFCCC & CBD
SDG India Index — NITI Aayog
HDI: health, education, income — UNDP since 1990
Gender Gap — WEF; GHI — Concern & Welthungerhilfe
Polluter pays & precautionary principles

cards.title: Poverty lines
cards.body: Expert groups estimated poverty: **Alagh (1979)** — calorie norms; **Lakdawala (1993)**; **Tendulkar (2009)** — 21.9% poor in 2011–12; **Rangarajan (2014)** — 29.5% in 2011–12. Official consumption-based poverty estimates have not been updated on the same basis since; check the latest surveys.

cards.title: Multidimensional poverty
cards.body: The **Global MPI** (UNDP and OPHI) measures deprivations in **health, education and living standards**. **NITI Aayog's national MPI** adds indicators such as maternal health and bank accounts, using NFHS data, and reported a sharp fall between NFHS-4 (2015–16) and NFHS-5 (2019–21).

cards.title: International poverty line
cards.body: The **World Bank** line was **$2.15 a day** (2017 PPP); in 2025 it was updated to **$3.00 a day** (2021 PPP). Changes in PPP data shift poverty counts, so compare figures only on the same basis.

cards.title: Measuring inequality
cards.body: The **Lorenz curve** plots cumulative income/consumption share against cumulative population share. The **Gini coefficient** ranges from **0 (perfect equality)** to **1 (perfect inequality)**. The **Palma ratio** compares the top 10% with the bottom 40%.

cards.title: Financial inclusion
cards.body: **PMJDY (2014)** — bank accounts for all; **JAM trinity** (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) enables **Direct Benefit Transfer**. **MUDRA (2015)** — loans for micro enterprises (Shishu, Kishore, Tarun). Payments banks and small finance banks; **RBI's Financial Inclusion Index** (0–100) since 2021.

cards.title: Safety-net programmes
cards.body: **MGNREGA (2005)** — legal guarantee of 100 days of wage work per rural household per year. **NFSA (2013)** — subsidised grain to up to 75% rural and 50% urban population; **5 kg per person per month** for priority households, **35 kg per household** for Antyodaya. **DAY-NRLM** — self-help groups.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Absolute poverty is measured against a fixed line; relative poverty compares with others in society. 'Inclusive growth' was the theme of the **11th Five-Year Plan** (2007–12).

cards.q: The Gini coefficient value of 0 indicates:
cards.explain: 0 means everyone has the same income.

cards.q: Which committee estimated 21.9% poverty for 2011–12?
cards.explain: The Tendulkar methodology gave 21.9%.

cards.q: Under NFSA, Antyodaya households are entitled to:
cards.explain: AAY households get 35 kg per household per month.

notes.p: Poverty can be **absolute** (inability to meet a minimum standard) or **relative** (deprivation compared with others). It can be **chronic** or **transient**. Amartya Sen's **capability approach** views poverty as deprivation of basic capabilities — health, education, freedom — not just low income. This broader view underlies multidimensional measures.

1. **Alagh Task Force (1979)**: poverty line from minimum calories (2,400 rural, 2,100 urban).
2. **Lakdawala (1993)**: state-specific lines; consumer price indices.
3. **Tendulkar (2009)**: moved away from calorie anchoring; included health and education spending; uniform consumption basket for rural and urban.
4. **Rangarajan (2014)**: higher lines and separate basket.

The household consumption surveys (**HCES**) of **2022–23** and **2023–24** released by MoSPI have revived the debate; researchers using them report large declines in extreme poverty, but no new official line has been adopted on the old basis — check the latest position before quoting a number.

Inequality has income, wealth, regional, gender and social dimensions. Consumption inequality in India is lower than income or wealth inequality. Causes include unequal access to education and health, informal employment, and asset concentration. Policies to reduce it include progressive taxation, public services, minimum wages, land reforms and targeted transfers.
Financial inclusion gives the poor safe savings, credit, insurance and pensions:
points: **PMJDY**: zero-balance accounts, RuPay card, overdraft facility
**PMJJBY** (life) and **PMSBY** (accident) — low-cost insurance
**Atal Pension Yojana** — pension for unorganised workers
**Stand-Up India** — loans for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs
**Self-help groups** and **microfinance** — group lending
**UPI** and digital public infrastructure have widened access to payments

notes.p: Wage employment: **MGNREGA**, with work demanded by the worker, wages paid by the Centre, social audits and a 15-day rule for work or unemployment allowance. Food security: the **NFSA** and the **PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana**, which provides free foodgrains to NFSA beneficiaries (extended for five years from January 2024). Housing: **PMAY**. Income support: **PM-KISAN** — ₹6,000 a year to landholding farmer families in three instalments. Self-employment: **DAY-NRLM** and **DAY-NULM**.

Statements on committee methodologies, scheme features (who funds, who is eligible) and index sources are common. Learn one distinguishing feature for each scheme — for example, MGNREGA is **demand-driven** and a **legal right**.

A worked check: 'Under MGNREGA, at least one-third of beneficiaries should be women' — **true** (the Act gives priority to women so that at least one-third of beneficiaries are women). 'MGNREGA wages are fixed by each state independently' — **false**; the Centre notifies state-wise wage rates. Small details like these decide the answer, so read the Act's key provisions once.
Recall.
points: Tendulkar 21.9%; Rangarajan 29.5% (2011–12)
Global MPI — UNDP & OPHI; national MPI — NITI Aayog
World Bank line $3.00/day (2021 PPP) from 2025
Gini 0 = equality; Lorenz curve
PMJDY 2014; JAM; DBT; MUDRA 2015
MGNREGA 100 days; NFSA 75%/50% coverage
PM-KISAN ₹6,000 per year

cards.title: Key terms
cards.body: **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)** — average children per woman over her lifetime; **replacement level ≈ 2.1**. **Dependency ratio** — dependants (0–14 and 65+) per 100 people aged 15–64. **Demographic dividend** — growth potential when the working-age share rises.

cards.title: Demographic transition
cards.body: Stage 1: high birth and death rates. Stage 2: death rates fall, births stay high → rapid growth. Stage 3: birth rates fall. Stage 4: both low, population stabilises. India is in the **later stages**, with wide variation between states.

cards.title: Where India stands
cards.body: **NFHS-5 (2019–21)** reported a national **TFR of 2.0**, below replacement. UN estimates suggest India became the **world's most populous country in 2023**. Southern and western states have low fertility and are ageing faster; some northern states still have above-replacement fertility.

cards.title: Data sources
cards.body: **Census** (every ten years; last held 2011), **Sample Registration System (SRS)** for birth, death, infant and maternal mortality rates, **NFHS** for health and family indicators, and **PLFS** for employment.

cards.title: Population policy
cards.body: India launched an official **family planning programme in 1952** — among the first in the world. The **National Population Policy 2000** aimed at replacement-level fertility and a stable population by **2045**, stressing voluntary, rights-based family planning and maternal and child health.

cards.title: Reaping the dividend
cards.body: A young population is an asset only if there are **jobs, skills, health and education**. Key levers: raising **female labour force participation**, skilling (Skill India, PMKVY), quality schooling, and labour-intensive manufacturing and services.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: A falling dependency ratio is the core of the dividend. As fertility keeps falling and life expectancy rises, the **old-age dependency ratio** will rise — so the dividend window is time-limited.

cards.q: Replacement-level fertility is approximately:
cards.explain: A TFR of about 2.1 keeps the population stable in the long run, ignoring migration.

cards.q: Which survey is the main source for India's infant mortality rate between censuses?
cards.explain: SRS provides annual vital rates such as birth, death and infant mortality rates.

cards.q: The National Population Policy 2000 aimed for population stabilisation by:
cards.explain: Its long-term objective was a stable population by 2045.

notes.p:
Population size, age structure and distribution shape labour supply, savings, public spending and politics. Prelims tests concepts (TFR, IMR, MMR, dependency ratio), data sources, and policy. Questions often contain trap words such as 'always' or 'only' — demographic outcomes vary widely across states.

The broad story is simple. In 1951 India's population was about 36 crore; by 2011 it had crossed 121 crore. Mortality fell first, thanks to public health, vaccines and food security; fertility fell later and more slowly, helped by female education, urbanisation, higher age at marriage and wider access to contraception. Today India's challenge is shifting from **controlling numbers** to improving the **quality** of its human capital — health, skills and jobs.
Learn the definitions precisely:
points: **Crude Birth/Death Rate:** per 1,000 population per year
**Infant Mortality Rate (IMR):** infant deaths (under one year) per 1,000 live births
**Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR):** maternal deaths per **1,00,000 live births**
**Sex Ratio (India):** females per 1,000 males; **Sex Ratio at Birth** reflects son preference
**Life expectancy:** average years a newborn is expected to live
**Median age:** age that divides the population in half

notes.p: As fertility falls, the share of children declines before the share of the elderly rises, so the share of **working-age people** peaks. This can raise **savings, investment and growth** — as seen in East Asian economies. India's working-age share is expected to remain high for the next few decades, but estimates of the exact window vary; use cautious language. Without jobs, the dividend can become a **'demographic burden'**, with youth unemployment and social stress.

Kerala, Tamil Nadu and several other states reached replacement fertility long ago, while Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya had higher fertility in NFHS-5. Consequences: **internal migration** from younger to older states, rising **elder care** needs in the south, and political debates over **delimitation** of seats after the freeze ends. The **Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI)** collects data on the elderly.

A region has 300 children (0–14), 600 working-age people (15–64) and 100 elderly (65+).

Step 1: Dependants = 300 + 100 = 400.
Step 2: Dependency ratio = (400 ÷ 600) × 100 ≈ **66.7**.
Step 3: Child dependency = 50; old-age dependency ≈ 16.7.

If fertility falls so children drop to 200 while working-age rises to 700, the ratio becomes (300 ÷ 700) × 100 ≈ **42.9** — a demographic dividend in action.

Expect definitions (MMR is per lakh live births, IMR per thousand), data sources, and policy statements. Avoid quoting precise recent mortality numbers unless sure; UPSC usually asks concepts rather than the latest decimal values.
Recall.
points: TFR replacement ≈ 2.1; NFHS-5 TFR 2.0
IMR per 1,000 live births; MMR per 1,00,000
Dependency ratio = dependants ÷ working-age × 100
Family planning programme since 1952
NPP 2000 — stabilisation by 2045
India most populous country from 2023 (UN estimates)
Dividend needs jobs, skills, health

chapters.title: Social Sector Initiatives: Health, Education, Nutrition

cards.title: Ayushman Bharat (2018)
cards.body: Two pillars: **Ayushman Arogya Mandirs** (earlier Health and Wellness Centres) for comprehensive primary care, and **PM-JAY** — health cover up to **₹5 lakh per family per year** for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation. In 2024 coverage was extended to all citizens aged **70 and above**, irrespective of income.

cards.title: Health programmes
cards.body: **National Health Mission** (NRHM 2005 + NUHM 2013); **Janani Suraksha Yojana** (2005) — cash for institutional delivery; **Mission Indradhanush** (2014) — full immunisation; **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission** (2021) — digital health IDs (ABHA). The **National Health Policy 2017** targeted public health spending of 2.5% of GDP by 2025.

cards.title: NEP 2020
cards.body: Replaces 10+2 with **5+3+3+4**; mother tongue or regional language as medium preferably till Class 5; focus on **foundational literacy and numeracy**; target **50% GER** in higher education by 2035; public education spending goal of **6% of GDP**.

cards.title: School schemes
cards.body: **Samagra Shiksha** (2018) merges SSA, RMSA and teacher education. **PM POSHAN** (2021) — the renamed mid-day meal scheme. **RTE Act** reserves **25%** of entry-level seats in private unaided schools for disadvantaged children.

cards.title: Nutrition
cards.body: **ICDS** (1975) runs **anganwadis** for children under six and mothers. **POSHAN Abhiyaan** (2018) targets stunting, undernutrition and anaemia; now under **Mission Poshan 2.0**. **PM Matru Vandana Yojana** (2017) gives cash support to pregnant and lactating women.

cards.title: Water, sanitation and energy
cards.body: **Swachh Bharat Mission** (2014) — toilets and ODF status; ODF Plus in phase II. **Jal Jeevan Mission** (2019) — functional household **tap connections** for every rural home ('Har Ghar Jal'). **PM Ujjwala Yojana** (2016) — LPG connections for poor women.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For any scheme learn four things: **ministry**, **target group**, **benefit**, and **funding pattern** (central sector = 100% Centre; centrally sponsored = shared with states). Most UPSC scheme questions test these.

cards.q: PM-JAY provides health cover of up to:
cards.explain: ₹5 lakh per family per year for hospitalisation.

cards.q: NEP 2020 replaced the 10+2 structure with:
cards.explain: Foundational (5), preparatory (3), middle (3), secondary (4).

cards.q: Jal Jeevan Mission aims to provide:
options: Tap water connections to rural households
cards.explain: It aims at functional household tap connections in rural areas.

notes.p:
Health, education, nutrition, water and sanitation shape **human capital**, which drives long-run growth and the demographic dividend. Under the Constitution, **health** and **school education** involve both levels of government — public health is a State subject, while education is in the **Concurrent List** (moved there by the 42nd Amendment). Hence most schemes are **centrally sponsored**, with cost-sharing between Centre and states.

For most centrally sponsored schemes the funding ratio is typically **60:40** (Centre:State), **90:10** for north-eastern and Himalayan states, and **100%** central for Union Territories without legislatures — though individual schemes may differ. Outcome monitoring increasingly uses dashboards and surveys such as NFHS, UDISE+ and the National Achievement Survey (now PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan). The big shift in recent years has been from building **infrastructure** (toilets, schools, clinics) to ensuring **outcomes** (use, learning, health).

India's approach combines **public provision** (primary health centres, district hospitals) with **insurance** for hospitalisation. Key challenges: high **out-of-pocket expenditure**, shortage of doctors and nurses in rural areas, and the rising burden of **non-communicable diseases**. Other initiatives: **Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana** (generic medicines), **TB Mukt Bharat** campaign, and **eSanjeevani** telemedicine. The **National Medical Commission** (2020) replaced the Medical Council of India.

Enrolment in primary school is near-universal, but surveys show weak **learning outcomes**. NEP 2020 responds with **NIPUN Bharat** for foundational skills, a national curriculum framework, **multiple entry and exit** in higher education with an **Academic Bank of Credits**, and a proposed single higher-education regulator. Programmes such as **PM SHRI** schools upgrade selected schools as models.

NFHS surveys show persistent **stunting**, **wasting** and **anaemia**. Strategies combine supplementary nutrition at anganwadis, school meals, **fortified rice** in public distribution, and behaviour-change communication. **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao** (launched 2015 at Panipat) addresses the child sex ratio and girls' education. **Mission Shakti** covers women's safety and empowerment schemes such as One Stop Centres.

Most Indian workers are **informal**. The **e-Shram** portal (2021) registers unorganised workers. Parliament passed **four Labour Codes** (wages; industrial relations; social security; occupational safety, health and working conditions) in 2019–2020, consolidating 29 central labour laws — check the latest status of their rules and implementation. Pension and insurance schemes such as APY, PMJJBY and PMSBY extend basic social security.

Questions test scheme features, the nodal ministry and constitutional basis. A worked check: 'PM POSHAN covers students of Classes 1–8 in government and government-aided schools, and balvatikas' — this is the scheme's stated coverage, so the statement is correct. Always look for subtle errors in target group or year.
Recall.

chapters.title: Agricultural Economy: MSP, Markets & Food Security

cards.title: Agriculture's place
cards.body: Agriculture and allied sectors contribute **under a fifth** of India's GVA but employ a much larger share of the workforce — **over two-fifths** in recent PLFS rounds. This gap shows low productivity per worker and disguised unemployment.

cards.title: Green Revolution
cards.body: From the mid-1960s, **high-yielding varieties** (HYV) of wheat and rice, irrigation, fertilisers and assured prices raised output, mainly in **Punjab, Haryana and western UP**. Associated scientists: **Norman Borlaug** and **M.S. Swaminathan**. Downsides: regional inequality, groundwater depletion, soil health decline.

cards.title: Minimum Support Price
cards.body: The government announces MSP for **22 mandated crops** on the recommendation of the **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)**, plus the **Fair and Remunerative Price** for sugarcane. Since 2018–19, MSP is set at least **1.5 times the A2+FL cost** of production.

cards.title: Cost concepts
points: A2 — paid-out costs (seeds, fertiliser, hired labour, fuel)
A2+FL — A2 plus imputed value of family labour
C2 — comprehensive cost: A2+FL plus rent and interest on owned land and capital

cards.title: Markets and reforms
cards.body: Most states regulate trade through **APMC** mandis. **e-NAM** (2016) links mandis electronically. The three **farm laws of 2020** were **repealed in 2021** after farmer protests. **FPOs** (Farmer Producer Organisations) help small farmers aggregate; a scheme for 10,000 FPOs began in 2020.

cards.title: Risk and inputs
cards.body: **PMFBY** (2016) crop insurance: farmer premium **2%** (kharif), **1.5%** (rabi), **5%** (commercial/horticultural). **Soil Health Card** (2015); **PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana** (2015) — 'Har Khet Ko Pani', 'Per Drop More Crop'; **Kisan Credit Card** (1998).

cards.title: WTO farm subsidy boxes
points: Amber box — trade-distorting (e.g., price support); capped (de minimis 10% of production value for developing countries)
Blue box — production-limiting payments
Green box — minimal distortion (research, extension, environment); not capped
Bali 2013 'peace clause' protects public stockholding for food security

cards.q: MSP is recommended by:
cards.explain: The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices recommends MSP.

cards.q: Under PMFBY, the farmer's premium for rabi food and oilseed crops is:
cards.explain: 1.5% for rabi, 2% for kharif, 5% for commercial/horticultural crops.

cards.q: Which WTO box covers subsidies that are not capped?
cards.explain: Green box subsidies cause minimal distortion and are not capped.

notes.p:
Indian farms are mostly **small and marginal** (below 2 hectares) — over four-fifths of holdings by number, according to Agricultural Census data. Fragmentation limits mechanisation and credit. Around half of the net sown area depends on **rainfall**, making output sensitive to the monsoon. Allied sectors — **livestock, fisheries, horticulture** — have grown faster than crops and now make up a large share of agricultural output.

Key structural problems include low **productivity** per hectare compared with global leaders, falling **groundwater** in the north-west, poor **post-harvest** storage and cold chains, high dependence on **informal credit** in some regions, and weak **price discovery** for perishables. Agricultural income is also exempt from central income tax, and agriculture itself is a **State subject** (Entry 14, State List), which is why reforms need state cooperation.

The **Food Corporation of India** (1965) and state agencies buy grain at MSP, store it as **buffer stock**, and supply the **Targeted Public Distribution System**. Under **decentralised procurement**, some states procure and distribute grain themselves. The system ensures food security and price stability but encourages a **wheat–rice bias**, burdens the subsidy bill and strains water in procurement-heavy states. Procurement is effective mainly for wheat and rice in a few states, so many farmers do not actually receive MSP.

After independence, states pursued:
1. **Abolition of intermediaries** (zamindari) — the most successful.
2. **Tenancy reforms** — security of tenure, fair rent; mixed results (West Bengal's **Operation Barga** is a well-known example).
3. **Land ceilings** — redistribution of surplus land; limited by evasion.
4. **Consolidation of holdings**.
Today's focus is on **land records digitisation** and leasing laws such as the model land leasing framework.
Different 'revolutions' are linked with sectors:
points: **White Revolution** — milk; **Operation Flood** (from 1970), led by **Verghese Kurien** through cooperatives (Amul model); India is the world's largest milk producer
**Blue Revolution** — fisheries
**Yellow Revolution** — oilseeds (Technology Mission on Oilseeds, 1986)
**Golden Revolution** — horticulture (fruits, vegetables, honey)
**Silver Revolution** — eggs/poultry

notes.p:
Suppose for a crop: A2 = ₹1,200 per quintal; family labour value = ₹300; rent and interest on owned assets = ₹500.

Step 1: A2+FL = 1,200 + 300 = ₹1,500.
Step 2: MSP at 1.5 × A2+FL = ₹2,250.
Step 3: C2 = 1,500 + 500 = ₹2,000; 1.5 × C2 = ₹3,000.

The gap (₹2,250 vs ₹3,000) is why farm groups demand MSP based on **C2** — as the **Swaminathan Commission** (National Commission on Farmers) recommended.
Expect questions on MSP and CACP, procurement, WTO boxes, PMFBY features, e-NAM, and allied sectors. Learn the cost concepts — they have appeared in Prelims.
Recall.
