chapters.title: Planning, Resource Mobilisation, Growth & Inclusive Development

cards.title: From Planning Commission to NITI Aayog
points: Planning Commission set up by executive resolution, **1950**
12 Five-Year Plans; last ended 2017
**NITI Aayog** replaced it on 1 January 2015
NITI: think tank, cooperative federalism, no fund-allocation power

cards.title: Plan models
points: 1st Plan (1951–56): agriculture; Harrod–Domar inspired
2nd Plan (1956–61): heavy industry; **Mahalanobis model**
Plan holiday (1966–69)
11th Plan: "faster and more inclusive growth"
12th Plan: "faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth"

cards.title: Resource mobilisation
points: Taxes: direct (income, corporate) and indirect (GST, customs)
Non-tax revenue: dividends, fees, spectrum
Borrowing: market loans, small savings, external
Disinvestment and **asset monetisation**
Fiscal discipline: **FRBM Act, 2003**

cards.title: Growth vs development
cards.body: **Growth** is the rise in output (GDP). **Development** includes improvements in health, education, incomes, freedoms and equity. Amartya Sen's **capability approach** underlies the Human Development Index.

cards.title: Inclusive growth
cards.body: Growth that is **broad-based across sectors and regions**, creates decent jobs, and lets the poor and marginalised share in gains. Tools: financial inclusion (PM Jan Dhan Yojana, 2014), skilling, MSME support, social protection, and investment in health and education.

cards.title: Employment issues
points: Large **informal** workforce
Low female labour force participation (rising recently)
Structural transformation: workers moving slowly out of farming
"Jobless growth" debate
Data: PLFS (periodic labour force survey)

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Inclusive-growth answers should name four dimensions — jobs, regions, social groups, gender — and end with human capital and MSME-led employment.

cards.q: NITI Aayog came into existence on:
cards.explain: It replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.

cards.q: The Second Five-Year Plan was based on the model of:
cards.explain: The Mahalanobis model emphasised heavy industries.

notes.p: "Indian Economy and issues relating to **planning, mobilisation of resources, growth, development and employment**"; "**Inclusive growth** and issues arising from it"; and "**Government budgeting**" (see the Fiscal Policy & Budget chapter). Mains questions are analytical: why growth has not created enough jobs, how to raise the tax-GDP ratio, or what inclusive growth requires.

India adopted **centralised planning** in 1950 through the Planning Commission, chaired by the Prime Minister, with the **National Development Council** (1952) bringing in states. Early plans built dams, steel plants and institutions. The Mahalanobis strategy of the Second Plan prioritised heavy industry and the public sector. Crises — wars, droughts — led to a **plan holiday** (1966–69) and the Green Revolution. After **1991**, planning became **indicative**, with markets playing a larger role.

In **2015**, **NITI Aayog** replaced the Planning Commission. It has no power to allocate funds; it acts as a **policy think tank**, promotes **cooperative and competitive federalism** (indices ranking states), monitors SDGs, and runs the Aspirational Districts Programme. Its Governing Council includes all Chief Ministers.

Government needs resources for development and welfare. Sources: **tax revenue** (India's tax-GDP ratio is modest compared with many advanced economies); **non-tax revenue** (RBI dividends, spectrum, PSU dividends); **borrowing** (government securities, small savings); **disinvestment**; and the **National Monetisation Pipeline (2021)**, which leases brownfield assets for upfront funds.

Reforms to raise resources: widen the tax base, rationalise GST rates, reduce exemptions, improve compliance with technology (faceless assessment, e-invoicing), property tax reform for local bodies, and better targeting of subsidies. The **FRBM Act, 2003** and later amendments set fiscal deficit and debt targets to keep borrowing sustainable. Private resources — savings, FDI, capital markets — matter as much as public ones.

India has been among the fastest-growing major economies, but challenges persist: much of the workforce is in **informal** jobs with low productivity; agriculture still employs a large share of workers relative to its output share; manufacturing's employment share has grown slowly; and **female labour force participation**, though improving, is low. Growth must translate into **productive employment** through labour-intensive manufacturing, MSMEs, construction, tourism, care economy and agri-processing.
Inclusive growth means expanding opportunity for all. Dimensions:
points: **Sectoral:** raise farm incomes and non-farm rural jobs
**Regional:** reduce gaps between states and districts (Aspirational Districts)
**Social:** SCs, STs, minorities, women
**Financial:** bank accounts, credit, insurance (Jan Dhan, Mudra, PMJJBY, PMSBY)
**Human capital:** quality education, health, skills
**Social protection:** pensions, food security, health cover

notes.p:
Question type: "Why has India's growth not generated enough jobs?"
**Reasons:** capital-intensive manufacturing, services growth in skilled segments, small firm size, rigid regulations historically, skill mismatch, low female participation.
**Steps taken:** labour codes, PLI, MSME definition revision, Skill India, PM Vishwakarma.
**Way forward:** labour-intensive sectors (textiles, leather, food processing, tourism), urban infrastructure, care economy, better data.
**Conclusion:** jobs as the bridge between growth and inclusion.
Key points.
points: Planning Commission 1950; NDC 1952; NITI Aayog 1 Jan 2015
Mahalanobis model in 2nd Plan; plan holiday 1966–69
Resources: taxes, non-tax, borrowing, disinvestment, monetisation
FRBM Act 2003
Growth ≠ development; capability approach (Sen)
Inclusive growth: sectoral, regional, social, financial, human capital
Jobs: informality, low FLFPR, structural transformation

cards.title: The 1991 crisis
points: Balance-of-payments crisis; forex reserves fell very low
Gold pledged to raise foreign currency
High fiscal deficit; Gulf War oil shock
IMF support with structural reforms

cards.title: LPG reforms
points: **Liberalisation**: end of most industrial licensing
**Privatisation**: disinvestment; fewer reserved public sector areas
**Globalisation**: lower tariffs, FDI and FPI opened, rupee made convertible on current account

cards.title: New Industrial Policy, 1991
points: Licensing abolished except for a short list
MRTP restrictions on large firms removed
Public sector reserved list cut sharply
Automatic approval for FDI in many industries
Technology agreements eased

cards.title: Recent industrial policy changes
points: **Make in India** (2014)
Corporate tax cut (2019)
**PLI schemes** (2020 onwards)
MSME definition revised (2020)
Four **Labour Codes**

cards.title: Effects of liberalisation
points: Higher growth; services and IT boom
More competition and consumer choice
FDI inflows; integration with global value chains
Criticism: jobless growth, agrarian neglect, inequality, premature deindustrialisation

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: A balanced Mains answer gives credit to 1991 reforms for growth and poverty reduction while noting incomplete reforms in factor markets (land, labour, power) and the manufacturing gap.

cards.q: The New Industrial Policy announced in July 1991 did NOT:
options: Reduce reserved sectors for the public sector
cards.explain: Bank nationalisation happened in 1969 and 1980, not in 1991.

cards.q: Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes reward firms on the basis of:
options: Incremental sales of goods manufactured in India
cards.explain: PLI gives incentives linked to incremental sales over a base year.

notes.p: From the **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956**, India followed a state-led model: the public sector held the "commanding heights", private industry needed **licences** for capacity and location, large firms faced **MRTP** controls, many products were reserved for small industry, and foreign investment was restricted (FERA, 1973). The model built a broad industrial base but led to inefficiency, the "licence-permit-quota raj", low productivity and slow growth.

In 1990–91, a **balance-of-payments crisis** struck: foreign exchange reserves fell to very low levels, oil prices spiked during the Gulf War, remittances fell and fiscal deficits were high. India pledged gold and sought IMF assistance.

The response was **LPG reforms**: the **New Industrial Policy (July 1991)** abolished licensing for all but a short list of industries, removed MRTP asset thresholds, reduced the public sector's reserved areas, and allowed automatic FDI approval in many industries. Trade reforms cut tariffs and removed quantitative restrictions; the rupee was devalued and later made **convertible on the current account**; financial sector reforms followed the **Narasimham Committee**.

notes.h: Effects of liberalisation on the economy
notes.p: Positives: higher and more stable growth, a **services and IT boom**, rising FDI, a larger middle class, better consumer choice, competitive firms, and a fall in poverty. Concerns: growth led by services rather than labour-intensive manufacturing; **jobless growth** debates; agrarian distress; rising **inequality** across regions and classes; informalisation of labour; and dependence on volatile capital flows. A useful phrase: India's reforms were **"product-market reforms with factor-market reforms lagging"** — land, labour and power markets changed slowly.
Recent measures:
points: **Make in India** (2014) to raise manufacturing
**Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code** (2016) for time-bound resolution
**GST** (2017) creating a common market
**Corporate tax reduction** (2019), including a lower rate for new manufacturing firms
**PLI schemes** across sectors such as electronics, pharma, auto, textiles and solar modules
**MSME definition** based on investment and turnover (2020)
**Labour Codes** consolidating 29 central laws into four
Industrial corridors, PM Gati Shakti, and the National Logistics Policy
Semiconductor mission and **Atmanirbhar Bharat**

notes.p: Manufacturing's share of GDP has remained broadly stagnant for years despite policy efforts, though sectors like mobile phone assembly have grown strongly under PLI. Challenges: high logistics and power costs, land acquisition, compliance burden, small firm size, skill gaps and limited R&D. Way forward: ease of doing business at state and district levels, cluster development, export orientation, technology upgrading of MSMEs, and stable trade policy.

Question type: "Evaluate the effects of liberalisation on Indian industry."
**Intro:** 1991 crisis and NIP.
**Positive effects:** competition, efficiency, FDI, auto and pharma growth, IT services.
**Negative effects:** small units facing competition, import dependence (electronics, APIs), regional concentration.
**Recent policy:** PLI, IBC, GST, labour codes.
**Conclusion:** second-generation reforms in factor markets needed.
Key points.
points: 1956 IPR: public sector commanding heights; licence raj
1991 BoP crisis; gold pledged; IMF
NIP July 1991: delicensing, MRTP limits removed, FDI automatic route
Trade and financial reforms; current account convertibility
Since 2014: Make in India, IBC, GST, tax cut, PLI, labour codes
Manufacturing share stagnant; factor-market reforms pending

cards.title: Syllabus scope
cards.body: "**Infrastructure**: energy, ports, roads, airports, railways etc." and "**Investment models**." Questions ask how to finance and deliver infrastructure efficiently.

cards.title: Flagship programmes
points: **Bharatmala** (roads, 2017); **Sagarmala** (ports, 2015)
**UDAN** regional air connectivity (2016)
**Dedicated Freight Corridors** (rail)
**National Infrastructure Pipeline** (2019)
**PM Gati Shakti** (2021) master plan; National Logistics Policy (2022)

cards.title: PPP models
points: **BOT (toll)**: private builds, collects tolls, transfers
**BOT (annuity)**: government pays fixed annuity
**BOOT/BOO**: own–operate variants
**EPC**: government funds; contractor only builds
**HAM**: hybrid — government pays part during construction, rest as annuity

cards.title: Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM)
cards.body: Introduced for highways in **2016**. The government pays **40%** of project cost during construction; the developer finances the rest and is repaid through annuities plus interest. Traffic risk stays with the government, reducing developer risk.

cards.title: Newer financing tools
points: **InvITs** and **REITs**: pooled vehicles for completed assets
**TOT** (toll-operate-transfer): lease operating highways for upfront payment
**National Monetisation Pipeline** (2021)
**NaBFID** (2021): development finance institution
Green bonds; municipal bonds

cards.title: Problems in PPPs
points: Land acquisition and clearance delays
Aggressive bidding and unrealistic traffic estimates
Contract renegotiation, disputes
Bank stress (twin balance sheet problem)
Kelkar Committee (2015) on revisiting PPPs

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Map each risk to who bears it: construction risk (developer), traffic risk (government under HAM, developer under BOT-toll), regulatory risk (government). Good PPP design allocates risk to whoever can best manage it.

cards.q: Under the Hybrid Annuity Model for highways, the government pays during construction about:
cards.explain: HAM provides 40% of project cost from the government during construction.

cards.q: In an EPC contract, the project is financed by:
cards.explain: In Engineering, Procurement and Construction, the government funds and owns; the contractor only builds.

notes.p:
Infrastructure — energy, transport, logistics, water, digital and urban services — raises productivity, connects markets and attracts investment. India's logistics costs have historically been high relative to leading economies, hurting competitiveness. Public capital expenditure has been raised sharply in recent budgets to crowd in private investment. Check the latest Budget for current figures.

Infrastructure has features that make financing hard: **large upfront costs**, **long gestation**, returns spread over decades, and risks from land, clearances and demand. Banks, which rely on short-term deposits, face **asset–liability mismatch** when lending for 20-year projects — a key reason for creating a development finance institution and deepening bond markets.
Key initiatives:
points: **Roads:** Bharatmala Pariyojana, expressways, PMGSY for rural roads
**Railways:** Dedicated Freight Corridors, station redevelopment, semi-high-speed trains, high-speed rail (Mumbai–Ahmedabad)
**Ports:** Sagarmala — port modernisation, coastal shipping, port-led industrialisation
**Airports:** UDAN for regional connectivity; PPP in major airports
**Energy:** renewable expansion, green hydrogen mission, transmission (green energy corridors), nuclear
**Integrated planning:** **PM Gati Shakti** National Master Plan (2021) — GIS-based coordination across ministries; **National Logistics Policy** (2022)

notes.p:
**Public funding (EPC):** the government pays and owns; the contractor builds. Simple but strains budgets.
**BOT-Toll:** the private partner finances, builds and recovers costs through user charges; bears traffic risk.
**BOT-Annuity:** the private partner builds; the government pays fixed annuities.
**Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM):** a middle path introduced in 2016 — the government funds 40% during construction, the developer arranges 60%, and the government pays annuities with interest over the concession; tolls are collected by the government.
**TOT:** the government leases operational highways for an upfront payment, recycling capital.
**InvITs/REITs:** trusts that pool income-generating assets and sell units to investors, letting developers recycle capital.

notes.h: Worked example: comparing risk under models
notes.p:
Consider a 100 km highway costing ₹1,000 crore.
**EPC:** government pays all ₹1,000 crore over construction; carries all financing and traffic risk.
**BOT-Toll:** developer raises ₹1,000 crore; recovers via tolls over, say, 20 years; carries traffic risk — if traffic is lower than projected, it may default.
**HAM:** government pays ₹400 crore (40%) during construction; developer raises ₹600 crore and receives annuities plus interest; government collects tolls and bears traffic risk.
Insight: HAM revived highway PPPs after many BOT projects stalled because developers were unwilling to take traffic risk.

PPPs in India faced **land acquisition delays**, **aggressive bids**, poor traffic forecasts, renegotiation, and stressed loans that contributed to the **twin balance sheet** problem. The **Kelkar Committee (2015)** recommended better risk allocation, an independent regulator, dispute resolution mechanisms and protection for honest decisions by officials. Other reforms: a dedicated DFI (**NaBFID**), deeper corporate bond markets, credit enhancement, model concession agreements, and faster clearances.
Key points.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In cropping-pattern answers connect agronomy to policy: MSP, power subsidies and procurement shaped the rice–wheat cycle; diversification needs assured markets and procurement for alternatives.

cards.q: Which is the largest source of irrigation in India?
cards.explain: Groundwater via wells and tubewells irrigates the largest share of land.

cards.q: "Per Drop More Crop" is a component of:
cards.explain: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana promotes micro-irrigation under this component.

cards.q: Mustard and gram are typically:
cards.explain: They are sown in winter and harvested in spring.

notes.p: GS III: "**Major crops — cropping patterns** in various parts of the country, different types of **irrigation** and irrigation systems; **storage, transport and marketing** of agricultural produce and issues and related constraints; **e-technology** in the aid of farmers." Agriculture prices, MSP and food security are covered in the Agricultural Economy chapter; this chapter covers the production and marketing chain.

A **cropping pattern** is the proportion of area under different crops at a time. It depends on climate, soil, water, technology, prices and policy. **Rice** dominates the east, south and north-west; **wheat** the Indo-Gangetic plains; **cotton** the Deccan black soils; **pulses and oilseeds** rainfed central India; **plantation crops** (tea, coffee, rubber) the hills and Kerala.

The Green Revolution created a **rice–wheat monoculture** in Punjab and Haryana, supported by MSP procurement and free or cheap power — leading to falling water tables, soil degradation and stubble burning. **Crop diversification** to pulses, oilseeds, millets (Shree Anna), horticulture and livestock improves nutrition, incomes and sustainability, but needs assured prices and markets.

Only around half of the net sown area is irrigated; the rest depends on the monsoon. **Groundwater** (wells and tubewells) is the largest source, followed by canals and tanks. Problems: over-extraction, inefficient flood irrigation, unfinished projects, siltation of tanks, and inequity between head and tail ends of canals.

Solutions: **micro-irrigation** (drip saves water and fertiliser), **PMKSY**, completing projects under AIBP, participatory irrigation management (water users' associations), **Atal Bhujal Yojana** for community groundwater management, watershed development, and pricing power and water to encourage efficiency.

Post-harvest losses are significant, especially for perishables, because of inadequate **cold storage**, packhouses and transport. Grain is stored by **FCI** and state agencies; private warehousing is regulated by **WDRA**, whose **negotiable warehouse receipts** allow farmers to borrow against stored produce.

Marketing is governed by state **APMC** Acts. Issues: few mandis per area, commission agents, market fees, delayed payments and fragmented markets. Reforms: **e-NAM**, model APMC and contract farming laws, **Farmer Producer Organisations** for collective bargaining, Operation Greens for tomato-onion-potato, and direct procurement by processors. The 2020 farm laws were repealed in 2021 after protests, so reforms now proceed through states and voluntary models.

Digital tools: **Soil Health Cards**, Kisan Call Centres, weather advisories (IMD, Meghdoot app), **remote sensing** and satellite data for crop area and yield estimation, **PMFBY** using technology for claim assessment, **e-NAM** for price discovery, **drones** for spraying and mapping, and the **Digital Agriculture Mission** with **AgriStack** (farmer IDs, crop sown registry). Constraints: digital literacy, connectivity, small holdings and data privacy.
Key points.
points: Kharif: rice, cotton, soybean; Rabi: wheat, mustard, gram; Zaid: summer crops
Rice–wheat cycle: water, soil, stubble issues; diversify
Groundwater: largest irrigation source; PMKSY; micro-irrigation
WDRA and warehouse receipts; cold-chain gaps
APMC, e-NAM (2016), FPOs (10,000 scheme)

chapters.title: Farm Subsidies, PDS, Buffer Stocks & Animal Husbandry

cards.title: Types of farm subsidies
points: **Input**: fertiliser, power, irrigation water, seeds
**Credit**: interest subvention on short-term crop loans
**Price**: MSP-based procurement
**Insurance**: PMFBY premium support
**Direct income**: **PM-KISAN** (₹6,000 a year in three instalments)

cards.title: Fertiliser subsidy
cards.body: **Urea** is sold at a statutorily fixed price, with the subsidy covering the gap. **P and K** fertilisers have been under **Nutrient Based Subsidy** since 2010. Cheap urea encourages overuse, distorting the N:P:K balance and harming soils.

cards.title: WTO boxes
points: **Amber box**: trade-distorting support, capped (de minimis 10% of production value for developing countries)
**Blue box**: production-limiting payments
**Green box**: minimally distorting (research, direct income support)
Bali **peace clause** (2013) protects public stockholding for food security

cards.title: PDS and NFSA
points: **NFSA, 2013**: up to 75% rural and 50% urban population covered
Priority households: 5 kg grain per person per month
**Antyodaya** households: 35 kg per household per month
Free grain under **PMGKAY** (extended from January 2024 for five years)
One Nation One Ration Card for portability

cards.title: PDS reforms
points: End-to-end computerisation; ePoS with Aadhaar authentication
Shanta Kumar Committee (2015): leakages, decentralised procurement, cash transfers option
Fortified rice distribution
Diversify to pulses, millets

cards.title: Animal husbandry
points: India is the **world's largest milk producer**
**Operation Flood** (1970), led by Verghese Kurien
Rashtriya Gokul Mission (2014): indigenous breeds
PM Matsya Sampada Yojana (2020): fisheries
Livestock as insurance for small farmers and landless households

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Distinguish "subsidies as investments" (irrigation, research, extension) from "subsidies as transfers" (cheap power, urea). Argue for shifting from price distortions to direct income support and public investment.

cards.q: Under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture, direct income support not linked to production falls in the:
cards.explain: Green box measures are minimally trade-distorting and not capped.

cards.q: Under NFSA 2013, Antyodaya Anna Yojana households are entitled to:
cards.explain: AAY households get 35 kg per household per month.

cards.q: Operation Flood is associated with:
cards.explain: Launched in 1970 by NDDB under Verghese Kurien, it made India a leading milk producer.

notes.p: GS III: "Issues related to **direct and indirect farm subsidies** and minimum support prices; **Public Distribution System** — objectives, functioning, limitations, revamping; issues of **buffer stocks and food security**; **technology missions**; **economics of animal rearing**." MSP mechanics are in the Agricultural Economy chapter; this chapter covers subsidies, PDS and livestock.

**Indirect subsidies** lower input prices: fertilisers, electricity for pumps, canal water, seeds, and interest subvention on crop loans (short-term loans through Kisan Credit Cards at subsidised rates, with extra relief for prompt repayment). **Direct subsidies** transfer money: **PM-KISAN** (₹6,000 a year to landholding farmer families), state schemes like Telangana's Rythu Bandhu and Odisha's KALIA, and premium support under **PMFBY**.

Indirect subsidies often benefit larger farmers more, encourage overuse of water and urea, and burden state finances (power utilities). Direct transfers are crop-neutral and less distorting but may exclude tenant farmers who do not own land.

Price support and procurement are counted as **Amber box** support under WTO rules. Developing countries' de minimis limit is 10% of the value of production. India uses the **peace clause** (Bali, 2013) to protect public stockholding for food security and seeks a permanent solution. **Green box** measures — research, extension, infrastructure, decoupled income support — are not capped.

PDS began as a rationing system during scarcity, became the **Revamped PDS** (1992) and then the **Targeted PDS** (1997). The **National Food Security Act, 2013** made food a legal entitlement for up to two-thirds of the population. Since January 2023, grain under NFSA is free (now under **PMGKAY**).

**Limitations:** leakages and diversion, exclusion errors, poor-quality grain, limited nutrition (mostly cereals), and high economic cost of FCI operations. **Revamping:** digitisation of ration cards, ePoS devices, **One Nation One Ration Card**, doorstep delivery in some states, fortified rice, inclusion of millets and pulses, and pilots of cash transfers. **Buffer stock** norms are set for each quarter; excess stocks raise storage costs, while shortages endanger security. Open Market Sale Scheme releases surplus to control prices.

**Technology missions** brought focused gains: the Technology Mission on Oilseeds (1986) drove the **Yellow Revolution**; the National Food Security Mission (2007) raised rice, wheat and pulse output; the **National Mission on Edible Oils – Oil Palm** (2021) aims to cut import dependence.

**Animal rearing** is vital for small and landless farmers: it provides regular income, nutrition, draught power and manure, and acts as **insurance** in bad crop years. India leads the world in milk production thanks to **Operation Flood** and cooperatives like **Amul**. Challenges: low productivity per animal, fodder shortage, disease (foot-and-mouth; National Animal Disease Control Programme), stray cattle, and weak veterinary services. Fisheries are supported by **PMMSY**.

A farmer buys 10 bags of urea (45 kg each) at a fixed retail price of about ₹242 per bag (check the current notified price). If the production/import cost is ₹2,000 per bag, the subsidy per bag is about ₹1,758; for 10 bags, about ₹17,580.
**Insight:** the farmer pays roughly one-eighth of cost, so urea is overused relative to P and K, worsening soil health. A shift to nutrient-neutral, per-hectare direct support could correct this — but must protect small and tenant farmers.
Key points.
points: Indirect: fertiliser, power, water, credit; direct: PM-KISAN
Urea fixed price; P&K under NBS since 2010
WTO: Amber (10% de minimis), Blue, Green; Bali peace clause
NFSA 2013: 75% rural, 50% urban; 5 kg/person; AAY 35 kg/household
PDS reforms: ePoS, ONORC, fortification, millets
Operation Flood 1970; Rashtriya Gokul Mission; PMMSY

cards.title: Why food processing?
points: Reduces post-harvest losses
Raises farm incomes through value addition
Creates rural jobs, especially for women
Boosts exports
Links farms to markets

cards.title: Policy support
points: Ministry of Food Processing Industries
**PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana** (2017): mega food parks, cold chains, agro-processing clusters
**PM FME** (2020): micro food enterprises; **One District One Product**
**PLI** for food processing (2021)
100% FDI under automatic route in food processing

cards.title: Upstream and downstream
points: **Upstream**: seeds, inputs, contract farming, procurement, aggregation via FPOs
**Downstream**: packaging, cold chain, logistics, branding, retail, exports
Supply chain management links both ends

cards.title: Land reforms: four pillars
points: **Abolition of intermediaries** (zamindari)
**Tenancy reforms**: security of tenure, fair rent, ownership rights
**Land ceilings** and redistribution of surplus
**Consolidation** of fragmented holdings

cards.title: Successes and failures
cards.body: Zamindari abolition largely succeeded. **Tenancy reforms** worked best in **West Bengal (Operation Barga, 1978)** and **Kerala**. **Ceilings** achieved limited redistribution because of benami transfers and loopholes. Consolidation succeeded mainly in Punjab, Haryana and western UP.

cards.title: Modern land agenda
points: **Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme**
**SVAMITVA** (2020): drone mapping of rural inhabited land
**ULPIN**: unique land parcel ID
Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act (2016)
Women's land rights

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Food processing answers should mention location factors (perishable raw material → near farms), the "missing middle" (cold chain, aggregation), and FSSAI standards. Land reform answers should end with tenancy legalisation and clear titles.

cards.q: Operation Barga, a tenancy reform programme, was implemented in:
cards.explain: Launched in 1978 to register sharecroppers (bargadars).

cards.q: SVAMITVA scheme uses drones to:
options: Map rural inhabited (abadi) land and issue property cards
cards.explain: It provides record-of-rights to rural households.

notes.p: Food processing covers primary processing (cleaning, grading, milling) and secondary/tertiary processing (ready-to-eat foods, dairy products, beverages, meat and fish products). India is a leading producer of milk, fruits, vegetables and cereals but processes a relatively small share of its perishables, so **post-harvest losses** are high. Processing adds value, reduces waste, stabilises prices, creates jobs and raises exports — making it a bridge between agriculture and industry.

Location factors: **perishable, weight-losing raw materials** pull primary processing close to farms (sugar mills, dairy chilling centres, fruit pulping); finished products locate near markets or ports. Clusters such as **mega food parks** offer shared infrastructure.

**Upstream requirements:** quality raw material, aggregation through FPOs, contract farming, farm-gate infrastructure. **Downstream requirements:** cold chain, packaging, logistics, branding, retail and export certification. Gaps in the middle — aggregation, grading and cold storage — are the biggest constraints. **FSSAI** sets standards; export requires meeting international norms.

Schemes: **PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana**, **PM Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises** (with One District One Product), **PLI for food processing**, **Operation Greens** (from TOP to TOTAL), and liberal FDI. Challenges: fragmented small farms, seasonal supply, high cost of credit, power and logistics, multiple regulations, low R&D and limited skilled workforce. Way forward: FPO-led aggregation, cold-chain PPPs, simple compliance for micro units, and branding regional products (GI tags).

At independence, land was concentrated with zamindars and intermediaries, and tenants had little security. Land reforms aimed at **equity and productivity**. The **First Amendment (1951)** created the **Ninth Schedule** to protect land reform laws from legal challenge.

**Abolition of intermediaries** brought tenants into direct contact with the state — largely completed by the 1950s–60s. **Tenancy reforms** sought security of tenure, fair rent and ownership; many states drove tenancy underground rather than reforming it. **Ceilings** fixed maximum holdings, but evasion through benami and family partitions limited surplus land. **Consolidation of holdings** improved efficiency where implemented. **Bhoodan** (Vinoba Bhave, from 1951) collected donated land, though much was of poor quality.

The agenda now is **clear titles and efficient land markets**: digitising records under DILRMP, **SVAMITVA** property cards, **ULPIN**, conclusive titling, legalising tenancy (NITI Aayog's **Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016**) so that tenants can access credit and insurance, and protecting **women's and tribal land rights**. Land disputes clog courts; clear titles also enable credit and investment.

Question type: "Land reforms in India succeeded only partially. Discuss."
**Successes:** zamindari abolition; Operation Barga in West Bengal; Kerala reforms; consolidation in Punjab.
**Failures:** ceilings evaded; tenancy pushed underground; poor records.
**Reasons:** weak political will, landed elite influence, poor records.
**Present agenda:** digital records, leasing laws, women's rights.
**Conclusion:** from redistribution to recognition and security.
Key points.
points: Processing reduces losses, adds value, creates jobs
PM Kisan SAMPADA (2017), PM FME + ODOP (2020), PLI (2021)
Upstream: aggregation; downstream: cold chain, retail, export
Land reforms: intermediaries, tenancy, ceilings, consolidation
First Amendment 1951: Ninth Schedule
Operation Barga 1978; Bhoodan 1951
Today: DILRMP, SVAMITVA, ULPIN, leasing law

cards.title: Ecosystem structure
cards.body: An ecosystem has biotic parts (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic parts (light, water, soil). Energy flows **one way** through trophic levels; nutrients cycle. Only about **10%** of energy passes to the next level (Lindeman's ten per cent law).

cards.title: Ecological pyramids
points: Pyramid of **energy** – always upright
Pyramid of **biomass** – can be inverted in oceans (small phytoplankton biomass supports larger zooplankton)
Pyramid of **numbers** – can be inverted, e.g. one tree supporting many insects

cards.title: Key terms
points: **Ecotone** – transition zone between two ecosystems (e.g. mangroves between land and sea)
**Edge effect** – greater diversity in an ecotone
**Keystone species** – has a disproportionate effect on its ecosystem
**Endemic species** – found only in one region

cards.title: Biodiversity hotspots
cards.body: Conservation International identifies **36** hotspots worldwide. India has parts of **four**: the **Himalaya**, **Indo-Burma**, **Western Ghats & Sri Lanka**, and **Sundaland** (which includes the Nicobar Islands).

cards.q: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
cards.explain: Energy is lost at each trophic level, so the energy pyramid is always upright.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT a biodiversity hotspot covering part of India?
cards.explain: India has parts of Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, and Sundaland.

notes.p: **Ecology** is the study of interactions between living organisms and their environment. It builds up in levels: **organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere**.
points: **Ecosystem:** a functional unit of living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components interacting together
**Habitat:** the place where an organism lives; **niche:** its role and use of resources in that habitat
**Ecotone:** a transition zone between two ecosystems (e.g. mangroves between land and sea, grassland between forest and desert); often richer in species — the **edge effect**
**Biome:** a large region defined by climate and dominant vegetation (tropical rainforest, desert, tundra)

notes.p: Energy enters ecosystems through **producers** (green plants) via photosynthesis and flows to **consumers** and **decomposers**.
points: **Trophic levels:** producers → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary consumers → tertiary consumers
**10% law (Lindeman):** only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next
Energy flow is **unidirectional**; nutrients **cycle** (carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus cycles)
**Grazing food chain** starts with green plants; **detritus food chain** starts with dead organic matter
**Ecological pyramids:** pyramid of energy is always upright; pyramid of biomass in oceans can be inverted
**Biomagnification:** toxic substances like DDT or mercury increase in concentration at higher trophic levels

notes.p:
**Biodiversity** is the variety of life at three levels: **genetic**, **species** and **ecosystem** diversity. India is one of the world's **megadiverse countries** and has **four biodiversity hotspots**: **Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, and Sundaland** (Nicobar Islands).

The hotspot concept was introduced by **Norman Myers**. To qualify, a region must have at least **1,500 endemic vascular plant species** and must have lost at least **70%** of its original habitat.
points: **Endemic species:** found only in a particular area
**Keystone species:** has a large effect on its ecosystem relative to its numbers (e.g. tigers as top predators)
**Flagship species:** a popular species used to attract support for conservation (e.g. the tiger, the Great Indian Bustard)
**Indicator species:** shows the health of an ecosystem (e.g. lichens for air pollution)

notes.p: A simple acronym to remember major threats:
points: **H**abitat loss and fragmentation
**I**nvasive alien species (e.g. Lantana, water hyacinth)
**P**ollution
**P**opulation growth (human pressure)
**O**ver-exploitation (poaching, overfishing)
**Climate change** is now an added major threat

notes.p: The **International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)** publishes the **Red List**. Main categories in decreasing risk order:
points: Extinct (EX) → Extinct in the Wild (EW)
**Critically Endangered (CR) → Endangered (EN) → Vulnerable (VU)** — together called 'threatened'
Near Threatened (NT) → Least Concern (LC)
Data Deficient (DD) and Not Evaluated (NE)
Species' status gets updated — check the latest Red List before quoting

notes.p: Prelims frequently asks about **ecological concepts** (food chains, ecotones, biomagnification), **species in the news** with their IUCN status and habitats, and **hotspots**. The 'how many of the above' format is common. Mains GS III asks about **biodiversity loss**, the value of ecosystem services, and conservation strategies.
Key points.
points: Organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere
Ecotone: transition zone with edge effect
10% law; energy flows one way, nutrients cycle
Biomagnification: DDT, mercury increase up the food chain
India's 4 hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Sundaland
Hotspot: ≥1,500 endemic plants + ≥70% habitat lost
Threatened = CR, EN, VU
HIPPO + climate change = main threats

cards.title: Protected area types
points: **National Park** – highest protection; no grazing or private rights
**Wildlife Sanctuary** – some activities permitted
**Conservation and Community Reserves** – added by the 2002 amendment to the Wildlife Act
**Biosphere Reserve** – core, buffer and transition zones; part of UNESCO's MAB programme when recognised internationally

cards.title: Key laws
points: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 — amended in 2023 and renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 — enacted after the Bhopal gas tragedy
Biological Diversity Act, 2002
National Green Tribunal Act, 2010

cards.title: Flagship programmes
cards.body: **Project Tiger** began in **1973**; the National Tiger Conservation Authority is statutory under the Wildlife Act. **Project Elephant** began in 1992. Cheetahs were reintroduced at **Kuno National Park**, Madhya Pradesh, in 2022 — the first intercontinental translocation of a large carnivore to India.

cards.title: Global conventions
points: **Ramsar** (1971) – wetlands
**CITES** (1973) – trade in endangered species
**CBD** (1992) – biodiversity; Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing
**IUCN Red List** – categories like Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Protected area counts and Ramsar site numbers change frequently. For Prelims, check the latest figures on the MoEFCC / PIB website a month before the exam rather than relying on older notes.

cards.q: The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in:
cards.explain: It was passed in 1986 as an umbrella law after the 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy.

cards.q: The Ramsar Convention deals with:
cards.explain: Ramsar (Iran, 1971) is the convention on wetlands of international importance.

notes.p: **In-situ** conservation protects species in their natural habitats. **Ex-situ** conservation protects them outside their habitats.
points: **In-situ:** national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves, community reserves, biosphere reserves, sacred groves
**Ex-situ:** zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, cryopreservation
Example of a seed bank: the **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** (Norway)

notes.p: Most protected areas are notified under the **Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972**.
points: **National Park:** stricter protection; no human activity like grazing allowed generally; boundaries changed only by state legislature resolution
**Wildlife Sanctuary:** some activities may be permitted
**Conservation and Community Reserves:** added by the 2002 amendment; involve local communities
**Tiger Reserves:** under Project Tiger (launched **1973**); managed with the **National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)**, set up in 2006; have a core and a buffer zone
**Biosphere Reserves:** under UNESCO's **Man and Biosphere (MAB)** programme; zones are core, buffer and transition; the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve was India's first (1986)
**Ramsar sites:** wetlands of international importance under the **Ramsar Convention (1971)**; numbers are rising fast — check the latest count
Project Elephant: launched in 1992

notes.p: The Constitution supports environmental protection through **Article 48A** (DPSP: State shall protect environment and wildlife) and **Article 51A(g)** (duty of citizens). Both were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**. Courts have read the right to a healthy environment into **Article 21**.
points: **Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972:** schedules of protected species, hunting ban, protected areas; amended in 2022 to rationalise schedules and implement CITES
**Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974:** created pollution control boards
**Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980:** prior central approval for diverting forest land (amended in 2023 — check the current name and provisions)
**Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981**
**Environment (Protection) Act, 1986:** umbrella law passed after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984); basis for EIA notifications
**Biological Diversity Act, 2002:** created the **National Biodiversity Authority** (Chennai), State Biodiversity Boards and Biodiversity Management Committees
**Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006**
**National Green Tribunal Act, 2010:** NGT for speedy environmental justice

notes.p: India is party to many conventions.
points: **CITES (1973):** regulates international trade in endangered species
**Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD):** from the 1992 Rio Earth Summit; its protocols include **Cartagena** (biosafety) and **Nagoya** (access and benefit sharing)
**Convention on Migratory Species (CMS)** — also called the Bonn Convention
**Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022):** includes the '30x30' target to conserve 30% of land and ocean by 2030

notes.p: Prelims frequently asks about **protected areas in the news**, which protected area lies in which state, the **difference between national parks and sanctuaries**, laws and their provisions, and conventions. Mains GS III asks about the **conservation vs development** debate, forest rights, the role of local communities, and EIA's effectiveness.
Key points.
points: In-situ: national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves; ex-situ: zoos, seed banks
Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972; Project Tiger 1973; NTCA 2006
Biosphere reserves: core–buffer–transition; Nilgiri first (1986)
Article 48A and 51A(g): added by 42nd Amendment
EPA 1986 after Bhopal; Biological Diversity Act 2002; NGT Act 2010
Ramsar Convention 1971; check the latest site count
CBD protocols: Cartagena (biosafety), Nagoya (benefit sharing)

cards.title: The science in brief
cards.body: Greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases — trap outgoing heat. Rising concentrations from burning fossil fuels and deforestation are warming the planet, raising sea levels and intensifying heatwaves, floods and droughts.

cards.title: Climate treaty timeline
points: 1992 – **UNFCCC** adopted at the Rio Earth Summit
1997 – **Kyoto Protocol**: binding targets for developed countries
2015 – **Paris Agreement**: keep warming well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C; every country submits **NDCs**, updated every five years
Principle: **Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR)**

cards.title: India's commitments
cards.body: At COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) India announced **net zero by 2070**. Its updated NDC (2022) aims to cut emissions intensity of GDP by **45%** from 2005 levels by 2030 and to reach about **50%** of installed power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030 — a share India reported reaching in 2025.

cards.title: Ozone protection
cards.body: The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phased out ozone-depleting substances like CFCs and is considered the most successful environmental treaty. Its **Kigali Amendment (2016)** targets HFCs — they do not harm ozone but are powerful greenhouse gases.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Indian initiatives worth quoting: International Solar Alliance (launched with France, 2015), Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), National Action Plan on Climate Change with its national missions, and the Green Hydrogen Mission.

cards.q: The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol targets:
cards.explain: It phases down hydrofluorocarbons, potent greenhouse gases used in cooling.

cards.q: India's net-zero target year is:
cards.explain: Announced at COP26 in Glasgow, 2021.

notes.p: The **greenhouse effect** is natural and keeps the Earth warm enough for life. Greenhouse gases (GHGs) trap outgoing heat (infrared radiation). Human activities — burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture — have increased GHG concentrations, causing **global warming** and **climate change**.
points: Main GHGs: **carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), fluorinated gases (HFCs, PFCs, SF₆)** and water vapour
Methane has a much higher warming effect per molecule than CO₂ over short periods but stays in the atmosphere for a shorter time
**Global Warming Potential (GWP)** compares gases with CO₂
**Black carbon** (soot) is a short-lived climate pollutant

notes.p: Effects are already visible worldwide and in India.
points: Rising temperatures and more frequent heatwaves
Melting glaciers (including Himalayan glaciers) and sea-level rise
**Ocean acidification** harming coral reefs; coral bleaching
Erratic monsoons, floods and droughts affecting agriculture
Health risks: vector-borne diseases, heat stress
Climate-related migration and pressure on livelihoods

notes.p: Global action is organised under the United Nations.
points: **1988:** **IPCC** set up by WMO and UNEP to assess climate science
**1992:** **UNFCCC** adopted at the Rio Earth Summit; principle of **Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC)**
**1997:** **Kyoto Protocol** — binding emission cuts for developed (Annex I) countries; market mechanisms such as the Clean Development Mechanism
**2015:** **Paris Agreement** (COP21) — keep warming well below **2°C**, pursue efforts to limit it to **1.5°C**; all countries submit **Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)**
**2022 (COP27, Sharm el-Sheikh):** agreement to set up a **Loss and Damage** fund
**2023 (COP28, Dubai):** first **Global Stocktake** under the Paris Agreement
COP decisions and finance goals keep evolving — check the latest COP outcomes

notes.p: Do not confuse the ozone problem with climate change, though they are linked. The **Vienna Convention (1985)** and the **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phase out ozone-depleting substances like CFCs. The **Kigali Amendment (2016)** to the Montreal Protocol aims to phase down **HFCs**, which do not harm ozone but are powerful greenhouse gases.
India argues for **equity and climate justice**, since its historical emissions and per capita emissions are low compared to developed countries. Key initiatives:
points: **National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC), 2008:** eight national missions, including the National Solar Mission
**International Solar Alliance (ISA):** launched by India and France at COP21 in 2015; headquarters in Gurugram
**Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment):** promoting sustainable lifestyles
India announced a **net-zero by 2070** goal at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021)
Updated NDC targets and renewable capacity figures change — check the latest official data

notes.p: Prelims asks about **conventions and protocols** (which deals with what), gases and their sources, carbon markets, and India's initiatives. Mains GS III asks about **India's position** in climate negotiations, energy transition challenges, climate finance, and adaptation in agriculture and cities.
Key points.
points: IPCC 1988; UNFCCC 1992; Kyoto 1997; Paris 2015
Paris: well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C; NDCs
CBDR-RC is India's key principle
Montreal Protocol 1987 (ozone); Kigali Amendment 2016 (HFCs)
Loss and Damage fund agreed at COP27
NAPCC 2008 with eight missions
ISA: India + France, 2015; India's net-zero target: 2070

cards.title: A megadiverse country
cards.body: India has about **2.4% of the world's land** but around **7–8% of recorded species**, and is one of the **17 megadiverse countries**. It has **10 biogeographic zones** — from the Trans-Himalaya and Desert to the Western Ghats, Deccan, Gangetic plain, North-East, coasts and islands.

cards.title: Biodiversity hotspots
cards.body: Defined by Norman Myers: at least **1,500 endemic vascular plants** and **≥70% of original habitat lost**. Of 36 global hotspots, four include parts of India: **Himalaya**, **Indo-Burma**, **Western Ghats & Sri Lanka**, and **Sundaland** (Nicobar Islands).

cards.title: Species and where they live
points: Great Indian Bustard — Rajasthan, Gujarat grasslands (Critically Endangered)
Gharial — Chambal river (Critically Endangered)
Lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr — Western Ghats
Sangai deer — Keibul Lamjao floating park, Manipur
Hangul (Kashmir stag) — Dachigam
Hoolock gibbon — India's only ape, North-East
Olive Ridley turtles — mass nesting at Gahirmatha and Rushikulya, Odisha

cards.title: Flagship projects
cards.body: **Project Tiger** (1973), **Project Elephant** (1992), **Project Snow Leopard** (2009), **Project Dolphin** (2020). **Cheetahs** were reintroduced at **Kuno National Park** (Madhya Pradesh) from **September 2022**, brought from Namibia and South Africa.

cards.title: Key laws
cards.body: **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972** — amended in 2022 to rationalise schedules and implement CITES. **Biological Diversity Act 2002** (amended 2023) — **National Biodiversity Authority** (Chennai), State Biodiversity Boards and local **Biodiversity Management Committees**. **Forest Rights Act 2006**.

cards.title: Invasive species
cards.body: Alien species that spread aggressively and harm native ecosystems: **Lantana camara**, **Prosopis juliflora**, **water hyacinth (Eichhornia)**, **Parthenium** (congress grass). They are a major driver of biodiversity loss.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: UPSC frequently asks 'which of these is found in India', 'which is endemic to the Western Ghats', or matching species with protected areas. Build lists by region rather than by species.

cards.q: Which hotspot covers the Nicobar Islands?
cards.explain: The Nicobar Islands fall in the Sundaland hotspot.

cards.q: India's only ape is the:
cards.explain: The hoolock gibbon of north-east India is the only ape found in India.

cards.q: Cheetahs were reintroduced in India at:
cards.explain: Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh, from 2022.

notes.p:
India's diversity comes from its range of climates and landscapes and its position where three realms meet — **Indo-Malayan**, **Palaearctic** and **Afrotropical** influences. **Endemism** is highest in the **Western Ghats**, **North-East**, and the **Andaman & Nicobar Islands** — for example, many amphibians of the Western Ghats are found nowhere else. The **Zoological Survey of India** and **Botanical Survey of India** document species.

Biodiversity also has economic value: forests, fisheries, pollinators, wild relatives of crops and traditional medicine support millions of livelihoods. Losses come from **habitat destruction**, **invasive species**, **pollution**, **over-exploitation** and **climate change** — the HIPPO drivers. India's **National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan** was updated in 2024 to align with the global framework.
India uses several categories under the Wildlife Protection Act:
points: **National Parks** — strict protection; no grazing or private rights
**Wildlife Sanctuaries** — some activities allowed
**Conservation Reserves** and **Community Reserves** — added in 2002/2003, involving communities
**Tiger Reserves** — notified on NTCA recommendation, with core and buffer zones
**Biosphere Reserves** — 18 in India; many are in UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere network (check the current count)
**Ramsar sites** — wetlands of international importance; India has steadily added sites and now has around 90 or more (check the latest)

notes.p: IUCN categories (covered in the ecology chapter) are used to classify species. Notable threatened Indian species include the **Great Indian Bustard** (power lines are a major cause of deaths; the Supreme Court has directed measures in its habitat), **gharial**, **Jerdon's courser**, **white-rumped vulture** (crashed due to the veterinary drug **diclofenac**, banned for veterinary use in 2006), **Ganges river dolphin** (national aquatic animal) and **red panda**. Vulture conservation breeding centres, such as at Pinjore, aim to restore populations.

India is party to the **Convention on Biological Diversity** (CBD, 1992) and its **Cartagena** (biosafety) and **Nagoya** (access and benefit-sharing) protocols. The **Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework** (2022) set targets for 2030, including the '**30x30**' goal — conserving 30% of land and 30% of oceans. **CITES** regulates wildlife trade; **CMS** (Bonn Convention) protects migratory species — India hosted CMS COP-13 at Gandhinagar (2020).

Question: Which of these are endemic to the Western Ghats? (1) Nilgiri tahr (2) Lion-tailed macaque (3) Sangai.

Step 1: Nilgiri tahr — found in the Nilgiris and southern Western Ghats ✔.
Step 2: Lion-tailed macaque — endemic to the Western Ghats ✔.
Step 3: Sangai — Manipur, north-east ✘.
Answer: 1 and 2 only.
Expect species–habitat matching, protected-area facts, hotspot criteria and conventions. Use newspapers to note species in the news (reintroductions, new discoveries, status changes).
Recall.
points: 2.4% land, ~7–8% species; megadiverse
4 hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, W. Ghats & Sri Lanka, Sundaland
10 biogeographic zones
Project Tiger 1973; Elephant 1992; cheetahs at Kuno 2022
WPA 1972 (amended 2022); BDA 2002 (amended 2023)

cards.title: Air quality index
cards.body: India's **AQI** (2014) uses eight pollutants: **PM10, PM2.5, NO₂, SO₂, CO, O₃, NH₃ and Pb**. The **National Clean Air Programme** (NCAP, 2019) targets city-level reductions in particulate pollution. Delhi-NCR uses the **Graded Response Action Plan** (GRAP) and the **Commission for Air Quality Management** (2021).

cards.title: Two kinds of smog
cards.body: **Classical (London) smog** — smoke + fog + SO₂ in cool, humid conditions. **Photochemical smog** — NOₓ + volatile organic compounds + sunlight produce **ground-level ozone** and **PAN**; common in warm, sunny cities.

cards.title: Water quality terms
cards.body: **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand) — oxygen used by microbes to break down organic matter; high BOD = more pollution. **DO** (dissolved oxygen) — low DO kills fish. **Eutrophication** — excess nutrients (nitrates, phosphates) cause algal blooms and oxygen loss.

cards.title: Pollutants and diseases
points: Mercury — Minamata disease
Cadmium — itai-itai disease
Arsenic in groundwater — skin lesions, cancers (Bengal delta)
Fluoride — fluorosis
Nitrates in drinking water — blue baby syndrome
Lead — neurological damage in children

cards.title: Biomagnification
cards.body: Persistent chemicals such as **DDT** and **mercury** are not broken down, so their concentration **increases at higher trophic levels** — top predators carry the highest load. This is why fish-eating birds were badly affected by DDT.

cards.title: Waste rules (selected)
cards.body: **Solid Waste Management Rules 2016** — segregation at source. **Plastic Waste Management Rules** — ban on identified **single-use plastic** items from 1 July 2022. **E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022** and **Battery Waste Management Rules 2022** — **Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)**. **Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016** — colour-coded bins.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Key laws: **Water Act 1974** (the CPCB was created under it), **Air Act 1981**, **Environment (Protection) Act 1986** (after the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984), **National Green Tribunal Act 2010**.

cards.q: High BOD in a water body indicates:
cards.explain: Microbes need more oxygen to decompose more organic waste.

cards.q: Photochemical smog mainly involves:
cards.explain: Sunlight drives reactions forming ozone and PAN.

cards.q: Minamata disease is caused by:
cards.explain: Mercury poisoning from contaminated fish in Minamata, Japan.

notes.p:
Main sources in India: **vehicles**, **industry and power plants**, **construction dust**, **biomass and crop-residue burning**, household solid fuels and **road dust**. Winter episodes in north India are worsened by **temperature inversion**, low wind speed and stubble burning. **PM2.5** (fine particles under 2.5 micrometres) penetrates deep into the lungs and blood and is the most harmful common pollutant. Responses include **BS-VI** fuel standards (leapfrogged from BS-IV in 2020), electric mobility, cleaner cooking (Ujjwala), and flue-gas desulphurisation in thermal plants.

Indoor air pollution from burning wood, dung and kerosene is a major health risk for women and children. The **WHO air-quality guidelines** (revised in 2021) are much stricter than India's national standards, which is why Indian cities often meet national standards on some days yet exceed WHO levels almost all year.

Rivers are polluted by untreated **sewage** (the largest source), industrial effluents and agricultural run-off. The **Namami Gange** programme (2014) funds sewage treatment and river-front works. Groundwater faces **arsenic**, **fluoride**, **nitrate** and **uranium** contamination in different regions. Soil pollution comes from excess fertilisers and pesticides, industrial waste and plastics. **Microplastics** (smaller than 5 mm) are now found in water, soil, food and even human tissue.
The **waste hierarchy**: **reduce → reuse → recycle → recover (energy) → dispose** (landfill as last resort). Key ideas:
points: **Segregation at source** — wet (biodegradable), dry, and domestic hazardous waste
**Extended Producer Responsibility** — producers responsible for collecting and recycling their products after use
**Circular economy** — design products for long life and recycling
**Bio-medical waste** — yellow (anatomical, soiled), red (contaminated plastics), white/translucent (sharps), blue (glass)
**Waste-to-energy** — useful but must meet emission norms

notes.p: **Noise** is regulated by the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000, with lower limits in **silence zones** around hospitals and schools. **Thermal pollution** from power-plant discharges reduces dissolved oxygen. **Radioactive** pollution arises from mining, accidents and waste. **Light pollution** disturbs wildlife and astronomy. **Fly ash** from coal plants is now used in bricks and cement.

A pesticide is present at 0.02 ppm in water. If its concentration rises roughly tenfold at each trophic level — plankton, small fish, large fish, fish-eating bird — what level might reach the bird?

Step 1: plankton ≈ 0.2 ppm.
Step 2: small fish ≈ 2 ppm.
Step 3: large fish ≈ 20 ppm.
Step 4: bird ≈ **200 ppm**.
The numbers are illustrative, but they show why top predators suffer the most from persistent pollutants.

UPSC asks about pollutants in AQI, sources of specific pollutants, terms like BOD and eutrophication, provisions of waste rules, and the bodies that enforce them. Statements about which pollutant comes from which source are a regular feature.
Recall.

NCAP 2019; GRAP; CAQM
High BOD = high organic pollution

cards.title: What EIA is
cards.body: A process to **predict and evaluate the environmental and social effects** of a proposed project before approval, and to design mitigation. In India it is governed by the **EIA Notification, 2006** under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

cards.title: Stages of EIA
points: **Screening**: does the project need full EIA?
**Scoping**: decide terms of reference
**Public consultation**: public hearing and written responses
**Appraisal** by expert committees
Decision, then **post-clearance monitoring**

cards.title: Categories
points: **Category A**: appraised at the Centre (MoEFCC with Expert Appraisal Committee)
**Category B**: appraised by State-level authorities (SEIAA/SEAC)
B1 needs EIA report; B2 may be exempted from it

cards.title: Weaknesses
points: Consultant-prepared reports paid by project proponents
Poor-quality or copied data
Weak or token **public hearings**
Little cumulative or strategic assessment
Weak monitoring of clearance conditions
Ex-post facto clearances controversy

cards.title: Better practice
points: **Strategic Environmental Assessment** of policies and plans
**Cumulative impact** assessment for river basins and regions
Accredited, independent consultants
Real-time compliance monitoring
Strong public participation (PARIVESH portal for transparency)

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Answers on development vs environment should treat EIA as a tool for **sustainable development**, not an obstacle: cite the precautionary principle and polluter-pays principle recognised by Indian courts.

cards.q: EIA in India is currently governed mainly by the:
cards.explain: The 2006 notification under the Environment (Protection) Act governs EIA.

cards.q: Which stage of EIA decides the terms of reference for the study?
cards.explain: Scoping defines what issues the EIA must study.

notes.p: GS III lists "**Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation, environmental impact assessment**". EIA is a decision-making tool that aims to integrate environmental concerns into development planning by identifying impacts early, considering alternatives, involving affected communities and prescribing mitigation. It embodies the **precautionary principle** and **sustainable development**, which the Supreme Court has treated as part of Indian environmental law (Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum, 1996).

EIA began in the late 1970s with appraisal of river valley projects. The **1994 EIA Notification** made it mandatory for listed projects. The **2006 Notification** decentralised appraisal by creating State-level authorities, introduced the A/B categorisation, and formalised four stages: screening, scoping, public consultation and appraisal. A **draft EIA Notification 2020** proposed changes (such as post-facto approvals and reduced public consultation for some projects) that drew wide criticism and has not replaced the 2006 framework. Courts have ruled on **ex-post facto clearances** in recent years — check the latest Supreme Court position.

**Screening:** the project is checked against the schedule to see if it needs EIA and at which level.
**Scoping:** the Expert Appraisal Committee sets **terms of reference**.
**EIA study:** baseline data (air, water, soil, biodiversity, social), impact prediction, mitigation and an Environmental Management Plan.
**Public consultation:** a public hearing near the site and written comments; affected persons voice concerns.
**Appraisal:** experts examine the report and hearing outcomes and recommend approval with conditions or rejection.
**Monitoring:** compliance reports and inspections by regional offices.

Studies and courts have flagged: reports prepared by consultants paid by proponents (conflict of interest); **copy-paste** baseline data; poorly publicised hearings in languages people do not understand; **salami-slicing** of projects to avoid thresholds; failure to assess cumulative impacts of many projects in one area (for example, hydropower cascades in the Himalaya); weak monitoring of conditions; and limited capacity in State authorities. Exemptions and dilutions for "ease of doing business" raise concerns about environmental safeguards.

Other tools include **forest clearance** under the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 (amended and renamed in 2023), **wildlife clearance** by the National Board for Wildlife, **Coastal Regulation Zone** rules, **Environmental Supplement Plans**, the **National Green Tribunal** for disputes, and **pollution control boards**. Reforms: an independent environmental regulator (suggested by the Supreme Court in Lafarge, 2011), **strategic environmental assessment** for sectors and regions, cumulative impact studies, digital transparency via **PARIVESH**, and community monitoring.

Question type: "EIA in India has become a mere formality. Critically examine."
**Intro:** legal basis and purpose of EIA.
**Arguments for:** proponent-funded reports, weak hearings, high approval rates, poor monitoring, dilutions.
**Counter-arguments:** several projects have been modified or rejected; NGT and courts enforce conditions; PARIVESH improves transparency.
**Way forward:** independent regulator, accredited consultants paid from a common pool, cumulative and strategic assessment, community monitoring.
**Conclusion:** EIA must inform decisions, not just document them.
Key points.
points: EIA Notification 2006 under EPA 1986
Stages: screening, scoping, public consultation, appraisal; then monitoring
Category A (Centre), Category B (State SEIAA)
Problems: conflict of interest, poor data, weak hearings, no cumulative view
Reforms: SEA, cumulative assessment, independent regulator, PARIVESH
Precautionary and polluter-pays principles (Vellore, 1996)

cards.title: ISRO milestones
points: ISRO founded in **1969**; Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite
**Chandrayaan-3** landed near the lunar south pole on **23 August 2023** — now celebrated as National Space Day
**Aditya-L1** (launched September 2023) studies the Sun from the L1 Lagrange point
**NavIC** – India's regional navigation satellite system

cards.title: Launch vehicles
points: **PSLV** – workhorse for polar/sun-synchronous orbits
**GSLV** – geosynchronous launches with cryogenic upper stage
**LVM3** – heaviest; launched Chandrayaan-3 and is human-rated for Gaganyaan
**SSLV** – small satellites on demand

cards.title: Human spaceflight
cards.body: **Gaganyaan** is India's programme to send astronauts to low Earth orbit on an Indian rocket. In **2025**, IAF Group Captain **Shubhanshu Shukla** flew to the International Space Station on the Axiom-4 mission, becoming the first Indian to visit the ISS.

cards.title: Lagrange points
cards.body: Points where the gravity of two large bodies (Sun and Earth) balances the orbital motion of a small object, so it can stay in position relative to both. **L1**, about 1.5 million km from Earth towards the Sun, gives an uninterrupted view of the Sun — ideal for Aditya-L1.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For S&T, learn the 'why it matters' of each mission: its objective, the technology it demonstrates and its benefit to India. That gives you material for both Prelims and GS III.

cards.q: Chandrayaan-3's lander touched down near the Moon's:
cards.explain: Vikram landed near the lunar south polar region on 23 August 2023.

cards.q: Aditya-L1 is positioned around L1 because:
options: It is closest to the Moon
It gives a continuous view of the Sun
cards.explain: From L1 the Sun is never blocked by Earth or Moon, allowing continuous observation.

notes.p: The **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** was founded in **1969** under the vision of **Dr Vikram Sarabhai**, often called the father of the Indian space programme. The **Department of Space** was created in 1972.
points: **1975:** **Aryabhata**, India's first satellite, launched with Soviet help
**1980:** **Rohini** satellite launched by India's own **SLV-3**
**2008:** **Chandrayaan-1** — helped confirm the presence of water molecules on the Moon
**2013–14:** **Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission)** — India reached Mars orbit on its first attempt
**2023:** **Chandrayaan-3** — soft landing near the lunar south pole (23 August 2023)
**2023:** **Aditya-L1** — solar observatory placed around the **Lagrange point L1**
**Gaganyaan:** human spaceflight programme — check the latest mission status

notes.p: Different missions need different rockets and orbits.
points: **PSLV:** reliable workhorse; best for **Sun-synchronous** and low-Earth orbits
**GSLV:** uses a cryogenic upper stage; for heavier satellites to geosynchronous transfer orbit
**LVM3 (GSLV Mk III):** heaviest; launched Chandrayaan-3 and is planned for Gaganyaan
**SSLV:** small satellite launch vehicle for quick, low-cost launches
**Geostationary orbit:** about **35,786 km** above the equator; satellite appears fixed — used for communication and weather
**Low Earth Orbit (LEO):** closer; used for Earth observation and remote sensing
**Cryogenic engines** use liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen at very low temperatures

notes.p: Space technology supports **communication, weather forecasting, disaster management, navigation, agriculture and resource mapping**. India's regional navigation system is **NavIC (IRNSS)**. Recent reforms opened the sector to private players: **IN-SPACe** authorises and promotes private activities, and **NewSpace India Limited (NSIL)** is ISRO's commercial arm. The **Indian Space Policy 2023** defines roles of different actors.

The **Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)** was set up in **1958**. The **Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP)**, launched in 1983 and associated with **Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam**, developed several missiles.
points: **Prithvi:** short-range surface-to-surface ballistic missile
**Agni series:** ballistic missiles of increasing range
**Akash:** surface-to-air missile
**Nag:** anti-tank guided missile
**BrahMos:** supersonic cruise missile — joint venture of India and Russia
**INS Arihant:** India's first indigenous nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine
**INS Vikrant:** India's first indigenously built aircraft carrier (commissioned 2022)
**Tejas:** indigenous Light Combat Aircraft

notes.p:
India's **nuclear doctrine** follows **'No First Use'** and **credible minimum deterrence**. India tested nuclear devices in **1974 (Pokhran-I)** and **1998 (Pokhran-II)**. India has not signed the **NPT** or the **CTBT**. India is a member of the **Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR)**, the **Wassenaar Arrangement** and the **Australia Group**, but not the **Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG)**.

The government promotes self-reliance in defence through **'Atmanirbhar Bharat'** and positive indigenisation lists. Export and import figures change — check the latest data.

Prelims asks about **missions and their objectives**, orbits and launch vehicles, missile types, and technologies in the news (cryogenic engines, Lagrange points). Mains GS III asks about the **significance of the space programme**, private sector participation, and indigenisation of defence production.
Key points.

Aryabhata 1975; SLV-3/Rohini 1980
Chandrayaan-3 south-pole landing: 23 Aug 2023; Aditya-L1 at L1

cards.title: Genetic engineering
cards.body: **Recombinant DNA** technology inserts a desired gene into an organism. **CRISPR-Cas9** works like molecular scissors to edit genes precisely; Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

cards.title: GM crops in India
cards.body: **Bt cotton** (approved 2002) carries a gene from the bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis* that makes it resistant to bollworms. It remains the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India. GM crops are cleared by the **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)** under MoEFCC.

cards.title: Vaccines
points: Live attenuated – weakened pathogen (e.g. oral polio vaccine)
Inactivated – killed pathogen
Subunit/recombinant – only a protein piece
mRNA – instructs cells to make a viral protein
Viral vector – a harmless virus carries the gene (e.g. Covishield)

cards.title: Emerging tech missions
points: **National Quantum Mission** (approved 2023) – quantum computing, communication, sensing
**IndiaAI Mission** (approved 2024) – compute capacity, datasets, AI startups
**India Semiconductor Mission** – chip fabs and packaging units
**Digital Public Infrastructure** – Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker

cards.q: The only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India is:
cards.explain: Bt cotton has been commercially grown since 2002; Bt brinjal was put under moratorium in 2010.

cards.q: CRISPR-Cas9 is primarily a tool for:
cards.explain: It edits DNA at precise locations, earning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

notes.p: **Biotechnology** uses living organisms or their parts to make useful products. Its foundation is **DNA**, which carries genetic information, and **genes**, which are sections of DNA coding for proteins.
points: **Recombinant DNA technology:** cutting and joining DNA from different sources using **restriction enzymes** and **ligase**
**PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction):** makes millions of copies of a DNA segment; used in diagnostics such as RT-PCR tests
**Genetically Modified (GM) organisms:** have altered DNA for desired traits

**Bt cotton:** contains a gene from the bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis*, giving resistance to bollworms; the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India for a long time — check the current status of others like GM mustard
In India, the **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)** under the Environment Ministry approves GM organisms

notes.p: **CRISPR-Cas9** is a gene-editing tool that acts like 'molecular scissors' to cut DNA at a precise place. Its developers, **Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna**, received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020**.
points: **Gene therapy:** correcting faulty genes to treat diseases
**Stem cells:** can develop into many cell types; used in regenerative medicine
**mRNA vaccines:** instruct cells to make a protein that triggers immunity
**Genome sequencing:** reading the full DNA; India's **Genome India Project** aims to map genetic diversity
**Ethical issues:** designer babies, privacy of genetic data, biosafety

notes.p: **Artificial Intelligence (AI)** lets machines do tasks that need human-like intelligence. **Machine learning** learns patterns from data; **deep learning** uses neural networks with many layers; **generative AI** creates text, images and code.
points: Uses: healthcare diagnosis, crop advisories, language translation, governance services
Concerns: bias, deepfakes, job displacement, privacy, accountability
**Quantum computing** uses **qubits**, which can exist in superposition, enabling certain calculations far faster; India has a **National Quantum Mission**
**Semiconductors** are central to electronics; India has a semiconductor mission to build chip and display manufacturing — check the latest status

notes.p: These appear often in news-based questions.
points: **Blockchain:** a distributed, tamper-resistant ledger; basis for cryptocurrencies
**Internet of Things (IoT):** connected devices sharing data
**5G:** high-speed, low-latency mobile networks
**Nanotechnology:** materials at a scale of 1–100 nanometres
**Green hydrogen:** hydrogen produced by electrolysis using renewable energy; India has a **National Green Hydrogen Mission**
**Digital Public Infrastructure:** Aadhaar, UPI and other India Stack systems

notes.p: Emerging tech needs rules that protect people without stopping innovation. India passed the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**. Regulation of AI, biotech and data is evolving globally — check the latest policy developments.

Prelims asks **what a technology is and what it can do** — for example, the uses of CRISPR, what PCR detects, or properties of qubits — often in statement format. Mains GS III asks about **applications in India**, ethical concerns, regulation, and how technology can help governance and development.
Key points.

PCR amplifies DNA; basis of RT-PCR tests
