chapters.title: General Science: Physics in Everyday Life

cards.title: Motion and force
cards.body: **Newton's laws**: inertia; F = ma; every action has an equal and opposite reaction (rocket propulsion). **Mass** is constant; **weight** = mass × g, and changes with gravity. Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they are in continuous **free fall**.

cards.title: Pressure and floating
cards.body: Pressure = force ÷ area — a sharp knife cuts better. **Archimedes' principle**: a body in fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced. A ship floats because its hollow shape displaces water equal to its weight.

cards.title: Heat
cards.body: Heat moves by **conduction** (solids), **convection** (fluids) and **radiation** (no medium needed). Water's **high specific heat** moderates coastal climates and creates **sea breezes**. At high altitude, lower pressure lowers the **boiling point**; a **pressure cooker** raises it.

cards.title: Sound
cards.body: Sound needs a medium and travels **fastest in solids**, slower in liquids, slowest in gases (about **343 m/s** in air at 20°C). Humans hear about **20 Hz to 20 kHz**; **ultrasound** is above, **infrasound** below. The **Doppler effect** changes pitch as a source moves.

cards.title: Light phenomena
cards.body: **Refraction** — stars twinkle, pools look shallower. **Total internal reflection** — optical fibres, diamond sparkle, mirages. **Dispersion** — rainbow. **Scattering** — blue sky (short wavelengths scatter more), red sunrise/sunset, **Tyndall effect**.

cards.title: Eye defects
points: Myopia (short-sight) — concave (diverging) lens
Hypermetropia (long-sight) — convex (converging) lens
Presbyopia (age) — bifocal or progressive lenses
Astigmatism — cylindrical lens

cards.title: Electricity basics
points: Ohm's law: V = I × R
Power P = V × I; 1 unit = 1 kWh
Series: R = R₁ + R₂; parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂
Household supply in India: 230 V AC, 50 Hz
Fuse/MCB protects against overload

cards.q: A person with myopia should use:
cards.explain: A concave lens diverges light so the image forms on the retina.

cards.q: The sky appears blue mainly because of:
cards.explain: Shorter (blue) wavelengths scatter more strongly in the atmosphere.

cards.q: A 1,000 W heater used for 3 hours consumes:
cards.explain: Energy = 1 kW × 3 h = 3 kWh = 3 units.

notes.h: Why general science is asked this way
notes.p:
UPSC's general science questions test **conceptual understanding of everyday phenomena** — why a spoon looks bent in water, why a pressure cooker cooks faster, how a microwave heats food. NCERT science books (Classes 6–10) are the base. Learn the 'why' behind each phenomenon.

A good method is to keep a list of 'everyday puzzles' and their one-line explanations: ice floats because it is less dense than water; a cyclist leans while turning to provide centripetal force; a mirage forms because hot air near the road bends light upward by refraction and total internal reflection; clothes dry faster on windy days because moving air carries away water vapour and speeds evaporation; and thermos flasks reduce heat loss by all three modes — conduction, convection and radiation.
Key ideas:
points: **Inertia** — passengers jerk forward when a bus brakes suddenly
**Momentum** = mass × velocity; conserved in collisions; recoil of a gun
**Friction** — needed for walking; reduced by lubricants and ball bearings
**Gravity** — g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on earth; about one-sixth on the moon
**Centripetal force** — keeps satellites in orbit; banking of roads on curves
**Escape velocity** from earth ≈ 11.2 km/s

notes.p: **SONAR** uses ultrasound to detect underwater objects; bats and dolphins use **echolocation**. Medical **ultrasonography** images organs safely. The **electromagnetic spectrum**, from longest to shortest wavelength: **radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma**. Microwave ovens heat food by making water molecules vibrate; infrared is used in TV remotes and night vision; UV sterilises water and causes sunburn; X-rays image bones.

**Electromagnetic induction** (Faraday) — a changing magnetic field produces current; this runs **generators** and **transformers**. **Electric motors** convert electrical to mechanical energy. **Semiconductors** (silicon) underpin diodes, transistors, solar cells and **LEDs**. **Superconductors** carry current with zero resistance at very low temperatures.

**Nuclear fission** (splitting heavy nuclei such as uranium-235) powers reactors; **fusion** (joining light nuclei) powers the sun and is the goal of **ITER**, in which India is a partner. Radioactive emissions: **alpha** (least penetrating), **beta**, **gamma** (most penetrating). **Half-life** is the time for half the nuclei to decay. **Heavy water** (D₂O) is used as a moderator in many Indian reactors.

Worked example: a sample has 80 g of an isotope with a half-life of 5 years. After 15 years (three half-lives) it has 80 → 40 → 20 → **10 g** left.
Expect 'which phenomenon explains X' questions, application questions (fibre optics, LED, GPS, radar), and statement checks on waves and radiation. Practise linking concept to application.
Recall.

Archimedes: buoyancy = weight of fluid displaced
Sound fastest in solids; ~343 m/s in air
Blue sky — scattering; mirage — TIR
Myopia concave; hypermetropia convex

chapters.title: General Science: Chemistry in Everyday Life

cards.title: Acids, bases and pH
cards.body: pH runs from 0 to 14: **below 7 acidic**, **7 neutral**, **above 7 basic**. Human blood is slightly basic (about **7.4**). The stomach makes **hydrochloric acid**; **antacids** such as magnesium hydroxide neutralise excess acid. Acid rain has pH below about 5.6.

cards.title: Common compounds
points: Baking soda — sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO₃)
Washing soda — sodium carbonate decahydrate
Bleaching powder — calcium oxychloride (CaOCl₂)
Plaster of Paris — CaSO₄·½H₂O
Gypsum — CaSO₄·2H₂O
Common salt — sodium chloride

cards.title: Alloys
points: Brass — copper + zinc
Bronze — copper + tin
Stainless steel — iron + chromium + nickel (+ carbon)
Solder — lead + tin (lead-free versions also used)
Amalgam — any alloy of mercury

cards.title: Corrosion
cards.body: **Rusting** of iron needs both **oxygen and moisture**. Prevention: painting, oiling, **galvanisation** (zinc coating — zinc corrodes first, protecting iron), alloying (stainless steel) and **cathodic protection**.

cards.title: Carbon and fuels
cards.body: Carbon's **allotropes**: diamond (hardest, non-conductor), graphite (soft, conducts electricity), fullerenes and **graphene**. **LPG** is mainly propane and butane (an odorant is added to detect leaks); **CNG** and **biogas** are mainly methane.

cards.title: Air composition
cards.body: Dry air is about **78% nitrogen**, **21% oxygen**, **0.93% argon** and about **0.04% carbon dioxide**, with traces of other gases. **Carbon monoxide** is poisonous because it binds haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Fruit ripening: **ethylene** is the natural ripening hormone. Use of **calcium carbide** (which releases acetylene) for artificial ripening is banned under food safety rules because of health risks from impurities like arsenic and phosphorus.

cards.q: Which gas is the main constituent of biogas?
cards.explain: Biogas is mostly methane with carbon dioxide.

cards.q: Galvanisation is coating iron with:
cards.explain: Zinc coating protects iron from rusting.

cards.q: Brass is an alloy of:
cards.explain: Brass = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin.

notes.p:
Matter exists as **solids, liquids, gases**, and also **plasma** and **Bose–Einstein condensate**. **Physical changes** (melting, dissolving) are usually reversible; **chemical changes** (burning, rusting, cooking) form new substances. **Elements** have one kind of atom; **compounds** combine elements in fixed ratios; **mixtures** do not. Separation methods include filtration, distillation, chromatography and centrifugation (used to separate cream from milk).

Useful everyday chemistry: **sublimation** (camphor, naphthalene balls) changes solid directly to gas; **evaporation** causes cooling, which is why sweating and earthen pots (matkas) cool; **dry ice** is solid CO₂; and **carbon dioxide fire extinguishers** work by cutting off oxygen. Water is not used on oil or electrical fires because oil floats on water and water conducts electricity.

notes.h: Acids, bases and salts in daily life
notes.p: Everyday examples help memory:
points: Vinegar — acetic acid; lemon — citric acid; curd — lactic acid; tamarind — tartaric acid
Ant and bee stings inject **formic acid**; rubbing a mild base like baking soda helps
**Soil pH** affects crops — lime (calcium compounds) corrects acidic soils, gypsum helps reclaim alkaline (sodic) soils
Toothpaste is basic to neutralise acids that cause tooth decay
Baking powder (baking soda + a mild acid) releases CO₂ to make cakes rise

notes.p: **Hard water** contains calcium and magnesium salts and does not lather well with soap. **Temporary hardness** (bicarbonates) is removed by boiling; **permanent hardness** (chlorides and sulphates) needs washing soda or ion exchange. **Detergents** work even in hard water, unlike soaps. Drinking water is disinfected by **chlorination**, **UV** or **ozonation**; **reverse osmosis** removes dissolved salts.

**Polymers** include polythene, PVC, nylon, polyester and Teflon (non-stick coating). Most plastics are **non-biodegradable**; bioplastics such as PLA are compostable under industrial conditions. **Urea** contains about **46% nitrogen**; **neem-coated urea** slows nitrogen release and curbs diversion to industry. Food is preserved using salt, sugar, vinegar and permitted preservatives such as **sodium benzoate**; **antioxidants** and nitrogen flushing in chip packets prevent **rancidity** (oxidation of fats).

A copper vessel turns green over time; an iron gate turns brown.

Step 1: Copper reacts with moist CO₂ and oxygen to form a green **basic copper carbonate** coating.
Step 2: Iron reacts with oxygen and water to form **hydrated iron oxide** (rust).
Step 3: Silver articles turn black due to **silver sulphide** from sulphur compounds in air.
All three are **corrosion** — slow oxidation of metals.

Questions test chemical names of common substances, alloy composition, reasons behind daily phenomena, and applications (fire extinguishers, fertilisers, water purification). Read the NCERT Class 7–10 chemistry chapters once and revise the tables here.
Recall.
points: pH 7 neutral; blood ~7.4
Baking soda NaHCO₃; PoP CaSO₄·½H₂O
Brass Cu+Zn; bronze Cu+Sn
Rusting needs oxygen + moisture; galvanise with zinc
LPG propane/butane; CNG and biogas methane
Ethylene ripens fruit; calcium carbide banned

chapters.title: General Science: Cells, Human Body & Plants

cards.title: The cell
cards.body: The cell was first observed by **Robert Hooke** (1665). Key organelles: **nucleus** (DNA, control), **mitochondria** ('powerhouse', ATP), **ribosomes** (protein synthesis), **endoplasmic reticulum**, **Golgi apparatus** (packaging), **lysosomes** ('suicide bags'). Plant cells also have a **cell wall** and **chloroplasts**.

cards.title: Genetics basics
cards.body: **DNA** is a double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953). Humans have **46 chromosomes (23 pairs)**. Females are XX, males XY — the **father's** chromosome decides a child's sex. **Mendel** discovered the laws of inheritance using pea plants.

cards.title: Vitamins and deficiency diseases
points: A — night blindness
B1 (thiamine) — beriberi
B3 (niacin) — pellagra
B12 — pernicious anaemia
C — scurvy
D — rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults)
K — poor blood clotting
Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K; water-soluble: B group, C

cards.title: Blood
cards.body: **RBCs** carry oxygen via haemoglobin (mature human RBCs lack a nucleus; life about 120 days); **WBCs** fight infection; **platelets** help clotting. ABO groups (**Karl Landsteiner**): **O** is the universal donor and **AB** the universal recipient (for red cells), also considering the **Rh** factor.

cards.title: Glands and hormones
points: Pituitary — 'master gland'; growth hormone
Thyroid — thyroxine; iodine deficiency causes goitre
Pancreas — insulin and glucagon (blood sugar)
Adrenal — adrenaline ('fight or flight')
Pineal — melatonin (sleep cycle)

cards.title: Plant processes
cards.body: **Photosynthesis**: CO₂ + water + light (with chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen. **Transpiration** — water loss through stomata. **Nitrogen fixation** — *Rhizobium* bacteria in root nodules of **legumes**. Plant hormones: **auxin** (growth), **gibberellin** (stem elongation), **cytokinin** (cell division), **abscisic acid** (stress, dormancy), **ethylene** (ripening).

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Brain parts: **cerebrum** — thinking, memory; **cerebellum** — balance and coordination; **medulla oblongata** — involuntary actions such as breathing and heartbeat. The **liver** is the largest gland and makes **bile**.

cards.q: Scurvy is caused by deficiency of:
cards.explain: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.

cards.q: Which part of the brain maintains balance?
cards.explain: The cerebellum coordinates posture and balance.

cards.q: Nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium is found in root nodules of:
cards.explain: Rhizobium forms symbiosis with leguminous plants such as peas and pulses.

notes.p:
Living things are organised as **cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism**. **Whittaker's five-kingdom** classification groups life into Monera (bacteria), Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. **Viruses** are not placed in any kingdom — they lack cell structure and reproduce only inside host cells. **Prokaryotes** (bacteria) lack a true nucleus; **eukaryotes** have one.

Cell division happens by **mitosis** (two identical daughter cells; growth and repair) and **meiosis** (four cells with half the chromosome number; forms gametes). **Stem cells** can turn into many cell types and are used in research and some therapies, such as bone-marrow transplants. **Enzymes** are proteins that speed up reactions; they work best at particular temperatures and pH, which is why high fever can be dangerous.
Short summaries:
points: **Digestive:** salivary amylase begins starch digestion; stomach pepsin digests proteins; small intestine absorbs most nutrients; villi increase surface area
**Respiratory:** gas exchange in alveoli; oxygen carried by haemoglobin
**Circulatory:** four-chambered heart; arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins towards it; pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood
**Excretory:** kidneys filter blood in **nephrons**; dialysis substitutes for failed kidneys
**Nervous:** neurons transmit impulses; reflex actions are controlled by the spinal cord
**Skeletal:** an adult has 206 bones; the femur is the longest; the stapes (ear) the smallest

notes.p: A balanced diet needs carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. **Protein-energy malnutrition** causes **kwashiorkor** (protein deficiency, swollen belly) and **marasmus** (severe overall deficiency, wasting). Mineral deficiencies: **iron** — anaemia; **iodine** — goitre and impaired development (hence iodised salt); **calcium** — weak bones. India's fortification programme adds iron, folic acid and vitamin B12 to rice supplied through government schemes.

Genes carry instructions for proteins. **Mutations** change genes; some cause **genetic disorders** — **sickle cell anaemia** and **thalassaemia** (blood), **haemophilia** and **colour blindness** (X-linked, more common in males), **Down syndrome** (an extra chromosome 21). India launched a **National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission** in 2023, focused on tribal areas. Biotechnology tools such as **CRISPR** gene editing are covered in the emerging-technology chapter.

A patient with blood group **B** needs red cells. Who can donate?

Step 1: Group B red cells carry the B antigen; the patient's plasma has **anti-A** antibodies.
Step 2: Donor red cells must not carry the A antigen.
Step 3: Acceptable donors: **B** and **O**.
Step 4: Also match Rh — an Rh-negative patient should receive Rh-negative blood.
Answer: B or O (Rh-matched).

UPSC asks basic biology through applied contexts — nutrition programmes, genetic diseases, hormones, and plant biology in agriculture. Precise vocabulary matters: 'antigen' vs 'antibody', 'gene' vs 'chromosome'.
Recall.
points: Mitochondria — ATP; ribosomes — proteins
46 chromosomes; father's Y decides male sex
Vitamins: A night blindness, C scurvy, D rickets, K clotting
O universal donor; AB universal recipient
Pituitary master gland; insulin from pancreas
Cerebellum — balance; medulla — involuntary
Rhizobium in legumes; ethylene ripens fruit

cards.title: Diseases by pathogen
points: Bacteria: tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, diphtheria, leprosy, plague
Viruses: COVID-19, influenza, measles, polio, rabies, dengue, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis, Nipah, mpox
Protozoa: malaria (Plasmodium), kala-azar (Leishmania), amoebiasis
Fungi: ringworm, candidiasis
Worms: filariasis, roundworm

cards.title: Vectors
points: Female Anopheles mosquito — malaria
Aedes mosquito — dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever
Culex mosquito — lymphatic filariasis, Japanese encephalitis
Sandfly — kala-azar
Rat flea — plague

cards.title: Types of vaccines
cards.body: **Live attenuated** — BCG, MMR, oral polio. **Inactivated** — injectable polio (IPV), rabies. **Toxoid** — tetanus, diphtheria. **Subunit/recombinant** — hepatitis B, HPV. **Viral vector** and **mRNA** — platforms used for COVID-19 vaccines.

cards.title: Immunity
cards.body: **Innate** immunity is present from birth; **acquired** immunity develops after exposure. **Active** immunity — the body makes its own antibodies (infection or vaccine; long-lasting). **Passive** immunity — ready-made antibodies (mother's milk, antiserum; short-lived).

cards.title: India's public-health milestones
cards.body: **Universal Immunisation Programme** (1985). India was certified **polio-free in 2014** (last wild case in January 2011). **Maternal and neonatal tetanus** eliminated (2015). WHO validated India as having **eliminated trachoma** as a public-health problem (2024).

cards.title: Antimicrobial resistance
cards.body: **AMR** occurs when microbes evolve to survive drugs. Antibiotics work against **bacteria, not viruses** — misuse for colds speeds resistance. India's **Red Line campaign** marks prescription-only antibiotics. **One Health** links human, animal and environmental health.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Many diseases are **zoonotic** (from animals): rabies, Nipah (fruit bats), avian influenza, Kyasanur Forest Disease ('monkey fever', Karnataka), and likely COVID-19. Expect questions combining disease, pathogen and vector.

cards.q: Kala-azar is transmitted by:
cards.explain: The sandfly transmits Leishmania donovani.

cards.q: Which vaccine is a toxoid?
cards.explain: Tetanus vaccine uses inactivated toxin (toxoid).

cards.q: Antibiotics are NOT effective against:
cards.explain: Influenza is viral; antibiotics act on bacteria.

notes.p:
**Communicable diseases** spread through air (TB, measles), water and food (cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E), vectors (malaria, dengue), body fluids (HIV, hepatitis B and C) or contact. **Non-communicable diseases (NCDs)** — heart disease, diabetes, cancer, chronic respiratory disease — are now the leading cause of death in India. Risk factors include tobacco, alcohol, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity and air pollution. India runs screening for common NCDs at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.

**Neglected tropical diseases** such as kala-azar, lymphatic filariasis, leprosy and dengue mostly affect the poor; mass drug administration campaigns target filariasis. **Mental health** has gained policy attention through the **Mental Healthcare Act 2017**, which decriminalised attempted suicide in most cases, and the **Tele-MANAS** helpline. Emerging threats include new zoonoses, AMR and the health effects of heatwaves and air pollution.
India runs national programmes for key diseases:
points: **TB**: National TB Elimination Programme, with a national goal of ending TB ahead of the SDG target year of 2030; **Ni-kshay Poshan** provides nutrition support
**Vector-borne diseases**: malaria, dengue, chikungunya, kala-azar, filariasis, Japanese encephalitis
**HIV/AIDS**: NACO; free antiretroviral therapy
**Leprosy**: multi-drug therapy
**Mission Indradhanush**: catches up on missed immunisation
**HPV vaccination** against cervical cancer — India has an indigenous vaccine, **Cervavac**

notes.p: A vaccine exposes the immune system to a harmless form or part of a pathogen, so it builds **memory cells**. On real infection, the body responds faster. **Herd immunity** arises when enough people are immune that spread is limited, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated. **Cold chains** are essential; India's **eVIN** system tracks vaccine stocks and temperatures digitally, and the **CoWIN** platform managed COVID-19 vaccination.

**Edward Jenner** — smallpox vaccine (1796). **Louis Pasteur** — rabies vaccine and pasteurisation. **Robert Koch** — identified the TB bacterium. **Alexander Fleming** — penicillin (1928). **Banting and Best** — insulin (1921). **Ronald Ross** — showed in India (1897) that mosquitoes transmit malaria, winning the Nobel Prize in 1902. Smallpox was declared eradicated globally in **1980**.

Clues: viral disease, spread by **Aedes** mosquito, sudden high fever, severe joint pain, outbreaks after monsoon.

Step 1: Vector Aedes → dengue, chikungunya or Zika.
Step 2: Severe, often long-lasting **joint pain** is the hallmark of **chikungunya**.
Step 3: Dengue is more associated with low platelet counts and bleeding risk.
Answer: **Chikungunya**.

Expect pathogen/vector matching, vaccine types, statements on immunity and AMR, and disease programmes or outbreaks in the news. Phrase-check carefully: 'eliminated' (as a public-health problem) is not the same as 'eradicated' (zero cases worldwide). Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated so far.
Recall.
points: Malaria — Plasmodium via female Anopheles
Dengue/chikungunya/Zika — Aedes
Kala-azar — sandfly; filariasis — Culex
Live, inactivated, toxoid, subunit, mRNA vaccines
Active vs passive immunity
Polio-free 2014; trachoma eliminated 2024
Antibiotics don't work on viruses; AMR

chapters.title: S&T Developments, Indigenisation & IT, Robotics, Nanotech

cards.title: Syllabus lines
points: S&T developments and their **applications in everyday life**
Achievements of Indians in S&T; **indigenisation** of technology
Awareness in **IT, space, computers, robotics, nano-technology, bio-technology**

cards.title: Indigenisation milestones
points: **INS Vikrant**: first indigenous aircraft carrier (commissioned 2022)
**Tejas** light combat aircraft
Akash, Astra missiles; Pinaka rockets
UPI and digital public infrastructure
Indigenous 4G/5G stack; COVID-19 vaccines

cards.title: Missions to know
points: **National Supercomputing Mission** (2015): PARAM systems
**India Semiconductor Mission** (2021)
**National Quantum Mission** (2023)
**IndiaAI Mission** (2024)
**Anusandhan National Research Foundation** (2023 Act)

cards.title: Robotics
cards.body: Robots sense, decide and act. Applications: manufacturing automation, surgery, warehousing, agriculture, disaster response, defence (bomb disposal), and space. Concerns: job displacement, safety, accountability.

cards.title: Nanotechnology
cards.body: Working with materials at **1–100 nanometres**, where properties change (strength, conductivity, reactivity). Applications: targeted drug delivery, water filters, coatings, sensors, batteries. India launched the **Nano Mission** in 2007. Risks: toxicity and environmental effects are not fully understood.

cards.title: IT and computing awareness
points: **Cloud** computing; **edge** computing
**AI and machine learning**; generative AI
**Quantum computing** uses qubits
**IoT**, **5G** (launched in India in 2022)
**Blockchain**: distributed ledgers

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For every technology: define in one line, give 3–4 applications in Indian context, note concerns (ethical, security, employment), and name India's mission or policy.

cards.q: INS Vikrant, commissioned in 2022, is India's first indigenous:
cards.explain: It was built by Cochin Shipyard.

cards.q: Nanotechnology deals with structures typically in the size range of:
cards.explain: The nanoscale is usually taken as 1–100 nm.

notes.p:
Mains S&T questions are **application-oriented**: how a technology helps citizens, what India has achieved, and what policy is needed. Prelims-style facts on space and biotech are in the Space & Defence and Biotechnology chapters; this chapter covers **indigenisation** and **IT, computers, robotics and nanotechnology**.

"Applications in everyday life" means connecting science to ordinary experience: satellite-based weather forecasts and fishing-zone advisories, GPS/NavIC navigation, digital payments, telemedicine, LED lighting, water purification, vaccines and diagnostics. India's research ecosystem still spends a modest share of GDP on R&D, with business contributing less than in leading economies — a common point for "way forward" sections.

Indigenisation means designing and producing technology domestically to reduce import dependence and build strategic autonomy. Drivers: technology denial regimes historically (after Pokhran tests), security needs, and cost. Milestones:
points: Space: launch vehicles, Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan missions, NavIC
Defence: Tejas, INS Vikrant, Arihant-class submarines, Akash, BrahMos (joint), positive indigenisation lists
Digital: Aadhaar, UPI, CoWIN-type platforms, C-DOT telecom technology
Health: indigenous vaccines, low-cost diagnostics
Policy: Atmanirbhar Bharat, Make in India, Defence Acquisition Procedure preferences, iDEX for start-ups

notes.p: Examples useful in answers: **C.V. Raman** (Raman effect, Nobel 1930), **Homi Bhabha** (nuclear programme), **Vikram Sarabhai** (space programme), **M.S. Swaminathan** (Green Revolution), **APJ Abdul Kalam** (missiles), **Verghese Kurien** (dairy), **E. Sreedharan** (metro and Konkan rail), and scientists behind recent lunar and solar missions. Use them to illustrate indigenous capability and institution-building.

**Supercomputing:** PARAM series and the National Supercomputing Mission for weather, genomics and research. **Semiconductors:** fabs and assembly-testing units under the India Semiconductor Mission. **AI:** applications in agriculture advisories, health diagnostics, language translation (Bhashini), and governance; the **IndiaAI Mission** funds compute, datasets and start-ups. Concerns: bias, deepfakes, privacy, jobs and accountability. **Quantum:** the National Quantum Mission targets quantum computing, communication and sensing. **5G and IoT:** smart grids, telemedicine, precision farming.

**Robotics** combines sensors, actuators and control software. Uses in India: automotive assembly, surgery in large hospitals, warehouses, sewer-cleaning robots replacing manual scavenging, agricultural drones and defence robots. Issues: cost, skilling, job displacement.

**Nanotechnology** exploits properties at the 1–100 nm scale. Uses: nano-drug delivery for cancer, nano-silver water filters, nano-urea fertiliser, stronger lighter materials, better batteries and solar cells, sensors. Risks: unknown toxicity, environmental accumulation, need for regulation and safety standards.

Question type: "What is the significance of indigenisation in defence technology for India?"
**Why:** strategic autonomy, supply security in conflicts, foreign exchange savings, jobs and MSME growth.
**Progress:** INS Vikrant, Tejas, Akash, positive indigenisation lists, rising defence exports.
**Challenges:** engines and advanced electronics still imported; R&D spending; delays.
**Way forward:** private-sector participation, iDEX, co-development with partners, testing infrastructure.
**Conclusion:** self-reliance as capability, not isolation.
Key points.
points: Indigenisation: Vikrant (2022), Tejas, Akash, UPI, vaccines
Missions: Supercomputing 2015, Semiconductor 2021, Quantum 2023, IndiaAI 2024
ANRF Act 2023 for research funding
Nanoscale: 1–100 nm; Nano Mission 2007
Robotics: manufacturing, surgery, sanitation, defence
Always pair applications with concerns and policy

cards.title: Types of IPR
points: **Patents**: inventions; **20 years**
**Copyright**: creative works; generally author's life + 60 years in India
**Trademarks**: brand marks; 10 years, renewable
**Geographical Indications**: products tied to a place
**Industrial designs**; **plant varieties**; trade secrets

cards.title: Indian laws
points: Patents Act, 1970 (product patents restored in 2005)
Copyright Act, 1957
Trade Marks Act, 1999
Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999
Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001

cards.title: Section 3(d) and evergreening
cards.body: **Section 3(d)** bars patents on new forms of known substances unless they show enhanced **efficacy**. In **Novartis v Union of India (2013)**, the Supreme Court denied a patent for a modified form of the cancer drug Glivec, upholding the provision against **evergreening**.

cards.title: Compulsory licensing
cards.body: Under **Section 84**, the government can allow others to make a patented product if it is unaffordable or unavailable. India's first compulsory licence (2012) was granted to **Natco** for Bayer's cancer drug Nexavar.

cards.title: International framework
points: **TRIPS** Agreement under the WTO (1995)
**WIPO** administers treaties (Paris, Berne)
**Doha Declaration (2001)** on TRIPS and public health
WIPO treaty on genetic resources and traditional knowledge (2024)

cards.title: Protecting traditional knowledge
cards.body: The **Traditional Knowledge Digital Library** (TKDL) documents Indian traditional knowledge so patent offices can reject claims on it. India earlier fought patents on **turmeric** and **neem** uses.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: IPR answers need balance: innovation incentives vs access to medicines, farmers' rights and traditional knowledge. Mention the National IPR Policy (2016).

cards.q: Section 3(d) of India's Patents Act is mainly aimed at preventing:
cards.explain: It blocks patents on trivial modifications without enhanced efficacy.

cards.q: India's first compulsory licence (2012) was granted to:
cards.explain: Natco got a licence for Bayer's Nexavar (sorafenib).

cards.q: Which body administers the TRIPS Agreement?
cards.explain: TRIPS is a WTO agreement; WIPO administers other IP treaties.

notes.p: **Intellectual Property Rights** are legal rights over creations of the mind — inventions, literary and artistic works, brand names, designs and place-linked products. They give creators **exclusive rights for a limited time** in return for disclosure and to encourage innovation. Balancing private rights with **public interest** — access to medicines, seeds, knowledge — is the central policy challenge.
Main categories:
points: **Patents** (Patents Act, 1970): new, inventive, industrially applicable inventions; 20-year term
**Copyright** (Copyright Act, 1957): literary, artistic, musical works, software, films
**Trademarks** (Trade Marks Act, 1999): distinguishing marks; renewable every 10 years
**Geographical Indications** (GI Act, 1999): products with qualities due to origin — Darjeeling tea was among the first Indian GIs
**Designs** (Designs Act, 2000)
**Plant varieties** (PPV&FR Act, 2001): breeders' and farmers' rights
**Semiconductor layout designs** (2000 Act)

notes.p: The **Patents Act, 1970** allowed only process patents for food and drugs, enabling a strong **generic pharmaceutical industry** — India is often called the "pharmacy of the world". To comply with **TRIPS**, India reintroduced product patents in **2005**, but kept safeguards:
points: **Section 3(d)** against evergreening (Novartis case, 2013)
**Compulsory licensing** (Section 84; Natco–Bayer, 2012)
**Pre-grant and post-grant opposition**
Parallel imports and government use provisions

notes.p: **TRIPS (1995)** set minimum IP standards for WTO members. The **Doha Declaration (2001)** affirmed that TRIPS should not prevent members from protecting public health. Developed countries and pharmaceutical firms sometimes criticise India's safeguards; India appears on the US **Special 301** watch list. India co-sponsored a proposal for a **TRIPS waiver** for COVID-19 products; a limited decision on vaccines was adopted in 2022. In 2024, WIPO members adopted a treaty requiring disclosure of the origin of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge in patent applications — a long-standing demand of India and other biodiverse countries.

**Biopiracy** is patenting of traditional knowledge or biological resources without consent or benefit-sharing. India successfully challenged patents related to **turmeric** (wound healing) and **neem**. The **TKDL**, a database of traditional medicine formulations translated into several languages, lets patent examiners worldwide find prior art. The **Biological Diversity Act, 2002** requires approval and benefit-sharing for access to biological resources.

notes.h: National IPR Policy and way forward
notes.p: The **National IPR Policy (2016)** aims at awareness, generation of IP, legal framework, administration, commercialisation, enforcement and human capital ("Creative India; Innovative India"). Issues: patent backlog (being reduced with more examiners), low domestic patent filings relative to population (rising recently), weak commercialisation from universities, and piracy. Way forward: faster examination, IP courts, university technology transfer offices, and IP literacy among MSMEs and start-ups.
Key points.
points: Patents 20 yrs; trademarks 10 yrs renewable; copyright life + 60
Product patents reintroduced 2005 for TRIPS
Section 3(d): Novartis 2013; compulsory licence: Natco 2012
TRIPS (WTO, 1995); Doha Declaration 2001
TKDL against biopiracy; turmeric, neem cases
GI Act 1999; PPV&FR Act 2001
National IPR Policy 2016

cards.title: Policy frameworks
points: **Neighbourhood First** – priority to South Asian neighbours
**Act East Policy** (2014) – upgraded from the 1991 Look East Policy; focus on ASEAN and Indo-Pacific
**SAGAR** – Security and Growth for All in the Region (Indian Ocean); widened to **MAHASAGAR** in 2025
**Gujral Doctrine** (1996) – non-reciprocal goodwill towards smaller neighbours

cards.title: Regional groupings
points: **SAARC** – founded 1985 at Dhaka; 8 members; largely stalled
**BIMSTEC** – founded 1997; 7 members around the Bay of Bengal; bridges South and South-East Asia
**Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA)**

cards.title: Water and borders
cards.body: The **Indus Waters Treaty (1960)**, brokered by the World Bank, gave India the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) and Pakistan mainly the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab). India placed the treaty **in abeyance in April 2025** after the Pahalgam terror attack. The **Ganga Water Treaty (1996)** with Bangladesh shares Farakka flows.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For each neighbour, keep four headings: cooperation (trade, connectivity, energy), irritants (border, water, China factor), recent events, and the way forward. This structure answers almost any GS II neighbourhood question.

cards.q: Which rivers were allocated to India under the Indus Waters Treaty?
cards.explain: The eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — went to India.

cards.q: India's Act East Policy evolved from:
cards.explain: Look East (1991) was upgraded to Act East in 2014.

notes.p:
India's approach to its region is summed up in the **'Neighbourhood First'** policy, which focuses on connectivity, trade, development partnerships and people-to-people ties. It is supported by the **'Act East' policy** (upgraded from the 'Look East' policy of the 1990s) towards South-East Asia and the **SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region)** vision for the Indian Ocean, launched in 2015.

India shares land borders with **Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Afghanistan** (through the area of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir). Sri Lanka and the Maldives are maritime neighbours.
Each relationship has its own opportunities and challenges.
points: **Pakistan:** terrorism, Kashmir issue; the **Indus Waters Treaty (1960)**, brokered by the World Bank; the **Simla Agreement (1972)** made bilateralism the basis of resolving issues
**China:** boundary dispute along the **Line of Actual Control (LAC)**; the **Panchsheel** principles (1954); 1962 war; large trade deficit for India; Galwan clash (2020)
**Nepal:** open border under the **1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship**; hydropower cooperation; boundary differences
**Bhutan:** close partner; hydropower cooperation; strategic importance near the Doklam plateau
**Bangladesh:** **Land Boundary Agreement (2015)** settled enclaves; Teesta water sharing still pending; connectivity projects
**Sri Lanka:** fishermen issues in the Palk Strait; Tamil question; India's economic assistance during Sri Lanka's crisis
**Maldives:** security in the Indian Ocean; India–Maldives ties have seen ups and downs
**Myanmar:** gateway to South-East Asia; **Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project**; India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway

notes.p: Regional organisations provide platforms for cooperation.
points: **SAARC (1985):** eight members; largely stalled in recent years due to India–Pakistan tensions
**BIMSTEC (1997):** Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand — bridges South and South-East Asia; India sees it as an active alternative
**Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA)**
**Colombo Security Conclave:** maritime security cooperation

notes.p: China's growing presence in South Asia through the **Belt and Road Initiative (BRI)** — including the **China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC)**, which passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir — and investments in ports (for example Hambantota in Sri Lanka) is a strategic concern for India. India has not joined BRI, citing sovereignty concerns over CPEC. India responds through development partnerships, lines of credit, capacity building and connectivity projects.
A quick way to revise each neighbour is by listing one strength and one challenge.
points: **Bangladesh:** strong connectivity and trade / Teesta water, border management
**Nepal:** cultural and economic links / boundary disagreements, trust deficit
**Bhutan:** hydropower partnership / China's boundary talks with Bhutan
**Sri Lanka:** economic support and shared heritage / fishermen issue
**Myanmar:** gateway to the East / internal instability, border security
**Pakistan:** shared history and culture / cross-border terrorism
**China:** major trade partner / boundary dispute and trade deficit
**Maldives:** maritime security partner / political swings in ties

notes.p: Prelims asks about **places in the news** in neighbouring countries, rivers shared with neighbours, treaties and projects, and groupings with their members. Map-based questions are common. Mains GS II asks about **challenges and opportunities** in relations with a particular neighbour, the effectiveness of SAARC vs BIMSTEC, and China's influence in South Asia.
Key points.
points: Neighbourhood First; Act East; SAGAR (2015)
Indus Waters Treaty 1960 (World Bank); Simla Agreement 1972
Panchsheel 1954; LAC dispute with China
India–Nepal Treaty 1950; open border
India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement 2015
Kaladan project: Myanmar
SAARC 1985 (stalled); BIMSTEC 1997 (7 members)
India opposes CPEC on sovereignty grounds

cards.title: United Nations
cards.body: Founded in **1945**. The Security Council has **5 permanent members** with veto (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) and 10 elected members for two-year terms. India has served several terms as a non-permanent member and seeks a permanent seat along with reform of the Council.

cards.title: G20 and BRICS
points: India held the **G20 presidency in 2023**; at the New Delhi summit the **African Union** became a permanent member
**BRICS** expanded from 2024 (Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE joined; Indonesia in 2025)
India holds the **BRICS chair in 2026**

cards.title: Other groupings
points: **Quad** – India, USA, Japan, Australia; Indo-Pacific cooperation
**SCO** – India became a full member in 2017
**I2U2** – India, Israel, UAE, USA
**WTO** – trade rules; India pushes for food security and public stockholding

cards.title: Strategic autonomy
cards.body: India buys defence equipment from Russia, partners with the US in the Quad, and works with China in BRICS and SCO. This multi-alignment reflects 'strategic autonomy' — choosing partners issue by issue for national interest, a useful framing in GS II answers.

cards.q: Which body became a permanent member of the G20 during India's 2023 presidency?
cards.explain: The African Union was admitted at the New Delhi Summit in September 2023.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT a Quad member?
cards.explain: The Quad comprises India, USA, Japan and Australia.

notes.p: The **United Nations** was founded in **1945**; India is a founding member. Its main organs include the **General Assembly**, the **Security Council**, the **Economic and Social Council**, the **International Court of Justice** (at The Hague), the **Secretariat** and the Trusteeship Council (now inactive).
points: **UN Security Council:** 15 members — 5 permanent with veto (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) and 10 non-permanent elected for two-year terms
India has served as a non-permanent member several times and seeks a **permanent seat**; it is part of the **G4** (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) that pushes for UNSC reform
Specialised agencies: WHO, FAO, ILO, UNESCO, IMF and World Bank, among others

notes.p: Know their origin and role.
points: **IMF and World Bank:** created at the **Bretton Woods Conference (1944)**
**WTO:** set up on **1 January 1995**, replacing GATT; Ministerial Conference is the top decision-making body

**G20:** major economies; leaders' summits since 2008; India held the presidency in 2023 with the theme **'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam – One Earth, One Family, One Future'**; the African Union became a permanent member during India's presidency
**New Development Bank (NDB):** set up by BRICS; headquartered in Shanghai
**Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB):** headquartered in Beijing; India is a founding member

notes.p: India follows **multi-alignment** — engaging with many groups at once to protect its interests (often linked to the idea of **strategic autonomy**).
points: **BRICS:** Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa; expanded from 2024 — check the current member list
**SCO (Shanghai Cooperation Organisation):** India became a full member in 2017
**Quad:** India, USA, Japan, Australia — free and open Indo-Pacific
**ASEAN:** South-East Asian grouping (Timor-Leste was admitted as the 11th member in 2025); central to India's Act East policy
**Commonwealth**, **Non-Aligned Movement (NAM)** — India was a founding leader of NAM (Belgrade, 1961)
**I2U2** (India, Israel, UAE, USA) and the **India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC)**

notes.p: These matter for technology access.
points: India is a member of **MTCR (2016)**, **Wassenaar Arrangement (2017)** and **Australia Group (2018)**
India is **not** a member of the **Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG)**
**FATF:** sets standards against money laundering and terror financing; India is a member

notes.p: Multilateral forums give India a voice on rules that affect its growth and security — trade, climate, technology, finance and terrorism. India uses them to speak for the **Global South**, for example by hosting the **Voice of the Global South Summit** during its G20 presidency. At the same time, institutions like the UNSC, IMF and World Bank are criticised for reflecting the power balance of 1945 rather than today's world, so India argues for **reformed multilateralism**.

Prelims frequently asks about **membership** ('Which of the following countries are members of…?'), headquarters, origin, and functions of groupings. Mains GS II asks about **India's role in multilateral forums**, UNSC reform, the relevance of NAM today, and balancing groups like the Quad and SCO.
Key points.
points: UN 1945; UNSC: 5 permanent + 10 non-permanent
G4: India, Brazil, Germany, Japan — UNSC reform
Bretton Woods 1944: IMF and World Bank
WTO 1 January 1995
G20 India presidency 2023; African Union joined as permanent member
NDB: Shanghai; AIIB: Beijing
India: SCO since 2017; member of MTCR, Wassenaar, Australia Group; not NSG
Check latest BRICS and ASEAN membership

cards.title: Strategic autonomy
cards.body: India pursues **strategic autonomy** — partnering with many powers without formal alliances — described as **multi-alignment**. It engages the US, Russia, the EU, Japan and Gulf states, while managing a complex relationship with China.

cards.title: India–USA
points: Civil nuclear deal: framework 2005, **123 Agreement** 2008
**Major Defence Partner** (2016)
Foundational pacts: LEMOA (2016), COMCASA (2018), BECA (2020)
Cooperation in **Quad**, technology, space
Frictions: trade and tariffs, visas, Russia ties — check latest

cards.title: India–Russia
points: **Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership** (2010)
Major arms supplier; S-400; BrahMos joint venture
Kudankulam nuclear plant
Large oil imports since 2022
INSTC corridor; balancing Russia–China closeness

cards.title: India–China
points: Boundary dispute; **Galwan clash (2020)**
Disengagement understandings at friction points (2024)
Large trade deficit; supply-chain dependence
Concerns: CPEC through PoK, Indian Ocean presence
Engagement in BRICS and SCO

cards.title: Japan, EU, UK, France
points: **Japan**: Special Strategic and Global Partnership; Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed rail
**EU**: trade, technology and clean energy; free trade agreement talks — check current status
**UK**: trade agreement signed in 2025
**France**: Rafale, space, civil nuclear, International Solar Alliance co-founder

cards.title: West Asia and connectivity
points: Gulf: energy, diaspora, investment
**I2U2** (India, Israel, UAE, USA)
**IMEC** corridor announced at G20 (2023)
**Chabahar** port (Iran) for Afghanistan and Central Asia access

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Structure bilateral answers as: convergences (strategic, economic, people), divergences, recent milestones, and way forward. Keep facts that change fast (tariffs, deals) phrased with "recently" and verify before the exam.

cards.q: The "123 Agreement" refers to India's civil nuclear cooperation agreement with:
cards.explain: Named after Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act; concluded in 2008.

cards.q: Which grouping includes India, Israel, the UAE and the USA?
cards.explain: I2U2 is a minilateral on economic cooperation.

cards.q: BrahMos missile is a joint venture between India and:
cards.explain: BrahMos Aerospace is an India–Russia JV.

notes.p: India's foreign policy moved from **non-alignment** during the Cold War to **multi-alignment**: deep partnerships with several powers based on issue-wise convergence. The goals are security (especially vis-à-vis China and Pakistan), economic growth (trade, investment, technology, energy), a favourable regional order and a larger global voice (UN reforms, G20). GS II asks about "**bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests**".

Relations transformed after 2000: the **civil nuclear deal** (2005 framework, 2008 agreement and NSG waiver), **Major Defence Partner** status (2016), foundational defence agreements (LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA), joint exercises (Malabar, Yudh Abhyas), the **Quad**, and technology cooperation in semiconductors, AI and space. The Indian-American community and student flows are strong bridges.

Divergences include trade disputes and tariffs, immigration and visa rules, US sanctions affecting India's partners (CAATSA, Iran), and differing views on Russia. These have intensified recently — check the current state before the exam.

A time-tested partnership, upgraded to a **Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership** (2010). Russia has been a major defence supplier (S-400, Su-30MKI, joint production of **BrahMos**), a nuclear partner (**Kudankulam**) and a supporter at the UN. Since 2022, India has sharply increased discounted oil imports from Russia. Challenges: Russia's growing dependence on China, payment issues, delays in defence deliveries, and Western pressure. India has called for dialogue and diplomacy over the Ukraine conflict.

The relationship mixes **competition, cooperation and confrontation**. The **boundary dispute** along the LAC flared at **Galwan (2020)**, the deadliest clash in decades; disengagement understandings in 2024 eased tensions, followed by gradual steps to normalise ties. Economically, China is a top trading partner but India runs a large deficit and depends on Chinese inputs (APIs, electronics, solar). Concerns include **CPEC** through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, Chinese presence in the Indian Ocean and neighbourhood, and dam-building on the Brahmaputra. Cooperation continues in BRICS, SCO and climate negotiations.

**Japan:** trusted partner for infrastructure (high-speed rail, metros), investment and Indo-Pacific cooperation, including the Quad. **EU:** India's major trading partner with negotiations on trade, investment and geographical indications; carbon border measures are a concern. **UK:** a trade agreement was signed in 2025. **France:** strategic partner since 1998 — Rafale jets, Scorpène submarines, space and the **International Solar Alliance**.

**Gulf:** energy, remittances from a large diaspora, and investment (UAE CEPA, 2022). New formats include **I2U2** and the **India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC)**.

Question type: "How can India balance its relations with the US and Russia?"
**Convergence with US:** technology, Indo-Pacific, investment. **With Russia:** defence legacy, energy, Eurasian balance.
**Tensions:** sanctions, Russia–China ties, trade frictions.
**Approach:** strategic autonomy, diversified defence imports with indigenisation, rupee trade options, active diplomacy for peace.
**Conclusion:** India's interests, not bloc loyalty, guide choices.
Key points.
points: Multi-alignment and strategic autonomy
US: 123 Agreement 2008; MDP 2016; LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA; Quad
Russia: Special and Privileged Partnership 2010; S-400; BrahMos; Kudankulam
China: Galwan 2020; 2024 disengagement; trade deficit; CPEC
Japan: high-speed rail; EU trade talks; UK deal 2025; France: Rafale, ISA
West Asia: I2U2, IMEC, Chabahar, UAE CEPA

chapters.title: Indian Diaspora & Effects of Other Countries' Policies on India

cards.title: Syllabus lines
points: "Effect of policies and politics of **developed and developing countries** on India's interests"
"**Indian diaspora**"
"Important international institutions, agencies and fora — their structure and mandate" (see Global Institutions chapter)

cards.title: The diaspora
cards.body: India has one of the world's **largest diasporas**: **NRIs** (Indian citizens abroad) and **PIOs/OCIs** (foreign citizens of Indian origin). India is the **largest recipient of remittances** in the world (World Bank data).

cards.title: Engagement tools
points: **Pravasi Bharatiya Divas**: 9 January (Gandhi's return from South Africa, 1915)
**OCI card** (PIO card merged into OCI in 2015)
e-Migrate; Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana
Operations to evacuate citizens (e.g. Operation Ganga, 2022)
Know India Programme for diaspora youth

cards.title: Policies of developed countries that affect India
points: Visa and immigration rules (H-1B, student visas)
**Carbon border measures** (EU CBAM)
Tariffs and protectionism
Farm subsidies and WTO positions
Sanctions on Russia and Iran
Data and digital regulations; IPR standards

cards.title: Developing countries' policies
points: China's **Belt and Road Initiative** and debt diplomacy
Gulf labour laws and nationalisation of jobs
Regional instability (Afghanistan, Myanmar)
South–South cooperation and Global South solidarity

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For diaspora answers, cover economic (remittances, investment), soft power, political (lobbying), knowledge transfer — and challenges (labour exploitation in Gulf, racial attacks, dual citizenship demands, brain drain).

cards.q: Pravasi Bharatiya Divas is observed on 9 January because on that day:
options: Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in 1915
The first NRI law was passed
cards.explain: Gandhi returned to India on 9 January 1915.

cards.q: The EU's CBAM mainly affects Indian exports of:
options: Carbon-intensive goods like steel and aluminium
cards.explain: The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism prices embedded carbon in imports such as steel and aluminium.

notes.p:
The diaspora includes **Non-Resident Indians** (Indian citizens living abroad) and **Persons of Indian Origin** (foreign citizens of Indian descent, many holding **OCI** cards). Historic waves include indentured labour to Mauritius, Fiji, the Caribbean and Africa in the 19th century; professionals to the US, UK and Canada after the 1960s; and large labour migration to the Gulf from the 1970s.

India is the **world's largest recipient of remittances** according to World Bank data, which supports household incomes, especially in Kerala, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and other states.
Contributions:
points: **Economic:** remittances, investment, trade links, start-up networks
**Knowledge:** transfer of skills and technology; scientific collaboration
**Soft power:** culture, yoga, cuisine, cinema, leadership in global firms and politics
**Political:** advocacy in host countries (e.g. support during the civil nuclear deal)
**Crisis support:** relief funds and volunteer networks

notes.p:
Issues: exploitation of low-skilled workers in the Gulf (kafala system, wage theft), deaths and legal troubles abroad, racial attacks, **brain drain**, fraudulent recruitment agents, and occasional controversy where diaspora groups support anti-India activities.

Policy responses: **Emigration Act, 1983** and the **e-Migrate** system, Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana, Indian Community Welfare Fund, **Pravasi Bharatiya Divas**, OCI cards, and evacuation operations (Vande Bharat during COVID-19, Operation Ganga from Ukraine in 2022, Operation Kaveri from Sudan in 2023). A new emigration law to replace the 1983 Act has been proposed — check the latest status.

Decisions in Washington, Brussels or London shape Indian interests: **immigration and visa** rules affect IT professionals and students; **tariffs and protectionism** affect exports; the EU's **Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism** imposes costs on carbon-intensive exports like steel and aluminium; **farm subsidies** in rich countries distort global prices; **sanctions** on Russia and Iran complicate India's energy and connectivity plans (Chabahar); and strict **IPR** demands affect generic medicines. Monetary policy of the US Federal Reserve affects capital flows and the rupee. Climate negotiations raise issues of **climate finance** and common but differentiated responsibilities.

China's **Belt and Road Initiative** creates strategic and debt concerns in India's neighbourhood (e.g. Hambantota in Sri Lanka). Gulf countries' labour nationalisation policies affect Indian workers. Instability in Afghanistan, Myanmar or Bangladesh affects security and migration. At the same time, India leads **Global South** solidarity — the Voice of Global South Summits and the African Union's inclusion in the G20 during India's presidency (2023).

Question type: "Discuss the role of the Indian diaspora as a strategic asset."
**Intro:** size and spread; remittance leadership.
**Economic, knowledge, soft-power, political roles** with examples.
**Challenges:** Gulf labour issues, brain drain, divisive groups.
**Way forward:** a new emigration law, skilling for overseas jobs, mobility agreements, digital consular services.
**Conclusion:** a bridge between India and the world.
Key points.
points: NRI = Indian citizens abroad; PIO/OCI = foreign citizens of Indian origin
India: largest remittance recipient (World Bank)
Pravasi Bharatiya Divas: 9 January (1915)
Emigration Act 1983; e-Migrate; evacuation operations
Developed-country policies: visas, tariffs, CBAM, sanctions, IPR, subsidies
Developing countries: BRI, Gulf labour policies, regional instability
Global South leadership; AU joined G20 in 2023

cards.title: What GS IV tests
cards.body: GS Paper IV (250 marks) has two parts: **Section A** on theory — ethics, attitude, aptitude, emotional intelligence, thinkers, probity — and **Section B** with **case studies**. It tests your values and decision-making as a future civil servant, not memorised definitions.

cards.title: Ethics, morality, law
points: **Ethics** – systematic principles of right and wrong (often for a group or profession)
**Morality** – personal beliefs about right and wrong
**Law** – rules enforced by the State; something legal may still be unethical

cards.title: Attitude
cards.body: An attitude is a learned tendency to evaluate people, objects or ideas. Its three components (ABC model):
points: **Affective** – feelings
**Behavioural** – actions
**Cognitive** – beliefs and thoughts

cards.title: Emotional intelligence
cards.body: Popularised by **Daniel Goleman**, EI is the ability to understand and manage your own and others' emotions. Five elements: **self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills**. Example: a DM staying calm and empathetic while handling an angry crowd after a flood.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Build a bank of real examples — civil servants, freedom fighters, reformers — for each value: integrity, empathy, courage. One crisp example makes a theory answer stand out.

cards.q: Which is NOT one of Goleman's elements of emotional intelligence?
cards.explain: IQ is cognitive intelligence; Goleman's EI elements are self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.

cards.q: The three components of attitude are:
cards.explain: The ABC model: Affective, Behavioural, Cognitive.

notes.h: What GS Paper IV is about
notes.p: **GS Paper IV — Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude** tests your attitude and approach to issues of integrity and probity in public life, and your ability to solve problems faced by people in society. It has two sections: **Section A** (theory) and **Section B** (case studies). Unlike other papers, there is no single correct answer — the examiner looks for **clarity of values, balanced reasoning and practical solutions**.
Learn short, clear definitions you can use in answers.
points: **Ethics:** the study of what is right and wrong, good and bad in human conduct
**Morality:** an individual's or society's beliefs about right and wrong
**Values:** lasting beliefs that guide choices (e.g. honesty, compassion)
**Integrity:** consistency between one's values, words and actions — even when no one is watching
**Probity:** strict honesty and uprightness, especially in public life
**Conscience:** the inner sense of right and wrong; Gandhi called it the 'inner voice'
**Attitude:** a settled way of thinking or feeling about something; has cognitive, affective and behavioural components

notes.p: Different schools judge right action differently.
points: **Deontology (Kant):** duty-based; actions are right or wrong in themselves; act only by rules you could will to be universal; treat people as ends, never merely as means
**Consequentialism / Utilitarianism (Bentham, J.S. Mill):** right action produces the greatest good for the greatest number
**Virtue ethics (Aristotle):** focuses on character; virtue is the 'golden mean' between extremes
**Gandhian ethics:** truth, non-violence, ends and means both must be pure; 'Seven Social Sins'; trusteeship

**Indian traditions:** *nishkama karma* (action without attachment to results) from the Bhagavad Gita; Buddha's middle path; Kautilya's idea that the king's happiness lies in the happiness of his subjects
**Rawls:** justice as fairness; the 'veil of ignorance'

notes.p:
**Emotional Intelligence (EI)** is the ability to understand and manage your own emotions and those of others. **Daniel Goleman** popularised a model with five parts: **self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills**.

For civil servants, EI helps in handling public grievances, leading teams, resolving conflicts and staying calm under pressure. In answers, connect EI to real administrative situations such as handling protests or disasters.
Use examples and quotes from thinkers carefully — only when sure of the source.
points: Family, school, society, religion and law shape values
**Swami Vivekananda:** character building and service to humanity
**Dr B.R. Ambedkar:** constitutional morality, social justice
**Rabindranath Tagore:** humanism, freedom of the mind
**Socrates / Plato:** virtue as knowledge, justice in the state
Real-life role models: honest officers, social reformers and scientists

notes.p: Section A usually asks for **definitions with examples**, the relevance of a **thinker's quote** to today, the **difference between related terms** (e.g. ethics vs morality, integrity vs probity), and the role of family, society and education in building values. Case studies in Section B test application. Answers that use simple examples from public administration score better than long philosophical text.
Key points.
points: GS IV: Section A (theory) + Section B (case studies)
Integrity = consistency of values, words and deeds
Kant: duty; Mill/Bentham: greatest good; Aristotle: golden mean
Gandhi: purity of ends and means; trusteeship
Nishkama karma from the Bhagavad Gita
Goleman's EI: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills
Rawls: veil of ignorance
Always add examples from public life

cards.title: Foundational values
cards.body: The GS IV syllabus lists the values every civil servant needs:
points: Integrity, impartiality and non-partisanship
Objectivity
Dedication to public service
Empathy, tolerance and compassion towards the weaker sections

cards.title: Nolan Principles
cards.body: The UK Committee on Standards in Public Life (1995) set out seven principles of public life: **Selflessness, Integrity, Objectivity, Accountability, Openness, Honesty and Leadership**. India's **Second ARC** (4th Report, 'Ethics in Governance') drew on similar ideas.

cards.title: Probity in governance
cards.body: Probity means uprightness beyond mere legal compliance. Tools that promote it:
points: Right to Information Act, 2005
Citizen's Charters and grievance redress
Codes of conduct and codes of ethics
Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013
E-governance that reduces discretion

cards.title: Gandhi's Seven Social Sins
cards.body: Published in Young India (1925): politics without principle, wealth without work, pleasure without conscience, knowledge without character, commerce without morality, science without humanity, worship without sacrifice. Very useful for quotes in Essay and GS IV.

cards.q: Which is NOT a Nolan Principle?
cards.explain: The seven are Selflessness, Integrity, Objectivity, Accountability, Openness, Honesty and Leadership.

cards.q: 'Ethics in Governance' is the title of which report of the Second ARC?
cards.explain: The Fourth Report (2007) of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission is 'Ethics in Governance'.

notes.p: The **Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2nd ARC)**, chaired first by **Veerappa Moily**, studied ethics in governance in its **fourth report, 'Ethics in Governance'**. Commonly listed foundational values of civil services include:
points: **Integrity:** honesty in all actions
**Impartiality and non-partisanship:** treating everyone equally and serving the government of the day without political bias
**Objectivity:** decisions based on merit and evidence
**Dedication to public service**
**Empathy, tolerance and compassion towards the weaker sections**
**Accountability and transparency**

notes.p: **Probity** means not just avoiding corruption but following the highest standards of honesty. It is supported by laws and institutions.
points: **Right to Information Act, 2005:** transparency in government
**Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988** (amended in 2018 to also punish bribe-giving)
**Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**
**Central Vigilance Commission**
**Citizen's charters** and grievance redressal systems
**Codes of conduct** such as the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968
**Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014**

notes.p: The UK's **Committee on Standards in Public Life (Nolan Committee, 1995)** gave **seven principles of public life**, which are often quoted in Indian answers:
points: Selflessness
Integrity
Objectivity
Accountability
Openness
Honesty
Leadership

notes.h: Conflict of interest and ethical dilemmas
notes.p:
A **conflict of interest** arises when an official's personal interest could influence their public duty — for example, awarding a contract to a relative's firm. The right step is to **disclose and recuse**.

Common dilemmas for civil servants include personal values vs organisational orders, loyalty to seniors vs public interest, rules vs compassion, and transparency vs confidentiality. Resolve them using **constitutional values**, **law**, **public interest** and **conscience**, in that broad order of reference.

A useful test is to ask: *Would I be comfortable if this decision were published on the front page of a newspaper?* If the answer is no, the action probably fails the standard of probity, even if it is technically legal.

Good governance means **SMART** governance (Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent), service delivery with dignity, and using technology to reduce discretion and delays. **Mission Karmayogi** (National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building) aims to build role-based competencies — check its latest components.

Values matter most at the **cutting edge** of administration — the patwari, the police constable or the hospital clerk whom citizens meet first. Senior officers set the tone by **leading by example**, rewarding honesty, protecting whistle-blowers and making systems simple enough that discretion cannot be misused.

Questions ask you to **explain a value** and show its relevance with examples, discuss **codes of ethics vs codes of conduct**, analyse how laws like RTI promote probity, and resolve ethical dilemmas. Quotes from thinkers on public service are common. Use short examples from administration to support every point.
Key points.
points: 2nd ARC 4th report: 'Ethics in Governance'
Foundational values: integrity, impartiality, non-partisanship, objectivity, dedication, empathy
Nolan principles: 7 — selflessness to leadership
Code of ethics = broad values; code of conduct = specific rules
RTI 2005; PCA 1988 (amended 2018); Lokpal 2013; Whistle Blowers Act 2014
Conflict of interest: disclose and recuse
Mission Karmayogi: civil service capacity building

cards.title: A simple framework
points: 1. Identify the **stakeholders**
2. Spot the **ethical dilemma** (e.g. duty vs compassion)
3. List **options** with pros and cons
4. Choose a course and justify it with values and law
5. Suggest long-term systemic fixes

cards.title: Sample case
cards.body: You are a district officer. A contractor close to a local MLA offers a 'gift' and asks you to overlook poor road quality. Stakeholders: public, contractor, MLA, you. Best course: politely refuse, record the offer, order a quality inspection, act per rules and inform superiors. Long term: third-party audits and geo-tagged project monitoring.

cards.title: Ethical lenses
points: **Utilitarianism** (Bentham, Mill) – greatest good of the greatest number
**Kant's deontology** – act on duty; treat people as ends, never merely as means
**Virtue ethics** (Aristotle) – develop good character; the 'golden mean'
**Gandhian** – purity of means and ends; Talisman: think of the poorest person

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Never choose an extreme, illegal or passive option. Examiners reward answers that are lawful, compassionate, practical and that strengthen institutions — not ones that make you a lone hero.

cards.q: 'Act only on that maxim which you can will to become a universal law' is associated with:
cards.explain: This is Kant's categorical imperative.

cards.q: In a case study, the first step should usually be to:
cards.explain: Identifying stakeholders and the core dilemma frames the analysis of options.

notes.p:
Section B of GS IV has **case studies** that describe a real-life administrative or personal situation with an ethical dilemma. They test whether you can **identify the issues, weigh options and choose a practical, ethical course of action** — the way a district officer or senior official would.

There is rarely one 'perfect' answer. Examiners value **clarity, balance, legality, compassion and practicality**.

A good answer is usually **250 words** or as specified, written in points. Aim to show that you can stay calm, think of all affected people and act within the law while still being humane. Mentioning that you would **document decisions** and **inform appropriate authorities** shows administrative maturity.
Use a simple structure for every case.
points: **1. Understand the facts:** who is involved, what is at stake
**2. Identify stakeholders:** citizens, victims, officials, the organisation, society, yourself
**3. Identify ethical issues/dilemmas:** e.g. honesty vs loyalty, rules vs compassion, development vs environment
**4. List options:** usually 3–4, including the easy but wrong ones
**5. Evaluate each option:** merits and demerits — legal, ethical, practical
**6. Choose and justify the best course:** combine options if needed
**7. Suggest long-term measures:** systemic reforms to prevent the problem from repeating

notes.p:
Your decision should reflect:

These values often pull in different directions. Show the examiner that you have noticed the tension and explain why one value should carry more weight in that specific situation.
points: **Constitutional values:** rule of law, equality, justice, dignity
**Integrity and impartiality:** no favouritism or personal gain
**Compassion and empathy:** especially for weaker sections
**Accountability and transparency:** proper documentation, informing seniors
**Courage of conviction:** standing up against wrongdoing in a calm, lawful way
**Public interest above personal interest**

notes.p: Practise across these situations.
points: Pressure from seniors or politicians to bend rules
Corruption or a bribe offered directly or indirectly
Disaster management with limited resources
Conflict between development projects and displacement or environment
Workplace issues: harassment, gender sensitivity, team conflicts
Personal dilemmas: family needs vs professional duty
Use of technology and data: privacy, misinformation

notes.p:
These cost marks.

Also avoid copying the case text back into your answer; summarise it in one line and spend your words on analysis and action.
points: Choosing extreme options like resigning immediately or ignoring the issue
Being preachy without giving practical steps
Taking illegal shortcuts even for a good cause
Ignoring stakeholders or the long-term solution
Writing too much theory; keep it action-focused
Not answering every sub-question in the case

notes.p: Case studies typically end with specific questions such as 'What are the options available to you?', 'Evaluate each option' and 'Which would you adopt and why?'. Some cases ask you to identify the ethical issues involved. Read the questions first, then the case, so you know what to look for.
Key points.
points: Facts → stakeholders → issues → options → evaluation → decision → long-term fix
Balance law, ethics, compassion and practicality
Avoid extreme or illegal options
Inform seniors and document actions
Include short-term and long-term measures
Answer every sub-question
Practise cases from varied themes

chapters.title: Ethics & Human Interface: Determinants, Dimensions & Values

cards.title: Essence of ethics
cards.body: Ethics is the study of **what is right and good** in human conduct. Its essence lies in **reasoned choice** guided by values, concern for others, and responsibility for consequences.

cards.title: Determinants of ethics
points: **Individual**: conscience, character, upbringing, education
**Social**: family, culture, religion, peer groups
**Legal and institutional**: laws, codes of conduct
**Situational**: pressures, incentives, leadership

cards.title: Consequences of ethical conduct
points: For individuals: integrity, trust, inner peace
For organisations: credibility, efficiency, lower corruption
For society: social capital, rule of law, cohesion

cards.title: Dimensions of ethics
points: **Meta-ethics**: nature of moral terms
**Normative**: what we ought to do (theories)
**Applied**: business, bio, environmental, public administration ethics
**Descriptive**: what people actually believe

cards.title: Private vs public relationships
cards.body: In **private** relationships (family, friends) ethics stresses care, loyalty and trust. In **public** relationships (official roles) it stresses **impartiality, accountability and rule of law**. Conflicts arise when private loyalties intrude on public duty (nepotism).

cards.title: Values from great lives
points: **Gandhi**: truth, non-violence, purity of means
**Ambedkar**: dignity, equality, constitutional morality
**Vivekananda**: service to humanity as worship
**Lincoln**: humility, perseverance, unity
**Patel**: integrity, firmness, national unity

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For "lessons from lives of leaders" questions, quote a specific incident and draw an administrative lesson — e.g. Gandhi's talisman for policy design.

cards.q: Which branch of ethics deals with questions like "What does 'good' mean?"
cards.explain: Meta-ethics studies the nature and meaning of moral concepts.

cards.q: Appointing a relative to a public post over a better-qualified candidate primarily violates:
cards.explain: Public roles require impartial, merit-based decisions.

notes.p: GS IV begins with "**Ethics and Human Interface**: essence, determinants and consequences of ethics in human actions; dimensions of ethics; ethics in private and public relationships. Human values — lessons from the lives and teachings of great leaders, reformers and administrators; role of family, society and educational institutions in inculcating values." Answers need **clear definitions, real examples and an administrative angle**. Basic concepts and theories are in Foundations of Ethics; this chapter goes deeper into these syllabus lines.

The **essence** of ethics is choosing actions that respect others' dignity and promote good, based on reason and conscience rather than fear or self-interest alone.

**Determinants** of ethical behaviour:
points: **Personal**: conscience, character, emotional maturity, beliefs
**Family**: early moral training, role models
**Society and culture**: norms, religion, traditions, media
**Institutions**: laws, codes of conduct, organisational culture, leadership
**Situational factors**: peer pressure, incentives, authority (Milgram's obedience experiments show how authority shapes conduct)

notes.p: Ethical conduct builds **trust**, which reduces transaction costs, improves cooperation and legitimises institutions. Unethical conduct leads to corruption, poor service delivery, loss of public faith, and social conflict. In administration, a single act of integrity — refusing a bribe, reporting a fraud — can change institutional culture, while tolerated misconduct spreads through example.

notes.h: Ethics in private and public relationships
notes.p: In private life, ethics emphasises love, care, loyalty and forgiveness. Public roles require **impartiality, objectivity, accountability, transparency and the public interest**. The two can conflict: family pressure to favour relatives, friendships with people one regulates, or personal beliefs conflicting with constitutional duties. The guiding principle is that **public office is a trust**; private loyalties must not influence official decisions. Conflicts of interest should be declared and recusal practised.

notes.h: Lessons from great lives and role of institutions
notes.p:
**Gandhi** taught truth, non-violence and that means must be as pure as ends; his talisman asks whether an action helps the poorest. **Ambedkar** taught constitutional morality and dignity. **Vivekananda** linked spirituality to service. **Abraham Lincoln** showed moral courage and reconciliation. **Sardar Patel** showed administrative firmness. **E. Sreedharan** exemplified integrity and timely delivery in public projects.

**Family** gives first lessons in honesty and empathy; **society** reinforces values through norms and role models; **educational institutions** cultivate critical thinking, scientific temper and civic values. When these weaken — consumerism, broken families, rote learning — value erosion follows. Value education, mentoring, and examples set by public leaders help restore them.

A friend who runs a construction firm asks you, a municipal engineer, to "speed up" his approval. **Private relationship:** friendship and loyalty. **Public role:** impartiality and due process. **Ethical course:** decline special treatment politely, declare the relationship, recuse yourself if needed, and ensure the file is processed on merit and in turn. This preserves both your integrity and, in the long run, a healthier friendship.
Key points.
points: Essence: reasoned, value-guided choice with concern for others
Determinants: personal, family, society, institutions, situation
Dimensions: meta, normative, applied, descriptive
Private (care, loyalty) vs public (impartiality, accountability)
Public office is a trust; declare conflicts, recuse
Lessons: Gandhi, Ambedkar, Vivekananda, Lincoln, Patel
Family, society, education inculcate values

chapters.title: Attitude, Persuasion & Aptitude for Civil Services

cards.title: Attitude: ABC model
points: **Affective**: feelings towards an object
**Behavioural**: tendency to act
**Cognitive**: beliefs and thoughts
Attitudes are learned and relatively stable but can change

cards.title: Functions of attitudes (Katz)
points: **Utilitarian/adjustive**: gain rewards, avoid costs
**Ego-defensive**: protect self-image
**Value-expressive**: express core values
**Knowledge**: organise and simplify the world

cards.title: Social influence
points: **Conformity**: Asch's line experiments
**Compliance**: agreeing to a request
**Obedience**: Milgram's experiments on authority
Group norms and peer pressure

cards.title: Persuasion
points: **Elaboration Likelihood Model** (Petty & Cacioppo): central route (arguments) vs peripheral route (cues like celebrity, attractiveness)
Yale/Hovland approach: **source, message, audience**
**Cognitive dissonance** (Festinger): discomfort from inconsistency drives change

cards.title: Moral and political attitudes
cards.body: **Moral attitudes** concern right and wrong (e.g. views on honesty, euthanasia). **Political attitudes** concern governance and ideology (liberal, conservative, attitudes to state intervention). Civil servants must keep political attitudes from influencing official work.

cards.title: Foundational values for civil services
points: Integrity
Impartiality and non-partisanship
Objectivity
