Dedication to public service
Empathy, tolerance and compassion towards weaker sections

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Aptitude is potential to learn and perform; attitude is evaluative disposition. A civil servant needs both: aptitude for problem-solving and an attitude of service. Use examples like campaigns that changed public attitudes (Swachh Bharat, anti-smoking).

cards.q: In the ABC model of attitude, "B" stands for:
cards.explain: Affective, Behavioural and Cognitive components.

cards.q: Persuasion through a celebrity endorsement rather than strong arguments uses which route of the Elaboration Likelihood Model?
cards.explain: Peripheral route relies on cues rather than argument quality.

cards.q: Milgram's experiments are best known for studying:
cards.explain: Participants obeyed an authority figure to give apparent electric shocks.

notes.p: GS IV: "**Attitude**: content, structure, function; its influence and relation with thought and behaviour; moral and political attitudes; social influence and persuasion." And "**Aptitude and foundational values for Civil Service**: integrity, impartiality and non-partisanship, objectivity, dedication to public service, empathy, tolerance and compassion towards the weaker sections." Questions are conceptual with administrative examples.

An **attitude** is a learned, relatively enduring evaluation of a person, object, idea or event. Its **structure** is often described by the **ABC model**: affective (feelings), behavioural (action tendencies) and cognitive (beliefs). Attitudes vary in **strength**, **accessibility** and **consistency**.

Katz described four **functions**: utilitarian, ego-defensive, value-expressive and knowledge. Attitudes form through **direct experience**, **conditioning** (classical and operant), **observational learning** (role models), family, media and culture.

Attitudes influence thought (what we notice, how we interpret) and behaviour, but the link is not automatic. The **theory of planned behaviour** adds **subjective norms** and **perceived behavioural control**: people act on attitudes when social norms support them and they feel able to act. **Cognitive dissonance** explains how behaviour can change attitudes: when people act against their beliefs, they often adjust beliefs to reduce discomfort. Example: an official who once took small favours may justify them as "normal", showing how dissonance can entrench corruption — or, positively, how participation in a cleanliness drive can strengthen pro-hygiene attitudes.

People change attitudes and behaviour due to others: **conformity** (Asch), **compliance** (foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face techniques) and **obedience** (Milgram). These explain both the power of positive peer norms and the danger of unquestioning obedience to unlawful orders.

**Persuasion** depends on the **source** (credibility, trustworthiness), **message** (clarity, two-sided arguments for informed audiences, emotional appeal), and **audience** (involvement, prior beliefs). The **Elaboration Likelihood Model** suggests high-involvement audiences respond to strong arguments (central route), while low-involvement audiences respond to cues (peripheral route). Public campaigns — on vaccination, sanitation, girls' education or road safety — use both routes.
**Aptitude** is the natural or acquired capacity to learn and perform tasks — analytical ability, decision-making, communication, leadership. **Foundational values** shape how that aptitude is used:
points: **Integrity**: consistency of values and actions; honesty even when unobserved
**Impartiality and non-partisanship**: equal treatment; no political bias in official work
**Objectivity**: decisions based on evidence and merit
**Dedication to public service**: commitment beyond the call of duty
**Empathy, tolerance and compassion**: especially towards the weak and marginalised

notes.h: Worked example: changing attitudes in the field
notes.p: A district officer wants to improve girls' school attendance where parents resist. **Diagnosis:** cognitive (belief that education is not useful for girls), affective (safety fears), behavioural (girls kept home for chores). **Persuasion plan:** credible local sources (women teachers, SHG leaders, religious leaders), two-sided messages acknowledging safety concerns, success stories of local girls, practical fixes (escort groups, toilets, bicycles), and recognition for families. This uses both central and peripheral routes and addresses all three attitude components.
Key points.
points: Attitude: ABC (affective, behavioural, cognitive)
Katz functions: utilitarian, ego-defensive, value-expressive, knowledge
Theory of planned behaviour; cognitive dissonance (Festinger)
Asch (conformity), Milgram (obedience)
ELM: central vs peripheral route; source–message–audience
Foundational values: integrity, impartiality, objectivity, dedication, empathy
Aptitude = capacity; attitude = evaluation

cards.title: Definition
cards.body: **Emotional intelligence (EI)** is the ability to **perceive, understand, use and manage emotions** in oneself and others. Salovey and Mayer defined it (1990); **Daniel Goleman** popularised it (1995).

cards.title: Goleman's five components
points: **Self-awareness**
**Self-regulation**
**Motivation**
**Empathy**
**Social skills**

cards.title: Mayer–Salovey ability model
points: Perceiving emotions
Using emotions to facilitate thought
Understanding emotions
Managing emotions

cards.title: Why EI matters in governance
points: Calm decisions in crises
Handling angry citizens and protests
Leading and motivating teams
Negotiation with stakeholders
Resisting impulsive or biased decisions
Preventing burnout

cards.title: EI at a protest site
cards.body: A crowd blocks a highway after a road accident. An officer with high EI stays calm (self-regulation), listens to grievances (empathy), acknowledges the loss, announces compensation steps and an inquiry (social skills), and clears the road without force — de-escalating a potential law-and-order crisis.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Distinguish EI from IQ: IQ helps you get selected; EI helps you succeed and lead. Show EI through behaviours, not slogans.

cards.q: Which is NOT one of Goleman's five components of emotional intelligence?
cards.explain: Logical reasoning is a cognitive ability, not an EI component.

cards.q: The term "emotional intelligence" was first formally defined in an academic model by:
cards.explain: Salovey and Mayer (1990) proposed the model; Goleman popularised it.

notes.p: GS IV: "**Emotional intelligence** — concepts, and their utilities and application in administration and governance." Questions ask what EI is, why it matters for civil servants, and how it can be developed. Case studies often implicitly test EI — how you handle anger, pressure, grief or conflict.

EI is the capacity to recognise emotions, understand their causes and effects, and manage them to guide thinking and behaviour. Howard Gardner's idea of **multiple intelligences** (including interpersonal and intrapersonal intelligence) prepared the ground. **Salovey and Mayer (1990)** gave an **ability model** with four branches: perceiving, using, understanding and managing emotions. **Daniel Goleman** (1995) presented a broader **mixed model** with five components that became popular in management.
The five components:
points: **Self-awareness:** knowing one's emotions, strengths, weaknesses and triggers
**Self-regulation:** controlling impulses, staying calm, thinking before acting, adapting to change
**Motivation:** inner drive to achieve, optimism despite setbacks
**Empathy:** understanding others' feelings and perspectives, especially of the vulnerable
**Social skills:** communication, conflict resolution, teamwork, influence and leadership

notes.p: Civil servants deal with stress, uncertainty and emotionally charged situations: disasters, riots, protests, grievances, political pressure. EI helps to:
points: **Make balanced decisions** under pressure rather than react emotionally
**Build trust** with citizens and communities through empathy
**Lead teams** — motivating subordinates, managing conflict, giving feedback
**Negotiate** with stakeholders in land acquisition, labour disputes, inter-departmental issues
**Deliver services** with sensitivity (e.g. dealing with victims of violence)
**Maintain integrity** by recognising emotional manipulation and pressure
**Prevent burnout** and maintain mental health

notes.p:
EI can be learned. Methods: reflective journaling and self-assessment; mindfulness and meditation for self-regulation; seeking 360° feedback; active listening practice; exposure to diverse communities (field visits, village stays during training); role-plays and case-based training; mentoring; and learning from failures. Training academies increasingly include behavioural and soft-skills modules, and Mission Karmayogi emphasises behavioural competencies.

Organisations can also raise collective EI: leaders who acknowledge stress after a disaster deployment, hold debriefs, and recognise effort create teams that recover faster and serve citizens better. Grievance desks staffed by trained, empathetic personnel reduce conflict and repeat complaints.

EI is not a substitute for **ethics or competence**: a manipulative person can have high EI and use it to exploit others ("dark side" of EI). Measurement of EI is debated, and mixed models are criticised for overlapping with personality traits. Hence EI must be anchored in values like integrity and public service. In answers, show EI as a tool serving ethical goals.

A simple self-check before a tough decision: What am I feeling? Why? How are others likely feeling? What response serves the public interest best?
Key points.
points: EI: perceive, use, understand, manage emotions
Salovey & Mayer (1990) ability model; Goleman (1995) mixed model
Goleman: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills
Uses: crises, protests, leadership, negotiation, service delivery
EI can be developed: reflection, mindfulness, feedback, field exposure
EI must serve ethics; beware manipulation

chapters.title: Moral Thinkers & Philosophers: India and the World

cards.title: Indian thinkers (1)
points: **Buddha**: Middle Path, Eightfold Path, compassion (karuna)
**Mahavira**: ahimsa, **anekantavada** (many-sidedness of truth)
**Bhagavad Gita**: **nishkama karma** — duty without attachment to results
**Kautilya**: the king's happiness lies in the happiness of his subjects

cards.title: Indian thinkers (2)
points: **Thiruvalluvar** (Tirukkural): virtue, wealth, love
**Basavanna**: **kayaka** (work is worship), dasoha (sharing)
**Gandhi**: truth, non-violence, trusteeship, Seven Social Sins
**Vivekananda**: service to humanity; **Tagore**: universal humanism
**Ambedkar**: constitutional morality, liberty–equality–fraternity

cards.title: Greek thinkers
points: **Socrates**: "the unexamined life is not worth living"; virtue is knowledge
**Plato**: philosopher-king; virtues of wisdom, courage, temperance, justice
**Aristotle**: virtue ethics, **golden mean**, eudaimonia (flourishing)

cards.title: Modern Western thinkers
points: **Kant**: categorical imperative; treat humanity as an end
**Bentham**: utility, hedonic calculus
**J.S. Mill**: higher pleasures; **harm principle**
**Rawls**: **veil of ignorance**; difference principle (A Theory of Justice, 1971)
**Amartya Sen**: capabilities; niti vs nyaya

cards.title: Other traditions
points: **Confucius**: ren (humaneness), li (propriety), rule by virtue
**Machiavelli**: realism in politics — a contrast to moral idealism
**Social contract**: Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Quote a thinker only when it fits. For each thinker, remember one core idea and one administrative application — e.g. Rawls' veil of ignorance for designing fair welfare policy.

cards.q: "Anekantavada" is a principle associated with:
cards.explain: Jain doctrine of the many-sidedness of reality and truth.

cards.q: The "veil of ignorance" thought experiment was proposed by:
cards.explain: In A Theory of Justice (1971).

cards.q: Basavanna's concept of "kayaka" means:
cards.explain: Kayaka holds that honest work is a form of worship.

notes.p: GS IV asks for "**contributions of moral thinkers and philosophers from India and the world** to the concepts of morality". Questions may ask you to explain a quote, relate a thinker's idea to administration, or compare traditions. Short, accurate summaries and **applications** are what earn marks.

**Buddha** taught the Four Noble Truths and the **Eightfold Path**, the Middle Way between indulgence and austerity, and compassion. **Mahavira** emphasised **ahimsa**, aparigraha (non-possession) and **anekantavada**, which encourages humility and tolerance of other views. The **Bhagavad Gita** teaches **nishkama karma** — doing one's duty without attachment to rewards — relevant for officers facing pressures. **Kautilya's Arthashastra** combines realism with welfare: the king's happiness lies in the happiness of his subjects; it also lists ways officials embezzle funds — showing awareness of corruption.

**Thiruvalluvar's Tirukkural** covers virtue (aram), wealth (porul) and love (inbam), with guidance on just rule. **Basavanna** preached equality, **kayaka** and **dasoha**. **Gandhi** stressed truth, non-violence, purity of means, **trusteeship**, sarvodaya and the **Seven Social Sins** (politics without principles, wealth without work, pleasure without conscience, knowledge without character, commerce without morality, science without humanity, worship without sacrifice). **Vivekananda** saw service to people as worship; **Tagore** championed universal humanism; **Ambedkar** emphasised **constitutional morality** and social democracy.

**Socrates** held that virtue is knowledge and that self-examination is essential. **Plato** described a just state ruled by philosopher-kings and the four cardinal virtues. **Aristotle** founded **virtue ethics**: virtues are habits lying at a **golden mean** between extremes (courage between cowardice and recklessness), aimed at **eudaimonia** (human flourishing). Application: character building and habits matter more than rule-following alone.

**Kant** grounded morality in reason and duty: act only on maxims you could will as universal law, and treat humanity never merely as a means. **Bentham** and **Mill** developed **utilitarianism**: right actions maximise overall happiness; Mill added the distinction between higher and lower pleasures and the **harm principle** (liberty limited only to prevent harm to others). **John Rawls** proposed justice as fairness: principles chosen behind a **veil of ignorance** would guarantee basic liberties and allow inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged (**difference principle**). **Amartya Sen** focuses on **capabilities** and distinguishes **niti** (institutional rules) from **nyaya** (realised justice).
Examples:
points: Designing a welfare scheme: **Rawls** (benefit the least advantaged), **Gandhi's talisman**
Cost–benefit of a dam: **utilitarianism**, with Kantian limits on sacrificing displaced people
Officer under pressure: **Gita's** nishkama karma, **Kant's** duty
Tolerance in diverse society: **anekantavada**, Ashoka's dhamma
Corporate ethics: **Gandhian trusteeship**
Leadership by example: **Confucius**, Aristotle's virtues

notes.p: Key points.
points: Buddha: Middle Path; Mahavira: ahimsa, anekantavada
Gita: nishkama karma; Kautilya: welfare of subjects
Thiruvalluvar; Basavanna: kayaka, dasoha
Gandhi: truth, ahimsa, trusteeship, Seven Social Sins
Socrates, Plato (virtues), Aristotle (golden mean)
Kant (categorical imperative), Bentham & Mill (utility, harm principle)
Rawls (veil of ignorance), Sen (capabilities, niti–nyaya)

chapters.title: Ethical Governance, Accountability, Corporate Governance & Ethics in IR

cards.title: Sources of ethical guidance
points: **Laws**: binding, enforceable minimum
**Rules and regulations**: detailed procedures
**Codes of conduct and ethics**
**Conscience**: inner moral voice — guides where rules are silent
Tension: what is legal may not be ethical

cards.title: Code of ethics vs code of conduct
cards.body: A **code of ethics** states broad values (integrity, impartiality) to guide judgement. A **code of conduct** lists specific do's and don'ts (gifts, political activity, investments) — e.g. **CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964** and **AIS (Conduct) Rules, 1968**.

cards.title: Accountability types
points: **Political**: to legislature and voters
**Administrative**: hierarchy, audits
**Legal**: courts, tribunals
**Social**: media, civil society, social audits
**Professional**: peer standards

cards.title: Fighting corruption
points: **Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988** (amended 2018: bribe-giving an offence; prior approval for investigating officials for decisions in official duty)
Lokpal and Lokayuktas; CVC
2nd ARC 4th report: "Ethics in Governance" (2007)
E-governance, transparency, whistle-blower protection

cards.title: Corporate governance
points: Transparency, accountability, fairness to stakeholders
**Companies Act, 2013**: independent directors, CSR, vigil mechanism
**SEBI LODR** rules; **Kotak Committee** (2017)
Lesson from **Satyam** scandal (2009)

cards.title: Ethics in international relations and funding
points: Humanitarian intervention vs sovereignty; **Responsibility to Protect**
Refugees and migrants
**Climate justice**: common but differentiated responsibilities
Arms trade, sanctions harming civilians
Aid conditionality and debt traps; vaccine equity

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In answers on "legal vs ethical", give a crisp example (e.g. a legal but harmful tax-avoidance scheme) and argue that conscience and values must fill the gaps law cannot.

cards.q: After the 2018 amendment, the Prevention of Corruption Act:
options: Removed public servants from its scope
cards.explain: Section 8 now makes giving a bribe an offence, with some protection for those compelled who report.

cards.q: The Kotak Committee (2017) is associated with:
cards.explain: It was set up by SEBI to improve corporate governance standards.

notes.p: GS IV includes: "**Public/Civil service values and ethics in public administration**: status and problems; ethical concerns and dilemmas in government and private institutions; **laws, rules, regulations and conscience** as sources of ethical guidance; **accountability and ethical governance**; strengthening of ethical and moral values in governance; **ethical issues in international relations and funding**; **corporate governance**." It also lists probity elements: codes of ethics, codes of conduct, citizens' charters, work culture, quality of service delivery, utilisation of public funds and challenges of corruption. Probity and civil service values are covered in a separate chapter; this one focuses on institutions.

**Laws** set enforceable minimum standards; **rules and regulations** operationalise them; **codes** set expectations for professions; and **conscience** guides where all these are silent or flawed. Laws can lag behind moral understanding (untouchability was once socially accepted; marital rape debates continue), and rigid rule-following can produce injustice. Conscience must itself be informed by reason, constitutional values and dialogue — otherwise it may become mere personal bias. Gandhi's satyagraha and civil disobedience show conscience challenging unjust laws, but public servants should use **lawful channels** (dissent notes, reporting) rather than disobedience.

notes.h: Ethical concerns in government and private institutions
notes.p: Government: conflicts of interest, nepotism, misuse of discretion, political pressure, leakage of public funds, lack of transparency, and neglect of the vulnerable. Private: fraud and accounting manipulation, exploitation of workers, environmental harm, data misuse, unfair competition and misleading advertising. Common dilemmas: loyalty to the organisation vs public interest (whistle-blowing), profit vs safety, efficiency vs equity.

Accountability means **answerability plus enforceability**. Mechanisms: parliamentary control, audits by CAG, judicial review, RTI, social audits, grievance redress, Lokpal, CVC, media scrutiny. The **2nd ARC's 4th report, "Ethics in Governance" (2007)**, recommended a code of ethics for ministers and civil servants, a Public Services law, stronger anti-corruption agencies, protection for whistle-blowers, confiscation of illegally acquired property and simplification of procedures to cut discretion. Strengthening ethical values also requires leadership by example, ethics training, rewarding integrity and protecting honest officers.

Corporate governance is the system of rules and practices by which companies are directed and controlled, balancing interests of **shareholders, management, employees, customers, creditors and society**. The UK's **Cadbury Committee (1992)** shaped global norms. In India, after scandals such as **Satyam (2009)**, the **Companies Act, 2013** strengthened independent directors, audit committees, auditor rotation, **CSR**, and vigil mechanisms; SEBI's **LODR** regulations and the **Kotak Committee (2017)** recommendations improved board independence and disclosure. Ethical issues include insider trading, related-party transactions, greenwashing and treatment of minority shareholders.

notes.h: Ethics in international relations and funding
notes.p: IR involves moral questions: **humanitarian intervention** and **Responsibility to Protect** vs sovereignty; treatment of **refugees**; **climate justice** (historical emissions, CBDR); **arms sales** to conflict zones; **sanctions** that hurt civilians; nuclear ethics; and **vaccine equity** during pandemics. **Funding** raises issues of **aid conditionality**, debt sustainability ("debt traps"), transparency of loans, and whether donors impose their values. India's approach — development partnerships driven by partner priorities, Vaccine Maitri, humanitarian assistance — can be cited, alongside the principle of **Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam**.
Key points.
points: Sources: law, rules, codes, conscience; legal ≠ always ethical
Code of ethics (values) vs code of conduct (specific rules)
Accountability: political, administrative, legal, social, professional
PCA 1988, amended 2018; Lokpal; 2nd ARC 4th report (2007)
Corporate governance: Companies Act 2013, SEBI LODR, Kotak 2017, Satyam lesson
IR ethics: R2P, refugees, climate justice, sanctions, aid conditionality

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.body: CSAT is qualifying, but you must score 66/200 — and every year some strong GS candidates miss it. Comprehension forms a large share of the paper and is the most reliable way to clear it if you practise regularly.

cards.title: Question types
points: **Main idea / central theme** – what the whole passage argues
**Inference** – what logically follows, though not stated
**Assumption** – unstated premise the author relies on
**Corollary / implication** – a consequence of the argument

cards.title: Method
cards.body: Read the passage once with focus on the author's tone and conclusion. Then read the question and eliminate options that are **too extreme** ('always', 'only'), **outside the passage**, or **true but irrelevant**. Answer from the passage, not from your general knowledge.

cards.title: Mini drill
cards.body: Passage: 'Rising groundwater use for paddy in Punjab is lowering water tables.' Question: the author's assumption? Option 'Paddy needs more water than many alternative crops' is a valid assumption. Option 'Punjab should ban paddy' is too extreme — not assumed.

cards.q: In an inference question, the correct option must be:
options: Supported by the passage even if not stated
cards.explain: Inferences follow logically from the passage without being stated outright.

cards.q: Options containing words like 'always' or 'only' are often:
cards.explain: Absolute words make claims passages rarely support, so treat them with suspicion.

notes.p:
**CSAT (Prelims Paper II)** is qualifying: you need at least **33% (66 out of 200)**. Reading comprehension usually makes up a **large share** of the paper, so it is often the safest area to score in. But it also has **negative marking (one-third)**, so careless guessing can hurt.

Comprehension questions test whether you can understand **what the author is saying** — not what you personally believe.
Recognise the question type to answer quickly.
points: **Main idea / central theme:** what is the passage mainly about?
**Inference:** what can be logically concluded from the passage?
**Assumption:** what does the author take for granted without stating?
**Explicit detail:** facts directly stated
**Tone and purpose:** critical, optimistic, neutral, cautionary
**Most logical / rational corollary:** the most reasonable next step from the passage
**Vocabulary in context:** meaning of a word as used in the passage

notes.p: Try this approach and adjust it with practice.
points: Read the question stem first for short passages, so you know what to look for
Read the passage actively — note the topic, the author's view and key transition words (however, therefore, but)
Answer from the passage only; avoid outside knowledge
Eliminate options that are **too extreme** ('always', 'never', 'only'), **out of scope**, or **opposite** to the passage
For inference and assumption questions, choose the option that **must** be true according to the passage
Skip very long or confusing passages in the first round and come back

notes.p:
These two types confuse many aspirants.

Example: if a passage says rising temperatures are reducing wheat yields, the inference may be that climate adaptation in farming is needed; an assumption may be that temperature is a key factor in yield.
points: **Inference:** a conclusion that follows from what is stated
**Assumption:** an unstated premise the author needs for the argument to work
Test for assumption: if the negation of the option breaks the argument, it is likely the assumption
Neither should require outside facts

notes.p:
Reading speed and understanding grow with daily practice. Read **editorials** and reports, and summarise them in one or two lines. Solve **previous years' CSAT passages** under timed conditions and review every mistake — find out *why* the wrong option looked attractive.

Keep a small log of your errors by type — for example 'chose extreme option' or 'used outside knowledge'. Over a few weeks you will see a pattern, and fixing that one habit often adds more marks than reading more passages. Also practise **time management**: fix a rough time per passage and move on if you exceed it.

UPSC passages are often on **economy, environment, governance, society, ethics and science**. Many questions ask for the **'most logical and rational inference'**, the **'crux of the passage'** or the **'critical message'**. Options are usually close to each other, so careful elimination matters more than speed alone.
Key points.
points: CSAT qualifying: 33% (66/200); negative marking applies
Answer from the passage, not personal opinion
Eliminate extreme, out-of-scope and opposite options
Inference follows from text; assumption is unstated but necessary
Negation test for assumptions
Practise PYQ passages under time limits
Read editorials daily and summarise

cards.title: Must-know formulas
points: Percentage change = (Change ÷ Original) × 100
Average = Sum ÷ Number of items
Speed = Distance ÷ Time; km/h × 5/18 = m/s
Simple interest = P × R × T ÷ 100
Profit % = (Profit ÷ Cost price) × 100

cards.title: Successive percentages
cards.body: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. Net effect = 20 − 20 + (20 × −20)/100 = **−4%**. So a ₹100 item becomes ₹96, not ₹100.

cards.title: Average speed trap
cards.body: A car goes A→B at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. Average speed is **not** 50. For equal distances use 2xy/(x + y) = (2 × 40 × 60)/100 = **48 km/h**.

cards.title: Ratio sharing
cards.body: ₹1,200 is shared between A and B in the ratio 3:5. Total parts = 8, one part = 150. A gets 3 × 150 = **₹450**, B gets **₹750**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Do not try every question. In CSAT, aim for accuracy on comprehension and easy quant first, then return to harder items. Remember wrong answers carry a one-third negative mark.

cards.q: A number increases by 10% and then by another 10%. The total increase is:
Convert 72 km/h into m/s.
The average of 4, 8, 12 and 16 is:

notes.p: The CSAT quantitative section is based on roughly **Class X level** mathematics. Topics include **number system, percentages, ratio and proportion, averages, profit and loss, simple and compound interest, time and work, time-speed-distance, permutations and combinations, probability, and data interpretation**. Even aspirants from non-maths backgrounds can score well with concept clarity and practice.
Many questions rely on simple number properties.
points: **Divisibility:** by 3 if the sum of digits is divisible by 3; by 4 if the last two digits are divisible by 4; by 8 if the last three digits are divisible by 8; by 9 if the digit sum is divisible by 9; by 11 if the difference of alternate digit sums is 0 or divisible by 11
**HCF × LCM = product of two numbers**
**Unit digit cycles:** powers of 2, 3, 7 and 8 repeat in cycles of 4
**Remainder** questions often use cyclicity or simple factorisation
Prime numbers: 2 is the only even prime

notes.p: These are linked — learn them together.
points: Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100
Successive changes of a% and b%: net change = a + b + (ab/100)
Profit % = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100
**Simple Interest** = P × R × T ÷ 100
**Compound Interest** amount = P (1 + R/100)^T

notes.p: Use the **unit approach**: find work per day or distance per hour.
points: If A finishes a job in a days, A's one-day work = 1/a
Together: 1/a + 1/b of the work per day
Speed = distance ÷ time; convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18
**Average speed** for equal distances at speeds x and y = 2xy ÷ (x + y)
Relative speed: add speeds if moving in opposite directions, subtract if same direction
Trains crossing: distance = sum of lengths (for two trains) or train length + platform length

notes.p:
Quick rules:

Data interpretation questions present tables, bar charts or pie charts. Read the units and labels carefully, approximate where options are far apart, and calculate exactly only when options are close.
points: Average = sum ÷ number of items
Ratios: combine using a common term; mixtures use the **alligation** method
Permutations (order matters): nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!
Combinations (order doesn't matter): nCr = n! ÷ [r! (n − r)!]
Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes; always between 0 and 1

notes.p: CSAT quant questions are often **puzzle-like and word-based** rather than direct formula questions. Recent papers include many questions on **number properties, digits, and logical counting**. Options can be used for **back-substitution**. Since CSAT is qualifying, focus on accuracy in the questions you attempt rather than attempting everything.
Key formulas.
points: HCF × LCM = product of two numbers
Successive % change: a + b + ab/100
SI = PRT/100; CI amount = P(1 + R/100)^T
Average speed (equal distances): 2xy/(x + y)
nPr and nCr formulas
Probability lies between 0 and 1
Use options to back-solve

cards.title: Common topics
points: Number and letter series
Blood relations
Direction sense
Seating arrangement and puzzles
Syllogisms and statement–conclusion
Clocks, calendars and coding-decoding

cards.title: Series
cards.body: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ? — differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12. Answer: **42**. (Also n × (n + 1): 1×2, 2×3, … 6×7 = 42.)

cards.title: Direction sense
cards.body: Ravi walks 3 km north, turns right and walks 4 km. How far is he from the start? He is 3 km north and 4 km east, so distance = √(3² + 4²) = **5 km**, towards the north-east.

cards.title: Syllogism
cards.body: All pens are books. Some books are bags. Conclusion: 'Some pens are bags'? **Does not follow** — the books that are bags may not include any pens. Draw Venn diagrams to test every possibility.

cards.q: Find the next term: 3, 9, 27, 81, ?
cards.explain: Each term is multiplied by 3: 81 × 3 = 243.

cards.q: A is B's brother. C is A's mother. How is B related to C?
cards.explain: A and B are siblings and C is A's mother, so B is C's child (B's gender is not given).

notes.p: The reasoning part of CSAT checks how clearly you think. Common topics include **syllogisms, statement–conclusion and statement–assumption questions, blood relations, direction sense, seating arrangements, coding–decoding, series, clocks and calendars, and puzzles**. Most can be solved with a neat diagram and careful reading.
Syllogisms test conclusions from given statements.
points: Draw **Venn diagrams** for statements like 'All A are B' and 'Some B are C'
A conclusion is valid only if it is true in **every possible diagram**
'Some A are B' also means 'some B are A'
'All A are B' does not mean 'All B are A'
'No A is B' means 'No B is A'
Use only the given statements, even if they sound unrealistic

notes.p:
Visual tools make these quick.

**Coding–decoding:** look for letter shifts (e.g. each letter moved forward by one), reversals, or number values of letters (A = 1, B = 2 … Z = 26). Write the alphabet with positions once at the start of the exam to save time.
points: **Blood relations:** draw a family tree; use symbols for male/female and generations
**Direction sense:** draw the path; use Pythagoras for the shortest distance; remember left/right turns change with facing direction
**Seating arrangements:** fix the most certain clue first; for circular arrangements note whether people face the centre or outward
**Ranking:** total = rank from top + rank from bottom − 1

notes.p: These follow fixed rules.
points: **Clock:** the minute hand gains 5.5° per minute over the hour hand; angle = |30H − 5.5M|
Hands overlap 22 times in 24 hours
**Calendar:** an ordinary year has 1 odd day; a leap year has 2 odd days
A century year is a leap year only if divisible by 400
**Series:** look for differences, squares/cubes, alternating patterns or multiplication

notes.p:
Statement-based questions are similar to comprehension.

Practise with previous years' CSAT papers to see how UPSC frames reasoning. Time yourself, and after each attempt note which question types took the longest so you can plan which ones to attempt first in the real exam.
points: **Conclusion:** must follow directly from the statement
**Assumption:** taken for granted; often implicit
**Course of action:** should be practical and address the problem
**Strengthen/weaken:** find the option that affects the link between evidence and conclusion
Avoid extreme or unrelated options

notes.p: CSAT reasoning questions are usually framed as **puzzles and word problems**, with clues given in sentences. Questions on arrangements, counting, number puzzles and syllogism-style deductions appear regularly. Draw diagrams, write down fixed clues first and check each option against all clues.
Key points.
points: Syllogism: valid only if true in all diagrams
'All A are B' ≠ 'All B are A'
Ranking: total = top rank + bottom rank − 1
Clock angle = |30H − 5.5M|; overlap 22 times a day
Odd days: ordinary year 1, leap year 2
Century year is leap only if divisible by 400
Draw diagrams for directions and family trees
Use only given information

cards.title: What the topic covers
cards.body: CSAT lists '**interpersonal skills including communication skills**'. Questions usually appear as **passages** or **situations** testing whether you can identify clear, respectful and effective communication — and how messages get distorted.

cards.title: The communication process
cards.body: **Sender → message (encoding) → channel → receiver (decoding) → feedback**, with **noise** (anything that distorts the message) at every stage. Good communication closes the loop through feedback.

cards.title: Common barriers
points: Physical — distance, noise, poor connectivity
Semantic — jargon, ambiguous words, language gaps
Psychological — prejudice, anger, assumptions
Organisational — too many hierarchy levels, information overload
Cultural — different norms of politeness and gesture

cards.title: Active listening
cards.body: Give full attention, avoid interrupting, **paraphrase** to confirm understanding, ask clarifying questions, and notice **non-verbal cues** (tone, posture, eye contact). Research on communication suggests non-verbal signals carry much of the emotional meaning.

cards.title: Communication styles
cards.body: **Passive** — avoids expressing needs. **Aggressive** — expresses needs at others' expense. **Assertive** — states needs clearly and respectfully while respecting others. Assertive communication is usually the best answer in situational questions.

cards.title: Conflict-handling styles
points: Competing — win at any cost
Accommodating — give in to keep peace
Avoiding — postpone or sidestep
Compromising — each side gives up something
Collaborating — work together for a win-win solution

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In situation-based options, prefer answers that are **respectful, fact-based, solution-oriented and inclusive**. Reject options that are passive ('ignore it'), aggressive ('reprimand publicly') or evasive ('pass it to someone else').

cards.q: Repeating the speaker's point in your own words to confirm understanding is called:
cards.explain: Paraphrasing is a core active-listening technique.

cards.q: Which communication style respects both one's own needs and those of others?
cards.explain: Assertive communication is honest and respectful.

cards.q: Use of technical jargon with a lay audience is an example of a:
cards.explain: Semantic barriers arise from words and meanings.

notes.h: Why this matters for civil servants
notes.p: Administrators must explain policies to citizens, coordinate with colleagues, negotiate with stakeholders and manage teams. CSAT tests the **underlying skills** — understanding a message as intended, recognising tone and assumptions, and choosing constructive responses. Even when questions look like reading comprehension, they often test whether you grasp the speaker's **intent** and the **effect** of words.
The '**7 Cs**' are a useful checklist:
points: **Clear** — one main idea, simple words
**Concise** — no unnecessary detail
**Concrete** — specific facts and figures
**Correct** — accurate and grammatically sound
**Coherent** — logical flow
**Complete** — all information the receiver needs
**Courteous** — respectful and considerate

notes.p: **Verbal** communication includes spoken and written words. **Non-verbal** communication includes facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact, **paralanguage** (tone, pitch, pace) and even silence. When verbal and non-verbal messages conflict — someone says 'I'm fine' while looking upset — people tend to believe the non-verbal signal. **Empathy** — understanding another person's feelings and perspective — makes communication more effective, especially with citizens in distress.

Good **feedback** is specific, timely, focused on behaviour (not personality) and offered privately when critical. In **teams**, members play task roles (initiator, information-giver) and maintenance roles (encourager, harmoniser); dysfunctional roles (blocker, dominator) hurt outcomes. In **negotiation**, separating people from the problem and focusing on **interests rather than positions** helps reach agreement; knowing your best alternative to a negotiated agreement (**BATNA**) prevents bad deals.

Situation: A citizen arrives angry because a certificate has been delayed. Options: (a) Ask him to come back tomorrow. (b) Explain politely that rules must be followed and send him away. (c) Listen calmly, check the file status, explain the reason and give a clear timeline, escalating if the delay is unjustified. (d) Call security.

Step 1: Reject (a) and (b) — evasive and unhelpful.
Step 2: Reject (d) — aggressive and escalates conflict.
Step 3: (c) shows active listening, empathy, transparency and action.
Answer: **(c)**.

Most CSAT papers test this skill indirectly through comprehension passages — the author's tone, intent, or the most logical response. Read for the purpose of each passage, not just its facts.

A practical habit: after each passage, ask 'what does the author want the reader to do or believe?' and 'what tone does the author use — critical, neutral, optimistic, cautionary?'. Options that misread tone (calling a cautious passage alarmist, for instance) are common distractors. In situation-type items, imagine you must defend your choice before a fair senior officer and an affected citizen at the same time; the option you could defend to both is usually right.
Recall.
points: Sender–message–channel–receiver–feedback; noise
Barriers: physical, semantic, psychological, organisational, cultural
Active listening: attend, paraphrase, clarify
Assertive > passive or aggressive
Collaborating = win-win conflict style
7 Cs of communication
Prefer respectful, solution-oriented options

cards.title: What is tested
cards.body: The CSAT syllabus includes '**decision making and problem solving**'. Early CSAT papers (2011–13) had administrative-situation questions; these reportedly carried no negative marking. Recent papers test the skill mainly through **puzzles, logical deductions and reasoning-based comprehension** — check the official notice.

cards.title: A decision framework
points: 1. Define the problem and the goal
2. Identify stakeholders and constraints (law, rules, ethics, time, budget)
3. List options
4. Evaluate consequences — short-term and long-term
5. Choose, act and communicate
6. Review and learn

cards.title: What 'best' options look like
cards.body: The best answer is usually **lawful**, **humane**, **proactive**, **proportionate**, and **sustainable** — solves the root cause, not just the symptom. Extreme options (doing nothing, using force first, resigning, passing the buck) are usually wrong.

cards.title: Problem-solving tools
cards.body: **Root-cause analysis** (ask 'why' repeatedly), **cost–benefit analysis**, **prioritisation** (urgent vs important), **elimination** (rule out impossible options), and **working backwards** from the answer choices.

cards.title: Puzzle method
cards.body: Three friends P, Q and R sit in a row facing north. P is not at either end. Q is to the immediate right of P. Who sits at the left end? Since P is in the middle and Q is on P's right, the order is **R, P, Q** — R is at the left end.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In logic puzzles, draw a quick table or diagram, fill in **definite** clues first, then handle conditional clues. Never solve puzzles mentally — that is how marks are lost.

cards.title: Common biases
cards.body: **Confirmation bias** (seeking only supporting evidence), **anchoring** (over-relying on the first figure), **sunk-cost fallacy** (continuing because of past investment), and **groupthink**. Good decisions consciously guard against them.

cards.q: A project is failing, but the team wants to continue only because a lot has already been spent. This is an example of:
cards.explain: Past costs should not drive future decisions — the sunk-cost fallacy.

cards.q: As a district officer you learn a relief-material supplier is delivering short weight during a flood. The best first step is to:
options: Publicly blame the supplier on social media
Verify, ensure relief continues through alternatives, and act against the supplier under rules
cards.explain: It protects victims, follows due process and fixes the problem.

cards.q: Four tasks: A must precede B; C must follow B; D can be done anytime. Which order is valid?
cards.explain: Only D-A-B-C keeps A before B and B before C.

notes.p: Public officials often face situations with incomplete information, competing interests and time pressure. Good decisions balance **rules** (legality), **values** (fairness, compassion, integrity) and **outcomes** (effectiveness). In CSAT, you are not asked to recite theory but to recognise the most reasonable course of action or to reason logically from given information.
Useful distinctions:
points: **Programmed** decisions — routine, covered by rules (e.g., issuing a licence)
**Non-programmed** decisions — new, complex situations needing judgment (e.g., disaster response)
**Individual vs group** decisions — groups bring diverse ideas but risk groupthink
**Under certainty, risk and uncertainty** — the less information, the more judgment needed
**Rational model** vs **bounded rationality** (Herbert Simon) — people 'satisfice' rather than find the perfect option

notes.p:
Many CSAT 'problem solving' items are **arrangement, scheduling and selection** puzzles.

Worked example 1: Five people — A, B, C, D, E — are to be ranked by height. A is taller than B; C is shorter than B; D is taller than A; E is shortest. Who is the second tallest?
Step 1: D > A > B (from clues 1 and 3).
Step 2: C < B, and E is shortest → D > A > B > C > E.
Answer: **A**.

Worked example 2: A committee of 2 must be chosen from P, Q, R, S. P and Q will not serve together; R serves only if S serves. How many valid committees exist?
Step 1: All pairs: PQ, PR, PS, QR, QS, RS = 6.
Step 2: Remove PQ (conflict).
Step 3: R needs S, so remove PR and QR.
Step 4: Valid: PS, QS, RS = **3**.

Read every condition, including words like 'only if', 'at least', 'not necessarily'. 'R serves **only if** S serves' means R → S, not S → R. In situational questions, avoid options that break rules for good ends, that are passive, or that make promises beyond your authority.

Recent papers include many reasoning puzzles and data-sufficiency style questions. Practise with previous CSAT papers, timing yourself; aim for accuracy over speed since CSAT is **qualifying** at 33%.

A simple routine for each puzzle: (1) read all clues once without writing; (2) set up a grid or line diagram; (3) enter fixed clues; (4) branch on the most restrictive conditional clue and test each branch; (5) check the final arrangement against every clue. If a puzzle is still unresolved after about two minutes, mark it and move on — another question may be quicker marks.
Recall.
points: Define → stakeholders → options → evaluate → act → review
Best options: lawful, humane, proactive, proportionate
Root-cause analysis; cost–benefit; elimination
Biases: confirmation, anchoring, sunk cost, groupthink
Draw diagrams for puzzles
'Only if' = one-way condition
CSAT qualifying at 33%

cards.title: What appears
cards.body: CSAT data interpretation (Class X level) uses **tables, bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts**, plus **data sufficiency** questions. Most require percentages, ratios, averages and growth rates — speed comes from approximation.

cards.title: Core calculations
points: % change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100
Share % = part ÷ total × 100
Pie angle = share % × 3.6 (degrees)
Average = total ÷ number
If A is x% more than B, B is x/(100+x) × 100 % less than A

cards.title: Pie chart example
cards.body: A family spends ₹2,40,000 a year: food 30%, rent 25%. Food = **₹72,000**; rent = **₹60,000**. Food's sector angle = 30 × 3.6 = **108°**.

cards.title: Data sufficiency
cards.body: You must decide whether given statements are **enough** to answer — not compute the answer. Check statement I alone, II alone, then both together. Don't assume facts not given.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Read the **units**, the **base year**, and whether figures are absolute or percentages before calculating. Many wrong answers come from comparing percentages of different totals.

cards.q: A pie-chart sector representing 15% of the total has an angle of:
A value rises from 80 to 100. The percentage increase is:
cards.explain: Increase 20 on base 80 = 25%.

cards.q: If A's salary is 20% more than B's, then B's salary is less than A's by about:

notes.p: Spend the first few seconds understanding the chart: title, axes, units, legend, and total. Then read all questions in the set — some can be answered directly by observation. **Approximate** when options are far apart; calculate precisely only when options are close. Use fraction equivalents (e.g., 12.5% = 1/8) to speed up percentage work.

Production (in thousand tonnes) of a crop: State A — 2022: 120, 2023: 150; State B — 2022: 200, 2023: 220.

Q1. Which state had higher percentage growth?
A: (150 − 120)/120 = 30/120 = **25%**. B: (220 − 200)/200 = 20/200 = **10%**. Answer: **State A**, even though B's production is larger.

Q2. What is A's share of combined 2023 output?
150 ÷ (150 + 220) = 150/370 ≈ **40.5%**.

Lesson: absolute size and growth rate are different things — a common trap.

notes.h: Worked example 2: line graph and averages
notes.p:
Monthly rainfall (mm): Jan 10, Feb 20, Mar 30, Apr 40, May 50.

Q1. Average rainfall = 150 ÷ 5 = **30 mm**.
Q2. In which month was the increase over the previous month the highest in percentage terms?
Feb: 10/10 = **100%**; Mar: 10/20 = 50%; Apr: 10/30 ≈ 33%; May: 10/40 = 25%.
Answer: **February** — equal absolute increases mean falling percentage increases as the base grows.

Typical format: 'Is x > y? I: x = 2y. II: y > 0.'

Step 1: I alone — if y is negative, x = 2y is smaller than y; if positive, larger. **Not sufficient**.
Step 2: II alone — tells nothing about x. **Not sufficient**.
Step 3: Together — y > 0 and x = 2y gives x > y. **Sufficient together**.

Always test positive, negative and zero values when signs are unknown.
Errors to avoid:
points: Using the wrong base for percentage change
Adding percentages of different totals
Ignoring units (thousands vs lakhs, % vs absolute)
Reading the wrong bar or legend colour
Over-calculating when approximation would do
Assuming data not shown in the chart (in DS questions)

notes.p:
CSAT includes DI-style questions within quantitative aptitude, often in short tables or word problems. Since CSAT is qualifying, use DI to secure reliable marks — these questions are often more straightforward than puzzles. Practise with previous papers and timed sets.

DI questions may also hide inside word problems — for instance, a paragraph describing a town's population by age group, followed by questions on shares and ratios. Convert such text into a small table first. Remember that **percentage points** differ from **per cent**: a rise in a rate from 10% to 12% is a rise of 2 percentage points but a 20% increase in the rate.
Recall.
points: % change = change ÷ old × 100
Pie angle = % × 3.6
x% more ⇒ x/(100+x) less the other way
Growth rate ≠ absolute size
Equal absolute rises ⇒ falling % rises
DS: test each statement alone, then together
Approximate when options are far apart

chapters.title: General Mental Ability: Series, Coding, Directions & More

cards.title: What GMA covers
cards.body: Number and letter **series**, **coding–decoding**, **blood relations**, **directions**, **clocks and calendars**, **Venn diagrams**, **ranking and ordering**, and **analogies**. Most need a quick method plus a rough diagram.

cards.title: Number series
cards.body: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ? — differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12: answer **42**. (Also: n × (n + 1) for n = 1, 2, 3 …)

cards.title: Coding
cards.body: If CAT is written as DBU (each letter +1), then DOG is written as **EPH**. Always check whether the shift is constant, alternating, or reversed (A↔Z).

cards.title: Blood relation
cards.body: Pointing to a boy, Riya says, 'He is the son of my grandfather's only son.' Riya's grandfather's only son is Riya's **father**; his son is Riya's **brother**.

cards.title: Clock and calendar rules
points: Angle between hands = |30H − 5.5M| degrees
Hands coincide 11 times in 12 hours
Ordinary year = 1 odd day; leap year = 2 odd days
A century year is a leap year only if divisible by 400

cards.title: Directions
cards.body: Walk 3 km north, turn right and walk 4 km. You are now east of your northward path. Distance from start = √(3² + 4²) = **5 km**, towards the **north-east**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For Venn problems: Total = A + B − (A and B) + neither. In a class of 40, if 25 like tea, 20 like coffee and 10 like both, those liking neither = 40 − (25 + 20 − 10) = **5**.

cards.q: Find the next term: 3, 9, 27, 81, ?
cards.explain: Each term is multiplied by 3: 81 × 3 = 243.

cards.q: The angle between the hands of a clock at 2:20 is:
If 1 January of a non-leap year is a Monday, what day is 1 January of the next year?
cards.explain: A non-leap year has 1 odd day, so the day moves forward by one: Tuesday.

notes.p: General mental ability questions are **rule-based**: once you know the pattern types, they are quick and reliable. Unlike comprehension, they rarely depend on interpretation. Build a routine — identify the type, apply the method, verify with the options.
Common patterns:
points: **Differences**: constant, increasing (+2, +4, +6), or alternating
**Multiplication/division**: ×2, ×3, or alternating × and +
**Squares and cubes**: 1, 4, 9, 16 … or n² ± 1
**Letter series**: convert letters to positions (A = 1 … Z = 26); opposite pairs sum to 27 (A–Z, B–Y)
**Analogies**: find the relation in the first pair (tool–worker, part–whole, cause–effect) and apply it

notes.p:
Worked example 1 (clock): At 3:30, angle = |30 × 3 − 5.5 × 30| = |90 − 165| = **75°**.

Worked example 2 (calendar): If 15 August 2023 was a Tuesday, what day was 15 August 2024?
Step 1: Between these dates lies **29 February 2024**, so the gap is 366 days.
Step 2: 366 = 52 weeks + **2 odd days**.
Step 3: Tuesday + 2 = **Thursday**.

The principle: count odd days (remainder after dividing days by 7) and move the weekday forward.

For **direction** questions, draw axes with north at the top. A right turn while facing north means facing east; a left turn means west. Use Pythagoras for shortest distance. For **blood relations**, draw a family tree using symbols: + for male, − for female, horizontal lines for siblings or spouses, vertical lines for generations. Phrases like 'only son', 'mother's only daughter' usually point back to the speaker or a parent.

**Ranking**: if someone is 7th from the top and 12th from the bottom, the total = 7 + 12 − 1 = **18**. **Ordering**: convert statements to inequalities (A > B > C). **Venn diagrams**: use the inclusion–exclusion formula; for three sets, Total = A + B + C − (AB + BC + CA) + ABC + neither. Syllogisms are covered in the logical reasoning chapter.

UPSC CSAT papers include series, clocks, calendars, directions, ranking and counting puzzles each year in varying numbers. Practise 10–15 mixed questions daily for a few weeks before the exam.

Worked example (ranking): In a row of children, Asha is 9th from the left and Bina is 6th from the right. If they interchange positions, Asha becomes 15th from the left. How many children are in the row?
Step 1: After interchange, Asha takes Bina's old place, which is 15th from the left and 6th from the right.
Step 2: Total = 15 + 6 − 1 = **20**.
Recall.
points: Check differences first in number series
A–Z positions; opposite letters sum to 27
Clock angle = |30H − 5.5M|
Odd days: ordinary year 1, leap year 2
Rank total = top + bottom − 1
Venn: A + B − both + neither = total
Draw diagrams for directions and relations

cards.title: What the Essay paper is
cards.body: The Essay paper carries **250 marks**. Candidates write **two essays**, one from each of two sections (usually four topics per section), in **3 hours**, with a suggested length of about **1000–1200 words** each. Always confirm the current pattern in the notification.

cards.title: What examiners reward
points: Arrangement of ideas in an **orderly** way
**Concise, effective** expression
Staying **close to the subject** — no drifting
A **multi-dimensional** view balanced by a clear stand

cards.title: A reliable skeleton
points: **Introduction** (100–150 words): anecdote, story, quote or paradox that leads to the theme
**Body** (800–900 words): 4–6 dimensions, each with argument + example
**Counter-view** and its answer
**Way forward**
**Conclusion**: return to the opening image, end hopeful

cards.title: The 30-minute plan
cards.body: Spend about **30 minutes** brainstorming before you write. List dimensions (PESTEL: political, economic, social, technological, environmental, legal; plus ethical, historical, international), then order them into a flow. A planned essay reads like an argument, not a list.

cards.title: Decoding a philosophical topic
cards.body: Topic type: "A ship in harbour is safe, but that is not what ships are built for." Literal meaning: comfort vs purpose. Wider meaning: risk-taking in individuals, start-ups, science, foreign policy. Counter-view: reckless risk without preparation. Conclusion: calculated courage.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Never write a GS answer in essay form. Avoid sub-headings overload, bullet lists and long statistics tables. Use flowing paragraphs, each with one idea, linked by transition sentences.

cards.q: How many essays must be written in the UPSC Mains Essay paper (current pattern)?
cards.explain: Candidates write two essays, one from each section.

cards.q: Which is the best use of the first part of the exam time in the Essay paper?
options: Brainstorm dimensions and plan the flow
cards.explain: Planning for about 30 minutes produces an organised, multi-dimensional essay.

notes.p:
The Essay paper is worth **250 marks** — as much as a GS paper — and it is the one paper where preparation of facts matters less than **thinking and expression**. Scores vary widely across candidates, so a good essay can lift a rank significantly.

UPSC states that candidates are expected to keep close to the subject, to **arrange ideas in an orderly fashion** and to **write concisely**. Credit goes to effective and exact expression. Always check the latest notification for the current pattern; recent papers have had two sections, each with several topics, and candidates choose one from each.

Read all topics once. Strike out those you cannot explain in a single sentence. Prefer a topic where you can list **at least six dimensions** and **several concrete examples**.

Topics broadly fall into two kinds: **philosophical/abstract** (quotes, proverbs, values) and **issue-based** (technology, women, environment, economy). Philosophical topics allow creativity but need careful interpretation; issue-based topics reward knowledge but risk turning into a GS answer.
Spend roughly the first **30 minutes** on a rough outline. A simple method:
points: **Decode** the topic: literal meaning, deeper meaning, key words
**List dimensions**: political, economic, social, cultural, technological, environmental, ethical, legal, international, historical
**Add examples** to each: personalities, schemes, events, data you are sure of
**Order** the points: from individual to society to nation to world, or from past to present to future
**Decide your stand** and one counter-argument you will address

notes.p:
The **introduction** should catch attention and lead to the theme within 100–150 words. Options: a short story or anecdote (real or clearly imaginary), a quote, a contrast, or a question.

The **body** carries the argument. Write each paragraph around **one idea**: claim, explanation, example, link to the theme. Use **transition sentences** so that paragraphs flow ("Yet the economic story is only half the picture…"). Include a fair **counter-view** — showing the other side and then answering it shows maturity.

A **way forward** section should be practical and connected to the arguments made earlier, not a generic list.

The **conclusion** should tie threads together, ideally returning to the opening story or image, and end on an optimistic, forward-looking note — often linked to constitutional values or a vision of India.

Language should be **simple and precise**. Avoid jargon, slang, very long sentences, excessive quotes and unverified statistics. A few well-chosen examples beat a crowd of half-remembered numbers. Keep handwriting legible and leave some space between paragraphs.

Write at least **one full essay a week** in timed conditions in the months before Mains. After writing, check: Did I stay on topic? Is there a clear stand? Did each paragraph add a new dimension? Is the conclusion connected to the introduction? Get peer or mentor feedback and rewrite weak parts — rewriting builds skill faster than reading model essays.
Key points.
points: 250 marks; two essays, one from each section (verify current pattern)
Plan for ~30 minutes before writing
Decode topic → dimensions → examples → order → stand
Intro hooks the reader; body = one idea per paragraph
Include a counter-view and answer it
Conclusion returns to the opening and ends hopeful
Flowing prose, not GS-style bullets

cards.title: Recurring themes
points: **Values & philosophy**: truth, happiness, contentment, purpose
**Society**: women, education, family, youth
**Economy & development**: growth vs equity, work, technology
**Polity & governance**: democracy, justice, institutions
**Science & environment**: technology, climate, nature
**India & the world**: soft power, globalisation

cards.title: Build a personal bank
cards.body: Keep a notebook with **examples by theme**: a personality, a scheme, an event, a story, a quote. Each entry should say what it illustrates. Draw from GS reading so that preparation is shared across papers.

cards.title: Safe illustrative examples
points: **Gandhi** — means and ends, Talisman
**Ambedkar** — constitutional morality, social democracy
**APJ Abdul Kalam** — science with humility
**Kerala's literacy story**, **Amul** cooperative model
**Chandrayaan** missions — frugal innovation
**Self-help groups** — women's collective agency

cards.title: Interpreting quotes
cards.body: For a quote-based topic, explain the **literal sense**, the **deeper sense**, where it **applies** (individual, society, nation, world) and where it has **limits**. The limit section prevents a one-sided essay.

cards.title: Dimension map: "Technology is a double-edged sword"
cards.body: Benefits: health (telemedicine), inclusion (digital payments), governance (DBT). Risks: privacy, misinformation, job displacement, digital divide, cyber crime. Ethical lens: whose purpose does technology serve? Way forward: regulation, digital literacy, ethics by design.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use facts only when you are sure of them. "India is among the world's largest…" is safer than a precise but wrong number. Credibility lost on one false figure affects the whole essay.

cards.q: While writing on a quote-based topic, discussing its limits mainly helps to:
options: Make the essay balanced and mature
cards.explain: Acknowledging limits shows balanced, multi-dimensional thinking.

cards.q: Which example best illustrates "purity of means and ends"?
cards.explain: Gandhi held that just ends cannot be achieved by unjust means.

notes.p:
Essay topics change every year, but the **underlying themes repeat**: human values, the role of women, education, technology, development and environment, democracy and justice, and India's place in the world. Preparing **theme notes** with arguments and examples lets you handle almost any topic.

Recent papers have favoured **philosophical and abstract** topics (proverbs and quotes) more than direct issue-based ones. Such topics still need concrete content; abstraction is only the entry point.
Organise your bank by theme. For each, collect:
points: **Personalities**: Gandhi, Ambedkar, Tagore, Vivekananda, Nehru, Kalam, Verghese Kurien, social reformers
**Constitutional ideas**: Preamble values, fraternity, dignity, constitutional morality
**Schemes and institutions**: SHGs, cooperative movement, Panchayati Raj, digital public infrastructure
**Events and stories**: freedom movement episodes, scientific missions, disaster responses
**Literature and philosophy**: Upanishadic ideas, Buddha's middle path, Kabir, Thiruvalluvar

notes.h: Worked example: planning an abstract topic
notes.p:
Topic type: "Contentment is natural wealth; luxury is artificial poverty."

**Step 1 – Decode:** happiness comes from limiting wants, not multiplying them.
**Step 2 – Dimensions:** individual (mental health), society (consumerism, social comparison), economy (consumption-led growth vs sustainability), environment (resource use), philosophy (aparigraha, Stoics, Gandhi), governance (simple living by public servants).
**Step 3 – Counter-view:** contentment can breed complacency; growth lifts people out of poverty.
**Step 4 – Resolution:** contentment with what one has, ambition for what one can contribute.
**Step 5 – Conclusion:** sustainable lifestyles (for example India's LiFE idea) as a bridge between the two.

notes.h: Worked example: planning an issue-based topic
notes.p:
Topic type: "Education is the most powerful instrument of social change."

**Dimensions:** history (reformers like Phule and Savitribai Phule opening schools), constitutional (Article 21A, DPSP), economic (human capital), social (caste and gender mobility), political (informed citizenship), technological (digital learning and its divide).
**Challenges:** learning outcomes, dropouts, inequity.
**Way forward:** foundational literacy, teacher quality, mother-tongue learning, skill linkage.
**Conclusion:** education as liberation, echoing Ambedkar's call to "educate, agitate, organise".

Three traps lower essay scores. First, **topic drift**: writing a general essay on "technology" when the topic asks specifically about technology and human relationships. Re-read the topic after every two paragraphs. Second, **one-dimensional treatment**: only economic arguments, or only praise. Third, **GS-style listing** of schemes and data without an argument connecting them.

An easy self-check: could each paragraph be moved to a different essay without change? If yes, it is not tied tightly enough to your topic.

An example should **prove the point** made in that paragraph — introduce it in one or two lines and explain the link. Mix Indian and global, historical and contemporary, and personal-scale and national-scale examples. Avoid stacking quotes; two or three across an essay are plenty.
Key points.
points: Themes recur: values, society, economy, governance, science, environment, world
Keep a themed examples bank fed by GS reading
Quote topics: literal → deeper → application → limits
Every example must be explained, not just named
Use only facts you are sure of
Balance Indian and global examples

cards.title: What the optional is
cards.body: Mains has **two optional papers** (Paper VI and VII) of **250 marks each** — 500 of the 1750 written marks. You choose one subject from the list in the notification; literature of a listed language is also allowed.

cards.title: Four questions to ask
points: **Interest**: can I study this daily for a year?
**Background**: did I study it in graduation?
**Overlap** with GS/Essay
**Guidance**: books, test series, mentors, answer-copy availability

cards.title: Overlap is a bonus, not the rule
cards.body: Subjects like Public Administration, Political Science, Sociology, Geography, History and Anthropology overlap with GS. But a technical or literature optional you love can score well too. Interest and comfort beat popularity.

cards.title: Check the syllabus first
cards.body: Read the **official syllabus** of 2–3 shortlisted subjects and solve a few **previous year questions**. If the questions feel approachable after reading the syllabus, it is a good sign.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Avoid choosing an optional only because "it is scoring this year". Trends shift; marks depend on depth of preparation and answer quality.

cards.q: How many marks do the two optional papers together carry in Mains?
cards.explain: Two papers of 250 marks each = 500 marks.

cards.q: Which factor should weigh most when choosing an optional?
options: Genuine interest and comfort with the syllabus
cards.explain: Sustained interest and comfort drive depth and good answers.

notes.p:
The optional subject carries **500 marks** through two papers (Paper VI and Paper VII), roughly 28% of the written total. The list of optional subjects and their syllabi is given in the UPSC notification; always check the latest list.

Unlike GS, the optional demands **depth**: concepts, thinkers, theories and their application. A strong optional can offset average GS scores.
Weigh these together.
points: **Interest** — the single most important factor; you will read it many times
**Academic background** — prior study saves time but is not compulsory
**Syllabus size** and its stability
**Overlap** with GS, Essay and interview
**Availability of material**, test series and guidance
**Answer-writing nature** — analytical (humanities), numerical (engineering, maths) or literary

notes.p:
**Step 1:** Shortlist 3 subjects using interest and background.
**Step 2:** Read their official syllabi end to end.
**Step 3:** Read one basic book chapter from each.
**Step 4:** Attempt 5–10 previous-year questions from each, even roughly.
**Step 5:** Talk to people who have written the subject recently.
**Step 6:** Decide, and then stop second-guessing.

Overlap means time saved and better GS answers. **Public Administration** supports GS II governance and GS IV; **Political Science & IR** supports GS II polity and IR; **Sociology** supports GS I society and the Essay; **Geography** supports GS I and GS III environment and disaster management; **History** supports GS I; **Anthropology** has a compact syllabus with some overlap with society topics.

Science, engineering, medical, commerce, law and literature optionals have less overlap but suit candidates with a strong background. The time saved by overlap is useful only if you can actually score well in that subject.

Avoid switching optionals mid-preparation without strong reason; it costs months. Do not choose purely on "scoring" trends or a friend's choice. Do not underestimate a subject because its syllabus looks short — depth questions can be tough. Plan to complete the optional before Prelims-focused months, then revise after Prelims.

Make concise notes, practise answer writing from the start, and solve the last 10 years' questions topic-wise. Link current events to optional topics where relevant (for example, sociology with social issues). Join a test series about 4–6 months before Mains.

A practical timeline many candidates follow: finish the first full reading of the optional in about 4–5 months, take a sectional test series alongside, and revise it twice before Mains. During the Prelims phase keep it alive with short weekly revision so that you do not start from zero after Prelims. Keep a one-page list of thinkers, models, diagrams and case examples for each unit — these lift answers above the average and are quick to revise in the final weeks.
Key points.
points: 2 papers × 250 = 500 marks
Interest first, then background, overlap and guidance
Read the official syllabus and PYQs before deciding
Do not chase "scoring" trends
Do not switch mid-way without strong reason
Practise answers from the start

cards.title: The Personality Test
cards.body: The interview carries **275 marks** and is added to the Mains written total (1750) for the final merit of **2025**. A board of UPSC members and experts assesses your **personal suitability** for a public-service career.

cards.title: What the board looks for
points: Mental **alertness** and critical powers of assimilation
**Clear and logical** exposition
**Balance of judgement**
Variety and depth of **interest**
**Social cohesion** and leadership
**Intellectual and moral integrity**

cards.title: The DAF is your map
cards.body: Most questions come from your **Detailed Application Form**: name, home district and state, education, work experience, hobbies, achievements and service preferences. Prepare each line deeply.

cards.title: Current affairs and opinions
cards.body: Expect questions on major national and international issues. Give **balanced views**: acknowledge both sides, take a reasoned position, stay respectful of institutions.

cards.title: Handling an unknown question
cards.body: "Sir, I am not aware of this at the moment; I will read about it." Honesty is better than guessing. If you can reason towards an answer, say so: "I am not certain, but logically it could be…"

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Prepare a 1–2 minute introduction, know your district and state thoroughly, and practise mock interviews. Dress formally and comfortably, and listen fully before answering.

cards.q: How many marks does the UPSC CSE Personality Test carry?
cards.explain: The interview carries 275 marks.

cards.q: If asked a factual question you do not know, the best response is to:
cards.explain: Honesty and composure are part of integrity and judgement being assessed.

cards.q: Which document forms the main basis of interview questions?
cards.explain: The DAF provides the personal details the board draws on.

notes.p:
UPSC describes the interview as an assessment of **personal suitability for a career in public service** by a board of competent and unbiased observers. It is not a test of specialised or general knowledge alone — that has been tested in the written papers — but of **mental calibre**, character and attitude.

The Personality Test carries **275 marks**. Combined with 1750 Mains marks, it decides the final rank, so a strong interview can move a candidate many ranks up.
UPSC lists qualities such as:
points: Mental alertness and critical powers of assimilation
Clear and logical exposition
Balance of judgement
Variety and depth of interest
Ability for social cohesion and leadership
Intellectual and moral integrity

notes.p:
Fill the DAF carefully — every line can become a question.

**Name:** meaning or famous namesakes.
**Home district/state:** geography, economy, history, culture, current issues, administrative challenges.
**Education:** core concepts of your graduation subject and its applications.
**Work experience:** what you did, sector issues, why you are leaving it.
**Hobbies:** genuine depth; a hobby you cannot discuss becomes a liability.
**Service preferences:** why IAS/IPS/IFS etc., and roles in each.

Read a newspaper daily after Mains. For each big issue, know the **facts, the different viewpoints, and a balanced position**. The board often probes with a counter-question; stay calm, accept a valid point gracefully and explain your reasoning. Avoid extreme or partisan statements and respect constitutional institutions.

Take a few **mock interviews** with different panels, but do not over-do them; too many mocks lead to rehearsed, mechanical answers. After each mock, note questions you fumbled and prepare them. Record yourself answering common questions — "Tell us about yourself", "Why civil services?", "What will you do as a district magistrate facing a flood?" — and check for clarity, pace and filler words.

Situational questions test administrative judgement: answer with the same structure as ethics case studies — stakeholders, options, a lawful and humane decision, and long-term measures.

Arrive early with documents. Greet the board, sit when asked, maintain natural eye contact with the member asking and include others. **Listen fully**, pause briefly, then answer in a structured way. Keep answers concise unless asked to elaborate. If you do not know, say so honestly. Thank the board at the end. Mock interviews help with nervousness and body language but avoid memorised, rehearsed answers.

The interview usually lasts around half an hour, and different members may take up different areas. Treat it as a **conversation**, not an interrogation; the board is assessing how you think, not only what you know.
Key points.
points: 275 marks; final merit out of 2025
Tests personal suitability, not just knowledge
DAF is the main source of questions
Know your district, state, subject, hobbies, job
Balanced, reasoned views on current issues
Honesty when you do not know
Listen, pause, answer concisely

chapters.title: Age of Revolutions & the Industrial Revolution

cards.title: Why 18th-century revolutions matter
cards.body: GS I asks about world history "from the 18th century". The **American** and **French** Revolutions spread ideas of popular sovereignty, rights and republicanism; the **Industrial Revolution** changed how the world produced, lived and ruled colonies.

cards.title: American Revolution (1775–1783)
points: Cause: taxation without representation, mercantilist controls
**Declaration of Independence**: 4 July 1776
**Treaty of Paris (1783)** ended the war
**US Constitution (1787)**: federalism, separation of powers; Bill of Rights added 1791

cards.title: French Revolution (1789)
points: Causes: fiscal crisis, privileges of clergy and nobility, Enlightenment ideas
Storming of the **Bastille**: 14 July 1789
**Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen** (1789)
Slogan: **Liberty, Equality, Fraternity**
Ended in the rise of **Napoleon**

cards.title: Industrial Revolution
points: Began in **Britain**, second half of the 18th century
Textiles first: spinning jenny (Hargreaves), water frame (Arkwright), power loom (Cartwright)
**James Watt's** improved steam engine
Coal, iron, canals, then railways

cards.title: Why Britain first?
points: Coal and iron ore deposits
Capital from trade and colonies
Agricultural changes and enclosures freed labour
Banking, stable politics, overseas markets

cards.title: Effects
points: Urbanisation and factory towns
A new **working class** and labour movements
Rise of **socialist** ideas
Search for raw materials and markets fed **imperialism**
**Deindustrialisation** of Indian handicrafts

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Link world history to India: French ideals influenced Indian reformers and the Preamble's "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity"; the Industrial Revolution explains the drain of wealth and ruin of Indian handicrafts.

cards.q: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen is associated with:
cards.explain: It was adopted in France in 1789.

cards.q: Which was NOT a reason for the Industrial Revolution beginning in Britain?
cards.explain: Electricity became important only in the later Second Industrial Revolution.

notes.p:
Between roughly 1750 and 1850 the Atlantic world saw political revolutions in America and France and an economic revolution in Britain. Together they produced the modern ideas of **popular sovereignty, rights of citizens, nationalism and industrial capitalism**.

The **Enlightenment** supplied the ideas: **John Locke** (natural rights to life, liberty and property; government by consent), **Montesquieu** (separation of powers), **Rousseau** (the social contract and general will) and **Voltaire** (freedom of thought and critique of the church).

British attempts to tax the thirteen colonies after the costly Seven Years' War (for example the Stamp Act) provoked the cry "**no taxation without representation**". War began in 1775; the **Declaration of Independence** (4 July 1776) asserted that all men are created equal with unalienable rights. French support helped the colonists, and the **Treaty of Paris (1783)** recognised independence.

The **US Constitution (1787)** created a federal republic with separation of powers and checks and balances; the **Bill of Rights (1791)** added fundamental rights. Limits: slavery continued and women had no vote — a useful point for balanced answers.
