France faced bankruptcy, a rigid society of three **Estates**, and food shortages. The Estates-General met in 1789; the Third Estate declared itself the **National Assembly**. The fall of the **Bastille** (14 July 1789) became the symbol of revolution, and the **Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen** proclaimed liberty and equality before law.

The revolution abolished feudal privileges, executed the king, passed through the radical **Reign of Terror**, and ended with **Napoleon's** rise. Its legacy: nationalism, secular state, legal equality (Napoleonic Code) and the spread of democratic ideals across Europe.

Starting in **Britain** in the second half of the 18th century, production moved from hand to machine and from home to factory. Textile inventions came first, followed by **steam power**, iron and coal, canals and railways. A **Second Industrial Revolution** in the late 19th century, led by **Germany and the USA**, brought steel, electricity, chemicals and the internal combustion engine.

Social effects included crowded cities, child labour, poor working conditions, trade unions and factory laws. Intellectually, it produced both **classical liberal economics** (Adam Smith) and **socialist critiques** (Marx).

The 19th century saw **nationalism** redraw Europe's map. **Italy** was unified through Mazzini, Garibaldi and Cavour, and **Germany** under Bismarck — both completed by 1871. Nationalism inspired colonised peoples too, including Indian leaders who read Mazzini.

The Industrial Revolution created demand for raw cotton and markets for British cloth, contributing to the **deindustrialisation** of Indian handicrafts and the **drain of wealth** argued by Dadabhai Naoroji. Revolutionary ideals of liberty and equality shaped Indian reformers and, later, the Preamble.
Key points.
points: Enlightenment thinkers: Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Voltaire
American Declaration 1776; Treaty of Paris 1783; Constitution 1787
French Revolution 1789; Rights of Man; Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Industrial Revolution began in Britain, textiles and steam
Second Industrial Revolution: Germany, USA; steel, electricity
Italy and Germany unified by 1871
India: deindustrialisation and drain of wealth

cards.title: Causes of World War I (MAIN)
points: **M**ilitarism — arms race
**A**lliances — Triple Entente vs Triple Alliance
**I**mperialism — colonial rivalry
**N**ationalism — Balkans, revanche
Spark: assassination of **Archduke Franz Ferdinand** at Sarajevo (June 1914)

cards.title: World War I (1914–1918)
points: Allies: Britain, France, Russia (later USA, 1917)
Central Powers: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Ottoman Empire, Bulgaria
Trench warfare, new weapons
Russia exits after the 1917 revolution
Armistice: November 1918

cards.title: Peace and its problems
cards.body: The **Treaty of Versailles (1919)** imposed war guilt, reparations and territorial losses on Germany. The **League of Nations** was set up but the USA never joined. Empires collapsed — Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, German — and new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia appeared.

cards.title: Road to World War II
points: **Great Depression** from 1929
Rise of **fascism** (Mussolini, 1922) and **Nazism** (Hitler, 1933)
Japanese aggression in Manchuria (1931)
Policy of **appeasement**; Munich Agreement (1938)
Invasion of **Poland**: 1 September 1939

cards.title: World War II (1939–1945)
points: Axis: Germany, Italy, Japan
Allies: Britain, France, USSR (from 1941), USA (from Dec 1941), China
The **Holocaust**
Atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945)
**United Nations** founded 1945

cards.title: India and the wars
points: WWI: over a million Indian soldiers served abroad; Home Rule movement; Montagu declaration (1917)
WWII: India declared at war without consultation; Congress ministries resigned (1939)
Cripps Mission and **Quit India** (1942); **INA**

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For "consequences" questions, organise by political (empires fall, UN), economic (debt, Bretton Woods), social (refugees, women in workforce) and colonial (decolonisation) dimensions.

cards.q: The immediate cause of World War I was:
cards.explain: The Sarajevo assassination in June 1914 triggered the crisis.

cards.q: Which country never joined the League of Nations?
cards.explain: The US Senate did not ratify the Versailles treaty, so the USA stayed out.

cards.q: World War II began in Europe with Germany's invasion of:
cards.explain: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France then declared war.

notes.h: Causes of the First World War
notes.p:
Historians summarise the long-term causes as **MAIN**: militarism (an arms and naval race, especially between Britain and Germany), alliances (Triple Entente of Britain, France and Russia; Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy), imperialism (competition for colonies) and nationalism (Slav nationalism in the Balkans, French desire to recover Alsace-Lorraine).

The spark was the **assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand** of Austria-Hungary at Sarajevo in June 1914. Alliance commitments turned a regional crisis into a world war within weeks.

The war saw stalemate on the Western Front, trench warfare, machine guns, poison gas, tanks and submarines. The **USA joined in 1917**, while Russia withdrew after the **Bolshevik Revolution**. An armistice ended fighting in November 1918.

The **Paris Peace Conference** produced the **Treaty of Versailles (1919)**: Germany accepted war guilt, paid reparations, lost territory and colonies, and faced military limits. Four empires collapsed and new nation-states emerged on the principle of **self-determination** (Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points). The Middle East was divided under the **mandate system**. The harsh peace created resentment that later aided Hitler.

The **League of Nations** aimed at collective security but lacked enforcement power and key members. The **Great Depression** from 1929 caused mass unemployment and pushed voters towards extremes. **Fascism** came to power in Italy under Mussolini and **Nazism** in Germany under Hitler, both based on aggressive nationalism and authoritarianism. Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) and Italy invaded Ethiopia (1935); the League failed to stop them. Britain and France followed **appeasement**, culminating in the Munich Agreement (1938).

Germany's invasion of **Poland (1 September 1939)** started the war in Europe. Germany conquered much of Europe, then invaded the **USSR (1941)**. Japan's attack on **Pearl Harbor (December 1941)** brought the USA in. Turning points included Stalingrad, El Alamein, Midway and the Normandy landings (1944). Germany surrendered in May 1945; Japan surrendered after the **atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki** in August 1945.

The **Holocaust** — the genocide of about six million Jews — shaped the post-war human rights order, including the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)**.

Politically, the **United Nations (1945)** replaced the League; the USA and USSR emerged as superpowers, leading to the **Cold War**. Economically, the **Bretton Woods** conference (1944) created the IMF and World Bank, and the Marshall Plan rebuilt Western Europe. Weakened European powers could no longer hold empires, accelerating **decolonisation** — beginning with India in 1947.

In **WWI**, over a million Indian soldiers served overseas; the war brought price rise and discontent, the **Home Rule Leagues**, the **Lucknow Pact** (1916) and the **Montagu declaration** (1917). In **WWII**, the Viceroy declared India at war without consulting Indians, leading Congress ministries to resign (1939). The **Cripps Mission** (1942) failed, followed by **Quit India**, while Subhas Chandra Bose led the **INA**. The war weakened Britain and hastened independence.
Key points.
points: WWI causes: militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism
Spark: Franz Ferdinand assassinated, Sarajevo, 1914
Versailles 1919; League of Nations without USA
Depression 1929 → fascism, Nazism → appeasement
WWII: Poland 1939; Pearl Harbor 1941; atomic bombs 1945
Outcomes: UN, Bretton Woods, Cold War, decolonisation
India: Home Rule, Montagu declaration; Cripps, Quit India, INA

cards.title: Colonialism vs imperialism
cards.body: **Colonialism**: settling or directly ruling foreign territory and exploiting it. **Imperialism**: the broader policy of extending power over other lands, directly or indirectly. 19th-century "new imperialism" was driven by industrial capitalism's need for raw materials, markets and investment.

cards.title: Scramble for Africa
cards.body: European powers divided Africa at the **Berlin Conference (1884–85)**, drawing borders with little regard to ethnic or geographic realities. By the early 20th century only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

cards.title: Theories of imperialism
points: **J.A. Hobson**: surplus capital seeks outlets abroad
**Lenin**: imperialism as the "highest stage of capitalism"
**Dadabhai Naoroji**: drain of wealth from India
Civilising-mission justification: "white man's burden"

cards.title: Waves of decolonisation
points: Latin America: early 19th century
Asia after WWII: India (1947), Indonesia, Burma
Africa: Ghana (1957) first in sub-Saharan Africa; **1960, "Year of Africa"**
UNGA Resolution **1514 (1960)** on granting independence to colonial peoples

cards.title: Redrawing boundaries
points: Partition of India (1947)
Korea split at the 38th parallel
Germany divided; reunified 1990
USSR dissolved (1991) into 15 states
Yugoslavia broke up in the 1990s

cards.title: The Cold War (c.1947–1991)
points: Truman Doctrine and **Marshall Plan** (1947)
**NATO** (1949) vs **Warsaw Pact** (1955)
Berlin Wall (1961–1989)
**Cuban Missile Crisis** (1962)
India chose **non-alignment**

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Answers on decolonisation should mention both causes (weakened Europe after WWII, nationalist movements, UN and superpower pressure) and legacies (artificial borders, ethnic conflict, economic dependence, NAM).

cards.q: The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 is associated with:
options: Partition of Africa among European powers
cards.explain: It set rules for the European scramble for Africa.

cards.q: Which was the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence (1957)?
cards.explain: Ghana, under Kwame Nkrumah, became independent in 1957.

cards.q: The Non-Aligned Movement's first summit was held in 1961 at:
cards.explain: The first NAM summit was in Belgrade; Bandung (1955) was the Afro-Asian conference that preceded it.

notes.p:
European expansion began in the late 15th century with Portuguese and Spanish voyages. Early colonialism was **mercantilist** — trade monopolies, bullion and plantations worked by enslaved Africans. From the 19th century, **industrial imperialism** sought raw materials (cotton, rubber, minerals), captive markets and investment outlets. Britain, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Italy, the USA and Japan all built empires.

The **Berlin Conference (1884–85)** set ground rules for the partition of Africa, producing borders that still shape conflicts.

Colonial rule drained resources, destroyed local industries, introduced cash crops at the expense of food security, created artificial borders and used **divide and rule**. It also unintentionally introduced modern education, railways and print, which nationalists used to organise. A balanced answer acknowledges these contradictions while making clear that exploitation was the core purpose. Racial hierarchies and the "civilising mission" were used to justify rule, and their social effects outlasted empire itself.
After 1945 the colonial order collapsed rapidly because:
points: European powers were economically and militarily exhausted by WWII
**Nationalist movements** had grown strong — India's example inspired others
The **UN Charter** endorsed self-determination; UNGA Resolution 1514 (1960) declared colonialism must end
Both superpowers, for different reasons, opposed old European empires
Public opinion in Europe shifted

notes.p:
Some transfers were negotiated (India 1947, Ghana 1957); others followed **armed struggle** (Indonesia against the Dutch, Algeria against France until 1962, Vietnam against France). In 1960 seventeen African countries became independent. Portugal's African colonies became free only in the mid-1970s.

New states faced artificial borders, ethnic conflict, weak institutions and economic dependence — sometimes called **neo-colonialism**. Many joined the **Non-Aligned Movement** (first summit Belgrade, 1961), following the Afro-Asian **Bandung Conference (1955)**.

The rivalry between the US-led capitalist bloc and the Soviet-led communist bloc shaped world politics from about 1947 to 1991. Key moments: Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan (1947), Berlin blockade, **NATO (1949)** and **Warsaw Pact (1955)**, Korean War, the Berlin Wall (1961), the **Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)**, Vietnam War, détente, and Soviet intervention in Afghanistan (1979). Reforms under Gorbachev, the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989), German reunification (1990) and the **dissolution of the USSR (1991)** ended it.

India followed **non-alignment**, keeping strategic autonomy while engaging both blocs.

Many 20th-century borders were redrawn: post-WWI treaties created new European states and Middle Eastern mandates; partitions divided India, Korea, Germany and Palestine; the end of the Cold War broke up the USSR, Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia. These events explain many present-day disputes — a useful link for GS II international relations answers.
Key points.
points: Mercantilist then industrial imperialism
Berlin Conference 1884–85: partition of Africa
Theories: Hobson, Lenin, Naoroji's drain
Decolonisation: India 1947, Ghana 1957, "Year of Africa" 1960
UNGA Resolution 1514 (1960); Bandung 1955; NAM Belgrade 1961
Cold War: NATO 1949, Warsaw Pact 1955, Cuba 1962, USSR ends 1991
Legacies: artificial borders, neo-colonialism

chapters.title: Political Philosophies: Capitalism, Socialism, Communism & More

cards.title: Liberalism and capitalism
points: **John Locke**: natural rights, limited government
**Adam Smith**, *The Wealth of Nations* (1776): free markets, the "invisible hand"
Private property, profit motive, competition, limited state role

cards.title: Socialism
cards.body: A family of ideas favouring **social or public ownership** of key means of production and a fairer distribution of wealth. Early "utopian" socialists included **Robert Owen** and **Saint-Simon**; Britain's **Fabian Society** favoured gradual, democratic reform.

cards.title: Marxism and communism
points: **Marx and Engels**, *The Communist Manifesto* (1848)
History as **class struggle**; capitalism exploits workers through surplus value
Predicted revolution, a proletarian state, then a classless society
Applied in Russia (1917) and China (1949)

cards.title: Fascism
cards.body: Ultra-nationalist, authoritarian ideology that glorified the state and leader, suppressed dissent and rejected both liberal democracy and communism. Examples: **Mussolini's Italy** and **Hitler's Germany**.

cards.title: India's synthesis
points: **Democratic socialism** and mixed economy under Nehru
"Socialist" added to the Preamble by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**
Gandhian **trusteeship** and decentralisation
DPSPs reflect welfare-state goals
Liberalisation since 1991 increased market role

cards.title: Comparing the three
cards.body: Capitalism: private ownership, market prices, freedom with inequality risks. Socialism: state/social ownership of key sectors, welfare, risk of inefficiency. Communism (Marxist ideal): no private property, classless society; in practice, one-party states with central planning.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: UPSC asks these as concepts with historical illustrations. Define each ideology, give its key thinker and text, show where it was applied, and evaluate its successes and failures.

cards.q: *The Communist Manifesto* (1848) was written by:
cards.explain: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote it in 1848.

cards.q: The word "Socialist" was added to India's Preamble by the:
cards.explain: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added "Socialist", "Secular" and "Integrity".

notes.p: The GS I syllabus mentions **communism, capitalism and socialism** and their forms and effect on society. These ideas shaped revolutions, the Cold War, decolonised states and India's own constitutional choices. Answers should combine **definition, thinkers, historical application and evaluation**.

**Liberalism** emphasises individual liberty, rule of law, consent of the governed and limited government — rooted in **Locke** and developed by **J.S. Mill** (*On Liberty*). **Capitalism** is an economic system based on private ownership, markets and profit. **Adam Smith** argued that self-interest in competitive markets promotes general welfare through an "invisible hand".

Strengths: innovation, efficiency, growth. Weaknesses: inequality, booms and busts, neglect of public goods. The Great Depression led to **Keynesian** ideas of state intervention and to the **welfare state** in Western Europe after 1945.
Socialism arose as a response to industrial capitalism's inequalities. Forms include:
points: **Utopian socialism** — model communities (Owen, Saint-Simon, Fourier)
**Scientific socialism / Marxism** — revolutionary transformation via class struggle
**Fabian / democratic socialism** — gradual reform through elections and welfare
**Social democracy** — markets plus strong welfare state (Nordic model)

notes.p:
Marx held that the economic base shapes society, history moves through **class struggle**, and capitalism would be overthrown by the working class. **Lenin** adapted Marxism to Russia, leading the **Bolshevik Revolution (1917)**; the USSR pursued central planning and rapid industrialisation under Stalin at huge human cost. **Mao** led China's revolution (1949), emphasising peasants.

Achievements claimed: rapid industrialisation, literacy, social security. Failures: authoritarianism, purges, famines, inefficiency and eventual collapse or reform (USSR in 1991; China's market reforms from 1978).

Fascism rose after WWI amid economic crisis and fear of communism. It exalted the nation and leader, used propaganda and violence, and rejected pluralism. **Nazism** added racial ideology, leading to the Holocaust. Their defeat in 1945 discredited these ideas and shaped the post-war rights framework.

**Worked comparison for answers:** on the question of who owns factories, capitalism says private owners, democratic socialism says a mix with public ownership of key sectors, and Marxist communism says the collective/state. On political freedom, liberal democracies protect multiparty competition, while communist and fascist states in practice concentrated power in a single party or leader.

India chose a **mixed economy**: public sector in strategic industries with private enterprise elsewhere, guided by planning. Nehru's democratic socialism, Gandhi's **trusteeship** and **Sarvodaya**, and Ambedkar's emphasis on social democracy shaped the Constitution's DPSPs. The **42nd Amendment (1976)** added "Socialist" to the Preamble, and the Supreme Court has interpreted it as democratic socialism aimed at reducing inequality, not abolishing private property. The **1991 reforms** moved India towards a market-friendly model while retaining welfare commitments.
Key points.
points: Liberalism: Locke, Mill; capitalism: Adam Smith (1776)
Socialism: utopian, Marxist, Fabian, social democratic
Communist Manifesto 1848; Russia 1917; China 1949
Fascism: Mussolini; Nazism: Hitler
Welfare state and Keynesianism after Depression
India: mixed economy, democratic socialism, trusteeship
"Socialist" in Preamble via 42nd Amendment (1976)

chapters.title: Salient Features of Indian Society & Diversity

cards.title: Salient features
points: **Pluralism**: many religions, languages, castes, tribes
**Caste** as a social structure
**Joint family** and kinship networks (changing)
**Patriarchy**
Village-agrarian base, rapid urban change
**Syncretic** traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

cards.title: Forms of diversity
points: **Religious**: all major world religions present
**Linguistic**: 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule
**Ethnic/tribal**: hundreds of Scheduled Tribes
**Caste**: thousands of jatis
**Regional**: geography, food, dress, festivals

cards.title: Unity in diversity
cards.body: Bonds of unity: shared history and freedom struggle, the **Constitution**, pilgrimage networks, a common market, festivals, cinema, sport and federal democracy. Diversity is the fact; unity is a continuing political and cultural project.

cards.title: Key sociological concepts
points: **Sanskritisation** (M.N. Srinivas): lower castes adopting upper-caste customs to rise in status
**Dominant caste** (Srinivas)
**Westernisation** and **modernisation**
**Little and Great traditions** (Redfield, applied by Marriott)

cards.title: Caste: change and continuity
cards.body: Change: urbanisation, education, reservations, inter-caste marriage, decline of pollution rules. Continuity: endogamy, caste in politics and networks, discrimination and atrocities. Caste has moved from ritual hierarchy towards **interest group** and identity.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use sociological terms (Sanskritisation, dominant caste, secularisation) and examples from your own state — they make GS I society answers stand out.

cards.q: The concept of "Sanskritisation" was given by:
cards.explain: M.N. Srinivas introduced Sanskritisation and the dominant caste concept.

cards.q: How many languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule?
cards.explain: There are 22 scheduled languages.

notes.p: The syllabus begins with "**salient features of Indian society, diversity of India**". Questions ask about the nature of diversity, whether it is a strength or challenge, how caste, family and religion are changing, and what holds India together. Answers should combine **sociological concepts, constitutional values and current examples**.
Indian society is marked by:
points: **Pluralism and syncretism** — coexistence and blending of traditions
**Caste and tribe** as basic units of social organisation
**Kinship and family** — joint families giving way to nuclear forms but with strong ties
**Patriarchy** — gendered roles, now being challenged
**Village base** — still a large share of people live in rural areas
**Tradition and modernity** co-existing — ritual alongside technology
**Unity in diversity** — a shared civilisational and constitutional identity

notes.p: **Religious:** Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism, Judaism and tribal faiths. **Linguistic:** four major language families (Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austro-Asiatic, Tibeto-Burman) and 22 scheduled languages. **Ethnic and tribal:** hundreds of notified Scheduled Tribes with distinct cultures. **Caste:** varna as a broad idea, jati as the working reality. **Regional:** varied ecology produces varied livelihoods, cuisines and customs.

**Strength:** cultural richness, soft power, tolerance traditions, a large and varied talent pool, resilience through federalism.

**Challenges:** communal and caste conflict, regional and linguistic tensions, discrimination against minorities and tribal groups, and identity-based politics.

The Constitution manages diversity through **fundamental rights** (Articles 14–17, 25–30), **federalism**, **linguistic states**, **reservations**, **Fifth and Sixth Schedules** for tribal areas and **secularism**.

**Family:** nuclearisation, smaller size, more working women, but continued kin support; new issues of elderly care. **Marriage:** later marriages, more choice, persistence of dowry and endogamy. **Caste:** weakening of ritual purity rules but persistence in marriage and politics — M.N. Srinivas noted the "dominant caste" whose power comes from land, numbers and political clout. **Religion:** growing visibility in public life alongside private secularisation. **Village:** more connected to cities through migration, roads and mobile phones.

**Tribal communities** face their own changes: land alienation, displacement by projects and mining, migration for work, and assimilation pressures, balanced by protections such as the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006).

Question type: "Is diversity a source of strength or weakness for India? Discuss."
**Intro:** define diversity with two quick facts (22 scheduled languages; major world religions present).
**Body 1 – strengths:** pluralism, federal accommodation, soft power, examples like linguistic states easing tensions.
**Body 2 – challenges:** communal riots, inter-state disputes, caste violence.
**Body 3 – how the Constitution manages it.**
**Conclusion:** diversity is a strength when institutions ensure equality and fraternity.
Key points.
points: Features: pluralism, caste, kinship, patriarchy, village base, syncretism
22 scheduled languages; four language families
Sanskritisation and dominant caste: M.N. Srinivas
Caste: ritual weakens, identity persists
Constitution manages diversity via rights, federalism, schedules
Answer with concepts + constitutional values + local examples

cards.title: What the syllabus asks
cards.body: "Role of women and women's organisation" sits in GS I; women-related schemes, laws and institutions also appear in GS II (vulnerable sections). Prepare the **social, economic and political** dimensions.

cards.title: Historic women's organisations
points: **Women's Indian Association** (1917)
**All India Women's Conference** (1927)
**SEWA** (1972, Ela Bhatt) — informal women workers
**Kudumbashree** (Kerala, 1998) — SHG network

cards.title: Key laws
points: Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
POSH Act, 2013 (workplace sexual harassment)
Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 — 26 weeks
Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 — one-third seats in Lok Sabha and state assemblies

cards.title: Persistent challenges
points: Low female labour force participation (improving recently)
Unpaid care work burden
Violence and safety
Skewed child sex ratio in some regions
Under-representation in legislatures and boards

cards.title: Women as agents of change
cards.body: From the **Chipko** movement to SHG-led microenterprise, women's collectives have shaped environmental, economic and political change. Reserved seats in panchayats (73rd/74th Amendments; several states give 50%) created a large base of elected women leaders.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Frame answers around agency, not only victimhood: show women as leaders, entrepreneurs and organisers, then discuss barriers and policy responses.

cards.q: SEWA, an organisation of self-employed women, was founded by:
cards.explain: Ela Bhatt founded SEWA in Ahmedabad in 1972.

cards.q: The 106th Constitutional Amendment (2023) provides for:
options: One-third reservation for women in Lok Sabha and state assemblies
cards.explain: Known as the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam; it takes effect after delimitation following the next census.

notes.p: Women's position has been shaped by patriarchy, caste and class, but also by reform movements and constitutional guarantees. Reformers like **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**, **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar**, **Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule**, **Pandita Ramabai** and others challenged sati, child marriage and the denial of education. Women participated widely in the national movement — Sarojini Naidu, Kasturba Gandhi, Aruna Asaf Ali, Usha Mehta and many others.

Early organisations such as the **Women's Indian Association (1917)** and the **All India Women's Conference (1927)** demanded education, franchise and legal reform. After independence, women's groups campaigned against dowry deaths, rape laws and domestic violence (1970s–80s), leading to legal changes. **SEWA** organised informal women workers; **Kudumbashree** and the national SHG movement under DAY-NRLM built economic collectives. The **National Commission for Women** (set up in 1992 under the NCW Act, 1990) is the statutory body for women's rights.

Constitution: Article 14 (equality), 15(3) (special provisions for women and children), 16 (equal opportunity), 39(a) and 39(d) (livelihood, equal pay), 42 (maternity relief), 51A(e) (renounce practices derogatory to women), and 243D/243T (reservation in local bodies).

Laws: Dowry Prohibition Act (1961), PWDV Act (2005), POSH Act (2013), Criminal Law (Amendment) Act (2013) after the Justice Verma Committee, Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act (2017), and the **106th Amendment (2023)**. Landmark judgments include **Vishaka (1997)** guidelines on workplace harassment and **Shayara Bano (2017)** on instant triple talaq.
Women face:
points: **Economic:** low labour force participation, wage gaps, concentration in informal work, unpaid care work
**Social:** son preference, dowry, early marriage in some regions, restrictions on mobility
**Safety:** domestic violence, sexual violence, cyber harassment
**Political:** low share in Parliament and state assemblies
**Health:** anaemia and nutrition gaps (see NFHS reports for current data)

notes.p: Schemes include **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015)**, **Mission Shakti** (safety and empowerment), **PM Ujjwala Yojana** (clean cooking fuel), **Stand-Up India** and **Mudra** loans for women entrepreneurs, and **DAY-NRLM** for SHGs. Beyond schemes, the way forward includes affordable childcare, safe transport, skill training aligned with jobs, property rights in practice, gender budgeting and changing social norms through education and media.

Question type: "Discuss the role of women's organisations in social change in India."
**Intro:** from reform-era associations to SHGs.
**Body:** pre-independence (WIA, AIWC — franchise, Sarda Act on child marriage, 1929); post-independence (anti-dowry and anti-rape campaigns leading to legal change; SEWA and SHGs for economic agency; environmental movements like Chipko).
**Limitations:** urban, upper-class bias of early bodies; fragmentation.
**Conclusion:** collective action turns rights on paper into rights in practice.
Key points.
points: WIA 1917; AIWC 1927; SEWA 1972; Kudumbashree 1998
NCW: statutory, 1992 (Act of 1990)
Laws: Dowry 1961, PWDV 2005, POSH 2013, Maternity 2017
106th Amendment 2023: one-third seats, after delimitation
Vishaka (1997); Shayara Bano (2017)
Show women as agents, not only victims

chapters.title: Urbanisation & Globalisation: Effects on Indian Society

cards.title: Urbanisation in India
cards.body: Census 2011 recorded about **31%** of Indians as urban (around 377 million). Growth comes from natural increase, rural–urban migration and reclassification of villages as towns (**census towns**). Check the next Census for updated figures.

cards.title: Urban problems
points: Slums and housing shortage
Water scarcity and urban flooding
Traffic, pollution, **urban heat islands**
Solid waste
Informal jobs, weak social security
Weak, under-funded municipalities

cards.title: Policy responses
points: **74th Amendment** (1992): urban local bodies
Smart Cities Mission and AMRUT (2015)
PMAY-Urban (2015): housing
Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban)
Metro rail and transit-oriented development

cards.title: Globalisation: social effects
points: New jobs in IT and services; a growing middle class
Consumerism and changing lifestyles
Nuclear families, more women in some jobs
Cultural mixing — and **glocalisation**
Pressure on small farmers, artisans and informal workers
Rising inequality between regions and skills

cards.title: Glocalisation example
cards.body: Global fast-food chains in India offer vegetarian and regional menus; global streaming platforms commission Indian-language content. Global forms adapt to local tastes — evidence that globalisation is not simple Westernisation.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For "remedies" in urbanisation answers, include municipal finance (property tax reform, municipal bonds), integrated planning, affordable rental housing, public transport and climate-resilient drainage.

cards.q: Which constitutional amendment gave constitutional status to urban local bodies?
cards.explain: The 74th Amendment (1992) added Part IXA on municipalities.

cards.q: A "census town" in India is:
options: A settlement meeting urban criteria but without a statutory urban local body
A town declared by the state government only
A village with a railway station
cards.explain: Census towns satisfy population, density and non-farm workforce criteria but are not statutory towns.

notes.p:
Urbanisation is the increase in the share of population living in towns and cities. The Census uses two categories: **statutory towns** (with a municipality, corporation, cantonment or notified area) and **census towns** (minimum population of 5,000, density of at least 400 per sq km, and at least 75% of male main workers in non-agricultural work). Census 2011 showed about 31% urban population; urban growth is concentrated in large metropolitan regions and peri-urban areas.

Urbanisation in India is often called **"pseudo-urbanisation"** or poverty-driven, since much migration is distress-driven rather than pulled by good jobs.
Key problems:
points: **Housing and slums** — informal settlements lacking tenure and services
**Water and sanitation** — scarcity alongside flooding from encroached drains and lakes
**Transport and pollution** — congestion, air pollution, road accidents
**Waste** — overflowing landfills, poor segregation
**Climate risks** — heat islands, floods, cyclones in coastal cities
**Governance** — weak municipal finances and limited devolution of the 18 functions in the Twelfth Schedule
**Social** — isolation, crime, informal labour without social security

notes.p:
Strengthen **urban local bodies** with funds, functions and functionaries; reform property tax and use municipal bonds; adopt **integrated land-use and transport planning**; expand public transport and walking/cycling infrastructure; promote **affordable rental housing** and in-situ slum upgrading; restore lakes and drains; adopt waste segregation and decentralised processing; develop smaller towns to reduce pressure on metros.

Schemes such as Smart Cities, AMRUT, PMAY-Urban and Swachh Bharat (Urban) address parts of this agenda; evaluate them by outcomes, not announcements.

Peri-urban areas deserve special mention: villages on city edges urbanise without planning, so they get the problems of cities (traffic, waste, land speculation) without urban services. Bringing them under planning authorities early is cheaper than retrofitting later.
Globalisation intensified after the **1991 reforms**: more trade, investment, migration, technology and media flows. Social effects are mixed:
points: **Positive:** jobs in IT/ITES and services, a larger middle class, exposure to global ideas, women's employment in some sectors, diaspora links and remittances
**Negative:** job insecurity and informalisation, pressure on farmers and artisans facing global competition, rising inequality, consumerism and debt
**Culture:** both homogenisation (global brands, English) and **revival/hybridity** (regional cinema, yoga going global, glocal products)
**Family:** nuclearisation, migration of the young, elderly left behind
**Identity:** in reaction, some assertion of local and religious identities

notes.p:
Question type: "Effects of globalisation on Indian women."
**Positive:** employment in IT, BPOs, garment exports; exposure to rights discourse; global networks for women's movements.
**Negative:** low-wage, insecure jobs in export sectors; double burden of paid and unpaid work; commodification in media.
**Uneven:** urban educated women gain more than rural women.
**Conclusion:** policies on skills, safety and social security decide whether globalisation empowers.
Key points.
points: ~31% urban (Census 2011); census vs statutory towns
Problems: housing, water, transport, waste, climate, weak ULBs
74th Amendment; Twelfth Schedule: 18 functions
Schemes: Smart Cities, AMRUT, PMAY-U, SBM-U
Globalisation post-1991: jobs, consumerism, inequality
Glocalisation shows adaptation, not just Westernisation

chapters.title: Social Empowerment: Caste, Tribe, Disability & Gender Minorities

cards.title: Meaning
cards.body: **Social empowerment** means enabling disadvantaged groups to gain dignity, voice, resources and control over their lives — through rights, representation, education, livelihoods and changing social attitudes.

cards.title: Constitutional toolkit
points: Art 15(4), 16(4): special provisions and reservation
Art 17: abolition of untouchability
Art 46: promote educational and economic interests of SCs/STs
Art 330, 332: reserved seats in legislatures
Art 338, 338A, 338B: National Commissions for SCs, STs, Backward Classes

cards.title: Key laws
points: Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955
SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
PESA, 1996 and Forest Rights Act, 2006
Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019

cards.title: Landmark judgments
points: **Indra Sawhney (1992)**: OBC reservation upheld; 50% ceiling; creamy layer
**NALSA (2014)**: transgender persons as "third gender"
**Janhit Abhiyan (2022)**: EWS quota upheld

cards.title: Beyond reservation
cards.body: Empowerment also needs quality schooling, skills, credit (Stand-Up India), land and forest rights, protection from violence, and representation in leadership — plus social reform that changes attitudes.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use the triad **rights – resources – representation** to structure empowerment answers, and end with attitudinal change through education and fraternity.

cards.q: Which Article abolishes untouchability?
cards.explain: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice.

cards.q: The NALSA judgment (2014) is associated with:
options: Recognition of transgender persons as third gender
cards.explain: NALSA v Union of India recognised transgender persons' rights and identity.

notes.p:
Social empowerment is the process by which marginalised groups — **Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, OBCs, minorities, persons with disabilities, transgender persons, the elderly and women** — gain the capacity to make choices and act on them. It operates at three levels: **individual** (education, confidence, income), **collective** (organisations, movements) and **structural** (laws, institutions, social norms).

The Constitution's vision of "justice, social, economic and political" and Ambedkar's emphasis on **social democracy** are the foundation.

Tools include Article 17, reservations in education, jobs and legislatures, the **Protection of Civil Rights Act (1955)** and the **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (1989)**, post-matric scholarships and the **National Commission for Scheduled Castes** (Article 338). Challenges: atrocities, manual scavenging (prohibited by the 2013 Act yet persisting), discrimination in housing and private jobs, and uneven benefits within groups. Debates include **sub-classification** within SC quotas — the Supreme Court in 2024 allowed states to sub-classify; check the latest position.

Protections include the **Fifth and Sixth Schedules**, **PESA (1996)** extending self-rule to Fifth Schedule areas, the **Forest Rights Act (2006)** recognising individual and community forest rights, and the **National Commission for STs** (Article 338A). Challenges: land alienation, displacement by dams and mines, poor health and education outcomes, and loss of language and culture. Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (**PVTGs**) need special focus; PM-JANMAN targets them.

notes.h: Persons with disabilities and transgender persons
notes.p:
The **Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016** expanded recognised disabilities to 21, provided reservation in government jobs and higher education, and mandated accessibility — aligned with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The **Accessible India Campaign** targets barrier-free buildings, transport and websites.

For transgender persons, the **NALSA judgment (2014)** affirmed self-identification and rights; the **Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019** prohibits discrimination, though activists criticise its certification process. The **Navtej Singh Johar (2018)** judgment decriminalised consensual same-sex relations.

**OBCs:** Mandal Commission recommendations, 27% central reservation upheld in **Indra Sawhney (1992)** with a creamy-layer exclusion; constitutional status for the National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B, 102nd Amendment). **EWS:** 10% reservation via the **103rd Amendment (2019)**, upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022). **Minorities:** Articles 29–30 protect cultural and educational rights; the **Sachar Committee (2006)** documented Muslim socio-economic backwardness. **Elderly:** Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007.

Question type: "Reservation alone cannot ensure social empowerment. Comment."
**Intro:** reservation's role in representation (examples: SC/ST legislators, officers).
**Limits:** benefits captured by better-off sections; private sector and informal jobs uncovered; quality of school education; social prejudice persists.
**Complements:** foundational learning, skills, credit, land and forest rights, strict enforcement of atrocity laws, social audit.
**Conclusion:** reservation is necessary but not sufficient; fraternity completes justice.
Key points.
points: Empowerment = rights + resources + representation + attitudes
STs: Fifth/Sixth Schedules, PESA 1996, FRA 2006, PVTGs
RPwD Act 2016: 21 disabilities
NALSA 2014; Transgender Act 2019; Navtej Johar 2018
Indra Sawhney 1992; 103rd Amendment EWS (2019)

cards.title: Communalism
cards.body: An ideology that treats a religious community as a **political unit** with interests opposed to other communities. It differs from religiosity; one can be deeply religious without being communal.

cards.title: Bipan Chandra's three stages
points: **Communal nationalism**: interests of a religious group are distinct
**Liberal communalism**: interests of different communities are different
**Extreme communalism**: interests are antagonistic and hostile

cards.title: Regionalism
cards.body: Loyalty to a region based on language, culture, economy or history. It can be **positive** (demand for development, cultural pride, federal bargaining) or **negative** (sons-of-the-soil hostility to migrants, secessionism).

cards.title: Indian vs Western secularism
points: Western (French *laïcité*): strict separation of religion and state
Indian: **equal respect** for all religions; state may intervene for reform (e.g. temple entry)
Rajeev Bhargava: **principled distance**
"Secular" added to Preamble by 42nd Amendment (1976)
S.R. Bommai (1994): secularism is part of the **basic structure**

cards.title: Drivers of communalism
points: Colonial **divide and rule**, separate electorates (1909)
Vote-bank politics
Economic competition and rumours
Misinformation on social media
Historical grievances revived

cards.title: Linguistic reorganisation as positive regionalism
cards.body: The States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali) led to the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956**. Fears that language-based states would weaken unity proved largely unfounded; they deepened democracy and administrative ease.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Present communalism and regionalism with causes, consequences and a balanced remedy set: law and order, fast justice, education, inter-community dialogue, responsible media, and development that is regionally balanced.

cards.q: Which case held secularism to be part of the basic structure?
cards.explain: S.R. Bommai v Union of India (1994) affirmed secularism as basic structure.

cards.q: "Principled distance" as a description of Indian secularism is associated with:
cards.explain: Political theorist Rajeev Bhargava used this term.

cards.q: The States Reorganisation Act was passed in:
cards.explain: It reorganised states mainly on linguistic lines in 1956.

notes.p:
Communalism is the belief that people who follow the same religion have common secular interests — political, economic, social — that are different from, and possibly opposed to, those of other religious communities. Historian **Bipan Chandra** described its progression from communal nationalism to liberal and then extreme communalism.

In India it grew under colonial rule: census categories, **separate electorates** (Morley-Minto Reforms, 1909), and political mobilisation along religious lines culminated in **Partition**. After independence, riots and tensions have recurred, often linked to electoral mobilisation, rumours and local economic rivalry.

Consequences: loss of life and property, ghettoisation, erosion of trust, economic damage, radicalisation and threats to internal security.

Remedies:
points: Impartial, prompt policing and justice; accountability for riot violence
Political parties refraining from religious mobilisation; Model Code and RPA provisions enforced
Education promoting scientific temper and fraternity (Article 51A)
Inter-community peace committees and civil society dialogue
Countering misinformation; responsible media
Inclusive development reducing competition-driven tensions

notes.p:
Regionalism arises from linguistic identity, uneven development, historical memory and perceived neglect by the Centre. Forms include **demands for separate states** (Telangana created in 2014), **inter-state disputes** over river water and borders, **sons-of-the-soil** movements against migrants, and in extreme cases **secessionism**.

It is not always negative: regional parties and movements have strengthened **federalism**, pushed for development and protected cultural identity. The key is whether regional assertion seeks a better place within the Union or rejects the Union. Remedies: balanced regional development, fiscal federalism, cultural recognition, and dialogue through bodies like Inter-State Councils and Zonal Councils.

The Constitution did not originally use the word "secular", but its provisions were secular: **Articles 25–28** (freedom of religion), **Articles 29–30** (minority rights), Article 15 (non-discrimination) and Article 325 (no separate electorates). The **42nd Amendment (1976)** added the word to the Preamble, and **S.R. Bommai (1994)** declared secularism part of the basic structure.

Indian secularism differs from the Western separation model: the state maintains **equal respect** (sarva dharma sambhava) and **principled distance**, intervening to reform practices that violate rights (abolishing untouchability, temple-entry laws, ending instant triple talaq) while supporting religious minorities' institutions.

Debates include the **Uniform Civil Code** (Article 44, a DPSP), state management of temples, religious conversions, the role of religion in elections (Section 123(3) of the RPA treats appeals on grounds of religion as a corrupt practice) and majoritarian or minority communalism. Balanced answers should defend constitutional values while acknowledging the complexity of reform within religious communities.

Question type: "Distinguish between communalism and regionalism, and suggest measures to counter their negative forms."
**Define both** with one example each.
**Similarity:** both are identity-based and can be politically mobilised.
**Differences:** basis (religion vs region/language); regionalism can be positive federal assertion, communalism is by definition divisive.
**Measures:** law and justice, inclusive development, education, media responsibility, federal dialogue.
**Conclusion:** fraternity as the binding value.
Key points.
points: Communalism: religious community as political unit (Bipan Chandra's 3 stages)
Separate electorates 1909 deepened communal politics
Regionalism can be positive or negative; Telangana 2014
SRC → States Reorganisation Act 1956
Indian secularism: equal respect, principled distance
42nd Amendment added "Secular"; S.R. Bommai 1994
RPA Sec 123(3): religious appeals are corrupt practice

cards.title: The policy cycle
points: Agenda setting
Formulation (options, consultation)
Adoption (law, scheme, budget)
**Implementation**
Monitoring and **evaluation**
Feedback and redesign

cards.title: Design problems
points: One-size-fits-all schemes
Poor targeting: **inclusion and exclusion errors**
Unrealistic timelines and targets
Too many overlapping schemes
Little consultation with users or states

cards.title: Implementation problems
points: Capacity gaps at district and block level
Delays in fund flow
Leakages and corruption
Weak convergence across departments
Output focus instead of outcomes
Poor data and grievance redress

cards.title: Tools that help
points: **DBT** using the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile)
**Social audit** (mandatory under MGNREGA)
**Outcome budgeting**; DMEO evaluations
**Aspirational Districts Programme** (2018): ranking on indicators
PRAGATI reviews; dashboards
Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy (2014)

cards.title: Behavioural design
cards.body: Swachh Bharat combined toilets with **behaviour change** campaigns and community recognition. Policy works better when it accounts for social norms, not only infrastructure — an idea from **behavioural economics** ("nudges").

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In "issues in design and implementation" questions, separate design flaws from delivery flaws, give a scheme example for each, and end with outcome-focused monitoring and community participation.

cards.q: Inclusion error in welfare targeting means:
cards.explain: Inclusion error = ineligible beneficiaries included; exclusion error = eligible people left out.

cards.q: Social audit is a statutory requirement under:
cards.explain: Section 17 of MGNREGA mandates social audits by the Gram Sabha.

notes.p:
GS II asks about "government policies and interventions for development in various sectors and **issues arising out of their design and implementation**". Questions take a scheme or sector and ask what went right, what went wrong and how to improve. Mastering a **framework** lets you handle any scheme.

The second half of the syllabus line — "issues arising out of their design and implementation" — is the core. Examiners want you to diagnose *why* outcomes fall short and suggest specific, realistic fixes, not to list scheme features. Keep a short note on 10–15 flagship schemes with their objective, design feature, one achievement, one problem and one reform.

Public policy moves through stages: **agenda setting** (a problem gains attention through data, media, courts or movements), **formulation** (options studied by ministries, NITI Aayog, committees), **adoption** (a law, scheme or budget provision), **implementation** (by ministries, states, local bodies and frontline workers), **evaluation** (audits, surveys, independent studies) and **feedback**. In India, many central schemes are **Centrally Sponsored Schemes** implemented by states with shared funding, so Centre–state coordination is vital.
Common design weaknesses:
points: **Uniform templates** that ignore regional diversity
**Targeting errors** from outdated or incomplete beneficiary lists
**Fragmentation** — many small schemes with overlapping aims
**Input-based** goals (money spent, structures built) rather than outcomes
**Limited consultation** with beneficiaries, states and experts
**Unfunded mandates** passed to states and local bodies

notes.p:
Even good designs falter in delivery: **capacity gaps** (vacancies, training), **fund flow delays** through multiple layers, **leakages** and middlemen, **poor convergence** between departments (nutrition needs health, water, sanitation and women's welfare to work together), **weak monitoring**, and limited **grievance redress**. Frontline workers — ASHAs, anganwadi workers, teachers, patwaris — are overburdened but central to success.

The **Second Administrative Reforms Commission** and many evaluation studies stress that implementation fails most often at the **interface between departments** and at the **last mile**, where discretion, documentation demands and lack of information shut out the poorest.

Take **MGNREGA** as an illustration.
**Design strengths:** demand-driven legal guarantee, wage payment through bank accounts, social audit, Gram Sabha planning.
**Implementation issues:** delays in wage payment, uneven demand across states, quality of assets, administrative capacity.
**Improvements tried:** DBT, geo-tagging of assets, electronic muster rolls.
**Way forward:** timely funds, convergence with agriculture and water schemes, stronger social audits.

The same template — design, delivery, data, redress — can be applied to PMAY, Jal Jeevan Mission or PM-KISAN.

Reforms that work across sectors: **DBT** to cut leakages; **outcome budgeting** and third-party evaluation (NITI Aayog's DMEO); **real-time dashboards**; **Aspirational Districts** style competition and convergence; **social audits** and community monitoring; **capacity building** (Mission Karmayogi); **rationalising** schemes; giving states flexibility through untied funds; and **behavioural insights** to change habits. Data protection and inclusion safeguards must accompany digital delivery so that the poorest are not excluded by technology failures.
Key points.
points: Policy cycle: agenda → formulation → adoption → implementation → evaluation
Design flaws: uniformity, targeting errors, fragmentation, input focus
Delivery flaws: capacity, funds, leakages, convergence, redress
Tools: DBT/JAM, social audit, outcome budget, DMEO, Aspirational Districts
MGNREGA as a template for evaluation
Behavioural nudges and community participation

chapters.title: Development Processes: NGOs, SHGs & Civil Society

cards.title: The development "industry"
cards.body: Beyond government, development involves **NGOs, self-help groups, cooperatives, donors, charities, CSR, community organisations and institutional stakeholders**. GS II asks about their role, effectiveness and regulation.

cards.title: NGO legal forms
points: **Trust** (public charitable trust under state laws)
**Society** (Societies Registration Act, 1860)
**Section 8 company** (Companies Act, 2013)
Foreign funds regulated by **FCRA, 2010** (amended 2020)
NGO-DARPAN portal for registration with government

cards.title: Self-Help Groups
points: Small groups (often 10–20 women) saving and lending together
**SHG–Bank Linkage Programme** led by NABARD (from 1992)
**DAY-NRLM** (2011) scales SHGs nationally
Kerala's **Kudumbashree**: a widely studied model

cards.title: Corporate Social Responsibility
cards.body: Under **Section 135** of the Companies Act, 2013, qualifying companies must spend at least **2% of average net profit** of the preceding three years on CSR activities listed in Schedule VII.

cards.title: Concerns
points: Accountability and transparency of NGOs
Dependence on donor priorities
Misuse of foreign funds; FCRA compliance
SHG debt stress where livelihood links are weak
Government–NGO trust deficit

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Show NGOs and SHGs as partners of the state — reaching the last mile, innovating and voicing the poor — while noting the need for accountability. Use one example each: Kudumbashree, SEWA, Pratham, Akshaya Patra.

cards.q: The SHG–Bank Linkage Programme was pioneered by:
cards.explain: NABARD launched it in 1992.

cards.q: Under the Companies Act, 2013, CSR spending for qualifying companies is at least:
options: 2% of average net profit of the last three years
cards.explain: Section 135 sets 2% of average net profit of the three preceding years.

notes.p: The syllabus mentions "the role of **NGOs, SHGs, various groups and associations, donors, charities, institutional and other stakeholders**". Development is no longer the state's job alone: civil society organisations deliver services, innovate, mobilise communities, monitor government and advocate rights. Market actors contribute through CSR and social enterprises, and international donors fund programmes.

NGOs work in service delivery (education, health), rights advocacy (RTI movement by MKSS), research and policy, disaster relief and environmental protection. Examples: **Pratham** (learning assessments through ASER reports), **SEWA** (women workers), **Akshaya Patra** (mid-day meals partnership), **Goonj** (resource redistribution), and many local groups.

Strengths: flexibility, local knowledge, trust of communities, innovation. Weaknesses: uneven quality, limited scale, dependence on funding, governance lapses in some organisations, and occasional political or foreign-influence concerns.

NGOs register as trusts, societies or Section 8 companies, and seek tax exemptions under the Income Tax Act. Foreign contributions are regulated by the **Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010**, amended in **2020** to bar sub-granting to other organisations, cap administrative expenses at 20%, and require receipt in a designated SBI account in New Delhi. Supporters say this improves accountability; critics say it burdens small NGOs. A transparent, risk-based regulation with clear timelines is the balanced view.

**SHGs** are small, homogeneous groups, mostly of women, who save regularly, lend internally and access bank credit as a group. NABARD's **SHG–Bank Linkage Programme** (1992) and the **Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana–National Rural Livelihoods Mission** (2011) have made India's SHG movement one of the world's largest. Impacts: financial inclusion, women's agency and leadership, social capital. Challenges: graduation from credit to sustainable enterprise, market links, regional imbalance, and over-indebtedness.

**Cooperatives** (Part IXB, inserted by the 97th Amendment, 2011 — later read down for state cooperatives by the Supreme Court in 2021) and the new **Ministry of Cooperation (2021)** form another pillar; Amul is the iconic example.

**CSR** under Section 135 has channelled large funds into education, health and rural development, though spending is concentrated in a few states and sectors. Philanthropic foundations and international donors (multilateral banks, UN agencies, bilateral donors) fund programmes and research. Effective partnership requires aligning with government priorities, measuring outcomes and avoiding duplication.

Question type: "SHGs have transformed rural women's lives but face limits. Discuss."
**Achievements:** savings habit, credit access, leadership in panchayats, collective action on social issues (Kudumbashree, Jeevika in Bihar).
**Limits:** low-income micro-enterprises, poor market access, debt stress, elite capture.
**Way forward:** producer groups and federations, digital and market linkages, skill training, convergence with MGNREGA and agriculture schemes.
**Conclusion:** from savings groups to enterprise collectives.
Key points.
points: Stakeholders: NGOs, SHGs, cooperatives, donors, CSR, communities
NGO forms: trust, society (1860 Act), Section 8 company
FCRA 2010; 2020 amendment: no sub-granting, 20% admin cap
SHG–Bank Linkage (NABARD, 1992); DAY-NRLM (2011)
CSR: Section 135, 2% of average net profit
97th Amendment (2011) cooperatives; Ministry of Cooperation (2021)

NCPCR as statutory protector

**RPwD Act, 2016**; Accessible India Campaign

cards.title: Evaluating a mechanism
cards.body: NCPCR can inquire into child rights violations and recommend action but has no power to enforce. Strength: visibility and monitoring. Weakness: recommendatory nature, vacancies at state level. Reform: time-bound action-taken reports and adequate staff.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use the structure: constitutional basis → laws → schemes → institutions → performance gaps → reforms. Mention data sources generically ("NFHS", "NCRB reports") rather than quoting uncertain numbers.

cards.q: The POCSO Act, enacted in 2012, deals with:
cards.explain: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012.

cards.q: Which body is a constitutional (not statutory) commission?
cards.explain: NCSC is under Article 338; the others are statutory.

cards.q: The e-Shram portal is meant for:
cards.explain: It builds a national database of unorganised workers for welfare delivery.

notes.p: GS II: "**Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections** of the population by the Centre and States and the **performance** of these schemes; **mechanisms, laws, institutions and bodies** constituted for the protection and betterment of these vulnerable sections." Expect questions on a group (children, elderly, disabled, tribals), a law, or an institution's effectiveness.

The Preamble promises justice, equality and dignity. Key provisions: Articles 14–17 (equality, non-discrimination, abolition of untouchability), 21 and 21A (life with dignity, education), 23–24 (against trafficking and child labour), 39(e)–(f) (protection of children and workers), 41 (public assistance in old age, sickness and disablement), 46 (weaker sections), and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for tribal areas.
Highlights:
points: **SC/ST:** PoA Act (1989), scholarships, Stand-Up India, Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers Act (2013)
**Tribals:** FRA (2006), PESA (1996), Eklavya Model Residential Schools, PM-JANMAN for PVTGs
**Children:** RTE (2009), POCSO (2012), JJ Act (2015), Mission Vatsalya, Poshan 2.0, PM POSHAN
**Elderly:** 2007 Act, NSAP pensions, health cover under PM-JAY for older persons (check current eligibility)
**Disabled:** RPwD Act (2016), Accessible India, UDID cards
**Transgender persons:** 2019 Act, SMILE scheme
**Workers:** e-Shram, PM-SYM, Labour Codes, One Nation One Ration Card

notes.p:
Achievements include near-universal school enrolment, expanded social pensions and wider health coverage. Gaps commonly noted: **low awareness** among beneficiaries, **exclusion** due to documentation and digital failures, small pension amounts, **delays** in scholarships, weak enforcement of protective laws (low conviction rates under some Acts — see NCRB reports), poor accessibility of public infrastructure, and **fragmented** schemes.

Institutions such as NCSC, NCST, NCW, NCPCR and NHRC often lack enforcement powers, face vacancies and see their recommendations ignored.

Universal registries (e-Shram) linked to benefits; **proactive, automatic enrolment** rather than application-based; **grievance redress** with timelines; **social audits**; adequate funding and staff for commissions with mandatory action-taken reports; **convergence** at district level; gender and disability budgeting; and community-based monitoring by SHGs and panchayats.

A rights-based approach — treating welfare as an entitlement with legal backing, as with the National Food Security Act or RTE — tends to improve accountability compared with discretionary schemes, though it needs budget support to be meaningful.

Question type: "Examine the effectiveness of laws for the protection of children in India."
**Laws:** RTE, POCSO, JJ Act, Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act as amended in 2016, Prohibition of Child Marriage Act (2006).
**Gains:** enrolment, child-friendly procedures under POCSO, special courts.
**Gaps:** pendency in special courts, under-reporting, weak child welfare committees, learning gaps.
**Reforms:** fast-track courts, trained staff, awareness, school safety audits.
**Conclusion:** law plus capacity plus community vigilance.
Key points.
points: Groups: SC/ST, women, children, elderly, PwD, minorities, transgender, workers
Children: RTE 2009, POCSO 2012, JJ 2015
Elderly: 2007 Act; NSAP pensions
PwD: RPwD 2016; Accessible India

cards.title: Pillars of good governance
points: **Transparency**: information is open
**Accountability**: answerability + consequences
Responsiveness and rule of law
Participation, equity, efficiency

cards.title: RTI Act, 2005
points: Reply within **30 days**; **48 hours** if life or liberty is involved
**Section 4**: proactive disclosure
**Section 8**: exemptions (security, privacy, etc.)
Central and State Information Commissions hear appeals
2019 amendment: Centre sets tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners

cards.title: Citizens' Charter
cards.body: A public statement by an organisation of its **services, standards, timelines and grievance redress**. Introduced in India in 1997, inspired by the UK (1991). The 2nd ARC recommended the **Sevottam** model for service-delivery excellence. Many states have **Right to Services** Acts that make timelines legally binding.

cards.title: Other accountability tools
points: **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**
Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014
Social audit; CAG audits
CPGRAMS grievance portal
Citizen report cards

cards.title: E-governance landmarks
points: National e-Governance Plan (2006)
**Digital India** (2015)
Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker, UMANG
**GeM** (2016): public procurement
State pioneers: **Bhoomi** (Karnataka land records), **Akshaya** (Kerala)

cards.title: E-governance models
points: **G2C**: government to citizen (certificates, DBT)
**G2B**: government to business (GST, MCA21)
**G2G**: between agencies (e-Office)
**G2E**: government to employees

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Pair every e-governance benefit with a risk: speed vs digital divide, data use vs privacy, automation vs exclusion errors. Mention the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 as the privacy framework.

cards.q: Under the RTI Act, information concerning life or liberty must be supplied within:
cards.explain: Section 7(1) provides 48 hours for life or liberty matters.

cards.q: The "Sevottam" model relates to:
options: Service delivery excellence and citizens' charters
cards.explain: Recommended by the 2nd ARC for citizen-centric administration.

cards.q: Bhoomi, an early e-governance success, computerised:
cards.explain: Bhoomi digitised land records (RTCs) in Karnataka.

notes.p: GS II asks about "important aspects of governance, **transparency and accountability, e-governance** — applications, models, successes, limitations and potential; **citizens' charters**, transparency and accountability and institutional and other measures". Good governance requires that citizens can **see** what government does (transparency), **question** it (answerability) and ensure **consequences** for failure or misconduct (enforcement).

The **RTI Act, 2005**, born from grassroots campaigns such as MKSS in Rajasthan, gives citizens the right to request information from public authorities. Public Information Officers must reply within 30 days (48 hours for life or liberty). **Section 4** requires proactive disclosure. **Section 8** lists exemptions such as national security, cabinet papers (until decisions are taken) and personal information. Appeals lie to the first appellate authority and then to the **Information Commissions**.

Issues: pendency and vacancies in commissions, weak proactive disclosure, attacks on RTI activists, the **2019 amendment** giving the Centre power over commissioners' tenure and pay, and the **DPDP Act, 2023** amending Section 8(1)(j) on personal information, which critics say narrows access.

A **Citizens' Charter** lists services, standards, time limits and grievance redress. India began them in 1997, but many charters became formalities — prepared without consultation, unknown to citizens and lacking remedies. The **Second ARC** recommended the **Sevottam** framework: charter, grievance redress and service-delivery capability. **Right to Public Services** laws in many states (Madhya Pradesh was among the first in 2010) make timelines legally enforceable with penalties on officials.

Accountability architecture includes the **CAG**, Parliament's **Public Accounts Committee**, the **CVC**, **Lokpal and Lokayuktas** (2013 Act), the **Whistle Blowers Protection Act (2014)**, **social audits** (MGNREGA), **CPGRAMS** for grievances, and judicial review. Civil society tools: citizen report cards (pioneered by the Public Affairs Centre, Bengaluru), community score cards and participatory budgeting.

E-governance uses ICT to deliver services, improve efficiency and increase transparency. Successes: **DBT** reducing leakages, **UPI** and digital public infrastructure, **DigiLocker**, **GeM** for transparent procurement, **e-Courts**, online land records, **CoWIN**-style platforms, and state initiatives like Bhoomi and Akshaya.

Limitations: the **digital divide** (rural, elderly, women, disabled), connectivity gaps, authentication failures causing exclusion, **cybersecurity** and **privacy** risks, lack of interoperability, and the need for process re-engineering rather than mere digitisation. Potential: AI for grievance analysis, open data, vernacular interfaces and assisted access through Common Service Centres.

Question type: "E-governance is not just about technology but about re-engineering governance. Discuss."
**Intro:** definition and models (G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E).
**Body:** examples where process change mattered (GeM, Bhoomi); failures where only forms went online.
**Issues:** digital divide, privacy, capacity.
**Way forward:** process re-engineering, assisted digital access, DPDP compliance, cyber hygiene, citizen feedback.
**Conclusion:** e-governance as a means to good governance.
Key points.
points: RTI: 30 days / 48 hours; Sec 4 proactive; Sec 8 exemptions
2019 RTI amendment; DPDP Act 2023
Citizens' Charter 1997; Sevottam (2nd ARC); Right to Services Acts
Lokpal 2013; Whistle Blowers 2014; CPGRAMS; social audit
NeGP 2006; Digital India 2015; GeM 2016
Models: G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E
Limits: digital divide, privacy, exclusion

cards.title: The "steel frame"
cards.body: **Sardar Patel** defended the All India Services as the "steel frame" holding the Union together, giving administrative continuity and national integration. **Article 312** allows Parliament to create All India Services; **Article 311** protects civil servants from arbitrary dismissal.

Link between citizens and the state
