points: Hierarchy and rules
Impersonality and merit-based recruitment
Specialisation and records
Strengths: predictability, fairness
Weaknesses: red tape, rigidity, status quo

cards.title: Key challenges
points: Politicisation and frequent **transfers**
Generalist vs specialist debate
Resistance to change; risk aversion
Corruption and weak accountability
Outdated performance appraisal

cards.title: Reforms
points: **Mission Karmayogi** (2020): competency-based capacity building
**Lateral entry** of domain experts
**Civil Services Boards** and minimum tenure (T.S.R. Subramanian case, 2013)
Outcome-based appraisal; 360° feedback
2nd ARC 10th report on personnel administration

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Present civil servants as neutral, committed public servants: neutral to political parties but committed to constitutional values and citizens' welfare.

cards.q: Which Article empowers Parliament to create new All India Services?
cards.explain: Article 312, on a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds majority.

cards.q: Mission Karmayogi is related to:
cards.explain: It is the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building (2020).

notes.p: In a parliamentary democracy, elected ministers decide policy while **permanent civil servants** advise and implement. The Constitution provides for recruitment by UPSC and State PSCs (Articles 315–323), protection against arbitrary dismissal (**Article 311**), the doctrine of pleasure (**Article 310**) and creation of All India Services (**Article 312**). The IAS, IPS and IFoS serve both the Union and states, supporting cooperative federalism.
Civil servants:
points: Provide **expert, neutral advice** to ministers, including unwelcome facts
**Implement** laws and programmes down to the village
Maintain **law and order** and regulate economic activity
Manage **crises** — disasters, pandemics, elections
Ensure **continuity** when governments change
Act as **custodians of constitutional values**: rule of law, equality, fairness
Facilitate **citizen participation** and grievance redress

notes.p:
Civil servants must be **politically neutral** — serving any elected government with equal loyalty — yet **committed to constitutional values** and public welfare. The 1970s debate on a "committed bureaucracy" raised concerns about loyalty to a party rather than the Constitution. The **All India Services (Conduct) Rules** and the Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules lay down expectations of integrity, impartiality and political neutrality.

In practice, neutrality means giving frank advice in writing, implementing lawful decisions faithfully even when one disagreed, refusing unlawful orders, and treating every citizen equally regardless of their politics. **National Civil Services Day** (21 April) marks Patel's 1947 address to probationers, where he urged officers to speak their minds fearlessly.

Frequent **transfers** used as punishment; **political interference**; risk aversion due to fear of investigation; **generalist** officers handling complex technical sectors; outdated appraisal systems; corruption; and a culture of procedure over outcomes. In **T.S.R. Subramanian v Union of India (2013)**, the Supreme Court directed **Civil Services Boards** for transfers and postings, minimum tenure, and recording of oral instructions in writing.

The **Second Administrative Reforms Commission** (10th report, "Refurbishing of Personnel Administration") suggested mid-career reviews, domain specialisation, performance agreements and a Civil Services law. Current initiatives: **Mission Karmayogi** (iGOT platform for continuous learning), **lateral entry** at senior levels, **e-Office** and digital workflows, **360° appraisal**, and Aspirational Districts as a model of outcome-based administration. Police reform directions from **Prakash Singh (2006)** — fixed tenure, separation of investigation from law and order, Police Establishment Boards — remain partially implemented.

Question type: "Is the civil service still a steel frame or has it become a steel cage?"
**Steel frame:** national unity, disaster response, elections, continuity.
**Steel cage:** red tape, rigidity, risk aversion, colonial mindset.
**Reforms:** Karmayogi, lateral entry, tenure protection, outcome-based appraisal, citizen-centric culture.
**Conclusion:** from rule-bound administration to responsive governance.
Key points.
points: Art 310 (pleasure), 311 (protection), 312 (AIS), 315–323 (PSCs)
Patel: "steel frame"
Roles: advice, implementation, regulation, crisis, continuity
Neutral to parties, committed to Constitution
T.S.R. Subramanian 2013: Civil Services Boards, fixed tenure
Mission Karmayogi 2020; lateral entry; 2nd ARC 10th report
Prakash Singh 2006 on police reform

cards.title: Hazard vs disaster
cards.body: A **hazard** is a potentially damaging event (earthquake, flood). It becomes a **disaster** when it overwhelms a community's capacity to cope. Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability ÷ Capacity (a common conceptual formula).

cards.title: Disaster Management Act, 2005
points: **NDMA** chaired by the Prime Minister
**SDMA** chaired by the Chief Minister
**DDMA** chaired by the District Collector/Magistrate
**NDRF** for specialised response
**NIDM** for training and research
Act amended in 2025 — check new provisions

cards.title: Disaster management cycle
points: **Prevention and mitigation** (before)
**Preparedness** (early warning, drills)
**Response** (rescue, relief)
**Recovery**: rehabilitation and reconstruction — "Build Back Better"

cards.title: Sendai Framework (2015–2030)
points: Four priorities: understand risk; strengthen risk governance; invest in resilience; enhance preparedness and Build Back Better
Seven global targets (reduce deaths, affected people, losses; increase early warning, etc.)
India's National Disaster Management Plan (2016, revised 2019) is aligned with Sendai

cards.title: Odisha's cyclone story
cards.body: After the 1999 super cyclone, Odisha built cyclone shelters, set up the Odisha State Disaster Management Authority and a rapid-action force, and trained communities. With accurate IMD forecasts, mass evacuations during later cyclones (Phailin 2013, Fani 2019) kept deaths far lower — a model of preparedness.

cards.title: Funding and global initiatives
points: NDRF/SDRF (response funds) and NDMF/SDMF (mitigation funds)
**Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure** (CDRI), launched by India in 2019
Heat Action Plans (Ahmedabad pioneered in 2013)

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Write disaster answers along the cycle: before (mitigation, preparedness), during (response), after (recovery), plus institutions and community participation.

cards.q: Who chairs the National Disaster Management Authority?
cards.explain: The PM is the ex officio chairperson of NDMA.

cards.q: The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction covers the period:
cards.explain: It succeeded the Hyogo Framework (2005–2015).

notes.p: A **hazard** becomes a **disaster** when exposure and vulnerability meet limited capacity. Disaster management shifted globally from a **relief-centric** approach to **disaster risk reduction (DRR)** — reducing vulnerability before events occur. India is exposed to floods, cyclones, droughts, earthquakes, landslides, heatwaves, tsunamis and industrial accidents, and urbanisation and climate change are increasing risks.

The **Disaster Management Act, 2005** (enacted after the 2004 tsunami) created a three-tier structure: **NDMA** (PM-chaired, lays down policy and guidelines), **SDMAs** (CM-chaired) and **DDMAs** (district collector-chaired, with elected representatives). The **National Executive Committee** coordinates at the Centre. The **NDRF** is a specialised force drawn from central armed police forces; states have **SDRFs**. **NIDM** handles training and research. The Act was **amended in 2025**, including provisions on urban disaster management and disaster databases — check details.

Plans: **National Policy on Disaster Management (2009)**, the **National Disaster Management Plan (2016, revised 2019)**, and state and district plans. Finance Commissions fund response and mitigation through national and state funds.

**Mitigation:** structural (embankments, cyclone shelters, earthquake-resistant buildings) and non-structural (land-use zoning, building codes, insurance, awareness).
**Preparedness:** early warning systems (IMD for cyclones and heat, **INCOIS** for tsunamis, **CWC** for floods), evacuation plans, mock drills, stockpiles.
**Response:** search and rescue, medical care, relief camps, communication.
**Recovery:** rehabilitation, reconstruction and livelihood restoration using **Build Back Better** principles.

The **Hyogo Framework (2005–2015)** was followed by the **Sendai Framework (2015–2030)**, with four priorities and seven targets. Related agendas include the SDGs and the Paris Agreement. India hosted the Asian Ministerial Conference on DRR in 2016, where the Prime Minister announced a **ten-point agenda** on DRR, and launched the **Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure** in 2019. India also offers humanitarian assistance and disaster relief abroad (for example after earthquakes in Nepal and Türkiye).

Challenges: weak enforcement of building codes; unplanned urban growth in floodplains; inadequate urban drainage; limited local capacity; slow post-disaster recovery; poor data on losses; and new risks such as **heatwaves**, **glacial lake outburst floods** and **urban floods**.

Way forward: risk-informed development planning, community-based DRR, heat action plans, impact-based forecasting, multi-hazard early warning, disaster insurance, resilient infrastructure, school and hospital safety, and integrating DRR with climate adaptation.

Question type: "Urban flooding is a man-made disaster. Discuss."
**Causes:** encroachment of lakes and drains, impervious surfaces, poor solid-waste management clogging drains, unplanned growth, extreme rainfall due to climate change.
**Examples:** recurrent city floods in Mumbai, Chennai and Bengaluru.
**Measures:** NDMA urban flood guidelines, sponge-city approaches, restoration of wetlands, early warning, drainage master plans.
**Conclusion:** governance failure turns rain into disaster.
Key points.
points: Hazard + vulnerability − capacity → disaster
DM Act 2005 (amended 2025): NDMA (PM), SDMA (CM), DDMA (Collector)
NDRF, SDRF, NIDM; NDMP 2016, revised 2019
Cycle: mitigation, preparedness, response, recovery
Sendai 2015–2030: 4 priorities, 7 targets
CDRI 2019; Odisha model; heat action plans

cards.title: Syllabus line
cards.body: "**Linkages between development and spread of extremism**." The classic case is **Left-Wing Extremism (LWE)** in central and eastern India; the logic also applies to other insurgencies.

cards.title: Origins
points: **Naxalbari** uprising, West Bengal (1967)
Splits and regrouping through the 1970s–90s
**CPI (Maoist)** formed in 2004 by merger of the People's War Group and MCC
Affected belt across parts of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, Maharashtra and neighbouring areas

cards.title: Development deficits that fuel extremism
points: Land alienation and displacement by projects
Denial of **forest rights**; exploitation by middlemen
Absence of roads, schools, health services
Weak governance and policing
Social exclusion of tribals and Dalits

cards.title: Government strategy
points: **National Policy and Action Plan (2015)**: security + development + rights and entitlements
**SAMADHAN** doctrine (2017)
Roads, mobile towers, bank branches in LWE areas
Aspirational Districts; Eklavya schools
Surrender and rehabilitation policies

cards.title: Trend
cards.body: LWE violence and the number of affected districts have declined substantially over the past decade. The government set **March 2026** as a target to end LWE; check the latest official status.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Never present LWE as only a law-and-order problem or only a development problem. Show the two-way link: development gaps feed extremism, and extremism blocks development (destroying roads, schools).

cards.q: CPI (Maoist) was formed in 2004 by the merger of:
cards.explain: People's War Group and Maoist Communist Centre of India merged.

cards.q: The Naxalbari uprising (1967) took place in:
cards.explain: Naxalbari is in Darjeeling district, West Bengal.

notes.p: Extremism refers to ideologies and movements that reject the constitutional order and use or advocate violence. The syllabus asks about its **linkage with development**: when development bypasses or harms communities — through displacement, exploitation and absence of services — grievances can be mobilised by extremist groups. Conversely, extremism obstructs development by attacking infrastructure and intimidating officials, creating a vicious cycle.

LWE began with the **Naxalbari** peasant uprising in 1967 led by Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal. After state crackdowns and splits, groups such as the People's War Group (Andhra Pradesh) and the Maoist Communist Centre (Bihar) grew. Their merger into the **CPI (Maoist)** in 2004 consolidated the movement, which the then Prime Minister (in 2006) described as the single biggest internal security challenge. The movement is concentrated in forested, mineral-rich, tribal-majority regions — the so-called "**Red Corridor**".
Root causes identified by expert groups (e.g. the Planning Commission's 2008 expert group on development challenges in extremist-affected areas):
points: **Land:** alienation of tribal land, non-implementation of land ceilings, displacement without adequate rehabilitation
**Forests:** historical denial of rights; harassment by forest officials (addressed by the Forest Rights Act, 2006)
**Livelihoods:** poverty, exploitative traders and contractors
**Governance:** absence of the state — no schools, clinics, roads; corruption
**Social:** exclusion and humiliation of tribals and Dalits
**Mining and industry:** benefits flowing outside while communities bear costs

notes.p: The **National Policy and Action Plan (2015)** combines security operations, development interventions and ensuring rights. Security: central armed police deployment, state special forces (Greyhounds of Andhra Pradesh as a model), intelligence-led operations, fortified police stations. **SAMADHAN** (2017) lists elements like smart leadership, aggressive strategy, motivation, actionable intelligence, dashboards, technology, action plans and **no access to financing**. Development: **Road Requirement Plans**, mobile connectivity, banking, Eklavya schools, skill centres, Aspirational Districts, and implementation of **PESA** and **FRA**. Local recruitment (e.g. Bastariya Battalion) and surrender-cum-rehabilitation schemes help.

Sustain security gains while filling the **governance vacuum** quickly: functional schools, health centres and anganwadis; honest implementation of forest rights; fair compensation and consent in mining; benefit-sharing through District Mineral Foundations; local governance under PESA; protection of human rights to avoid alienation; and dialogue with those willing to give up violence.

Question type: "Analyse the linkages between development and the spread of LWE."
**Intro:** Red Corridor overlaps with tribal, forested, mineral-rich regions.
**Development gaps → extremism:** land, forests, services, displacement.
**Extremism → under-development:** attacks on roads, schools, telecom.
**Response:** 2015 action plan, SAMADHAN, roads and towers, PESA/FRA.
**Conclusion:** inclusive development plus rights-respecting security.
Key points.
points: Naxalbari 1967; CPI (Maoist) 2004 (PWG + MCC)
Root causes: land, forests, services, displacement, exclusion
2015 National Policy and Action Plan; SAMADHAN 2017
Development: roads, towers, banks, Eklavya schools, Aspirational Districts
PESA 1996 and FRA 2006 implementation
Two-way link: deficits feed extremism; extremism blocks development

cards.title: Syllabus line
cards.body: "Role of **external state and non-state actors** in creating challenges to internal security" and "security challenges and their management in **border areas**; linkages of organised crime with terrorism".

cards.title: State actors
points: Cross-border terrorism as state policy (**proxy war**) by Pakistan-based networks
Historic external support to North-East insurgents
Information warfare and cyber operations
Use of drones for weapons and drug drops across borders

cards.title: Non-state actors
points: Terror groups: Lashkar-e-Taiba, Jaish-e-Mohammed, Hizbul Mujahideen
Global jihadist networks (ISIS, al-Qaeda) radicalising online
Insurgent groups in the North-East
Drug cartels, arms smugglers, hawala operators
Misuse of NGOs and social media

cards.title: Jammu & Kashmir
points: Article 370 provisions abrogated (August 2019); J&K reorganised into two UTs
Pahalgam terror attack (April 2025) and **Operation Sindoor** (May 2025)
Focus on counter-infiltration, terror financing and youth outreach

cards.title: North-East
points: Ethnic and secessionist insurgencies since the 1950s
**AFSPA** (1958) gradually reduced in many areas
Peace accords: e.g. Bodo (2020), Karbi Anglong (2021)
Naga framework agreement (2015) talks
Manipur ethnic violence (from 2023)

cards.title: Legal and institutional tools
points: **UAPA, 1967** (amended 2019: individuals can be designated terrorists)
**NIA** (2008 Act, amended 2019)
**NATGRID**, Multi-Agency Centre
PMLA and FATF-standard financing controls

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Present internal security threats with the "4C" lens: causes, capabilities of actors, consequences, and counter-measures (legal, institutional, technological, diplomatic, developmental).

cards.q: The 2019 amendment to UAPA allowed the government to:
cards.explain: Earlier only organisations could be designated.

cards.q: The National Investigation Agency was set up in the aftermath of:
cards.explain: The NIA Act was passed in December 2008 after the 26/11 Mumbai attacks.

notes.p: India faces internal security challenges in **Jammu & Kashmir** (cross-border terrorism), the **North-East** (ethnic insurgencies), **Left-Wing Extremism** areas, and from **urban terror** and online **radicalisation**. Many are aggravated by **external actors** — hostile states and non-state networks that exploit grievances, porous borders and technology.

**Pakistan** has been accused by India and many international forums of using terror groups as instruments of policy — a strategy of "bleeding India through a thousand cuts". Instruments include training, financing and infiltration of militants, drones for weapons and narcotics, and propaganda. In the North-East, insurgent groups historically found sanctuary in neighbouring countries; cooperation from Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar at various times has helped dismantle camps. Cyber operations and disinformation campaigns by state-linked actors are newer threats.

Terror organisations (LeT, JeM), global jihadist groups, insurgent outfits, organised crime syndicates, drug traffickers, counterfeit currency networks and hawala operators form overlapping networks. **Linkages of organised crime with terrorism** are seen in narco-terror (for example along the Punjab border), arms smuggling and funding through fake currency. Social media and encrypted apps enable radicalisation and recruitment.

**J&K:** after the abrogation of Article 370 provisions and reorganisation in 2019, the government reports a decline in stone-pelting and local recruitment, though targeted attacks continued. The **Pahalgam attack (April 2025)** on tourists led to **Operation Sindoor**, in which India struck terror infrastructure across the border. Key measures: counter-infiltration grid, smart fencing, terror-financing probes, de-radicalisation and outreach.

**North-East:** insurgencies arose from identity, autonomy and development concerns. Accords (Mizo 1986, Bodo 2020, Karbi Anglong 2021, NLFT 2019), ceasefires, development (Act East connectivity) and phased reduction of **AFSPA** have reduced violence, but the ethnic conflict in **Manipur** from 2023 and the porous Myanmar border show continuing fragility.

Laws: **UAPA**, **NIA Act**, **PMLA**, Arms and Explosives Acts, the new criminal laws (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, includes terrorism as an offence). Institutions: NIA, Intelligence Bureau, R&AW, Multi-Agency Centre, **NATGRID**, NSG, state ATS units. International: India pushes for the **Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism** at the UN (proposed in 1996), cooperates through FATF, and uses UN sanctions listings. Concerns include low conviction rates under UAPA, long pre-trial detention, and the need to balance security with civil liberties.

Question type: "Discuss the role of external state and non-state actors in India's internal security challenges."
**State actors:** proxy war, infiltration, drones, disinformation.
**Non-state actors:** terror groups, narco-terror, hawala, online radicalisation.
**Regions:** J&K, Punjab border, North-East.
**Responses:** border management, intelligence integration, terror-financing controls, diplomacy (FATF, UN listings), development and outreach.
**Conclusion:** whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach.
Key points.
points: External state actors: proxy war, drones, cyber, disinformation
Non-state: LeT, JeM, ISIS networks, narco-terror, hawala
J&K: Article 370 provisions abrogated 2019; Pahalgam and Operation Sindoor 2025
North-East: accords, AFSPA reduction, Manipur violence
UAPA (2019 amendment), NIA (2008), NATGRID, MAC

chapters.title: Cyber Security, Communication Networks & Social Media

cards.title: Syllabus line
cards.body: "Challenges to internal security through **communication networks**, role of **media and social networking sites** in internal security challenges, **basics of cyber security**; money-laundering and its prevention."

cards.title: Cyber threats
points: **Malware** and **ransomware** (e.g. attack on AIIMS Delhi servers, 2022)
**Phishing** and financial frauds; "digital arrest" scams
Attacks on **critical information infrastructure** (power, banking, telecom)
Cyber espionage by state-linked actors
Deepfakes and disinformation

cards.title: Legal framework
points: **IT Act, 2000** (amended 2008): Sec 66F cyber terrorism; Sec 69A blocking
**IT Rules, 2021**: intermediary due diligence
**Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**
**Telecommunications Act, 2023**

cards.title: Institutions
points: **CERT-In**: national nodal agency for incident response
**NCIIPC**: protects critical information infrastructure
**I4C**: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (MHA)
National cyber crime reporting portal and **1930** helpline
National Cyber Security Coordinator (NSCS)

cards.title: Media and social networks
points: Spread of rumours leading to mob violence
Radicalisation and recruitment online
Hostile propaganda and information warfare
Live coverage compromising operations (lesson from 26/11)
Positive: alerts, crowd-sourced help, counter-narratives

cards.title: Global context
points: India has not joined the **Budapest Convention**
UN General Assembly adopted a **UN Convention against Cybercrime** (December 2024)
Bilateral cyber dialogues; Quad cyber cooperation

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Cyber answers: threat → vulnerability (low awareness, imported hardware, skill gap) → framework (laws, CERT-In, NCIIPC, I4C) → gaps → way forward (updated policy, skilling, public–private partnership, cyber hygiene).

cards.q: Which agency is the national nodal agency for responding to cyber security incidents?
cards.explain: CERT-In functions under Section 70B of the IT Act.

cards.q: Which section of the IT Act deals with cyber terrorism?
cards.explain: Section 66F, added in 2008, defines cyber terrorism.

notes.h: Why cyber and communication security matter
notes.p: India is among the world's largest digital populations, with digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI), e-governance and digitised critical sectors. This expands the **attack surface**. Cyberspace is borderless, attribution is hard, and attackers can be criminals, hacktivists, terrorists or state-linked groups. The 2020 power outage in Mumbai and the 2022 AIIMS ransomware attack highlighted risks to critical services (attribution in such cases is often contested).

Cyber security protects **confidentiality, integrity and availability** (the **CIA triad**) of data and systems. Common threats: malware, ransomware, phishing, denial-of-service attacks, supply-chain compromises, insider threats and zero-day exploits. Basic defences: strong authentication (multi-factor), patching, encryption, backups, network segmentation, security audits, incident response plans and user awareness ("**cyber hygiene**").

Laws: the **IT Act, 2000** (amended 2008) defines offences, cyber terrorism (66F), blocking powers (69A), protected systems (70) and intermediary liability (79); the **IT Rules, 2021** set obligations for platforms; the **DPDP Act, 2023** protects personal data; the **Telecommunications Act, 2023** updates telecom law.

Institutions: **CERT-In** (incident response; directions requiring reporting of incidents within six hours, 2022), **NCIIPC** (critical infrastructure), **I4C** under MHA for cyber crime coordination, sectoral CERTs, the Defence Cyber Agency, and the National Cyber Security Coordinator. The **National Cyber Security Policy, 2013** is widely considered due for update.

notes.h: Communication networks, media and social media
notes.p:
Encrypted messaging, VoIP, satellite phones and the dark web make interception harder for agencies. **Social media** can spread rumours that trigger communal violence or lynching, hostile propaganda and deepfakes, and enable terror recruitment and financing. **Traditional media** coverage of operations can aid terrorists — during 26/11 live broadcasts showed security positions; guidelines now restrict such coverage. On the positive side, social media helps in disaster alerts, citizen reporting and counter-narratives.

Balance: blocking and takedown powers must follow due process and proportionality (**Shreya Singhal, 2015** struck down Section 66A); internet shutdowns should meet tests laid down in **Anuradha Bhasin (2020)**.

Challenges: shortage of skilled professionals, dependence on imported hardware and software, low user awareness, fragmented institutions, poor reporting by firms, cross-border jurisdiction, and slow investigation of cyber crime by state police.

Way forward: a new cyber security strategy, a dedicated law for critical infrastructure, trusted-source procurement, capacity building of police and courts, public–private information sharing, cyber insurance, international cooperation (mutual legal assistance, norms), and digital literacy campaigns.

Question type: "Discuss the role of social media in internal security challenges and suggest measures."
**Threats:** rumours and mob violence, radicalisation, foreign propaganda, deepfakes, coordination of riots.
**Benefits:** early warning, public communication, crowdsourced help.
**Measures:** IT Rules compliance, fact-checking, platform accountability, digital literacy, quick police response, due-process safeguards.
**Conclusion:** secure but free digital public sphere.
Key points.
points: CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability
CERT-In, NCIIPC, I4C, 1930 helpline
Shreya Singhal 2015; Anuradha Bhasin 2020
Not in Budapest Convention; UN cybercrime convention 2024
Social media: rumours, radicalisation, deepfakes — and benefits

chapters.title: Money Laundering, Terror Financing & Organised Crime

cards.title: Three stages of money laundering
points: **Placement**: dirty cash enters the financial system
**Layering**: complex transactions hide the trail
**Integration**: money re-emerges as apparently legitimate wealth

cards.title: Methods
points: **Hawala** informal transfers
Shell companies and benami holdings
**Trade-based** laundering (over/under-invoicing)
Real estate, bullion, casinos
Crypto-assets and online gaming

cards.title: Indian laws
points: **PMLA, 2002** (in force 2005); Enforcement Directorate
**Benami Transactions Act** (amended 2016)
**Black Money Act, 2015** (foreign assets)
**Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018**
**NDPS Act, 1985** for drugs

cards.title: Institutions
points: **Enforcement Directorate** (PMLA, FEMA)
**FIU-IND**: receives suspicious transaction reports
NCB, DRI, NIA (terror funding)
RBI and SEBI KYC/AML rules

cards.title: FATF
cards.body: The **Financial Action Task Force** (1989) sets global anti-money-laundering and counter-terror-financing standards. India became a member in **2010**. Its "grey list" puts pressure on non-compliant countries.

cards.title: Organised crime–terror nexus
points: Narco-terror through Golden Crescent (Afghanistan–Pakistan–Iran) routes
Fake Indian currency notes
Arms and human trafficking
Extortion funding insurgent groups
BNS 2023 defines organised crime as an offence

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use the "follow the money" angle: choking finance weakens terror and organised crime. Mention Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (2022), which upheld key PMLA provisions, and concerns about low conviction rates and due process.

cards.q: In money laundering, "layering" refers to:
options: Moving funds through complex transactions to hide their origin
cards.explain: Layering obscures the audit trail.

cards.q: FIU-IND primarily:
options: Receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports
cards.explain: The Financial Intelligence Unit analyses and disseminates financial intelligence.

cards.q: India became a full member of FATF in:
cards.explain: India joined FATF as a member in 2010.

notes.p: Money laundering is the process of making illegally obtained money appear legitimate. It enables corruption, tax evasion, drug trafficking and **terror financing**, distorts markets (especially real estate), erodes tax revenue and damages a country's financial credibility. **Terror financing** differs in that funds may come from legal sources but are used for terrorism; both are tackled together under AML/CFT frameworks.

Laundering usually passes through **placement**, **layering** and **integration**. Common methods in India include **hawala** (informal value transfer based on trust), **shell companies**, **benami** property, **trade-based money laundering** through over- or under-invoicing, round-tripping via tax havens, cash-intensive businesses, real estate, gold, and newer channels such as **crypto-assets**, online betting and mule bank accounts used in cyber frauds.

The **Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002** criminalises laundering of proceeds of scheduled offences, allows attachment and confiscation, and requires banks and other reporting entities to maintain records and report suspicious transactions. The **Enforcement Directorate** investigates; **FIU-IND** (2004) analyses reports. In **Vijay Madanlal Choudhary (2022)**, the Supreme Court upheld the ED's powers of arrest, search and the reverse burden of proof; critics raise concerns about low conviction rates and due process, and some aspects are under review.

Other laws: **Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016**, **Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015**, **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018**, **UAPA** (terror funding), **NDPS Act** and FEMA. Crypto-asset service providers were brought under PMLA reporting in 2023.

**FATF** sets 40 recommendations and conducts mutual evaluations; its grey and black lists carry economic consequences — Pakistan was on the grey list for years until 2022. India's own mutual evaluation was adopted in 2024 with a positive outcome — check the report for details. Other tools: tax information exchange (Common Reporting Standard), mutual legal assistance treaties, the **Egmont Group** of FIUs, and the UN Convention against Corruption.

notes.h: Organised crime and its links with terrorism
notes.p: Organised crime includes drug trafficking, arms smuggling, human trafficking, extortion, counterfeit currency, cyber fraud and contract killing. Links with terrorism: **narco-terror** in Punjab and J&K using cross-border drones, insurgents in the North-East financing themselves through extortion and smuggling, and terror groups using criminal networks for logistics. India lies near the **Golden Crescent** and **Golden Triangle** opium regions. The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** introduced organised crime as a specific offence; state laws like **MCOCA (1999)** already existed.

Beneficial ownership registries; data analytics across agencies (tax, banking, customs); faster trials; stronger oversight of hawala and crypto; asset recovery; capacity building of state police; and cooperation with neighbours on drugs and fake currency. Safeguards against misuse and timely trials maintain legitimacy.
Key points.
points: Stages: placement, layering, integration

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For border questions, split by neighbour: each border has a distinct threat profile (terror on Pakistan border, illegal migration and smuggling on Bangladesh, PLA posture on China, open-border misuse on Nepal, insurgent movement on Myanmar).

cards.q: With which country does India share its longest land border?

cards.explain: It develops villages along the northern (China) border.

notes.p: India shares roughly **15,000 km** of land borders with Bangladesh, China, Pakistan, Nepal, Myanmar, Bhutan and Afghanistan (through PoK), and has a long coastline with island territories in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea. Borders cross deserts, glaciers, rivers, jungles and densely populated plains, and some segments are disputed or undemarcated. Managing them involves **security, trade facilitation and development** of border populations.

**Pakistan:** infiltration, cross-border terrorism, drone drops of drugs and arms, ceasefire violations along the LoC.
**China:** undemarcated LAC, PLA infrastructure build-up, transgressions; India responds with roads, tunnels and forward infrastructure.
**Bangladesh:** porous, riverine border; illegal migration, cattle and fake currency smuggling; the 2015 Land Boundary Agreement resolved enclaves.
**Nepal and Bhutan:** open borders under friendship treaties — misuse by criminals and third-country nationals.
**Myanmar:** insurgent movement and drug trafficking through hilly terrain; the government moved to end the Free Movement Regime and fence the border (2024).
**Coast:** the 26/11 attackers came by sea, exposing gaps in coastal security.

The **Group of Ministers (2001)** after Kargil recommended "**one border, one force**", leading to the current allocation of BSF, ITBP, SSB and Assam Rifles. Measures include fencing and floodlighting, the **Comprehensive Integrated Border Management System** using sensors, radars and cameras, **Integrated Check Posts** for trade and travel, the **Border Area Development Programme**, the **Vibrant Villages Programme**, and roads, tunnels and airstrips built by BRO. Coastal security now has a **three-tier** structure: Navy, Coast Guard and state marine police, with coastal radar chains and fishing-boat identification.

**Armed forces** (Army, Navy, Air Force) under the Ministry of Defence defend against external aggression and aid civil authorities. **CAPFs** under MHA: BSF, ITBP, SSB and Assam Rifles (borders; Assam Rifles is administratively under MHA but operationally under the Army), **CRPF** (internal security, counter-insurgency, LWE), **CISF** (industrial and infrastructure security), and **NSG** (counter-terrorism). **State police** handle law and order, a State List subject; CAPFs assist states when required.

Issues: overuse of CAPFs in internal duties, fatigue and stress, vacancies, modernisation needs, and police reforms directed in **Prakash Singh (2006)**. In higher defence, the **CDS** post and the **Department of Military Affairs** (from 2020) aim at jointness and integrated theatre commands.

Question type: "Analyse the challenges of managing the India–Bangladesh border."
**Nature:** long, porous, riverine, densely populated, enclaves resolved in 2015.
**Challenges:** illegal migration, cattle and drug smuggling, fake currency, fencing gaps in riverine stretches, local livelihoods across the border.
**Measures:** BOLD-QIT smart fencing, coordinated border management plan with Bangladesh, ICPs, border haats.
**Conclusion:** security with cooperation and livelihood sensitivity.
Key points.
points: ~15,000 km land border; longest with Bangladesh
BSF (Pak, BD), ITBP (China), SSB (Nepal, Bhutan), Assam Rifles (Myanmar)
GoM 2001: one border, one force
CIBMS, BOLD-QIT, ICPs, Vibrant Villages (2023), BRO
Coastal security: Navy, Coast Guard, marine police
CRPF, CISF, NSG mandates; police = State subject
CDS and DMA from 2020; theatre commands
